Bharat Connect Conference Rising Stars – Sept - 2026
India @2047: Post-Conference Institutional Compendium
5 Oct 2026
Sector structural theses and macroeconomic outlook from our flagship investor summit, framed against India's
journey to a developed economy by 2047.
A Note of Gratitude

engaged attendance made this flagship event an extraordinary success: institutional fund managers, domestic
mutual funds, sovereign wealth allocators, global FPIs, family offices and retail investors. The breadth of
discussion, valuation cross-examination and long-term capital allocation dialogue reflected deep conviction in
India's structural compounding trajectory.
To corporate leadership and IR teams. We are equally grateful to the promoters, board members, CXOs and
Investor Relations professionals of every participating company. Your coordination of executive access, granular
operational visibility, detail on supply-chain realignment and transparent multi-year capex roadmaps made this
summit a benchmark forum for institutional discovery.
To the Arihant Capital team. Finally, we thank every member of the Arihant Capital family whose dedication made
this summit possible. From research, institutional sales and corporate access to events, operations and
technology, your tireless effort and attention to detail delivered a seamless experience for investors and
companies alike.
The India @2047 Lens
Every theme debated at the summit maps to a building block of Viksit Bharat @2047, India's goal of becoming a
developed nation by the centenary of independence. The private capex cycle now under way is, in our view, the first
leg of that two-decade build-out.
• World-class infrastructure: H2 tender acceleration, freight corridors and wagon fleet expansion. Sectors: infra
EPC, cement, railways, logistics.
• Energy transition and grid security: renewable evacuation, Green Energy Corridors and 220–400 kV upgrades.
Sectors: power T&D, cables, captive renewables.
• Manufacturing self-reliance: import substitution at 50–70% shorter lead times and Make-in-India defence.
Sectors: capital goods, defence electronics, auto components.
• Rising, premiumising consumption: urban premiumisation, the branded shift and formalisation. Sectors: durables,
staples, jewellery, real estate.
• Healthy and sustainable society: Tier-2/3 healthcare, China-plus-one pharma and EPR-led recycling. Sectors:
hospitals, APIs/CDMO, circular economy.
• Deep, inclusive financial system: stable credit costs and trail-based wealth revenues. Sectors: NBFCs, MFIs, capital
market intermediaries.
• Digital and AI-led productivity: digital engineering, cloud migration and domain AI platforms. Sectors: enterprise
IT and digital solutions.
Macro Architecture: Cyclical Inflection and the H2 Capex Rebound
The H1 slowdown is reversing into a broad execution rebound, with capacity utilisation past the 75–85% threshold
that triggers private capex.
• Private capex inflection gathering momentum: First-half moderation was driven by election administration,
prolonged heatwaves and monsoon interruptions. Utilisation across heavy engineering, capital goods, metals and
infrastructure fabrication has now crossed the 75–85% tipping range. Healthy balance sheets, low debt-to-equity
and well-capitalised banks are turning this into sustained brownfield and greenfield commitments.

[[page 2]]

2
• Resilient domestic consumption: Structural demand across passenger mobility, commercial vehicles, housing,
branded staples and lifestyle retail remains sound. Urban premiumisation supports mix and realisation gains, while
normalised reservoirs and stable farm-gate prices support rural incomes and farm machinery adoption.
• Compelling sectoral valuation disconnects: Headline indices trade near historical bands, but dislocations have
opened in core manufacturing, power transmission, transport EPC, real estate and specialised consumption.
Businesses with the following profile still trade at attractive multiples to multi-year cash-flow potential:
• visible 15–25%+ compounding runways,
• robust internal cash generation, and
• sustainable ROCE above 20%.
This sets up an asymmetric risk-reward ahead of cyclical earnings acceleration.
Macro Sensitivity: Tail-Risk Matrix and Mitigants
We view the major macro risks as unlikely, with buffers in place at both the economy and corporate level.
• Severe or delayed monsoon
Impact: temporary rural wage compression, short-term mass FMCG volume moderation, localised food inflation
(e.g. maize, paddy).
Mitigants: expanded irrigation, healthy reservoir storage, counter-cyclical government buffer releases.
• Geopolitical friction (West Asia, Black Sea)
Impact: Cape of Good Hope re-routing, container shortages, freight spikes, transit lags.
Mitigants: domestic supply chains, backward integration, diversified sourcing.
• Trade regulation (e.g. EU CBAM)
Impact: compliance costs and export margin pressure on carbon-intensive goods.
Mitigants: captive renewable power, greener production.
• Commodity volatility
Impact: pressure on EPC and manufacturing execution spreads.
Mitigants: Price Variation Clauses, back-to-back hedging on domestic and global exchanges.
Monsoon: Ground metrics confirm the recent monsoon's impact on core corporate fundamentals has been negligible.
An erratic or severely delayed cycle remains a theoretical tail risk only.
Corporate insulation: Major engineering and EPC order books carry formulaic PVCs or back-to-back hedges that lock
in execution spreads. Accelerating adoption of captive solar, wind and waste-heat recovery is structurally lowering
unit costs and defending EBITDA margins against external shocks.
Sector Deep Dive: Operational Takeaways and Structural Drivers
Capital Goods and Power Transmission
• Power T&D and high-voltage grid transformation: T&D networks face sustained multi-year structural deficits.
Renewable evacuation lines, Green Energy Corridors, data-centre power build-outs and grid modernisation
(including underground cabling) are driving double-digit tender pipelines. Order backlogs stretch 6–8 quarters,
with mix shifting to 220–400 kV transformers and MV/HV cables carrying 12–25% margins.
• Industrial capital goods and precision automation: Private capex is lifting demand for mixing machinery, process
automation, forming equipment and precision tooling. Domestic OEMs are winning share from European and East
Asian imports with equivalent specifications at 50–70% shorter lead times, backed by captive fabrication and local
design.
Infrastructure EPC, Cement and Logistics
• Civil infrastructure, highways and industrial EPC: After administrative pauses in early FY27, central and state
tendering is accelerating into H2. Leaders benefit from clean balance sheets, faster working-capital settlement
(TReDS, bank guarantees) and integrated PEB and captive aggregate capabilities.
• Cement and building materials: The sector is entering an accelerated volume phase on infrastructure spending
and housing demand. Leaders are adding brownfield and greenfield clinker and grinding capacity, defending
margins against petcoke and coal volatility through captive solar, wind and WHRS.
• Marine and multimodal logistics: Integrated operators are capitalising on tight global container capacity through
buy-and-lease strategies and expanding liquid tank container fleets. An acute global shortage of offshore support
vessels lets niche diving support vessel operators secure multi-year inspection and maintenance charters at rising
day-rates and high cash returns.

[[page 3]]

Railways, Defence and Automotive
• Railway modernisation and rolling stock: Dedicated freight corridors, coach upgrades and track expansion are building multi-
year pipelines. Freight targets require significant wagon additions over the next five to six years, driving capacity scaling across
wagons, bogies, coach components and signalling.
• Defence and strategic electronics: Make-in-India and Make-II procurement is unlocking multi-year opportunities. Domestic
players in precision guidance, defence displays, aerospace sub-assemblies and specialised forgings are entering commercial
production with high value-add and sticky customers.
• Automotive premiumisation and electrification: Two-wheeler and CV volumes are expanding on rural stabilisation, festive
retail and urban fleet replacement. Rising electronic and aesthetic content per vehicle, PV premiumisation and EV scale-up are
widening the addressable market for Tier-1 suppliers.
Real Estate
• Residential metro corridors and redevelopment: Demand remains structurally strong on income growth, lifestyle upgrades
and consolidation toward organised tier-1 developers. Asset-light redevelopment and JDAs cut upfront land capital while
unlocking high-velocity inventory in prime metro corridors.
• Commercial office and warehousing: Leasing is steady on GCC expansion, BFSI growth and domestic corporate demand. Tech-
enabled mandate platforms are institutionalising sales and CRM, shortening liquidation cycles.
Consumer Discretionary, Staples and Retail
• Consumer durables: Appliance leaders are adding year-round categories (air purifiers, BLDC fans, high-efficiency cooling) to
reduce summer seasonality. Energy-rating and BIS mandates are shifting share from unorganised fabricators to organised
brands.
• Branded staples and specialty FMCG: Modern trade and quick commerce are driving volume in branded staples, edible oils
and packaged foods. Players with farm-gate procurement and captive processing manage commodity spreads while capturing
the unbranded-to-branded shift.
• Lifestyle retail and organised jewellery: Elevated bullion prices are pushing consumers toward lightweight diamond, studded
gold and lifestyle jewellery. Organised players continue to gain share from standalone jewellers via company-owned and shop-
in-shop formats.
Healthcare, Pharma and Circular Economy
• Hospitals: Rising insurance penetration, medical value travel recovery and Tier-2/3 secondary and tertiary demand support
growth. Capital-efficient bed additions break even at lower occupancy, generating healthy ROCE and cash flows.
• APIs and CDMO: China-plus-one diversification continues to benefit domestic producers, who are backward-integrating into
precursors and commercialising regulated-market formulations and CDMO platforms.
• Recycling: EPR mandates and carbon-tracking regimes such as CBAM are consolidating secondary metals and rubber recycling.
Organised recyclers with captive green power and automated lines hold a clear cost moat.
Banking, NBFCs and Financial Services
• Credit growth and risk discipline: Diversified NBFCs and MFIs are seeing credit costs stabilise on tighter underwriting, lower
marginal borrowing costs and branch rationalisation. Digital lending distributors and supply-chain financiers are scaling on
transaction data and anchor ecosystems, with near-zero NPAs and superior asset turnover.
• Capital market intermediaries: Wealth and retail broking franchises are pivoting toward trail-based distribution, PMS and
institutional clearing to insulate earnings from retail derivatives volatility.
Enterprise Technology
• Enterprise transformation and agentic AI: IT services firms are shifting from legacy maintenance to higher-margin digital
engineering, cloud migration and domain-specific AI platforms. Proprietary frameworks, automated compliance engines and
platform-agnostic architectures enable margin expansion without linear headcount growth.
Strategic Synthesis: Institutional Takeaways
Three pillars underpin the institutional case heading into H2, and they are the near-term expression of the India @2047 build-out:
1. Operating leverage inflection: Capacity added over the past 12–24 months is moving from under-absorbed fixed costs to
peak utilisation, unlocking rapid operating leverage and positive free cash flow.
2. Formulaic margin protection: Power equipment, engineering and EPC players are insulated from commodity swings through
contractual pass-through structures and backward-integrated manufacturing.
3. Valuation disconnect vs. earnings visibility: Meaningful valuation gaps persist across core cyclical, infrastructure and
consumer sectors relative to multi-year compounding visibility, setting a strong base for outperformance as private capex
accelerates.

Accord Transformer & Switchgear Ltd
Outlook: Accord Transformer is well-positioned for strong growth ahead. Management guides 70-80% revenue growth with PAT margins
expanding to 9-10% in FY27E, supported by an interim capacity boost to 1,700-1,800 MVA. The new Bhiwadi facility will scale capacity
fivefold to 5,000-8,000 MVA by FY29-FY30, opening entry into higher-margin EHV transmission transformers at 20-25% margins. An INR
1.7 bn order book, improved customer diversification, and key vendor approvals provide near-term visibility, while a conservative debt
profile and positive operating cash flows offer financial flexibility. With India's transmission network only 20% complete and replacement
demand across transformers creating a multi-decade runway, the long-term outlook remains firmly positive.
Revenue and Profitability
• Management guides 70-80% revenue growth for FY27E, with PAT margin expanding to 9-10%, an improvement of roughly 2
percentage points.
Revenue Mix and Margins
• The business spans transformers, compact substations, renewable energy orders, and EHV transmission transformers. EHV
transformers carry higher profitability at 20-25% margins due to lower raw material intensity relative to engineering fees.
Capex and Capacity Expansion
• The two units at Bhiwadi, Rajasthan (NCR) have 1,200+ MVA of installed capacity running at over 80% utilisation. Interim shop-floor
modifications and machinery additions have unlocked 300-400 MVA, taking existing capacity to 1,700-1,800 MVA.
• A 220,000 sq ft land parcel near the Alwar highway will expand capacity fivefold to 5,000-8,000 MVA at a capex of INR 600-700 mn,
funded through internal accruals and debt, without a QIP or preferential issue.
• The new facility will begin operations in phases next financial year, at 50% utilisation in year one, ramping up to 80-90% by FY29-
FY30.
Order Book and Breakup
• The order book stands at INR 1.7 bn (excluding H1FY27 execution) and is deliverable over 12 months, with over INR 1 bn expected to
be executed in H2FY27. Breakup: compact substations INR 250 mn, renewable energy INR 600-700 mn, a Gujarat Electricity Board
order via EPC contractor Rajesh Power INR 870 mn, and a recent INR 200 mn wind energy order from Aditya Birla.
• The order book is intentionally capped below INR 2 bn due to manufacturing bottlenecks; multi-year backlogs are expected post-
expansion.
Customers and Tenders
• Customer diversification has improved, reducing exposure to Torrent Power. Key vendor approvals have been secured from UGVCL,
Blue Pine, Megha Engineering, KEC International, Sterling and Wilson, Damodar Valley Corporation, and Aditya Renewables.
Transformers and EHV Progression
• Existing products cover medium power transformers up to 20 MVA and solar inverter duty transformers. The new plant will enable
entry into high-voltage transmission transformers, starting with the 315 MVA/220 kV class and scaling to 500 MVA and 400 kV after
PGCIL EHV approvals. Each rating step requires six months of prototyping, external lab testing and a one-year operational track
record. EHV margins are 20-25%.
Package Substations, EV, and Automation
• Accord is now an integrated electrical infrastructure solutions provider offering switchgear panels, package substations
(PSS)/compact substations, bus systems, e-houses, EV charging, and automation for utilities, EPC, and industrial expansion. Compact
substations contribute INR 250 mn to the order book.
Renewables and Higher Ratings
• The company has completed dynamic short-circuit testing for a 17.6 MVA inverter duty transformer (IDT), the highest solar IDT rating.
Solar IDTs must handle severe harmonics, requiring grounding filters, while wind turbine transformers must handle load fluctuations,
requiring a specialised internal design. Accord has recorded zero transformer failures over 12 years and has the largest installed base
of wind turbine transformers in India.
Pricing, PVC, and Procurement
• Price variation clauses cover INR 870 mn of the INR 1.7 bn order book. Transformer oil prices fell from INR 200/litre in March to INR
128-130/litre as the number of global producers expanded from 2-3 to 18-20. CRGO steel prices have settled at INR 180-300/kg versus
the COVID peak of INR 450/kg, aided by the JSW-JFE tie-up and BIS licences for Baosteel. RIP bushings face extended lead times, with
domestic supply limited to Crompton Greaves and Yashu, but two new domestic manufacturers next year should ease lead times.
Working Capital and Debt
• Debt-to-equity stood at 0.18x as of 31 March 2026. Operating cash flows turned positive in FY26 after the company phased out high
open-credit arrangements with Torrent Power. Working capital comprises 80-90 debtor days and 100-110 inventory days, a 3.5-4
month cycle in line with industry norms. No working capital limits were utilised as of the conference date; discussions are ongoing to
scale up cash credit limits.

Adani Power Ltd
Outlook: Adani Power offers a rare combination of scale, cost leadership, and earnings visibility in India's thermal space, with ~18
GW operating, 95% contracted, and a ~24-27 GW pipeline targeting ~45 GW by FY36 at 20-30% lower project cost than peers.
Backed by ~INR 234.31 bn FY26 EBITDA, ~INR 130 bn PAT, AA+ rating, and ~2.12x net debt/EBITDA, the equity-first capex model
funds a ~INR 2,200 bn build largely through internal cash flows. With ~14 GW of ~22 GW thermal bids already won, a healthy state
bid pipeline, coal pass-through economics making new PPAs annuity-like, and optionality in hydro and nuclear, the near- to
medium-term outlook is positive on volume growth, margin stability, and return on assets, though execution timelines,
equipment supply, and PPA tie-ups for balance capacity remain the key monitorables.
Capacity and Growth Trajectory
Adani Power operates ~18 GW of thermal capacity today, making it India's largest private thermal producer and second-largest
overall, with 95% tied up in long-term and medium-term contracts primarily with state discoms. The company is building another
~24-27 GW, targeting ~45 GW by FY36, with 60% of under-construction capacity at brownfield sites. Management targets a 3.5-4
year construction cycle per 1,600 MW unit, and capacity addition should begin this year and accelerate over the next three years.
Cost Leadership and Execution Moat
Equipment for the entire under-construction pipeline has already been ordered from BHEL and L&T, locking in prices ahead of the
market and giving 20-30% project cost advantage versus the current market benchmark of ~INR 120-140 mn per MW. The
company also benefits from proximity to coal mines, pre-owned land, water and evacuation infrastructure, and an equity-first
funding model that avoids ring-fenced project finance and lowers interest during construction. Roughly 4.8 GW of boilers will be
imported, staying within domestic content thresholds.
Bid Wins and Pipeline Visibility
Of ~22 GW of thermal bids awarded under the revised PPA regime, Adani Power has won ~14 GW, implying a ~67% strike rate.
Pending bids include ~4,000 MW each from Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat, ~3,860 MW from West Bengal, ~3,200 MW from
Rajasthan, ~1,320 MW from Uttarakhand, and a recently approved 1,600 MW bid from Andhra Pradesh. Management expects
untied capacity to be contracted within roughly one year.
Financial Position and Capital Allocation
FY26 EBITDA stood at ~INR 234.31 bn on a continuing basis, or ~INR 212.85 bn excluding one-time regulatory recoveries, implying
~40% margins. PAT is ~INR 130 bn, net debt/EBITDA is ~2.12x, and the domestic credit rating is AA+. The ~24 GW pipeline needs
~INR 2,200 bn, funded by ~INR 1,200-1,400 bn of operating cash flow over six years and ~INR 600 bn of debt from banks and
capital markets with 3-7 year tenures.
Market Dynamics and Thermal Relevance
India's electricity demand is expected to grow ~45% from ~1.7 trillion units to ~2.5 trillion units by 2032, requiring ~USD 500 bn of
investment. Peak demand is seen rising from ~270 GW to ~400 GW by FY32, and thermal capacity of over 300 GW will be needed
to bridge the gap that renewables cannot serve during morning and evening shoulder hours. The new PPA regime provides coal
price pass-through, alternate coal cost pass-through, and two-part tariffs where capacity charges effectively make new PPAs
annuity-like, reducing earnings volatility.
Diversification into Hydro and Nuclear
Adani Power holds ~24% of Jayaprakash Power Ventures (~400 MW hydro plus 1,820 MW thermal) and has received an LOI under
a resolution plan for GVK Energy's 300 MW Alaknanda hydro plant. In Bhutan, it has an MOU for 5,000 MW of hydro development
with an initial 570 MW Wangchu project, where it holds 49% in the JV, with power to be supplied to India and Bhutan seasonally.
In nuclear, the target is 10 GW over ~10 years, pending notification of rules under the SHANTI Act, with site surveys and
technology provider discussions already underway. Thermal will remain the dominant revenue source for at least the next six to
seven years, with hydro commissioning likely from FY32 onward.
Competitive Positioning
Management notes that NTPC has so far pursued only Section 62 nomination-based brownfield projects, while Tata Power has not
entered competitive thermal bidding. Adani Power's differentiation rests on site access near coal mines, lower logistics costs, land
availability, shared infrastructure at brownfield sites, and pre-ordered equipment.
Receivables and Counterparty Risk
State discom payments have become regular, aided by the PRAAPTI portal and late payment surcharge rules, with collections
typically within ~70 days. Gujarat and Rajasthan pay early to claim rebates. No state is flagged as a structural collection risk. On
Godda, which supplies ~10% of Bangladesh's power and ~25% of the connected grid region's requirement, payments are steady
and at least equal to monthly billing, with roughly half of outstanding amounts being unbilled or not yet due and overdues at ~2-
2.5 months.

Afcons Infrastructure Ltd
Outlook: Afcons Infrastructure expects a stronger second half, with management confident of achieving its ~INR 300 bn order
inflow guidance and potentially surpassing it, supported by over 50% already secured and a ~INR 1,500 bn pipeline across roads,
railways, metros, and ports. Execution of the Croatia railway project is slated to begin in FY28 after design and mobilisation, while
Vadhavan Port awaits the government's approach road before work starts next year. The overseas revenue mix is expected to rise
to ~40:60 this year from ~25:75, with a long-term target of ~30:70, aided by a couple of international orders. Gross debt is
projected at ~INR 35 bn by FY27 with a 50:50 term loan-working capital mix, funded via receivable releases and mobilisation
advances. EBITDA margins are guided at ~11%+, and UP Jal Jeevan receivables are being monetised through a phased completion
strategy, with payments beginning to flow.
Order Inflow Guidance and Pipeline
Management maintained guidance of ~INR 300 bn order intake for the year, having already secured ~INR 160 bn (over 50% of the
target) by Q1. Confidence is supported by a robust pipeline of ~INR 1,500 bn mentioned in the Q1 presentation, with several
projects in final tender-opening stages. Inflows are expected to be spread across roads, railways, metros, and ports, with some
orders likely in Q3 and Q4. Management expressed optimism about achieving, and potentially surpassing, the guidance.
UP Jal Jeevan Mission Receivables
The UP Jal Jeevan Mission remains a pain point, with ~INR 4 bn of receivables, of which only a small fraction has been received.
The UP government has changed contractual terms, linking payments to completion of last-mile connectivity. Afcons, being a
Phase 3 participant, has adopted a strategy of first completing projects that are already 70-80% complete, realising payments, and
using those funds to complete remaining connectivity rather than deploying fresh capital. Payments have started flowing in bits
and pieces, with government assurance on releasing payments for completed work.
Croatia Railway and Vadhavan Port Projects
For the Croatia railway project, initial design, mobilisation, and preparatory works (~6-7 months) have begun, with full execution
expected from FY28 onwards. For Vadhavan Port, work is yet to commence, as the government must first provide the approach
road needed to move equipment for the breakwater work; execution is expected to start next year.
Debt Profile and Capital Expenditure
Gross debt is expected to reach ~INR 35 bn by the end of FY27, despite ~INR 7-8 bn capex this year. The debt mix will shift from
two-thirds working capital and one-third term loan to a 50:50 split by year-end. Improvement in net working capital will be driven
by release of stuck receivables and mobilisation advances from newly won orders. Capex will be funded through collections and
receivable releases.
Overseas Mix, Currency Risk, and Payment Security
The long-term target is ~30% overseas and ~70% domestic revenue. With the Croatia order, the mix has shifted to ~25:75, and
management targets ~40:60 for this year, with a couple more international orders expected. Focus geographies include Africa, the
Middle East, neighbouring countries, and Southeast Asia, with a recent foray into Europe. Foreign currency exposure is naturally
hedged as projects are in USD or EUR, with expenditures in matching currencies. Overseas projects are funded by multilaterals
with full financing tie-ups before commencement. Bangladesh projects are funded by the Government of India, with Exim Bank of
India releasing payments directly to Afcons' accounts in India, ensuring no payment issues.
Africa Market Strategy and Competition
In Africa, Afcons targets sovereign projects, including EPC+F where it facilitates financing. Competition exists from Chinese and
Turkish players, but Afcons focuses on projects where it has expertise, including roads and bridges, with men and machinery that
can be moved across African countries. The company holds the record for the fastest completed core projects in Africa.
Margin Outlook
Overseas projects carry ~200-300 bps higher margins than domestic. At a portfolio level, management maintains guidance of
~11%+ EBITDA margins despite some lower-margin road projects and drag from JJM. While this year has been slightly lower, the
11% margin guidance is maintained going forward.
Arbitration Claims
Arbitration is an ongoing process with outstanding claims. While it is difficult to pinpoint a number or quarter, some arbitration
awards are expected every year as hearings come up.
Labour Shortages
Labour shortages persist in some fast-track projects, particularly a refinery project with restrictions on labour (no mobile phones,
limited facilities). However, most projects are technically complex and mechanised, requiring less heavy labour.

Akiko Global Services Ltd
Outlook: The company is targeting strong revenue growth, with FY27 guidance of INR 3.25-3.5 bn and FY28 core-business revenue

Core Distribution Business
• Akiko Global's established financial distribution business generates leads for credit cards, personal loans, business loans,
mortgages and home loans through digital marketing and a 20-year-old partner network.
• FY26 revenue stood at INR 1.77 bn, with credit cards contributing 35% and loans accounting for 65%; personal loans
constituted 82% of loan-segment revenue.
• The company operates a hybrid sourcing model comprising digital lead generation, a centralised customer assistance team and
a partner-led distribution network, with credit card distribution margins of 14-15% after operating costs.
• Management expects the core business to sustain strong growth, supported by a 10-20% monthly increase in the centralised
team and rising lead volumes.
Revenue Guidance & Profitability
• FY27 revenue is guided at INR 3.25-3.5 bn, compared with INR 1.77 bn in FY26, and the company targets INR 5.5-6 bn in FY28
from the core business, excluding Akiko Pay.
• The company expects to sustain growth through higher lead generation, deeper lender relationships and operating leverage,
while maintaining cost discipline and reinvesting profits into the business.
• Management expects cash flow to turn positive in the near term, potentially by Q3FY27, as collections improve and working
capital pressure eases following the reduction in home loan and mortgage business.
Akiko Pay – Customer Acquisition & Monetisation
• Akiko Pay is being developed as a customer-facing financial platform to complement the core distribution business, enabling

• The app is currently generating 2,000-3,000 daily downloads, with ~5,000 customers enrolled in the newly launched Version 2;

• Management is targeting the first 100,000 customers to validate unit economics before scaling, with customer acquisition
costs expected at INR 10-20 per customer, based on early experience.
• Monetisation will come from credit card and loan commissions, wallet transactions, prepaid payment services, discounted gift
cards, travel bookings and other partner-led offerings.
• Akiko Pay could generate INR 300-400 per customer per month, although this refers to the overall existing customer base and
requires further validation as engagement and monetisation scale.
• The company expects Akiko Pay to achieve a 20-30% PAT margin within six months, with the potential for significantly higher
margins over time, subject to customer activation, repeat usage and product-level economics.
Product Expansion & Technology
• Akiko Pay's Android application is live, while the iOS launch was expected shortly after the conference; wallet-to-bank
transfers and prepaid payment features are already operational.
• UPI Scan-and-Pay, mutual funds and insurance are planned for rollout by the end of Q3FY27, subject to the relevant
integrations and regulatory approvals.
• The company has applied for a TPAP licence to enable UPI transactions on the platform and expects to integrate insurance
following the anticipated receipt of its insurance distribution licence.
• The platform leverages the existing customer database of over 25 mn and lender relationships to drive cross-selling, with
management aiming to limit incremental technology and customer acquisition expenditure.
Dubai Business
• Akiko Global operates a financial distribution business in Dubai, supported by a 150-member team and relationships with
leading banks, including Emirates, FAB, Citibank and Dubai Islamic Bank.
• The business was affected by geopolitical disruptions over the past two years, although operations have started recovering;
management expects revenue of INR 40-50 mn in Q3FY27 and over INR 100 mn in Q4FY27.
• Management indicated that the Dubai business operates at high margins, in a broad range of 20-50%.

Financial Performance & Margin Expansion

HRMS & Payroll Expansion

outsourcing opportunities from Western markets.
Product Pipeline & New Offerings

covering ~42 countries.

Workday Partnership & Global Expansion

All Time Plastics Ltd
Outlook: The company faces near-term challenges from crude-linked polymer price volatility, geopolitical uncertainty, raw
material availability and export logistics, which have affected revenue growth and margins. The company is targeting ~20%
production growth; however, this remains contingent on improved demand visibility, raw material availability and container
availability, with some customer programmes currently on hold. Order visibility remains adequate, but customers are adopting a
cautious approach towards new commitments amid uncertainty over tariffs and global trade flows. Near-term margin pressure is
expected to persist due to elevated fixed costs at the Khatalwada and Guwahati facilities, alongside delays in passing on higher
raw material costs to customers.
Margin Recovery and Capacity Utilisation
• The Khatalwada facility is currently operating below its optimal utilisation level, resulting in under-absorption of fixed costs
and pressure on profitability.
• Management expects the company to regain its historical margin profile at ~75-78% overall capacity utilisation, with margins
potentially exceeding historical levels at ~85% utilisation.
• The company has a combined installed capacity of ~41,000 tonnes across its three plants and is undertaking a further 1,500-
tonne expansion, taking capacity to ~42,500 tonnes this year.
• The company has ordered 14 new machines for Khatalwada, expected to arrive over the next two months, while the remaining
planned machinery deployment has been deferred pending greater clarity on demand and geopolitical conditions.
• Capacity expansion will continue organically, with incremental machine additions based on business requirements and the
nature of new customer programmes.
Raw Material Costs and Pricing
• The company continues to face challenges in passing on higher polymer prices, with the recent increase in crude oil and
polymer prices putting pressure on margins.
• Pricing adjustments for the largest customer follow a transparent pass-through mechanism at approximately eight-week
intervals, while the timing of recovery from other customers remains challenging.
• Management clarified that inventory gains are not a meaningful earnings lever, given the pass-through pricing mechanism and
the company's current difficulty in fully recovering raw material cost increases.
• Raw material procurement lead times have increased from 3-4 weeks to 7-8 weeks, particularly for supplies from the Middle
East, requiring longer procurement planning cycles and higher operational flexibility.
IKEA Relationship and Customer Stickiness
• IKEA remains the company's largest customer, with a relationship spanning over 28 years; the company supplies products to
IKEA globally and also participates in joint product development.
• The company accounts for approximately 5-6% of IKEA's global plastic houseware sourcing, positioning it as a strategic supplier
within IKEA's global sourcing network.
• Customer stickiness is supported by product quality, on-time delivery, tooling capabilities, compliance standards and social
audits, making supplier replacement a time-consuming process.
• New product development typically takes 16-26 weeks following RFQ selection, including tooling and product development,
while IKEA provides a rolling 52-week forecast to support procurement and inventory planning.
• Price remains one of several considerations in supplier selection, alongside landed cost, quality, service levels and compliance;
a price differential of 10-12% could prompt buyers to evaluate alternatives, although switching is not immediate.
Customer Diversification and Export Opportunities
• The company is engaging with several prospective customers across Europe and the US, with some relationships having
progressed beyond initial sales and pilot stages.
• New customer acquisition remains challenging amid raw material volatility and uncertainty over tariffs, with some prospective
programmes currently on hold.
• The company continues to evaluate opportunities across export markets while maintaining its focus on India-based
manufacturing, given the current cost competitiveness of its domestic manufacturing base.
Global Competitiveness and Trade Dynamics
• Turkish manufacturers benefit from geographical proximity to European customers and zero-duty access, resulting in shorter
delivery timelines and potential landed-cost advantages.
• All Time Plastics believes its competitiveness is supported by lower labour costs than China, broadly comparable power costs
and potentially improved landed economics for European customers as trade arrangements evolve.
• India may have a slight disadvantage versus China in polypropylene procurement costs; however, logistics economics and
manufacturing capabilities remain important considerations for customers.
• Supplier decisions are based on overall landed cost, quality, compliance and supply-chain reliability rather than tariff
advantages or manufacturing lead times alone.

Almonds Global Securities Ltd
Almonds Global Securities is a broking and wealth entity that has, over the years, promoted sizeable businesses in green energy
(ethanol) and infrastructure engineering. It is now undertaking a two-stage restructuring to simplify a holding structure that the
company believes is confusing public shareholders and suppressing value. Through the demergers, shareholders will receive
mirror shares in the infra and green energy businesses, and the company sees the restructuring as the central value-unlocking
event over the next 18 months.
Structure and Restructuring
• The group holds roughly 60% in the geospatial and infra business and 40% in Premier Green; a scheme has been filed to
demerge the infra consulting business into a separately listed entity, with every public shareholder of Almonds receiving
mirror shares.
• Under the first scheme, shareholders will receive 666 shares of Almond Infra (face value INR 10) for every 10,000 shares of
Almonds Global Securities (face value INR 1), with listing to follow immediately as a vertical split; a second scheme will later
spin off Premier Green, with the swap ratio yet to be finalised.
• Post restructuring, promoter holding (through Avonmore) is expected at 51% in Almonds Global, ~30-32% in Premier Green
and 68% in Almond Infra. SEBI has directed the broking entity to exit businesses where it has given guarantees.
Green Energy (Premier Green Innovations)
• The business has two distilleries: a Himachal plant operating for around nine years and producing ENA (60% for potable liquor,
40% for cosmetics), and a 200 KLPD ethanol unit running above rated capacity. Last year's revenue was INR 7.07 bn, with
EBITDA of INR 800 mn and PAT of INR 400 mn.
• A new 250 KLPD ethanol plant in Odisha was commissioned in February, with 70% long-term offtake from oil companies; it ran
at ~20% utilisation through the allocation gap but should operate at close to 90% from 1 November as grain ethanol allocation
rises and sugar allocation falls.
• The company expects revenue of ~INR 9-9.5 bn this year at an EBITDA margin of ~10% and PAT of ~INR 500 mn (weighed down
by Odisha depreciation), rising towards INR 13 bn next year on full Odisha operations. Total term loans are ~INR 2.5 bn at 4-
4.5%, plus INR 500 mn of working capital debt.
• Grain economics: gross margins of ~15% and EBITDA margins of 10-11% at current maize prices; ethanol prices are not
expected to rise, but higher DDGS prices are offsetting elevated maize costs. At least three more projects are in the pipeline.
Infra Engineering (Almond Infra Consultant)
• The business is led by a former NHPC chairman with ~8 specialist directors; 80% of billing is from transportation (roads and
railways) and 20% from urban projects, with specialisation in geospatial and digital twin work under Gati Shakti.
• Last year's billing was INR 1.3 bn, and is guided at a minimum of INR 1.65 bn this year; new order intake has already crossed
INR 2 bn, and the company targets at least INR 3.5 bn of fresh orders versus INR 1.5-1.6 bn last year, aiming for 30%+ annual
growth.
• EBITDA margin is ~12% (11.5% last year) and is expected to reach 20% over three to four years as the share of lead consultant
mandates rises; geospatial contributes only ~INR 150 mn of billing, but at 30-35% margins. The EGE acquisition (hydroelectric)
adds tunnel engineering capabilities, with ~INR 200 mn of billing on a Nepal project.
Financial Services
• A focused player with ~INR 12 bn of wealth under management, serving family offices; the ambition is to be the investment
banker to small caps (INR 1-1.5 bn) and grow them into mid caps, taking minority stakes alongside advisory mandates.
• Marquee mandates include Momentum (formerly Urban Harvest), which raised funds at an INR 6.5 bn valuation and has now
been re-mandated at INR 22 bn, Dalchini and Green Jewels (5% owned, with Amazon and Singularity each investing INR 450
mn); the target is four to five transactions a year at a minimum fee of INR 50 mn each.
Promoter Buying
• The promoters have completed their 5% creeping acquisition allowance through a mix of preferential issue and market
purchases, citing value in the stock and the intent to raise their shareholding; no further purchases are planned.
Guidance & View
The company guided to Premier Green revenue of ~INR 9-9.5 bn this year, rising towards INR 13 bn next year at an EBITDA margin
of ~10%; infra billing of at least INR 1.65 bn, with fresh orders of INR 3.5 bn and 30%+ growth; the Almond Infra listing within
seven to eight months and Premier Green within ~18 months; and promoter holding settling at 51% in Almonds Global, 30-32% in
Premier Green and 68% in Almond Infra.
The sum-of-the-parts unlocking is the clear thesis, and the underlying ethanol and infra businesses are genuinely scaling, but value
realisation depends on the demergers completing on schedule and the unlisted businesses achieving listing and valuation
discovery. Given the structural complexity and the promoter-led, Fairfax-style model, execution and disclosure cadence (which the
company is now committing to) will determine any re-rating.

Amir Chand Jagdish Kumar (Exports) Ltd
Amir Chand is transitioning from a pure-play basmati rice exporter to a broader kitchen staples FMCG platform under the
"Aeroplane" brand. The company closed FY26 at ~INR 23 bn in revenue and is leveraging its existing distributor network to layer on
adjacent products (atta, besan, sugar, cooking oil). The onboarding of Rashmika Mandanna and Fatima Sana Sheikh as brand
ambassadors, combined with senior FMCG hires from Pepsi and Procter & Gamble, signals a serious push toward premiumisation
and consumer brand recall. Near-term earnings are supported by strong export demand and rising domestic basmati prices; in the
medium term, the FMCG playbook could materially widen the revenue and margin envelope.
Basmati Industry Tailwinds
The domestic basmati market is seeing a structural shift from unbranded/loose to branded/packaged. About INR 400 bn of the
market is already branded, but the company estimates the total addressable market at INR 1,500 bn.
Roughly INR 40 bn of the market is migrating from unpacked to packed products every year, driven by rising disposable incomes
and premiumisation.
Basmati rice prices have moved up by >25% season-on-season. Export demand remains robust, with buyers willing to absorb
higher freight and product costs.
Revenue & Margin Profile
FY26 revenue was ~INR 23 bn, of which exports contributed ~INR 8.4 bn (~37% of sales).
The company is number one in Gujarat and Kerala (under the Alibaba brand). Gujarat, Kerala, and UP account for 35-40% of
domestic revenue.
Direct HoReCa sales contribute ~20% of revenue, rising to 30-35% including distributor-led HoReCa sales. The premium segment
currently accounts for ~25% of the mix.
Current EBITDA margins are 7-8%, versus 9-10% for peers. The company expects to bridge this gap as brand awareness improves.
The sustainable margin target is 14-15% over time, aided by the shift to organised retail.
FMCG Diversification Strategy
Product selection was driven by a distributor survey: the company identified what its existing distributors were already selling
(atta, sugar, cooking oil, besan) and added those SKUs under the Aeroplane brand.
The plan is to add 5-6 new products annually, targeting a portfolio of 30-40 products over 5-6 years.
The TAM for adjacent categories is large: atta ~INR 1,000 bn, sugar ~INR 1,000 bn and besan/maida ~INR 300-400 bn.
FMCG products are sourced (not manufactured), so capital intensity is low. The main investment is in branding and sales team
expansion.
Capacity & Capex
The company is using ~50% of its installed capacity. No significant capex is required up to INR 60 bn in revenue.
Between INR 60 bn and INR 80 bn revenue, some packing/production line additions may be needed.
Beyond INR 80 bn, a new mega unit may be required, with a replacement value of INR 5-6 bn. The company has a 2-3 year window
before reaching that point.
Export Markets & Geopolitical Risks
The company is present in 38 countries directly and ~50 including re-exports. Exports are concentrated in the Middle East, with a
presence also in Australia, parts of Africa and the US (low penetration).
Margins are geography-agnostic; brand pull, not geography, determines realisation. Indian margins are now comparable with those
in the US and Europe.
The Strait of Hormuz disruption pushed freight costs to Oman from ~USD 400 to ~USD 4,000 (10x) at the peak. Demand remains
very strong, but container availability is a bottleneck.
Export headwinds were offset by higher domestic sales; overall top line is growing despite the logistics challenge.
Guidance
FY27 revenue is guided to grow ~27-28% over FY26. Sustainable EBITDA margins are targeted at 14-15% as brand spends scale and
the organised retail mix rises.
The company sees no near-term supply constraint on basmati procurement; crop damage from floods/weather events has
historically been marginal (3-4%).

Business Model & Positioning
• The company is transitioning from pure conversion/job-work towards integrated wind tower supply.
• The integrated model can materially increase absolute revenue and EBITDA, albeit at lower margins.

Order Book & Revenue Visibility
• The company has booked 356 towers worth ~INR 3,800 mn, along with an additional order of INR 1,330 mn.

Aptus Pharma Ltd
Asset Light Prescription Generation Model
• Aptus Pharma operates a branded generics model focused on prescription generation through doctor engagement, similar to
Mankind Pharma and Corona Remedies. The company owns its brands, controls quality, and manages the entire distribution
channel from super stockists down to medical representatives. Manufacturing is fully outsourced to WHO-GMP-certified
contract manufacturers under loan licence and purchase order arrangements. This allows Aptus to scale with minimal capex
while directing resources toward brand building and market expansion.
Revenue Mix across Three Verticals
• Acute therapies contribute roughly 40% of revenue, OTC and wellness account for 20-21%, and chronic and semi-chronic
therapies make up ~30%. The remainder comes from export-related services. The Pharma Formulation vertical drives core
prescription revenues, while the Consumer Products vertical is being built around skincare, haircare, and personal care. The
International Business vertical currently generates commission income by facilitating export orders through contract
manufacturers.
Product Portfolio Expansion
• The company currently offers 250+ formulations across 18+ therapeutic segments spanning anti-infectives, gastro, cardiac,
diabetic, respiratory, neuro, and pain categories. Chilkul, the company's gastro (PPI) brand, is its flagship prescription product.
Aptus targets 350 products across 25+ therapeutic segments by the end of FY27 and aims for 600+ products across 30+
segments over the next three years with the addition of new divisions.
Distribution Network and Geographic Footprint
• Aptus has built a network of 10,000+ doctor relationships, 25,000+ retail touchpoints, 250+ distributors, and 200+ field
personnel. Gujarat remains the core geography, but post listing, the company has expanded into Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan
and other states, taking its presence to seven states. The company focuses on Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities where larger pharma
companies have limited penetration, creating a differentiated distribution moat.
Own Manufacturing Plant in Two to Three Years
• Aptus currently has no owned manufacturing facility and operates entirely through CDMO and loan licence arrangements with
two Gujarat-based plants plus additional PO-based partners. The company plans to operationalise its own plant within two to
three years, at which point approximately 20% of products will be manufactured in-house. This is expected to improve
margins, strengthen quality control, enable direct product registration for exports, and support the pan-India scale-up.
Export Opportunity
• At present, export revenue is limited to commission income earned by routing overseas orders to contract manufacturers
under NDA-based sharing arrangements. Once its own plant is operational and registered for international markets, the
company plans to directly export to Africa, Latin America, and select Asian markets. However, Aptus has stated that
approximately 80% of future revenue will continue to come from the domestic Indian market.
Margin Compression from Expansion Spending
• EBITDA margin contracted from 19.7% in FY25 to 16.0% in FY26 as the company invested aggressively in manpower
recruitment and geographic expansion. Gross margin also declined from 63.2% to 54.1% on account of a higher share of traded
goods. The company acknowledged that margin percentage has taken a backseat as it prioritises top-line growth, distribution
build-out and meeting mainboard migration criteria. EBITDA improvement is expected in the coming periods as operating
leverage kicks in.
Capital Allocation and Mainboard Migration
• Aptus declared a 2-for-3 bonus issue in May 2026 to expand its equity base, which is a prerequisite for migrating from the BSE
SME platform to the mainboard. There is no dividend history as all surplus capital is being deployed toward expansion. The
company's roadmap for mainboard listing is clear, with revenue scale being the primary criterion it is working toward.

Aptus Value Housing Finance India Ltd
The company runs a two-entity structure (the standalone housing finance company and its wholly owned NBFC subsidiary, Aptus
Finance), operated independently with separate compliance, risk and borrowing functions and no cross-support. It reiterates a long-
term framework of 20%+ AUM growth and 20% ROE, with current run-rate growth of 22-24%, underpinned by high-yielding fixed-
rate products, wider spreads than peers and conservative leverage. Asset quality pressure last quarter was an execution-led
collection issue rather than borrower income stress, and collections are improving this quarter.
Structure and Borrowing
The group comprises two separate companies, the standalone HFC and its wholly owned NBFC subsidiary, Aptus Finance, with
separate compliance and risk functions and independent borrowing. The earlier HFC guarantee on NBFC borrowing has been fully
removed, so the HFC does not support the NBFC's growth.
The incremental cost of borrowing is ~8% in the HFC and slightly higher in the NBFC. On AUM of ~INR 136.48 bn, the company raises
funds only four times a quarter (three in the HFC and one in the NBFC) and holds higher month-end liquidity to negotiate better
rates.
Over the last six months, funds were raised at broadly the same rates as earlier, but there is now less room for further declines; any
move will track the repo rate, with liabilities repricing first and assets following. Around 80% of products are fixed-rate, which are
priced higher than floating-rate products and provide a runway advantage, and spreads are higher than those of several
competitors.
Digitisation and Underwriting
Operations are fully digital, with an in-house LOS and LMS (the Diva platform, also used by larger entities such as the Shriram
Group) and no paperwork in sourcing; every file is digital from sourcing to collection.
Given the focus on Tier 2, 3 and 4 cities, branch staff must still visit the customer's home and business premises to underwrite, so a
templatised sourcing or underwriting model does not apply; technology is an enabler of growth rather than a replacement for field
presence.
A bureau scrub is conducted after every quarter-end at the borrower and household level to check the loans customers have taken,
under a standing arrangement with the credit bureaus.
Growth, Leverage and Product
Guidance is for 20%+ growth, with 22-24% AUM growth this year and more than 20% in the foreseeable future; a 20% ROE is seen as
achievable given current realisations. Housing finance growth bounced back in Q1 and is expected to continue.
Internal accruals are strong, with PAT of ~INR 9.43 bn last year and ~INR 2.61 bn in Q1 alone, so leverage is unlikely to rise quickly; it
will build gradually as growth picks up and a new NBFC product is added.
A new NBFC product is under consideration: since some products carry an LTV of only 40% and the quarterly bureau check shows
customers borrowing two-wheeler or other loans for working capital, the company may lend more to the same customer using the
same underwriting; no separate licence is needed to add a product.
Mix, Capital and Asset Quality
At a consolidated level, ~48% of the book is home loans and 29% is NBFC (mostly LAP), with the balance in quasi-home loans, top-up
loans and insurance; the company intends to broadly maintain the current mix, with the NBFC growing slightly faster off a smaller
base.
The capital stance is conservative by design: home loan capital consumption is only ~35%, so capital burn is low and internal
accruals are strong. The irregular cash flows of Tier 2-4 customers, often without ITR or GST records, require customer visits and
manual assessment, which is time-consuming, so the same product cannot be grown at 35-40%.
Last quarter saw a collection efficiency challenge in the NBFC segment driven by execution and the company's own people rather
than borrower income stress; collection efficiency is improving as of late Q2 and the trend is expected to continue.
Newer states such as Maharashtra and Odisha have only ~10-12 branches each, against 300+ in the southern states; a new branch in
a new state takes 6-10 months to reach a run-rate of ~INR 7-8 mn of disbursements per branch per month, versus ~INR 10 mn
within 8-9 months in the older states.
Guidance
The company guided to 20%+ AUM growth (22-24% this year), a 20% ROE, a broadly unchanged mix of ~48% home loans and 29%
NBFC, and only a gradual rise in leverage given strong internal accruals; the cost of funds is expected to hold near current levels,
with limited further downside.

Arman Financial Services Ltd
A rural-focused NBFC spanning microfinance, micro-enterprise, secured MSME (micro-LAP) and two-wheeler loans, with a portfolio
of ~INR 27-28 bn. The company reports stable asset quality despite macro headwinds; the microfinance crisis is seen as largely
behind it, but a cautious stance is maintained since the recovery owes more to better selection than to rising real rural incomes.
Demand is slower than expected but healthy for the sector; the company targets AUM of ~INR 50 bn over two to three years and
expects a stronger H2.
Structure and Scale
The book is ~70% microfinance and ~30% secured MSME (micro-LAP) and two-wheeler loans. The listed parent, Arman, holds the
NBFC licence, while its wholly owned subsidiary, Namra, is the NBFC-MFI; the split is driven purely by the differential regulation of
microfinance.
The portfolio of INR 27-28 bn is spread across 11 states, with ~530 branches, 5,300-5,400 employees and 0.65-0.70 mn customers.
Microfinance and Asset Quality
There are no ECBs outstanding, so FCNR flows are not a direct benefit; any advantage would be indirect if excess bank liquidity leads
to favourable rates. MFI customers have deleveraged significantly, and industry guardrails have restored asset quality to around the
pre-crisis March 2024 level.
The recovery is weighted more towards better selection than favourable ground-level macros; real incomes remain broadly flat in
inflation-adjusted terms, so this is not the time to push the accelerator despite favourable headline numbers. The crisis is seen as
behind, but caution continues.
Rejection rates remain very high: for every 100 inquiries, only 20-24 customers receive disbursements. Underwriting has been
revamped to stop relying on JLG as a risk mitigant, using better technology, bureau data and feet on the street, with ~90% of assets
covered and 72-75% of defaults covered under CGFMU.
Demand, Drought and Insurance
Q2 asset quality is stable despite expected pressure from West Asia, oil prices and trade issues, with no alarming stress. Demand
and inquiries have risen, but not to accustomed levels, so Q1 and Q2 volumes are modest, which the company views as a sign of a
healthier, evolving industry rather than a negative.
Maharashtra is only 2-3% of the book, so the drought declaration is immaterial at the company level; a drought can take zero-DPD
rates down to 94-95% in affected cohorts, and the key risk is a cascading cliff effect where even unaffected borrowers stop paying,
which happens in only ~2 of 10 cases. Bihar, Odisha and eastern UP saw excessive rain and Nepal floods, but these were handled
well by the sector.
There is no commission or pass-through insurance income in the P&L; the company prefers to charge transparent interest rather
than earn insurance side income, so the draft IRDAI regulations have no impact and may even be marginally positive by lowering
customer rates. It flags that the draft could be highly disruptive for rural distribution, given tiny commissions of INR 8-12 per policy.
Funding, CGFMU Accounting and Outlook
Borrowings are diversified across PSU and private banks, ECBs (none currently), PTC securitisation, DAs, and retail and listed NCDs; if
the weighted average cost of borrowing rises meaningfully, it is passed on to customers where the market allows. On the liability
side, ~50-55% is bank borrowing and 20-25% NBFC borrowing, both floating; only retail NCDs are fixed-rate. A credit rating
surveillance is due in October or November, with a possible upgrade worth 20-30 bps on the cost of borrowing.
The CGFMU premium is paid upfront once every financial year on the prior year-end book and recognised pro rata each quarter
under other expenses (hence the rise in other expenses over two years), with incremental premium prorated for new live loans. The
first claim is expected to be filed in Q3 (only one claim is allowed per financial year) and will be booked as a claim receivable that is
extinguished on receipt; peers' experience suggests claims are paid if filings are correct.
The company works to two-to-three-year targets rather than five-to-ten-year visions (currently AUM of INR 50 bn) and expects Q3
and Q4 volumes to beat H1 as macros improve, with liquidity, staff and technology in place to serve demand safely. It takes
customers up the ladder from microfinance to larger secured MSME tickets to retain them.
On the recent 10-11% fall in the stock, the company said nothing has changed operationally and that it was not due to Elevation
(SAIF) exiting. The promoters have no intention of buying shares in the open market purely to support the price, nor of selling their
stake (~90-95% of family wealth is in Arman) absent an exceptional offer.
Guidance
The company targets AUM of ~INR 50 bn over two to three years, expects H2 to be materially better than H1, and guides to stable
asset quality with high rejection rates, ~90% CGFMU asset coverage and a possible rating upgrade worth 20-30 bps on the cost of
funds.

Astral Ltd
Astral is a building materials company across four verticals: pipes (flagship), adhesives, bathware and paints. Management
maintained its FY27 guidance across all verticals: double-digit growth in pipes, 15-20% in adhesives (India), 25-30% in bathware and
25-30% in paints (Q1FY27 paints growth was 48%). For the first time in 2-3 years, value growth is expected to exceed volume
growth, supporting overhead absorption and margins after a period of falling realisations and inventory losses. PVC price increases
have been passed on, while CPVC (5-10% range), adhesive and paint price hikes are being implemented from 1 October 2026. The
CPVC compounding (backward integration) plant is on track for completion by December 2026, trials during January-March 2027
and commercial operations from 1 April 2027, meeting ~70% of requirements. Capacity utilisation is ~57-58%, so no new capacity
announcement is planned this year. Astral holds ~10% market share, with agri pipes at ~8% of the mix. The key factors to monitor
are CPVC plant commissioning and cost savings, realisation trends, PVC/CPVC price volatility and trade measures, market share
gains and the scale-up of bathware and paints.
FY27 Guidance & Demand
• Pipes (flagship vertical) are growing as per the guidance of minimum double-digit growth; management sees no challenge to
this.
• Adhesives are on track for 15-20% growth in India; Q1 was good and Q2 is going well.
• Bathware is expected to grow 25-30% (at least 25%), and paints 25-30%, with Q1FY27 paints growth at 48% and Q2 also going
well.
• For the first time in 2-3 years, value growth is expected to be much higher than volume growth; earlier, falling realisations
pressured overhead absorption and margins, along with continuous inventory losses.
• Secondary demand remains good, distributor inventory of PVC is very low, and CPVC inventory may be slightly higher due to
quarter-end schemes and the 1 October price hike. Price hikes have had no impact on demand so far.
Pricing & Raw Materials
• PVC price increases have been passed on to the market; the INR 2-3 support continues until 30 September and will also be
passed on from 1 October 2026.
• CPVC price increases are being implemented across the industry from 1 October 2026; Astral has communicated a 5-10% range
across products (pipes, fittings, brass fittings).
• Q2 chemical/crude-led cost increases in adhesives and paints have not yet been passed on; price hikes are planned from
October 2026.
• On PVC resin MIP: the floor price of INR 83-84/kg is not expected to be disturbed, as the MIP has been extended for six months
and the industry is working with the government on countervailing/anti-dumping duty.
• India meets only ~30% of its CPVC and ~40% of its PVC requirement locally, and is expected to remain in deficit even after new
Reliance and Adani PVC capacities. Raw material sourcing is not a challenge (Reliance, DCW, Chemplast and imports).
CPVC Backward Integration
• The CPVC compounding plant is on track for completion by December 2026, with trials in January-March 2027 and commercial
readiness by 1 April 2027; the full-year benefit will accrue in FY28.
• Capex of ~INR 1.5 bn will be offset by working capital savings from reduced dependence on imported CPVC; Gujarat government
subsidies (GST, capital, power) are expected to provide INR 0.8-0.9 bn of benefit, directly aiding ROCE.
• The plant is expected to meet ~70% (roughly two-thirds) of the company's CPVC requirement. Quantification of savings will be
provided after trials.
• Savings will be deployed with a balanced approach (aggressive market share gains in weaker markets and some margin
expansion), with the primary focus on market share, since Astral already has the highest margins in the industry.

Avonmore Capital & Management Services Ltd
Avonmore Capital is the ultimate holding and operating investment company behind the Almonds group, presenting itself as a
Fairfax-style promoter and operator that incubates, builds and selectively exits businesses, rather than a passive holding company.
Through the ongoing restructuring, it will hold 55% of the financial services business and remain the ultimate owner of the green
energy and infra businesses, while running a separate minority investment portfolio. The company argues that its market
capitalisation of ~INR 3.6 bn deeply undervalues the aggregate of these assets.
Structure and Value Unlocking
• Avonmore will hold 55% of the financial services business (Almonds Global Securities), remain the ultimate owner of the green
energy and infra businesses, and continue investing in companies its financial services arm advises, such as Green Jewels,
Dalchini and Parflex.
• Almond Finance, a 100% subsidiary, is merging into Avonmore with no new shares being issued, while Almonds Global
Securities is demerging its green energy and infra businesses, capturing value at the Avonmore level. The complex structure
arose from continually recycling group capital into new businesses and is now being unwound through demergers and
consolidation.
• Three businesses are described as significant: financial services with revenue of ~INR 550-600 mn, green energy with revenue
of ~INR 10+ bn and infra with revenue of ~INR 1.5+ bn.
Portfolio and Investments
• The company has promoted five majority businesses over time: insurance (exited to Willis Towers Watson at an INR 5.5 bn
valuation on an INR 5 mn investment), financial services, green energy (Premier Green), infra engineering, and Skiffle
Healthcare (written off).
• Minority holdings include ~9% in Parflex (packaging), ~6% in Green Jewels (biocrude, backed by Amazon, Circularity and
Zerodha) and smaller stakes in Dalchini and others; the minority portfolio is valued at ~INR 300 mn.
• The model targets two to three new minority or majority transactions a year and one to two exits, keeping a financial partner
and operating management partner in each business; one large acquisition is near closing with Avonmore to hold ~20-25%.
Financials and Valuation
• Avonmore's FY26 standalone revenue was INR 1.91 bn, and consolidated revenue was ~INR 1.9 bn, with PAT of ~INR 220 mn;
the latest quarter showed revenue of ~INR 500 mn and PAT of ~INR 170 mn. Green energy revenue is not consolidated; only
the minority share of its profit is.
• Green energy is valued at ~INR 10 bn (last fundraise), implying roughly 25x PAT (current-year PAT is ~INR 550 mn on EBITDA of
~INR 1 bn); infra consulting, with an order book of ~INR 4 bn, is yet to raise private capital, so its valuation will emerge on
listing.
• Group debt sits in green energy (~INR 2 bn fund-based plus ~INR 250 mn non-fund-based) and infra (INR 100 mn fund-based
plus INR 300 mn non-fund-based); broking and financial services carry no debt. Contingent liabilities of ~INR 3.58 bn relate
only to group bank guarantees for Premier Green and infra borrowings, with no litigation.
Ethanol Expansion and Outlook
• No further greenfield ethanol plants are planned; the company will move into ethyl acetate, e-methanol and polyethylene to
consume surplus ethanol, and may acquire other ethanol players. Maize availability is rising by ~30% a year, so grain prices are
not expected to climb further.
• Infra will list within seven to eight months and green energy within ~18 months; other portfolio companies may list over three
to five years as subsequent fundraises set valuation benchmarks.
Guidance & View
The company guided to retaining 55% of the financial services business, listing infra within seven to eight months and green
energy within ~18 months, moving ethanol downstream into ethyl acetate, e-methanol and polyethylene rather than adding
greenfield capacity, and executing two to three transactions a year with one to two exits. It projected FY27 PAT of ~INR 350-400
mn versus INR 220 mn last year and committed to quarterly earnings calls and to disclosing valuations of unlisted businesses.
The holding-company discount thesis is plausible given the demonstrated insurance exit and the scale of the green energy and
infra assets, but realising it depends on the demergers completing, the unlisted businesses listing and the market accepting an
operator rather than a holding-company framing. Improved disclosure cadence is a positive, though sum-of-the-parts investing
here requires conviction in the promoter-led model and patience on exit timing.

Baheti Recycling Industries Ltd
Financial Performance and Guidance
• The H2FY27 order book of INR 2.5+ bn from five key clients, with a six-month execution window, provides a floor for second-half performance
and supports full-year FY27 guidance of INR 10 bn.
• Management is "more than on track" to achieve and "overachieve" FY27 guidance, with an FY28 target of INR 13.5 bn (35% growth), including
INR 1.5-2 bn from aluminium wire rod business, reflecting conservative phasing of new product ramp-up.
• The wire rod project's FY28 revenue guidance of INR 1.5-2 bn represents only 30-40% of its INR 5 bn run-rate potential, reflecting realistic
capacity utilisation phasing and customer acquisition cycles.
Operational Metrics
• Installed capacity has expanded to 40,800 tonnes (from 30,000-38,000 tonnes previously) through equipment optimisation, including the
migration from 750 kg to 1-tonne electric furnaces, improving both nameplate capacity and operational yield.
• Current utilisation stands at ~60%, with a target of 70-75% in FY27; reaching an 85% threshold would trigger a further INR 300 mn brownfield
expansion in FY28.
• EBITDA margins expanded from 4-5% to 7-8% through three discrete improvements: enhanced furnaces improving yield by 1-2%, new
segregation plants reducing labour costs, and the solar plant delivering annual energy savings of INR 18 mn; management targets sustained 8-
10% margins going forward.
• Rotary furnace recovery rates of 92-93% (theoretical maximum of 95%) indicate strong process competency; asset turnover of 14-15x (vs. 6-7x
for peers) reflects superior capital efficiency and operational discipline.
Aluminium Wire Rod Projects
• The INR 320-330 mn capex (INR 250 mn in Phase 1 and INR 70-80 mn in Phase 2) will deliver a combined annual capacity of 25,000 tonnes,
generating run-rate revenue of INR 5 bn, an exceptional revenue-to-capex multiple of ~15x.
• Wire rod addresses two distinct segments: aluminium alloy rods for the steel industry (deoxidisers), serving ArcelorMittal, Tata Steel and
Jindal Steel, with 50% of capacity absorbed from day one (INR 1.25-1.5 bn), and cable conductor products, reducing concentration risk.
• Management targets 65-70% utilisation in the first year, translating into annualised revenue of INR 3.25-3.5 bn; the original November 2026
commissioning has been revised to December 2026/Q4FY27 due to labour and supply chain disruptions, followed by a one-month trial period.
• Wire rod will operate at partial utilisation in FY28, explaining the conservative revenue contribution of INR 1.5-2 bn despite a run-rate
potential of INR 5 bn.
Raw Material Sourcing and Hedging
• Baheti sources 85% of its scrap through imports and 15% domestically, with 20-30% from Europe and the balance from the US, South Africa
and the Dubai-Jeddah corridor; US scrap is INR 20-25 per tonne cheaper than European scrap, enabling geographic cost optimisation.
• EU scrap export restrictions (repeatedly delayed to May 2027) would have limited impact due to alternative sourcing routes and re-export
hubs continuing supply to India with minimal cost escalation.
• Natural hedge: Scrap is purchased at a specified percentage of LME (e.g., 80% at Mundra), and products are sold at LME (prior month) plus the
USD rate (prior month) plus a delta premium, creating a month-on-month lag that insulates earnings from commodity moves over 12-month
cycles.
• Scrap discounts are expected to remain stable (fluctuating only 1-2% around prevailing levels) as high EBITDA margins (8-10%) maintain
competitive equilibrium; increased secondary aluminium demand will not significantly narrow LME-to-scrap discount spreads.
Customer Profile and Competitive Positioning
• The company has deliberately shifted from small distributors to large OEMs (Bajaj Auto, TVS Motor, Royal Enfield, Bosch, ArcelorMittal, Tata
Steel, Jindal Steel), providing better demand visibility, stronger negotiation leverage, and margin improvement opportunities through service
differentiation.
• One major customer is a 100% EOU with US headquarters, providing natural carbon-compliant sourcing demand ahead of 2028 CBAM
implementation and enabling sticky long-term relationships.
• Customer conversations focus on indexed pricing (LME + Delta) rather than margin squeezing, decoupling customer purchasing behaviour
from supplier profitability concerns and enabling margin defence/expansion.
• India's secondary aluminium sector benefits from structural tailwinds: high European primary smelting costs driving secondary aluminium
demand, India's policy support for recycled content standards, and anti-dumping protection on Chinese aluminium products.
• Industry consolidation thesis: regulatory requirements (carbon tracking, IATF compliance, CBAM) will force smaller unorganized players out,
positioning Baheti (as a listed, main-board player with compliance infrastructure) to capture market share similar to pharmaceutical industry
consolidation.
• The company forecasts 30% CAGR through 2030 vs. sector 8-9%, indicating aggressive market share capture potential.
Other Highlights
• EBITDA margins are targeted at 8-10% (upper quartile for secondary aluminium), with the aluminium wire rod project expected to deliver 6-
10% EBITDA margins, consistent with the core business.
• Current installed capacity of 40,800 tonnes at 70-75% utilisation supports revenue of INR 10 bn (~INR 245 mn per 1,000 tonnes of capacity);
the FY28 target of INR 13.5 bn (35% growth) is supported by higher capacity utilisation and early wire rod commercialisation.
• Post-capex margins are expected to stabilise in line with the previous year's performance, maintaining 8-10% EBITDA even as the business
scales and wire rod operations mature.
• The current working capital structure requires upfront payment for imports, while customers pay on 60-day terms, necessitating short-term
borrowings of INR 2 bn (March 2026), which are expected to rise to INR 3 bn post-expansion; these are transactional facilities (bill
discounting), not permanent debt.
• Positive operating cash flow is expected to materialise in 2-3 years (FY29-FY30) through inventory compression, extended supplier payment
terms as volumes scale, and working capital leverage from higher-margin wire rod business; H1FY27 results expected to show meaningful
improvement.
• The timeline for positive OCF appears credible as revenue scales beyond 2x the current base and operational processes mature, with cash
conversion improving as scale strengthens supplier relationships and working capital efficiency.

Balance Sheet Health & Cash Generation

new ~INR 700-800 mn facility in Madhya Pradesh approaching commercial operations by November, the company is poised to

Company Background and Positioning
Bhadora Industries has operated in cable manufacturing for nearly four decades, marketing products under the brand Vijuth
Cables. The company has built its presence primarily in the power transmission and distribution ecosystem, serving discoms,
utilities, EPC companies, and institutional customers across India. Its key strengths include a deep approval base, vendor
registrations, execution track record, and long-standing customer relationships, all of which take considerable time to build in this
industry.
IPO and Capital Deployment
The company listed on the NSE Emerge platform last year through an IPO, with proceeds directly linked to manufacturing
expansion. Funds have been substantially deployed toward a new facility that is approaching commissioning, marking a transition
from the investment phase to operations and ramp-up.
Product Portfolio Expansion
Historically focused on LT cables including LT power cable, aerial bunch cable, service cable, and control cables in both PVC and
XLPE variants, the company is now expanding into 33 kV HT cables. The incremental portfolio includes LT power cable, 11 kV, 22
kV, 33 kV, control cables, instrumentation cables, solar cables, and other specialised cables. This expansion offers both higher
capacity and a significantly broader addressable market, enabling participation in projects previously inaccessible due to voltage
or product limitations.
New Manufacturing Facility
The company is investing ~INR 700-800 mn in a new facility in Madhya Pradesh, spread across ~15 acres. Commercial operations
are expected to begin around early to mid-November. The plant is significantly larger, more automated, and designed for a wider

Demand Drivers

solar-wind hybrid projects, industrial infrastructure including data centres, and exports. The strategy is to build a diversified
business across utilities, EPCs, renewables, industrial projects, data centres, and international markets rather than depending on
any single segment.
Market Development Strategy
The company is moving from an inquiry-led to a project-led approach, engaging earlier in the project cycle to understand EPC
contract awards, cable requirements, procurement timelines, and optimal engagement stages. With select large EPC customers, it
is exploring capacity booking, exclusive partnerships, and long-term supply arrangements to create better visibility and capacity
planning.
Structural Advantages
Utility and institutional approvals take years to build, creating an advantage for established manufacturers. Strong EPC
relationships built on quality, consistency, and execution reliability are difficult to replicate. The central location in Madhya
Pradesh provides a geographical advantage for serving North, West, Central, and South India competitively, as freight forms an
important part of delivery cost for heavy cable products.

• PAT is expected at INR 3-3.25 bn, implying 38-50% YoY growth.
• FY27 closing order backlog is expected at USD 1.3-1.4 bn, representing ~65-70% growth YoY.
• North America contributes ~70% of revenue, while India accounts for only 6-7%.
Hyperscaler Positioning
• Black Box has established relationships with major hyperscalers including Meta, Oracle and Google, with management focused
on deepening existing customer relationships rather than expanding indiscriminately.
• The company expects to hire 1,000+ professionals during FY27 for data-centre hyperscale connectivity rollout.
• Management believes its experience over the last 4-5 years and conversion of long-term customer engagements into large
contracts provide a platform for continued order wins.
• Black Box does not supply fibre; its role is primarily design, deployment, connectivity, networking and maintenance of digital
infrastructure.
Competitive Position
• Management clarified that Black Box is services-led and product-attached, rather than a fibre manufacturer or supplier.
• Its scope includes discovering, designing, deploying and managing infrastructure, whereas companies such as STL, Corning and
CommScope participate in fibre supply.
• In the US, management sees a large addressable market and believes its established hyperscaler relationships and execution
capabilities support further share gains.
Data-Centre Opposition
• Management acknowledged constraints around land, power and water, which can create local or project-specific opposition.
• However, management expects the broader AI infrastructure buildout to continue given increasing demand for digital services
and computing capacity.
• Some individual projects may face delays, but management does not currently expect these issues to materially alter the
overall growth trajectory.
Hyperscaler Contracting Model
• Contracts are a mix of direct and indirect arrangements.

• Newer contracts are increasingly routed through general contractors/EPC companies for balance-sheet and project-

• However, hyperscalers continue to control key decisions including vendor evaluation, pricing, partner selection, execution and

Inorganic Growth Strategy
• Black Box has already completed an acquisition in Brazil, strengthening its capabilities in the largest Latin American market.
