• Management intends to remain disciplined on capital allocation, including structures such as 60% upfront and 40% deferred

Hyperscaler Buildout Model
• Management highlighted three broad models used by hyperscalers:
◦ Self-build, where hyperscalers own the underlying infrastructure.
◦ Colocation, where they lease data-centre capacity and deploy their own compute infrastructure.
◦ NeoCloud, where they use fully populated GPU-enabled infrastructure.
• Even when hyperscalers own the asset, they require multiple partners for land, power, MEP, connectivity, networking and
other infrastructure.
• Black Box focuses primarily on connectivity and networking, which management considers critical for moving data between
servers and end users.
Adjacency Opportunities
• Management is evaluating opportunities to move one step towards compute and one step towards MEP.
• Compute could be an opportunity particularly in enterprise, colocation and smaller cloud environments where customers may
require managed compute.
• On MEP, the company is exploring the electrical/low-voltage portion rather than full mechanical and plumbing services.
• Management is also evaluating partnerships and acquisitions to expand its addressable market.
• However, management believes the existing connectivity and networking opportunity itself is sufficiently large to support
significant growth.
Revenue Recognition
• Revenue recognition varies by business:
◦ Time & Material: revenue recognised based on work performed/hours billed.
◦ Annuity/maintenance: revenue recognised ratably over the contract period.
◦ Projects: revenue recognised based on progress/percentage of completion.
◦ Product sales: revenue recognised upon product supply.
• Management stated that revenue recognition follows applicable accounting standards.
Receivables Normalisation
• Management attributed the increase in receivables primarily to quarter-end revenue skewness, particularly in March.
• ~65% of March-quarter revenue was generated during March, with a significant portion coming in the final 2-3 weeks.
• This resulted in receivables temporarily increasing at the reporting date.
• Management stated that these receivables were substantially collected within ~60 days and expects September numbers to
show a significant reduction in receivables versus March.
Hyperscaler Service Scope
• Black Box provides inside-plant fibre connectivity, rack/server connectivity, white-space fit-outs, wireless and network
infrastructure.
• Cabling and fibre infrastructure form a significant part of the connectivity offering.
• Black Box does not provide physical security infrastructure, as hyperscalers generally maintain their own security systems.
• The company is therefore positioned primarily around the connectivity and networking layer of data-centre infrastructure.
India Opportunity
• India currently contributes only ~6-7% of revenue, with the company generating roughly INR 5 bn from its India business.
• Management is currently more focused on hyperscaler opportunities in the US, where large-scale infrastructure deployment is
already underway.

BLS International Services Ltd
Business and Financials
• BLS is a tech-enabled visa, consular and citizen services provider. It is a top-two global player, with ~17% revenue share and ~10%
volume share.
• It operates in 100+ countries for 46 client governments, and has processed 490+ mn applications to date.
• The digital business sits in BLS E-Services, in which BLS International holds ~51-53%.
• FY26 consolidated revenue was ~INR 30 bn (37% CAGR over FY22-26) and EBITDA INR 8.19 bn (66% CAGR, ~27% margin). PAT was
INR 7.24 bn (60% CAGR).
• Visa and consular services account for ~65% of revenue and ~90% of EBITDA. FY26 revenue was INR 18.4 bn and EBITDA INR 7.38
bn (~40% margin versus ~15% in FY22).
• Net revenue per application was ~INR 3,300 in FY26.
• Operating cash flow was ~INR 9 bn and ROE was ~30% (diluted by acquisitions). Net worth is ~INR 25 bn and cash ~INR 16 bn as of
30 June.
Q1FY27
• Revenue was INR 8.91 bn (+25%), EBITDA INR 2.52 bn (+24%, 28.3% margin) and PAT ~INR 2.2 bn (+11.5%).
• Visa and consular revenue was INR 5.6 bn (+21-22%) and EBITDA INR 2.26 bn (+22%). Net revenue per application rose ~11% to
INR 3,521.
• Visa volumes have been flat for a few quarters. Management says they are need-based and track travel-industry growth of ~8-
10%, with revenue per application driven by value-added services.
Guidance
• No formal guidance. On existing business and with no new tenders or M&A, management expects ~20% revenue growth and 20-
25% EBITDA growth this year.
• Visa EBITDA margin is seen stabilising at 38-40%. Digital margins have bottomed and should improve. The consolidated margin
depends on mix (~32% if visa is above 70% of revenue).
• Effective tax is rising from ~9% to 12-13%, because Dubai now taxes at 9%. It should reach ~15% over time under Pillar Two norms.
• The Iran war had a minor impact on Middle East volumes, offset by other regions. Q1 still grew 15-20%.
Visa Model and Moat
• Contracts are exclusive and long-term (5-10 years). The business is asset-light with negative working capital, since fees are
collected upfront.
• Tenders come in three forms: global (e.g., Spain), a cluster of countries, or country-by-country (e.g., Italy in India).
• Pricing is fixed per tender in USD or EUR for the contract term. Europe and the US weight technicals 75% and price 25%, while
India awards contracts to the lowest (L1) bidder.
• Processing fees are ~70-75% of revenue, and the rest is value-added services (premium lounges, courier, insurance, mobile
biometrics).
• Spain is ~18-20% of revenue, with Germany, Italy, the US and Slovakia next. Key source markets are Algeria, Morocco, Dubai and
Canada, and no country exceeds 12-15%.
• Competition: VFS has 60%+ share and TLS Contact ~15%. Eligibility conditions in tenders, such as 1 mn applications a year, are
barriers to new entrants.
• BLS claims a cost and flexibility advantage over both.
Spain and Algeria Investigation
• The press reports concern a Spanish consul in Algeria and a junior official accused of taking money to approve visas in 2025.
• BLS says its Spanish lawyer found no mention of BLS in public documents, and that it has received no communication from
authorities or courts.
• Management says BLS does only non-judgmental work and expects no impact on pre-qualification. It operates directly in Algeria,
not through a partner.
Growth Drivers
• New tenders, with a bump to sales and profit when one is won.
• More value-added and consular services, such as passport renewal.
• About 50% of countries have not yet outsourced visa processing. Pilots are under way (e.g., Brazil), and South America is a new
frontier.
• M&A: the group has made 6+ acquisitions in 3 years. Visa M&A targets are scarce, so more deals are expected in digital.
• Citizenship by investment (a Dubai acquisition with 15+ country programmes) is a small adjacent business.
• The UK hotel business is an experiment. There is no intention to buy more hotels, and management would prefer hotel
management services.
Digital (Non-Visa)
• The digital business has three segments: banking correspondent services, G2C e-governance (including Aadhaar at 400+ centres)
and loan distribution (16 NBFCs and banks, 6,500 DSAs). About 750,000 people visit its centres daily, and cross-selling is expected
to lift margins.
• Management agreed visa and digital are very different businesses. Digital was listed separately for that reason, and the parent's
stake may fall as it raises equity. A separate call on the digital business was scheduled for the following day.

BMW Industries Ltd
BMW Industries is a ~40-year-old steel processing company with a legacy conversion business (TMT rebars, HR/CR coil processing,
galvanising, pipes & tubes) for Tata Steel and SAIL, and is now building a proprietary flat steel complex at Bokaro. Q1FY27 revenue
stood at INR 1,660 mn, with operating EBITDA of INR 336.9 mn (20.3% margin) and PAT of INR 191.2 mn (10.8% margin). The Bokaro
complex (capex ~INR 8.03 bn) will add ~550,000 TPA of galvanised, galvalume and ZAM capacity, of which ~200,000 TPA can be
further value-added into colour-coated products. Colour coating is being commissioned now (revenue from Q3FY27), galvalume and
cold rolling/pickling by Q4FY27, and galvanising in H1FY28. Management reiterated FY28 revenue of ~INR 32 bn, implying ~70-75%
revenue CAGR over FY25-28, with EBITDA and PAT CAGR of ~40-45% and ~35-40%, while blended EBITDA margin moderates to ~12-
13% as the business shifts to a raw material-inclusive model. Peak debt is expected at INR 7.5-8.0 bn by FY28-end. The key factors to
monitor are Bokaro commissioning timelines, ramp-up and offtake, distribution build-out, steel price volatility, debt levels and
working capital.
Business Model & Positioning
• The legacy conversion business converts customer-supplied billets into TMT rebars, and processes HR/CR coils through various
lines; raw material is supplied free of cost by customers.
• The company operates five plants in Jamshedpur and one in Kolkata; at Bokaro, it has a joint venture with SAIL and is setting up
the new flat steel complex. It is located close to the key HR coil manufacturing hubs of Jamshedpur and Bokaro.
• Legacy plants are dedicated to their respective customers (Tata Steel and SAIL) and are largely not fungible; utilisation depends
on customer demand and raw material availability.
• Zinc is a pass-through cost, so percentage margins fluctuate, while absolute margins remain broadly flat.
Q1FY27 Performance
• Q1FY27 revenue stood at INR 1,660 mn, operating EBITDA at INR 336.9 mn and PAT at INR 191.2 mn.
• Operating EBITDA margin was 20.3%, PAT margin 10.8%, ROE 9.4% and ROCE 9.5%; return ratios reflect Bokaro capex not yet
generating revenue.
• Q1 revenue from the CGL complex (rolling mill and galvanising complex at Jamshedpur) was INR 770 mn, and rolling mill
revenue was INR 250 mn.
• Pipes and tubes continue to ramp up, with better numbers expected in FY27 versus FY26 and FY25; logistics is a vertical the
company is positive on. The legacy business continues to perform as anticipated.
Bokaro Expansion
• The Bokaro flat complex will capture value across cold rolling, galvanising, galvalume, ZAM and colour coating, with ~550,000
TPA of GI/galvalume/ZAM capacity, of which ~200,000 TPA may be further value-added into colour-coated products.
• Colour coating is being commissioned now, with revenue expected from Q3FY27; galvalume and cold rolling/pickling are
expected towards Q4FY27; the galvanising facility will be commissioned in H1FY28, completing the plant.
• Total capex is ~INR 8.03 bn, funded by internal accruals and debt; INR 5.0-5.5 bn of debt has been tied up with SBI (lead), HDFC
Bank and Yes Bank.
• As of 30 June 2026, ~INR 3.4 bn had been spent, comprising ~INR 1.4 bn of internal equity and ~INR 2.02 bn of debt drawdown.
• Ramp-up is expected within one quarter, as these are simple facilities; ramp-up depends more on operating efficiency than
demand. Target utilisation for the greenfield capacity is ~80%.
• Bokaro carries raw material price exposure and will move with the steel cycle; the company will manage cycles to minimise
impact. HR coil prices are currently ~INR 55,000-56,000/tonne. The company does not buy billets and has no plans to do so at
Bokaro.

contribute INR 1.2-1.3 bn revenue and INR 120-140 mn EBITDA by H1FY28. In parallel, monetisation of the INR 2-2.2 bn estimated
land portfolio could provide an additional growth opportunity over the next 2-3 years. Improving working capital and maintaining
the distribution business growth will remain important for cash-flow generation.
Strong Distribution Business
• A 30-year-old business with a strong Tata Steel distribution network across Bihar and other markets.
• Revenue has grown at 20% CAGR over the last 30+ years, while net profit has grown at 24% CAGR.
• TTM revenue stands at INR 23-24 bn; distribution remains the core cash-generating business.
Fabrication Business Scaling up
• Fabrication capacity stands at 24,000 tonnes, with current utilisation at 20-25%.
• The order book has increased to 9,600 tonnes from 2,600 tonnes a year ago.
• Management targets 50% utilisation over the next 4-5 quarters and 85-90% utilisation over 8-10 quarters.
Fabrication to Become a Larger Profit Contributor
• Fabrication is currently a small part of revenue but already contributes 3-5% of EBITDA.
• Management expects fabrication to contribute 5% of revenue by H1FY28, implying INR 1.2-1.3 bn revenue and INR 120-140 mn
EBITDA.
• At full capacity, fabrication could contribute 20-25% of the company's earnings over the next 2-3 years.
Strong Order Pipeline and Entry Barriers
• The company is receiving orders from large players such as IOCL, BHEL, Adani and Megha Engineering.
• RDSO approval, technical capabilities, compliance and required scale create entry barriers in railway fabrication.
• Management expects increasing order sizes as execution track record improves.
Distribution Network Supports Fabrication Growth
• The existing dealer network and relationships with large infrastructure companies provide access to fabrication orders.
• Distribution inventory can also be used as fabrication raw material, improving sourcing flexibility.
• Value-added distribution such as bore piling can improve EBITDA margins from 3% to 5-6%.
Land Portfolio Provides Additional Value
• The company owns 60 acres across two Pune parcels and 16-17 acres in Kolkata.
• Management estimates the overall land portfolio value at INR 2-2.2 bn versus a bank valuation of INR 800-900 mn.
• Kolkata land may be developed through a real estate/hospitality project, while Pune land is planned for industrial/residential
plotting.
Land Monetisation in the Next 2-3 Years
• Management expects a concrete plan for the Kolkata land potentially by the Q2 investor communication.
• Pune projects could take another 6-12 months to finalise.
• Management expects meaningful monetisation activity within the next 2-3 years.
Working Capital Improvement Remains a Key Focus
• Weak operating cash flow in recent years was mainly due to higher inventory and slower dealer collections.
• The cash conversion cycle increased to 88-93 days from the targeted 65-70 days.
• Management expects inventory and receivables to improve, supporting better operating cash flow going forward.
Comfortable Leverage
• Debt stands below INR 2.5 bn, with debt/equity at 0.6-0.7x versus 2x before the IPO.
• The credit rating was upgraded from BBB+ to A- for an INR 4 bn facility.
• Management currently has no fundraise plans and intends to reduce debt through internal accruals.

Bombay Coated and Special Steels Ltd
Integrated Steel Processing Platform
Bombay Coated and Special Steels, established in 1983 and transitioning into steel processing in 2010, is an integrated steel service
centre and authorised primary service partner of JSW Steel. The company provides customised steel processing solutions, primarily
for the white goods industry, while increasingly targeting automotive applications. Its operations span ~66,000 sq m across four
plants in Bhiwandi, Vasai, Gilot and Sri City, supported by 23 processing lines and a workforce of 500+ employees.
Strong White Goods Franchise
White goods and home appliances contribute ~90% of revenue, with refrigerators and air conditioners being the key applications,
followed by washing machines and water heaters. The company supplies leading OEMs including Voltas, Havells, Amber
Enterprises, Godrej, PG Electroplast and Haier Appliances. Its processing portfolio includes slitting, cut-to-length, embossing and
shearing, with ~85% of sales undergoing two or more processing stages, providing greater value addition and customer stickiness.
Capacity & Pan-India Presence
Installed processing capacity stands at ~462,000 MT, with operations running 24x7. The pan-India footprint enables the company
to service OEM clusters across western, northern and southern India. The company is positioned as JSW Steel's only pan-India steel
service centre focused on the white goods segment, providing a strategic advantage in customer proximity and logistics.
JSW Partnership Provides Visibility
JSW Steel has a dominant position in India's appliance-grade coated steel market, with an estimated ~65% share. Bombay Coated
benefits from its strategic relationship with JSW, with raw material procurement and customer sales largely governed by quarterly
pricing arrangements. This structure provides protection against steel price volatility and supports relatively stable processing
margins.
Automotive Expansion – Key Growth Trigger
The company is diversifying beyond seasonal white goods demand through its upcoming Supa MIDC facility in Ahmednagar. The
11-acre site is strategically located between Pune and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, providing access to major automotive
manufacturing clusters. Phase 1 capex is estimated at INR 750-800 mn, with commercial operations targeted for December
2027/January 2028, subject to OEM technical approvals. The facility is expected to have a 60-70% automotive and 30-40%
appliance mix.
Deleveraging to Support Earnings
The company's debt-to-equity ratio has dropped to 2.0x, while asset turnover remains strong at 8x. The blended borrowing cost is
9.0-9.2%. Proposed IPO proceeds are primarily directed towards debt reduction, including INR 1-1.1 bn of short-term debt and INR
300 mn of long-term debt, along with INR 150-170 mn towards the buyback of Siemens-leased assets. Lower leverage should
reduce finance costs and improve earnings conversion as operations scale.
Management Guidance & Vision 2031
Management is targeting a significant scale-up by 2031, with:
• 1 mn MT annual steel selling capacity.
• Revenue of INR 60 bn.
• EBITDA of INR 3 bn.
• Continued expansion into automotive steel while maintaining its core white goods franchise.
• Supa MIDC expected to become an important contributor to the company's automotive growth from FY28 onwards.
Seasonality & Key Monitorables
White goods demand is typically strongest from October to May, while June-September remains comparatively weak. The
company witnessed softer utilisation during periods of unseasonal rainfall and weaker summer demand. Key monitorables include
the ramp-up of the Supa facility, OEM technical qualifications, automotive customer additions, utilisation across the expanded
network and the pace of deleveraging.
Investment View – Key Drivers
The key structural drivers are the company's pan-India processing footprint, strategic JSW relationship, high asset turnover, multi-
process value addition and established OEM relationships. The transition into automotive processing provides an opportunity to
diversify revenue and reduce dependence on seasonal appliance demand. Execution of the Supa MIDC project, however, will
remain critical to achieving the company's longer-term growth targets.

Canarys Automations Ltd
Outlook: Canarys Automations Ltd is executing a multi-year strategic transformation, shifting from legacy IT and engineering
services to AI-powered digital solutions and higher-margin proprietary product platforms. Supported by a 30+ year technology
heritage, the company is pivoting up the value chain to capture recurring licensing revenue across North America, APAC, and
domestic Indian markets. Management expects future scaling to be anchored by its flagship AI regulatory platform (ARIS),
international client additions following the Forira acquisition, and steady execution of its INR 4,409 mn order book.
FY26 Standalone & Consolidated Financial Performance
FY26 marked a landmark operational milestone as standalone total income crossed INR 1,000 mn for the first time, reaching INR
1,017 mn. Standalone EBITDA grew to INR 175 mn, with EBITDA margins expanding to 17.0% (up from 16.0% in FY25), while
standalone PAT reached INR 100 mn (PBT pre-exceptionals at INR 167 mn). On a consolidated basis, total income surged 121% YoY
to INR 1,997 mn, driven by international consolidation. Consolidated EBITDA stood at INR 245 mn (up 74% YoY, representing a
12.3% consolidated margin), while consolidated PAT increased 79% YoY to INR 148 mn.
Order Book & Business Segments
The total order book at the end of FY26 reached INR 4,409 mn, providing multi-year revenue visibility across a typical 2-3 year
execution timeline. Technology Solutions serves as the core growth vertical, accounting for INR 4,132 mn of total orders, a
significant expansion from INR 1,050 mn in FY25. The Water Resource Management (WRM) division contributed INR 276 mn to
the overall order backlog.
Strategic Acquisition – Forira
• In April 2025, Canarys completed the acquisition of Forira to accelerate its "land and expand" strategy across North America. In
FY26, Forira generated USD 11.68 mn (INR 970+ mn) in revenue, USD 0.77 mn in EBITDA, and USD 0.73 mn in PBT. The
acquisition added 58+ specialised consultants, expanded presence across AI, data engineering, cloud, cybersecurity, and digital
engineering, and granted direct access to 20+ Tier-1 enterprise clients across BFSI, healthcare, pharma, and retail.
Proprietary AI Strategy & the CAR Framework
• The company has deployed its proprietary CAR Framework (Canarys Automation Resilience), designed under a "smartify, not
replace" philosophy. The framework overlays an intelligent AI layer across 5 core enterprise pillars: CAR D (Design UX/UI), CAR
E (Engineering & deployment), CAR T (Testing & QA automation), CAR S (Support & proactive monitoring), and CAR G
(Governance, compliance, & ethics). Operationally, AI integration allows engineering teams to complete a project requiring 6
engineers and 16 weeks (960 hours) using only 3 to 4 engineers in 10-11 weeks. Currently, 70% of the company's 455-member
workforce is AI-enabled using tools like GitHub Copilot and DevOps CI/CD automation.
Flagship AI Product Platforms & WRM Segment
• Canarys is commercialising three domain-specific AI platforms:
◦ ARIS: Flagship AI-driven regulatory compliance platform for life sciences and drug discovery. Active pilots are underway
with 2 North American enterprise clients following completed PoCs and demos, operating on an ARR/SaaS subscription
model.
◦ ClubBase: AI platform targeting sports, hospitality, and premium golf/club ecosystems.
◦ Solaris: AI workflow engine for higher education and research institutions.
• Water Resource Management (WRM): Provides IoT monitoring, SCADA, telemetry, canal automation, and flood warning.
Installed base includes 300+ open channel flow meters, 800+ water level recorders, 2,500+ automatic rain gauges, and 400+
weather stations.
Go-To-Market & Sales Cycle Dynamics
Product-led sales cycles typically last 2-4 months (3-6 months for large enterprise accounts and under 3 months for mid-sized
firms). A key strategic advantage of product platforms is the ability to bypass lengthy vendor management system (VMS)
empanelment processes, enabling faster enterprise onboarding.
Margin Expansion & Strategic Outlook
Having historically grown at 20-22% YoY, the company expects its consolidated financial metrics to benefit structurally from a shift
in product mix. Proprietary product sales carry standalone EBITDA margins of 35-45%. As recurring product revenues (ARR) scale
over the next 18-24 months, management expects significant margin expansion without a proportional increase in headcount.
Global Operations & Partner Ecosystem
Canarys operates across India, the US and Singapore, with 48% of consolidated FY26 revenue coming from international markets.
The firm serves 212 clients across 20+ industries and 10+ countries, maintaining a 100% client retention rate. Its technological
ecosystem is anchored by strategic global partnerships with GitHub, Microsoft, SAP, GitLab, SonarQube, Snyk, LambdaTest, and
JFrog.

Capital Small Finance Bank Ltd
Capital SFB positions itself as a secured, full-suite bank focused on the middle-income group (MIG), anchored in Punjab and
Haryana and expanding contiguously into neighbouring states. The book is 97.4% secured, with 92% of it (ex-corporate)
collateralised by immovable property worth more than the loan. The bank is sufficiently capitalised for its FY29 vision, intends to
drive ROA expansion largely through NIM levers, and sees the bulk of its growth runway in business loans, agriculture and
mortgages within the geographies it already operates in.
Asset Side and Product Mix
• The bank lends to the middle-income group, with an average loan ticket of ~INR 1.9 mn; it does not lend below the poverty
line or to ultra-HNIs.
• Business loans are the largest book at ~27% of the portfolio, with an average ticket of INR 2.8 mn, growing 11% QoQ and 49%
YoY as of June; net NPA is below 0.7%. The bank aims to be the working capital provider and cash flow manager for borrowers
with turnover between INR 10 mn and INR 300-400 mn, at an LTV of 65-78%.
• Agriculture is the second-largest book, with an average ticket of INR 3 mn, lent only to progressive middle-income farmers
cultivating at least two crops a year, including at least one MSP crop; collateral is agricultural land at 50% LTV on the collector
value, so the effective LTV is better given the gap between market and collector values. The bank sits in the MSP value chain as
a nodal banker.
• Mortgages (housing and LAP) are among the best-performing books, with net NPA never exceeding 1% since inception; LAP
has gained traction over the last 15-18 months, and housing momentum is expected as the rate cycle turns. Only prime
property with a 13-year title track record and dual valuation is funded.
• The corporate book comprises lending to mid-sized NBFCs, with A- and above at 69.45% and BBB+ at ~30%; MFI exposure is
negligible at INR 3.1 mn. Consumption loans are an add-on (second or third hook) at 7-8% of the book.
Asset Quality
• Gross slippage runs at 1.25-1.75% each year, but net slippage is held at just 0.15-0.35% given the collateralised, primary-
banker model; FY24 gross slippage of ~INR 1,280 mn was met by recoveries of ~INR 1,110 mn.
• Credit cost has stayed in the 0.15-0.25% range across the 12-year history, with write-offs described as minuscule through
COVID, demonetisation and weather cycles.
Liabilities and Franchise
• Deposits are ~82% of the balance sheet, with 90%+ retail; the average term deposit ticket is INR 1.1 mn and the average
savings ticket ~INR 52,000. CASA has held at 35-38% for three years despite a top savings rate of just 3.1%.
• The cost of deposits is below 6%, optimised to 5.6% in the current quarter; term deposit rollover stays near 90%, reflecting
customer stickiness. Deposits have grown at a 19% CAGR since the SFB conversion and 17% YoY as of June.
• The growth philosophy is contiguous branch expansion, 'combing and carpeting' a geography before deepening; the bank is
the fourth- to fifth-largest private sector bank in Punjab and is deepening its presence in Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi, with
Jammu and Uttar Pradesh next.
Profitability and Levers
• Profit has grown every year since the SFB conversion, including through COVID, at a 26% CAGR (29% YoY in the June quarter);
NIM was 4.2% in Q1, matching FY25, after a brief compression in FY26 due to faster asset repricing.
• Current-quarter growth: NII 22%, PPOP 23% and PAT 29%. The average CD ratio is 83%, with the intent to move to the mid-to-
high 80s; this is the single largest NIM expansion lever, as 6.7%-yielding assets reprice to 11%.
• Fixed-rate advances have been raised from 39% in FY24 to ~50% to match the roughly 50% fixed-rate liability base, so margins
adjust automatically, with a one- to three-quarter lag, across rate cycles.
Guidance & View
The bank guided to doubling advances to INR 160 bn by FY29 (from FY26), a 1.5x increase in branch count, ROTA rising to 1.6% and
ROE to 15%+, funded entirely from existing capital, with no fresh equity anticipated through FY29. ROTA expansion will come
mainly from the NIM lever via a higher CD ratio, with a smaller opex benefit by FY29 and more thereafter.
The targets look credible given the proven secured underwriting, sticky retail deposits and a genuine CD ratio runway, though the
back-ended opex leverage and reliance on NIM mean that expanding the CD ratio without diluting asset quality is the key variable
to watch. The MIG niche remains underpenetrated, supporting the growth thesis.

Capri Global Capital Ltd
The company remains firmly on its five-year scaling roadmap, targeting AUM of INR 1,250 bn by FY31 from the current INR 400 bn,
with nearer-term milestones of INR 500 bn by FY27 and INR 650 bn by FY28. Growth is deliberately pursued at a defended yield
rather than at the cost of profitability, with gold loans set to rise from 48% to 55-60% of the mix over two to three years. The
company guides to 30%+ consolidated growth for the next two years, PAT of INR 14-15 bn this year, and a long-term ROA band of
4.2-4.5% with ROE of 18-21%.
Scale and Positioning
A listed, retail-focused NBFC with a market capitalisation of ~INR 240 bn, focused entirely on diversified, secured lending to the
underserved and underbanked self-employed non-professional segment, underwritten on cash flow assessment rather than income
proof.
The company has five lending products plus two fee-based businesses (car loan distribution and insurance distribution), with AUM
of INR 400 bn across 1,433 branches in 21 states, net worth of INR 76 bn, ~14,000 employees and 0.75 mn customers.
AUM has grown at a 51%+ CAGR over four years, built on a brick-and-mortar model rather than digital or unsecured lending, while
keeping yields and asset quality under control.
Gold Loan Franchise
Gold loan AUM stands at INR 190 bn, up 139%, and is now the largest segment at 48% of the mix. Branch productivity of INR 190 mn
of AUM per branch has been achieved in just four years, against INR 320 mn for Muthoot and INR 150-160 mn for Manappuram and
IIFL, despite a far shorter vintage.
The gold branch network has expanded from 124 branches in 2022 to 955, with 750 opened in two years. 97% of gold branches are
above the per-branch breakeven of INR 50 mn, the repeat customer ratio is close to 60%, and gold tonnage has risen from 3.5 to 20
tonnes.
The gold loan yield is ~18.5%, with a portfolio LTV of 73% and an average ticket of ~INR 0.19 mn. Industry-first transparency
practices include colour photographs of jewellery with stated purity, caratage and weight, and terms in English, Hindi and the
vernacular.
On competition and yield pressure, the view is that the market is large enough and customers, beyond a point, are not highly yield-
sensitive; the company stays in smaller, granular tickets, where RBI allows up to 85% LTV below INR 0.25 mn and yields are better.
Gold yields are expected to hold in the 16-18% band for NBFCs like Capri.
Other Lending Segments
MSME AUM grew a deliberate 18% as capital was steered to faster-growing gold, housing and construction finance; new customer
additions rose at a 27% CAGR. The company plays across ticket sizes: traditional MSME loans of INR 2-5 mn at a 15-15.5% yield,
micro-LAP below INR 0.5 mn at a 23% yield, and a new prime LAP product of INR 5-7.5 mn at 12.5-13%. The INR 2-5 mn band is the
most resilient. MSME is expected to grow 20-25% going forward.
Housing finance is run through a 100% subsidiary with AUM of INR 78 bn (up 42%), customer growth of 26%, a yield of ~13%, LTV of
57% and an average ticket of INR 1.5 mn. 25-30 branches were opened in the south over three quarters, and southern granularity is
expected to improve book quality. Housing is expected to grow 25-30%.
Retail construction finance stands at INR 63 bn across 290 projects, with an average ticket of INR 210 mn, confined to metro and Tier
1 markets and funding Tier 2 and 3 developers. Lifecycle credit cost is under 1%, ROA ~6%, yield ~17.5% and asset cover 2x. Its share
in the mix will continue to decline.
Fee Income and Technology
Insurance distribution across 22 partners generated INR 2.7 bn of premium and INR 1.5 bn of commission income last year. On the
IRDAI consultation paper, the PAT impact is estimated at 3-4% if implemented in full, though this is preliminary as final guidelines
are awaited.
The car loan distribution business is the largest third-party non-dealer distributor, run through a 100% subsidiary with no credit risk;
it originated ~INR 110 bn last year, generating INR 2.4 bn of gross and INR 960 mn of net fee income, with used car and credit card
distribution being added over the same 1,600-employee base.
A 150+ member in-house tech team has built the full loan journey (except the LMS) in-house, now driving productivity and cost
gains. Collections are fully in-house across 0-90+ DPD buckets through AI chatbot reminders, telecalling and field staff, monitored
on real-time dashboards.
Asset Quality and Liabilities
GNPA is 1.1% and NNPA 0.6%, the lowest among the top 20 NBFCs (FY26 GNPA: 0.9%). Credit cost has held in a 0.6-0.8% range over
five years and is expected to stay there, with perhaps a 10-20 bps uptick as gold rises to 55% of the mix.
Funding mix: 55% banks, 25% co-lending, 8% other FIs, 8% market borrowings and 2% NHB. The lender base widened from 20 to
40+ in a year. The incremental cost of borrowing is 8.8-8.9%, against 9.1% on the outstanding book; the cost of funds is expected to
hold near 9.1% even with a possible 50 bps repo hike, since most loans are MCLR-linked with a 6-12 month reset lag.

Captain Polyplast Ltd
Captain Polyplast is a Gujarat-based micro-irrigation company diversifying into Solar EPC (rooftop and solar water pumps) to reduce
single-segment volatility and leverage its existing dealer network. FY26 consolidated revenue grew 45% YoY to INR 4.19 bn, with
EBITDA of INR 460 mn (up 36%) at an 11% margin; micro-irrigation contributed ~85% of revenue and Solar EPC the balance ~15%, a
mix management targets moving toward roughly 50:50 within ~3 years. The company has commissioned a new 70,000 sq ft.
Ahmedabad plant (production from May 2026) to internalise components (filters, valves and connectors) that currently account for
~10% of system value and are sourced externally, with margin benefits expected as internalisation scales over the next three years.
Existing capacity can support up to ~INR 6 bn of micro-irrigation revenue without additional capex, with full utilisation targeted by
FY28. In Solar EPC, FY26 saw 1,500 off-grid pumps executed (~INR 420 mn), while in H1FY27 the company has already won 3,000
pumps worth ~INR 700 mn (1,000 completed and 2,000 under a 60-day execution cycle). The key factors to monitor are the pace of
Ahmedabad plant ramp-up and component internalisation, execution and tender wins beyond Maharashtra as PM Kusum 2.0 rolls
out, the Solar EPC revenue mix shift, and working capital/receivables tied to subsidy reimbursement timelines.
Business Model & Positioning
• Captain Polyplast designs, supplies, installs and provides agronomical services for end-to-end micro-irrigation systems,
comprising head units (filters, valves, connectors), underground PVC networks and drip lines.
• The company sells through direct farmer engagement, local sales/support teams and a dealer network, with a presence across
17 Indian states.
• Demand is largely driven by central and state subsidy programmes, under which the farmer typically funds 5-40% of system cost
upfront, with the balance reimbursed after third-party verification.
• The company has diversified into Solar EPC (rooftop and solar water pumps) to leverage its existing dealer network, reduce
micro-irrigation revenue volatility, and tap the large opportunity under PM Kusum and PM Suryaghar.
Micro-Irrigation Segment
• Management targets micro-irrigation revenue growth of 20-25% annually over the next few years.
• The company competes with larger peers such as Jain Irrigation and Mahindra EPC, differentiating itself through Israeli dripline
technology, end-to-end service, dealer reach and after-sales support.
• Existing installed capacity can support up to ~INR 6 bn of micro-irrigation revenue without additional capex, with full utilisation
targeted by FY28.
Solar EPC Segment
• The segment spans two sub-verticals, rooftop solar (residential: 2-10 kW; commercial: up to several hundred kW) and solar
water pumps, and contributed ~15% of FY26 consolidated revenue.
• Management targets a roughly 50:50 revenue split between Solar EPC and micro-irrigation within ~3 years.
• Rooftop carries lower working capital intensity but also lower EBITDA margins given high competition, while solar pumps carry
moderate working capital intensity (with some subsidy dependence) and margins/returns broadly comparable to micro-
irrigation.
• Solar pump orders and execution are currently concentrated in Maharashtra via the company's empanelment there, with
expansion into Rajasthan, UP, Haryana, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh expected once PM Kusum 2.0 empanelment is announced;
several Maharashtra tenders remain in the pipeline.
Manufacturing & Capacity Expansion

Career Point Edutech Ltd
Career Point has completed its pivot to an asset-light franchisee, content and enterprise-solutions model, which delivered a 64.1%
EBITDA margin in Q1FY27 on revenue of INR 143.1 mn (EBITDA INR 91.7 mn, PAT INR 79.5 mn). Management considers these
margins sustainable for a couple of years, with further upside as partner-institution capacity utilisation rises from ~25% of ~44,000
seats. A ~INR 2 bn government order book (executable till 2030, ~INR 700 mn each in FY27 and FY28) anchors FY27 revenue
guidance of close to INR 1 bn (contingent on execution of government projects) and FY28 revenue of INR 1.25-1.3 bn. Franchisee
test-prep remains the weak spot, with centres down from 40+ to 37 and the digitised-content fix still in development, against a
target of ~65 centres. CP Campus is being repositioned as a premium school (fee target up to INR 0.9 mn p.a.), and the university
has received ICAR accreditation. Key monitorables are execution of government projects, launch of digitised franchisee content and
centre count, NAAC re-application and online programmes, and the revenue-recognition change on franchisee licence fees.
Business Model & Positioning
Career Point exited corporate-operated classroom centres ~5 years ago as average realisations halved to ~INR 55,000-57,000 per
student, compressing offline margins from ~20% to single digits.
The current model earns per-student revenue from partner institutions without bearing the cost of running centres.
University students stay a minimum of 4 years and school students ~12 years, giving high visibility and a long tail of recurring per-
student revenue.
All enterprise clients together operate at ~25% of ~44,000 seats; because the model is asset-light, a modest rise in enrolment drops
disproportionately to profit with no additional capex.
Management described enterprise clients as a 'gold mine' and sees no reason to look elsewhere.
Enterprise-solutions revenue is expected at ~INR 260 mn in FY27 vs ~INR 180 mn last year (management clarified that this is the
amount charged to institutions).
The company holds preferred partnership status with various governments for test-prep services, which underpins the order book.
Government Order Book & Revenue Guidance
Order book stands at ~INR 2 bn, to be executed by 2030: ~INR 700 mn in FY27, ~INR 700 mn in FY28, ~INR 500 mn in FY29 and the
balance (~INR 100 mn) thereafter. Management expects to keep winning government orders.
FY27 total revenue is expected to be close to INR 1 bn, contingent on executing ~INR 700 mn of government projects.
FY28 revenue is expected at ~INR 1.25-1.3 bn.
University & Education Growth
The company is replicating the Kota outreach model beyond the 250-300 km radius of Kota and Hamirpur into cities such as Agra,
Nagaur and Udaipur; word-of-mouth drives flow once a student enrols from a city. Hostel student numbers have already doubled.
The university received ICAR accreditation (held by only 3-4 universities in Rajasthan), which management expects to attract
students from across the country.
The NAAC grade was downgraded from A+ to B+; management said this was due to an external factor, as grades awarded to
institutions across India were revoked. The company will re-apply for an A or A+ grade when the window opens, is confident of
obtaining it and will then start online programmes.
AI has been introduced as a compulsory module in every programme offered this year (from BA to Computer Science).
The formal-education student base grew 8-10% YoY.
Franchisee Test-Prep
Franchisee centres fell from 40+ last year to 37; the student base stayed almost flat. Management noted the company is currently
operating with 31 centres.
The target is ~65 centres, while retaining the existing 37; no date was given.
Faculty retention is costly and makes the franchisee model unsustainable in its current form. The planned fix is digitised,
standardised, expert-designed lectures delivered in a presentation format at centres; this is still under development.

Central Bank of India
Central Bank of India presented a clear post-PCA turnaround story, having been the last bank to exit PCA, with CRAR rebuilt to
18.28%, net NPA down to 0.49% and sustained profitability restored. The franchise leans on one of the strongest CASA ratios in
the industry at 46.61% and a predominantly rural and semi-urban branch network. The bank is confident of holding NIM above
3%, keeping net NPA below 1% and translating improving fundamentals into valuation as market trust builds.
Headline Performance
• Q1FY27 global business grew 18.29% to INR 8,333.2 bn, deposits 11.68% to INR 4,789.7 bn, CASA 11.16% to INR 2,228.9 bn and
advances 28.58% to INR 3,543.5 bn; the RAM segment grew 21.38% to INR 2,411.1 bn.
• Q1FY27 net profit grew 13.26% to INR 13.24 bn; gross NPA fell 53 bps to 2.60%, net NPA was flat at 0.49%, credit cost fell 28
bps to 0.40%, ROE was 14.92% and ROA just above 1%.
• FY26 total income was INR 401.71 bn (up 14.97%), operating profit INR 84.79 bn (up 24.37%) and net profit INR 24.69 bn (up
15.39%), after absorbing an INR 6.32 bn DTA recognition hit, without which ROA would have been above 1%.
Turnaround and Asset Quality
• Post-PCA, CRAR rose from 13.01% to 18.28% and CET1 from 11.06% to 16.54%; net profit moved from a loss of INR 24.39 bn in
FY20 to INR 30.49 bn in FY26 and INR 13.24 bn in the June quarter.
• Credit underwriting was strengthened by onboarding 1,000 trained credit officers posted across clusters and processing
centres, plus NACH mandate and monitoring changes that cut SMA-0 by 50%. The slippage ratio improved from 1.47% (FY25)
to 1.16% (FY26) and 0.40% (non-annualised) in Q1FY27, despite ~INR 4 bn of agricultural slippages in Maharashtra and UP.
Franchise and Distribution
• CASA at 46.61% is among the largest in the industry; 65% of branches are rural or semi-urban and around 3,000 branches carry
CASA above 50%. Cost of deposits at 4.60% and CD ratio at 74% leave headroom for growth.
• CRISIL upgraded the bank to AA+ long term and A1+ on certificates of deposit. The bank raised USD 925 mn (~INR 88 bn) in
FCNR(B) deposits, broadly diversified across customers.
Growth Initiatives
• A full-fledged wealth management vertical will launch by December or January, staffed by 40+ trained marketing officers with
prior experience and senior market hires. Bancassurance runs through Cent General and Cent Life across 4,615+ branches, with
no dent foreseen from the insurance consultation paper.
• Some 45 digital lending journeys are live, customer acquisition centres have been set up at 50+ locations, 300 marketing
officers and 53 lead district managers have been deployed, and a credit card business is planned for FY27-FY28.
Margins and Valuation
• NIM of 3.06% in June is guided to stay above 3% for the year, supported by RAM at 68% of advances and ~61% of advances
linked to EBLR. The cost-to-income ratio of 55.40% is trending down.
• Government holding has reduced from 89% to 81% post-OFS; book value is ~INR 41 per share, while the stock trades at INR 30-
31, below 1x price-to-book, which the bank attributes to a lag in market recognition of the improved asset quality.
Guidance & View
The bank guided to NIM holding above 3% for FY27, growth sustained above 20%, net NPA contained below 1%, CASA maintained
above 46% and a full wealth management launch by December or January, with a credit card rollout in FY27-FY28. The MD and
CEO's mandate runs until 30 September 2028.
The turnaround metrics are robust, and the CASA franchise and CD ratio headroom genuinely support growth, yet the sub-1x
price-to-book suggests that the market is still discounting the durability of PSU asset quality and the DTA-driven optics. A re-rating
hinges on several more quarters of clean slippage and the credibility of the wealth and card build-out.

Chamanlal Setia Exports Ltd
Outlook: The company is targeting a gradual revival in revenue growth through domestic brand expansion, new export customer
additions and deeper penetration across existing markets. Management aims to increase the domestic contribution from around
10% to 30% over the next 2-3 years, while targeting revenue of over INR 20 bn within the same period. Near-term profitability
remains supported by demand and disciplined procurement, although elevated freight costs, geopolitical disruptions and volatile
paddy prices remain key monitorables. The pace of domestic distribution expansion, export growth and working-capital discipline
will be critical to achieving a sustainable improvement in the company's earnings base.
Domestic Market
• Management plans to revive the Maharani brand across India to address the prolonged stagnation in turnover at INR 14-15 bn,
leveraging existing manufacturing capacity and distribution relationships.
• Domestic sales currently contribute ~10% of revenue, with management targeting a 30% share over the next 2-3 years, while
continuing to grow exports.
• The domestic expansion will commence in the current season, initially targeting Mumbai, Delhi, Ahmedabad and Baroda,
followed by expansion into southern markets.
• The company is evaluating both offline distribution and online channels, although online sales currently offer relatively limited
profitability due to high platform charges.
Export Market
• The company exports to 95 countries and aims to expand its presence to 100 countries, with its diversified geographical and
customer mix helping mitigate disruptions in individual markets.
• The company continues to pursue export growth through new customer additions, including four new customers in Russia,
alongside participation in international buyer-seller meets and food exhibitions.
• Export growth remains constrained by elevated freight costs, longer transit times and lower shipment frequency, particularly
across GCC and Middle Eastern markets.
• The company is exploring merchant trading opportunities, including a potential arrangement to source Japanese sushi rice for
onward exports to European markets.
Freight Costs and Geopolitical Disruptions
• Ocean freight rates have increased sharply, with Dubai freight rising from ~USD 200 to USD 5,500 per container, Europe from
USD 1,000-1,500 to USD 3,500-4,000, and the US from USD 1,500-2,000 to ~USD 10,000.
• The company generally prices exports on an FOB basis, factoring in its operating costs and profitability, while converting
shipments to CIF where required to manage transit and insurance risks.
• Higher war-risk insurance premiums and longer shipping routes are increasing logistical complexity, with some shipments
being delayed due to vessel capacity constraints.
• Management indicated that Q1FY27 profitability remained strong despite geopolitical disruptions and expects business
conditions to remain broadly supportive, although full-year margin guidance was not provided.
Procurement Strategy and Inventory Management
• The company is following a disciplined procurement strategy of buying and selling in line with confirmed demand, avoiding
excessive inventory accumulation amid elevated paddy prices.
• Paddy prices have increased by ~20-30% across varieties over the past year, while current prices remain higher than the
corresponding period last year.
• The company maintains ~2-3 months of old-rice inventory, as certain export markets, particularly Europe and the US, prefer
aged rice over freshly harvested produce.
• Management expects to build inventory selectively when prices become attractive, particularly if selling activity slows and
liquidity pressures emerge in the market.
• The upcoming procurement season will be influenced by crop yields, acreage, demand from Iran and the timing of price
corrections in the mandi market.
Iran Exposure and Industry Pricing
• The company does not undertake direct business with Iran, thereby limiting its direct exposure to payment-related risks and
cargo delays associated with the market.
• However, Iranian demand remains an important determinant of Indian basmati prices, with increased Iranian buying
historically supporting prices and its absence potentially triggering sharp corrections.

against an earlier expectation of 7-8%.
Near-Term Growth: Management expects India to deliver better growth in the coming quarters, supported by a healthy
underlying market and new model launches, while the company's performance is expected to remain closer to the industry
growth rate over the next few quarters.
Medium-Term Growth Strategy: CIE is prioritising growth through capacity expansion, customer diversification and increasing
content across existing automotive segments, with management indicating that the company expects to outperform the industry
over the medium term, although formal guidance is deferred.
Export Opportunity: The gradual decline in ICE vehicle production in developed markets could create long-term export
opportunities for Indian component manufacturers as lower volumes reduce the economics of automation in developed markets;
however, realisation will depend on cost competitiveness, quality and execution.
Iron Castings: The business is growing at 15%+ with healthy profitability, supported by export orders and a strong enquiry
pipeline; capacity is emerging as a constraint, with management evaluating a 30-40% expansion over the next 2-3 years,
preferably through brownfield or greenfield investments.
Gears & Composites: Both businesses are witnessing strong growth, driven by four-wheeler EV gears, three-wheeler EV body
parts and four-wheeler battery-related composite components, with profitability and returns remaining above or around company
averages.
Stampings: The business is expected to benefit from stronger order traction from Mahindra & Mahindra and Tata Motors,
following a period of strategic reassessment by customers; capacity expansion across Pune and other locations is being evaluated
to support the growth opportunity.
Aluminium Castings: Growth has been constrained by rationalisation of the Bajaj portfolio, which contributes ~INR 7 bn of the INR
12 bn business; management expects the Bajaj business to broadly stabilise at current levels over the next 2-3 years.
Aluminium Diversification: CIE is targeting greater exposure to four-wheelers through orders from Mahindra & Mahindra, Renault
and Tata Motors, with approximately INR 900 mn of existing orders; scaling this business will require larger die-casting machines
and potentially substantial capacity investments.
Aluminium Margin Improvement: The aluminium casting business currently operates at approximately 13% EBITDA margins, with
management targeting 15% through customer and product diversification; however, elevated aluminium prices and raw material
costs are expected to exert near-term pressure.
Forging & Crankshafts: The crankshaft business is expected to benefit from new model launches by Mahindra & Mahindra and
Maruti in CY27, followed by a potential demand boost from BS7 implementation in 2028-29; the company anticipates higher
content and market share, supported by investments in additional high-tonnage presses.
Bill Forge – 2W: The two-wheeler business continues to perform well, with CIE planning a 10% capacity addition by March to
address capacity constraints in races and crankshafts; management indicated that earlier capacity expansion could have supported
approximately INR 100 mn of additional monthly revenue.
Bill Forge – 4W: Growth has been affected by lower-than-expected conversion of the Stellantis order, which is expected to
contribute approximately INR 1 bn this year versus an earlier expectation of around INR 2 bn; management is evaluating
replacement opportunities, including GKM, while reviewing the broader strategy for this business.

Cineline India Ltd
MovieMax remains focused on sustaining its screen expansion, with 20-25 screens already under fit-out and ~25 additions
targeted in FY27. The increasing contribution from South India, improving industry footfalls, broader content pipeline and
recovery in regional/international films are expected to support occupancy growth. While ticket pricing in South India may remain
lower, management expects revenue per screen to remain broadly stable. Selective O&M/FOCO opportunities, premium formats
and continued favourable leasing economics provide additional growth levers, with management maintaining its commitment to
similar growth over the next three years.
Screen Expansion
• MovieMax has delivered 85 screens over the last three years, reflecting a strong expansion trajectory.
• For FY27, the company is targeting ~25 new screens, with 7 locations comprising 20-25 screens already under fit-out.
• These screens are expected to become operational across Q3 and Q4FY27, with the company currently on track against its
stated expansion plan.
• The company expects to maintain a similar pace of screen additions over the next few years.
South Expansion
• Historically, MovieMax has had a stronger presence in West and North India; however, a majority of new screens this year will
be added in South India.
• The geographic diversification is expected to create a more balanced exposure to box-office collections across regions.
• South India typically has government-regulated ticket pricing, resulting in higher occupancy but lower average ticket prices.
• Despite the lower ticket pricing, the company expects revenue per screen from South India to remain broadly similar to the
existing blended level.
Industry Recovery
• Management highlighted that H1FY27 has been the strongest first half for the cinema industry post-COVID, with higher
footfalls and box-office collections.
• Industry box-office collections have increased by approximately 12-13% YoY.
• The recovery is becoming more broad-based, with multiple INR 1+ bn and INR 2+ bn films contributing to collections.
• Regional content and international films have also shown stronger performance, supporting a healthier content mix.
Screen Renovation
• The 30 screens under renovation were part of the existing 77-screen base, which increased to 85 screens by FY26-end.
• Renovation activity was staggered throughout FY26 rather than all 30 screens being closed simultaneously.
• Individual auditoriums were renovated in phases, allowing cinemas to continue operating with reduced inventory rather than
complete shutdowns.
• The renovation activity contributed to lower footfalls in FY26, particularly in Q4.
Content Pipeline
• Management believes the Indian content pipeline remains robust, with India continuing to be one of the largest content-
producing markets globally.
• Film budgets are increasing, with several large-scale projects involving significant production and VFX investments.
• Content is increasingly being produced across bilingual/trilingual formats, enabling films to target multiple regional markets
simultaneously.
• The success of lower-budget films has also encouraged newer filmmakers to enter the industry.
• Management expects occupancy levels to improve over time, although actual performance remains dependent on the success
and mix of individual releases.
Occupancy Outlook
• Management expects occupancy levels to improve as the content pipeline broadens and newer formats of content gain
acceptance.
• H1FY27 performance has reinforced management's optimism around the cinema industry.
• MovieMax remains committed to similar growth year-on-year over the next three years, supported by continued screen
additions.
• Management did not provide a specific occupancy target given the inherent unpredictability of film performance.
Leasing Economics
• Management indicated that post-COVID cinema leasing deals have become more threshold-oriented and favourable for
multiplex operators.
• Real-estate owners increasingly recognise cinemas as important footfall drivers for malls, retail and F&B businesses.
• MovieMax follows a mix of revenue-share and threshold-based structures, depending on the property and economics.
• The company stated that its rent-to-revenue ratio has remained favourable, which was also reflected in its Q1 results.

Claycraft India Ltd
Business and Financials
• Claycraft is a ceramic tableware and drinkware maker, established in 1988, with 5,770+ SKUs, 132 distributors and 15,000+
retail points. It listed on NSE Emerge in June 2026.
• Own brands (Claycraft 84%, JCPL 13%) account for 95%+ of sales.
• Revenue was INR 1.45 bn in FY24, INR 1.52 bn in FY25 and INR 1.8 bn in FY26. The flat earlier years reflected post-Covid
demand normalisation.
• FY26 EBITDA was ~INR 420 mn (~23% margin) and PAT ~INR 270 mn (~15% margin).
• The product mix is mugs ~40%, dinnerware ~36% and tea and coffee ~17%. The channel mix is distributors ~55%, modern retail
~15%, corporate ~11% and HoReCa ~8%.
Capacity and Capex
• Current capacity is 6,000 MT across two plants. FY26 utilisation was 82% and is expected to exceed 90% this year, which
management sees as optimal.
• Plant 3 (Manda, Jaipur) adds 4,000 MT, taking capacity to 10,000 MT. It carries a revenue potential of INR 1.5-1.6 bn at full
utilisation.
• Commissioning is targeted for February 2027. Utilisation is expected at ~50% in the first year and full in 2-3 years.
• The higher-quality output targets five-star hotels (which currently import from Germany and Italy) and export buyers.
• Capex is ~INR 1.14 bn: INR 960 mn from the IPO (fresh issue, no OFS) and the balance from internal accruals.
• The company is net debt-free, with net worth of ~INR 1.67 bn as of March 2026, plus the INR 960 mn IPO proceeds. No
significant debt is expected, only working capital needs.
Exports and Industry Tailwinds
• Exports were under 0.2% of FY26 revenue. Management expects 6-7% this year and aims to double it each year for the next 3
years.
• The EU raised anti-dumping duty on Chinese ceramic tableware to 79% in February 2026. The UK (currently 17-35%) is
expected to follow.
• Orders were converted within 6-7 months. The UK is served by a sales director and one distributor, plus trade exhibitions.
• The priority is to sell under its own brand. OEM and white-label orders will be taken only if spare capacity is available.
• The industry is estimated to grow from INR 58 bn to INR 86 bn (D&B). Imports are ~10-15% of the market, with anti-dumping
duty on Chinese imports in India since 2017-18.
• BIS norms for ceramic tableware are expected. They would raise quality barriers against cheap imports.
Margins and Costs
• Category gross margins are ~22-26% across mugs, tea and coffee and dinnerware. Product-level margins are not tracked.
• Fuel and gas are ~23% of COGS. The Iran-war disruption caused delays and higher input costs but no production loss.
• A 12% price hike was taken in June. Whether it fully offsets costs will be reviewed after the September 2026 books are closed,
and a rollback or revision is possible. The market has absorbed it, given the supply deficit and festive demand.
• Distributor margin is a 14-17% markup. A&P spend was ~INR 35-40 mn in FY26.
• Finished goods inventory is ~100 days.
Competition
• There is no listed pure-play peer. Cello and Borosil are diversified, with ceramic under 1% of their portfolios.
• The MRP range is INR 49-30,000. Opalware tops out around INR 3,000, and unorganised clusters are small, so management
sees a large uncontested band.
• Management claims its capacity of ~200,000 pieces a day is the largest in the industry.
• Management declined to comment on future capex, project IRR and the finished goods versus raw material inventory split.

CMR Green Technologies Ltd
CMR Green Technologies is India's largest secondary aluminium recycler, with an installed capacity of 0.61 mn MT p.a. across 13
plants in 8 states and a market share ~6x its nearest domestic competitor by revenue. The business is anchored in liquid aluminium
supply to auto OEMs/tier-1s, with a growing wrought alloys push into billets, sheet ingots and UBC recycling, supported by three JVs
with Japanese partners (Toyota Tsusho, Nikkei MC Aluminium, Nippon Light Metal). Blended EBITDA has stabilised at INR 11-12.5/kg
over the last five quarters, aided by hedging since FY23, versus a historical range of ~INR 7-20/kg. Volume growth guidance stands at
~25% for FY27, moderating to an 11-13% CAGR through FY30. Net debt/equity rose to 0.81x in FY26 (from ~0.5x) on higher working
capital from elevated aluminium prices, with management targeting a reduction and positive operating cash flow by year-end. Key
monitorables are the working capital/debt trajectory, ramp-up of new capacity (Shoolagiri, Bawal), the revenue mix shift toward
wrought alloys/non-auto segments, EU/US scrap regulation, and EPR monetisation.
Business Model & Positioning
• CMR Green Technologies has been promoted by Mr. Mohan Agarwal since 1986, with the CMR Green business established in
2006 and its first plant near Tarapur/Palwal.
• The company is India's largest non-ferrous metal recycler by installed capacity and holds the highest revenue share in the
secondary aluminium market (~4x larger by capacity and ~6x larger by revenue than the nearest domestic player).
• The company operates 13 plants across 8 states with total installed capacity of 615,000 MT per annum; 11 plants serve auto-
casting, one (Odisha) is dedicated to UBC recycling with Hindalco as exclusive customer, and one (Tirupati) processes billets and
sheet ingots.
• The company holds a 40-45% volume share in automotive cast alloys and has supplied liquid aluminium via road transport
(~750°C, ~25-35 km radius) since 2013, following earlier boundary-adjacent supply from 2008.
• Aluminium products (molten ingots, billets) contribute ~80% of revenue, with the balance from non-ferrous metals (steel, brass,
copper, zinc, magnesium) derived from Zorba scrap.
• The company has three technology/market-access JVs, with Toyota Tsusho (2012), Nikkei MC Aluminium (2012) and Nippon
Light Metal (2025); no royalty or know-how fees are paid to partners.
• Key OEM customers include Maruti Suzuki and Yamaha, with tier-1 customers such as Toyota Industries, Rockman, Craftsman
and Gabriel; Hindalco is key in raw alloy recycling.
Sourcing & Technology
• Raw material is sourced from over 1,000 scrapyards across 13 countries, ~75% imported and ~25% domestic, with domestic
sourcing up from ~20-21% two years ago.
• A wholly owned US subsidiary procures raw material for Indian operations, making the sourcing chain vertically integrated end-
to-end.
• Scrap segregation technology includes heavy media flotation, base and colour sorting, and XRT/LIBS machines, backed by 8
copyrights and ~7 patents, including sensor-based "on-time, in-full" delivery scheduling on customer ladles.
• The company ranks 6th on the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment within the aluminium industry, noting recycled
aluminium uses only ~5% of the energy required for primary production.
• The company ranks among the top 15 in Great Place to Work, particularly within sourcing.
Margins & Hedging
• Management measures profitability on a per-kg blended EBITDA basis (industry norm) rather than as a percentage margin;
blended EBITDA was ~INR 12.7/kg in the latest quarter.
• EBITDA/kg was ~INR 10 in FY20-21, rose to INR 15-20/kg during COVID-driven volatility (FY21-22), fell to ~INR 7/kg in FY23-24,
and has since stabilised at INR 11-12/kg following hedging from FY23.
• Guidance for near-term EBITDA/kg is INR 12-12.5.

Revenue Mix & Market Opportunity

• Within India's ~5 mn tonne aluminium market, auto accounts for ~1 mn tonnes (~20%) and wrought alloys/extrusion for ~2 mn
tonnes (~40%, a ~15% CAGR segment used in buildings, data centres, solar panels and EVs), with the remainder largely non-

• The company holds first-mover advantage as the only Indian recycler producing billets through the recycled route using post-
consumer scrap.
• Management does not expect near-term equity dilution to fund ~20-25% growth given sufficient internal accruals, though it
remains open to dilution for inorganic opportunities (lead, copper, lithium-ion recycling) or to meet the requirement to reduce
promoter holding from ~84% to 75% within three years of listing.
EPR & Carbon Credits
• Aluminium EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) trading is not yet operational in India; CPCB guidance points to ~5% EPR
obligation by FY28, rising toward 10% by FY30-31.
• The company holds ~273,000 carbon credits to date, with ~60,000 added annually; currently unmonetised, these would be
booked as other income once monetisation mechanisms are established.
• Management does not expect EPR/carbon credits to become a material (10-15%) contributor to PAT but views them as an
incremental revenue stream and a potential driver of primary-player tie-ups, as EPR requirements may push primary producers
toward higher recycled-input usage.

Confidence Petroleum India Ltd
Confidence Petroleum India, the largest parallel marketer of LPG with ~33% share of the non-PSU segment (which is ~6% of the
market), operates an integrated 'supermarket of LPG and CNG' model spanning imports through time-chartered vessels, 68 bottling
plants, packed LPG in 2-425 kg cylinders, 310+ auto LPG stations, 15 LPG cylinder manufacturing plants and 50+ CNG stations in
Bengaluru under an exclusive agreement with GAIL. FY26 revenue stood at INR 47 bn, with EBITDA of INR 3.78 bn and PAT of INR
0.96 bn. Q1FY27 growth was driven by both higher prices and ~75% volume growth, as the company onboarded several HoReCa and
industrial customers (including Parle and Patanjali) during the West Asia supply disruption, signing 1-year agreements with many of
them. Monthly run-rates stand at ~80,000 MT of LPG imports and ~20,000 MT of packed LPG, with auto LPG at ~380,000-400,000
litres/day. Growth levers include 6-7 new bottling plants, 30-40 auto LPG stations under construction, scaling CNG stations to 100 in
Bengaluru and the upcoming Type-4 CNG cylinder plant. The key factors to monitor are retention of crisis-led volumes, LPG sourcing
and CP-linked pricing, margin per tonne, Type-4 approval and segment-level disclosures.
Business Model & Positioning
• The company has 30+ years of experience and is listed on BSE and NSE; it is promoted by Mr. Nitin Khara and Mr. Elesh Khara,
with a professional management team.
• Integrated model from procurement to retail: LPG is imported via time-chartered ships, unloaded at terminals and transported
in its own tankers to bottling plants or directly to customers.
• Network: 68+ bottling plants, 300+ direct industrial customers, 3,200+ direct HoReCa customers, 3,000+ dealers, 225+
HCVs/LCVs, 310+ auto LPG stations, 15 LPG cylinder plants, 50+ CNG stations, 3 high-pressure cylinder units, 82 CNG road
vehicles, DPT (denting, painting, testing) units and 2 propane-butane blending plants.
• The promoters started with a utensil shop, moved into LPG cylinder manufacturing for PSUs, then into packed LPG retail, and set
up bottling plants to serve it.
Industry & Market Position
• India's LPG market was ~35 MMT in the last financial year and is expected to reach 40-42 MMT by 2030.
• PSUs hold ~94% of the market and parallel marketers ~6%; the company holds ~33% of the parallel marketer segment and is the
largest among ~105 parallel marketers.
• Domestically produced LPG is reserved for PSU domestic supply, so commercial users (HoReCa, industries) must be served
through imported LPG.
• No parallel player is present across all segments; competition comes from small regional players, and Aegis Logistics is more
focused on terminals than nationwide retail.
Auto LPG
• The company operates 310+ auto LPG stations (the largest network), mainly in southern India, as well as in Rajasthan and
Maharashtra.
• Stations are company-operated on leased land, with no dealers or middlemen, under a hub-and-spoke, cash-and-carry model
with no credit.
• Capex is ~INR 10 mn per station, with a payback period of less than 18 months.
• 30-40 new stations are under construction, and the company is in talks to acquire small players that faced LPG availability issues
during the crisis.
• Current auto LPG volumes are ~380,000-400,000 litres/day.
Packed LPG
• Cylinders from 2 kg to 425 kg are sold directly, through dealers and to industries, with volumes of 20,000+ MT/month.
• The focus is on the commercial segment, as subsidised domestic LPG makes the company price-uncompetitive there; it will
enter the domestic segment if subsidies are removed.
• Strategically located bottling plants reduce four-way transportation costs, and customers receive credit for residual LPG in
returned cylinders, improving competitiveness versus PSUs in the commercial segment.

• During the crisis, the company onboarded many HoReCa and large customers such as Parle and Patanjali, and has signed 1-year

Bulk LPG & Sourcing

• LPG is sourced from refiners such as ADNOC and Basra Gas, from Qatar, the US (a cargo planned every month) and Europe; all

CNG Retail & Cylinder Manufacturing

• The Type-4 high-pressure cylinder plant is ready, with most approvals in place and only the final operational approval pending.
Financial Performance & Margins
• FY26 revenue stood at INR 47 bn, EBITDA at INR 3.78 bn and PAT at INR 0.96 bn.
• Q1FY27 growth came from both pricing and volumes, with volume growth of ~75%; prices have not yet normalised, and
management expects the growth to be sustained given new customer additions.
• Management is working to maintain the earlier indicated 10-15% QoQ volume growth and believes higher volumes will drive
margins through fixed cost absorption.
• Segment-wise revenue and margins are not disclosed as infrastructure is shared across segments; contribution from packed,
auto and bulk LPG is roughly equal, with bulk margins lower but on higher volumes.
• The distribution margin is at or slightly above the industry standard of ~INR 7,000/MT.
• Prices are reset monthly by state and region; the company is more price-competitive than PSUs in commercial and auto LPG but
not in domestic LPG. Volumes have grown ~10x over the last 5-7 years.

Cosmic CRF Ltd
Outlook: Cosmic CRF is navigating a soft demand environment in FY27 with railway and infrastructure ordering subdued due to
the West Asian crisis and constrained government spending, yet management guides for 25-30% higher top line than FY26 on the
back of swappable railway-infra capacity and expects H2 to be stronger than H1. The near-term earnings trajectory is underpinned
by the Amzen acquisition, which is awaiting procedural NCLT approval and is expected to begin commercial production within six
months, with FY27-28 seen at 20-25% capacity utilisation and full value unlocking by FY28-29. Over FY28-FY29, the company
projects tonnage rising to ~180,000-200,000 tonnes and then ~300,000-320,000 tonnes, with average realisations improving from
INR 70,000-80,000 to INR 100,000-125,000 per tonne, supported by wagon manufacturing, springs, forging, containers, sheet piles,
and defence items. EBITDA margins are guided to expand from ~14-15% in FY26 to ~18% by FY28 and potentially 20-21% if plans
materialise, aided by galvanising integration. The key monitorables are timely NCLT approval and funding of Amzen, execution
ramp-up, RDSO and DRDO approvals for forging, railway order revival from FY28, and working capital management for a ~INR 33-
35 bn revenue ambition.
Company Background and Listing Journey
Cosmic CRF Ltd, led by Chairman and Managing Director Aditya Vikram Birla, was incorporated on 21 December 2021 and took
over an asset from a company with turnover of ~INR 200 mn in 2021 through a business transfer agreement. The company listed
on the SME platform on 30 June 2023, one of the fastest listings in the SME segment. FY23 revenue stood at ~INR 1.21 bn, with
PAT of ~INR 65 mn; FY24 revenue rose to ~INR 2.55 bn, with PAT of ~INR 128 mn; FY25 consolidated revenue reached ~INR 4.01
bn, with PAT of ~INR 310 mn; and FY26 revenue reached ~INR 7.22 bn, with PAT of ~INR 510 mn, which would have been ~INR 578
mn but for ~INR 55-60 mn of legal costs related to the NCLAT battle against the H2 and H3 bidders for Amzen Transportation
Industries.
Capacity Expansion and Business Evolution
The original Singur (West Bengal) facility had an installed capacity of 12,000 tonnes but an achievable capacity of only ~8,000
tonnes. The company raised ~INR 300 mn through its listing to expand installed capacity to 24,000 tonnes per annum. Initially
present only in cold-rolled formed sections for railway wagons and coaches, it later diversified into infrastructure through the
acquisition of NS Engineering Projects Pvt Ltd in April 2024 via a Swiss challenge bid in the NCLT. NS Engineering had a total
capacity of 18,000 tonnes and was acquired for ~INR 900 mn gross, including takeover and rebuilding; its installed capacity now
stands at 65,000 tonnes. The company also entered springs manufacturing (castle and helical springs) through a wholly owned
subsidiary serving both railways and automobiles. A state-of-the-art forging unit for railways and defence is being set up.
Group Structure and Installed Capacity
Cosmic CRF Ltd is the holding company, housing the original CRF business for railways, and has two subsidiaries: NS Engineering
Projects, which manufactures infrastructure items, and a second subsidiary with two divisions, one manufacturing helical and
castle springs for railways and automobiles, and the other manufacturing railway and defence items through forging. Once the
forging unit is complete, total installed capacity across the group will be at least 131,000 tonnes, with ~90% achievable given the
swappable nature of the capacity and 24/7 operations. The Singur plant covers 5 acres, NS Engineering 8 acres, and the forging
and spring divisions 1 acre each. Amzen is a 72.5-acre plant with ~50 acres of additional attached land, totalling ~122 acres, with a
shed area of ~1.6 mn sq ft.
Amzen Transportation Industries Acquisition
Amzen, formerly Amtek Railcar, was a JV between Amtek Auto and American Railcar, designed for the South American and
Russian markets. Cosmic CRF bid for it in 2024 and received NCLT approval in April-May 2025, but faced an NCLAT challenge, which
ruled against it after 8-9 hearings over 8-9 months. The company took the matter to the Supreme Court and received a favourable
verdict. The LOI has been issued by the Committee of Creditors, and the matter is with the NCLT for procedural approval. The
acquisition price was INR 2.55 bn on a 30-day payment basis, negotiated down from INR 2.84 bn on a 6-12 month basis. The total
takeover cost, including CIRP costs of ~INR 110 mn, is ~INR 2.66 bn. Additional capex of ~INR 1.2 bn is planned, of which ~INR 300-
400 mn has been given as advances to machinery suppliers. The plant can manufacture wagons, coaches, containers (20-foot and
40-foot high cube), loco shells, sheet piles and defence equipment. First commercial production is expected within six months of
takeover, with 20-25% capacity utilisation in FY27-28 and full value unlocking in FY28-29. Amzen has a total capacity of 200,000
tonnes per annum. The plant has six sheds and can manufacture 200 wagons per month comfortably, 350 with additional effort
and 450 with full capex and RDSO clearances. The company is initially targeting 100 wagons per month for six months, which
translates into revenue of ~INR 4.5-5 bn annually. The 50 acres of attached land are under provisional attachment by the ED but
may come to the company, potentially adding ~INR 1 bn in value. Another 67-acre land parcel in Alwar is planned to be spun off to
repay debts.
