Market Outlook and Demand Environment
The railway sector is facing headwinds due to the West Asian crisis and government policy decisions. The government has not
delivered orders or payments as promised in budgets, creating softness in the infrastructure and railway sectors. India needs more
than 850,000 wagons to justify the INR 3,500 bn investment in DICC, but currently has only 450,000, requiring 400,000 additional
wagons over six years, implying demand of ~60,000 wagons per annum. Current industry capacity is only ~35,000 wagons per year.
From next year, the company expects a standard order flow of 45,000 wagons per annum, including private purchases, exports
and local tender-based procurement. A 100,000-wagon order is unlikely; instead, 35,000-45,000 wagons will be the norm. Railway
orders are expected to be more structured and larger from FY28. The BCN wagon order of 35,000 units created congestion, as it
was planned for fertiliser and grain transport but is not required now. The company believes the downcycle will end by the end of
this financial year, with tailwinds returning thereafter.
FY27 Guidance and Financial Projections
For FY27, the company guides to 25-30% higher revenue than in FY26 despite soft markets, with a very soft first half and a
stronger second half. It expects output of 125,000 tonnes at an average price of INR 70,000-80,000 per tonne. This includes
~110,000-120,000 tonnes from existing capacity at 85-90% utilisation and ~10,000-15,000 tonnes from the forging division, which
starts operations after April-May 2027. The forging division will initially operate at 40-45% capacity, as RDSO licences take 4-6
months and DRDO approvals 7-8 months. FY28 projections are ~180,000-200,000 tonnes at an average selling price of ~INR
100,000 per tonne, and FY29 projections are ~300,000-320,000 tonnes at ~INR 125,000 per tonne, potentially reaching 350,000
tonnes. At revenue of INR 33-35 bn, an EBITDA margin of 18-19% and a PAT margin of 12-13% are achievable. The company is
conservatively guiding to an 18% EBITDA margin but believes 20-21% is possible if plans materialise.
Capex Plans and Funding
The company will be in a capex cycle for the next two years, after which no capex will be needed for existing plants unless there
are further acquisitions. Cosmic CRF needs INR 10-40 mn for routine renewal and maintenance. NS Engineering needs no further
capex except INR 45-50 mn for air-wiping systems on the galvanising bath for efficiency and cost benefits. The spring division
needs no further capex, as it is complete and undergoing field trials and RDSO testing. The forging unit is an INR 500 mn project,
with bank financing of INR 282.8 mn and promoter equity of INR 210-220 mn, of which INR 210 mn has already been infused and
INR 10-20 mn remains; the bank is yet to disburse another ~INR 170 mn. The Amzen acquisition requires INR 2.55 bn upfront plus
INR 110 mn of CIRP costs (INR 2.66 bn in total), plus INR 1.2 bn of additional capex. The entire capex programme will be completed
by October-November 2027. Post-capex, total installed capacity will be ~385,000 tonnes with ~80% achievable utilisation,
translating into ~300,000-310,000 tonnes and revenue of ~INR 33-35 bn. Working capital at 120 days of turnover for an INR 33 bn
business would require ~INR 10 bn at some point. The company is working with advisors and merchant bankers on a debt-light
and equity-light structure. Internal accruals since inception are ~INR 1.2 bn, and the working capital limit is INR 800 mn. The
company has paid INR 600 mn to banks/the CoC and given INR 500 mn of advances for Amzen capex. It carries ~INR 500 mn on its
books and has invested INR 200-300 mn from current-year accruals into capex at CRF and NS.
Product Diversification and Market Opportunities
Amzen will address six sectors: defence (82 SQ items for DRDO through the GeM portal), containers (high cube 20 feet and 40
feet), coach building and body parts, wagon manufacturing, loco shells, and sheet piles. The company is the largest player in
industrial sheet piles in India with a 42% market share in the cold-rolled format, targeting 48-60% by supplying from the Amzen
facility in Punjab to West and North markets. Sheet pile conversion margins are 10%, but supplying the West and North from
Bengal erodes 7.5 percentage points of margin, making local manufacturing essential. The company expects an order book of INR
1 bn for sheet piles from day one of operations. Container orders of ~INR 500 mn are expected, with prototyping and testing
taking 4-5 months. The company has existing channels with Chittaranjan Locomotive Works and DLW for loco shells through Vasan
Soul Sealcasting and Comet Technocom, with 30-35 years of relationships. In wagon building, the West has no large wagon builder
after Jindal Rail Systems converted to Texvako West focusing on coaches and loco shells, and Modern India (now Radhika Modern)
not operating meaningfully. This makes Amzen the only large player in the region, attracting orders from JSW, Coal India, TIL,
Tesco, UltraTech and Gatex. The company will also bid for coach body parts for Modern Coach Factory Raebareli and RCF
Kapurthala.
Order Book and Execution
The current order book stands at INR 7.6 bn as of Q1, with 32% from railways and the rest from infrastructure. Execution timelines
range from a few weeks to 1.5 years (for extendable orders), and the company expects to complete this order book within the
year. The order book is largely raw material pass-through in nature.

Margin Outlook and Drivers
EBITDA margin for FY26 stood at ~14-15%. The company expects EBITDA to rise to 18% by FY28 and potentially 20-21% if plans
materialise. The key margin driver is galvanising strength. Previously only 20% of infrastructure items were galvanised; now 60%
are galvanised, yielding a benefit of INR 2,500 per tonne. Raw material prices have increased with E450 mild steel rising from INR
66 to INR 72 per kg and E250 Grade A from INR 58 to INR 62 per kg. Zinc prices have risen from INR 220-280 per kg to INR 440 per
kg, which is a concern but expected to normalise. The company expects an increase of at least 4.5-5% in basic pricing. The
company is taking new-age orders and expects selling price to grow from INR 70,000-80,000 per tonne to INR 100,000 per tonne in
FY28 and INR 125,000 per tonne in FY29 due to wagon, springs, forging, and container additions.
Key Risks and Challenges
The West Asian crisis and government policy decisions are creating headwinds in the infrastructure and railway sectors, and the
government has not delivered orders or payments as promised in budgets. NCLT procedural approval for Amzen is pending, with
30,000+ cases pending across NCLT benches in India. The company faced an NCLAT challenge from the H2 and H3 bidders,
requiring Supreme Court intervention. The 50 acres of attached land at Amzen are under provisional attachment by the ED, and
the 67-acre Alwar land has encroachment issues. Wagon builders broadly remain conservative, relying on supplier credit of 6-8
months rather than working capital debt, which limits their turnaround capability. Wagon manufacturing requires 86-90 types of
components from 80-90 vendors, and the absence of even one knuckle pin can delay RDSO testing and entire wagon production.
RDSO licences take 4-6 months and DRDO approvals 7-8 months. The company has never handled an asset as large as Amzen
before.

Outlook: Crizac is focusing on consolidating its strong UK position while expanding into the US, New Zealand, Canada and other non-

Strong UK Presence and Global Expansion
• The UK remains Crizac's core market, supported by long-standing relationships with major universities. The company has 450+
institutional partnerships, with several top institutions having relationships of 5+ years.
• The UK remains strong, while recent acquisitions have expanded the company's presence in the US, New Zealand and other
geographies.
• Management highlighted that global market share is still relatively low at ~2-3%, versus ~13% in India, providing scope for further
international expansion.
Healthy Application and Enrolment Trends
• Q1FY27 enrolment increased by 15%, despite geopolitical concerns, visa restrictions and anti-immigration policies in key

Revenue per Student: University Mix Effect
• Revenue per student declined to around INR 4.2 mn from INR 5.1 mn YoY.
• Management clarified that the decline is not due to lower commission rates, as university contracts generally run for 3-5 years.
• Revenue per student varies depending on the university mix and the applicable slab/volume-based incentives.
Strong Profitability and Cash Generation
• The company reported operating revenue of around INR 2 bn, with EBITDA margin of ~29% and PAT margin of ~22%.
• Crizac remains debt-free and generates close to INR 2 bn of cash annually, according to management.
• Management expects EBITDA margins to remain broadly around historical levels despite the current industry challenges.

• The company has successfully integrated its acquisitions over the last 1-1.5 years and is now open to pursuing larger acquisitions.

• Management indicated that acquisition payback is generally targeted at less than 2-3 years.
Technology and AI-Led Scalability
• Crizac's proprietary platform automates application screening, quality checks and submission to university portals.
• Around 90-95% of applications are currently submitted automatically through the AI-enabled platform.
• Management stated that the company has improved its systems and AI capabilities and can significantly increase application-
processing capacity with limited additional cost.
Ancillary Services
• Crizac has started offering additional services such as loans, accommodation, insurance, forex and immigration/visa-related
services.
• A separate team is working on these services.
• Management highlighted two objectives: improving student stickiness and increasing revenue per student, although no specific
revenue contribution target was provided.
Seasonality
• Around 65-70% of annual revenue is generated in H2, mainly Q3 and Q4.
• Q4 is the largest quarter, followed by Q3 and Q1, while Q2 is typically the leanest quarter due to limited admission intake.
• Management cautioned that the timing of admissions could shift between quarters due to changes in student decisions and
market conditions.
FY27: A Consolidation Year
• Management indicated that FY27 revenue is expected to be broadly flat versus FY26 as the company focuses on consolidating
operations and strengthening capabilities.
• From FY28, management expects normal growth of around 20-25%.
• EBITDA and PAT are expected to broadly track revenue performance, with management not expecting a major deterioration in
EBITDA margins.

The new seamless pipe plant is fully ready with no teething issues, already executing L&T orders and internal requirements, with
formal external billing starting next quarter. The facility is the only Indian producer of F91/F92 grades and very large diameter,
high-thickness pipes, competing only against Chinese imports. Seamless pipe EBITDA margins are expected at up to ~20%. No

A small FPGO data centre piping order has been received as a beginning, with hopes of more orders. The nuclear JV is progressing,
with partner discussions largely concluded and finalisation targeted by December, but the ~INR 1 bn greenfield plant (company

possible next year.
GE and Siemens HRSG Orders Remain FY28 Revenue Events
Formal GE orders, drawings, and documents are still awaited, promised before December, with billing only next year due to 3-4
months of procurement lead time. Siemens has issued an MOU for GT/balance-of-plant piping, with Anjar facility approval slated
for 6-8 October, but Siemens orders will also flow and execute largely next year. Neither delays the FY27 guidance, and
management views the extra breathing room positively.
Anjar Utilisation Ramp and Execution Constraints
Anjar is currently at ~40-50% utilisation, targeted to reach ~70% by end-FY27 and ~85-90% next year. The key bottlenecks to
scaling from ~INR 1.2-1.3 bn monthly execution towards ~INR 2+ bn are input/material availability, skilled labour scarcity, and
matching staffing capabilities, not capacity. Management is deliberately balancing capex to avoid overbuilding.
Balance Sheet and Non-Core Power Business
The effective interest rate is ~8.75-9%. The non-core power generation assets are debt-free, with only minimal working capital
debt, and no immediate divestment is planned given depressed valuations. Biomass pellet production has been added to make
the assets sustainable, with no cash loss expected in FY27 and ~5-10% EBITDA possible, while also supporting ESG obligations.
Capital Expenditure and Replacement Value
Total gross fixed assets are ~INR 7.4 bn on a consolidated basis. Management estimates that rebuilding just the piping capacity
today would require a minimum capex of over ~INR 6 bn. The current capex programme is sufficient to support the ~INR 25 bn
revenue level without aggressive expansion.

Denta Water and Infra Solutions Ltd
Denta Water and Infra Solutions is a Karnataka-focused water infrastructure company executing DBOT (design, build, operate and
transfer) projects across groundwater recharge, water revitalisation, drinking water supply, irrigation and, more recently,
wastewater and sewage treatment, positioning itself across the full water cycle from design and EPC to O&M. In business since 2016
and listed for about two years, the company has completed over 40 projects and has 38 ongoing projects. The order book stands at
over INR 8.5 bn as of June-end, excluding a newly won ~INR 3.5 bn order, with ~50% coming from Jal Jeevan Mission (~INR 2.8 bn)
and AMRUT (~INR 1.5 bn); revenue is 100% government-driven. FY26 revenue stood at ~INR 2.5 bn and management targets 20-
30% YoY growth with EBITDA margins of 25-30%, although margins have moderated to ~20% in recent quarters on project mix and
higher material costs. The company is debt-free, with bank limits largely non-fund-based. The key factors to monitor are margin
recovery amid cost escalation (no pass-through), execution of the large new order, conversion of 3-4 large bids (75-80% historical
success rate), expansion outside Karnataka and receivable cycles.
Business Model & Positioning
• A civil engineering contractor focused on groundwater recharge, water revitalisation, drinking water supply, irrigation and
water/wastewater management; most projects are DBOT, with assets transferred back to the agency after ~5 years of O&M.
• Integrated capabilities cover feasibility studies, design, EPC and O&M; management describes design as where value is created,
EPC as where value is realised and O&M as where value is compounded.
• Coverage spans raw water sourcing, water treatment plants, storage and distribution under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and AMRUT
2.0, and wastewater collection, treatment, reuse and recharge.
• The long-term ambition is to evolve into an engineering-led, technology-enabled water management platform, aiming to be one
of the most specialised companies rather than the largest contractor.
• Key strengths include domain knowledge, engineering capability, technology selection and the ability to work with the
government ecosystem.
• Project selection is disciplined, based on government fund allocation, project duration, financial viability and technical
feasibility; the company walks away from projects that do not match its core strengths or carry higher execution/financial risk.
• Execution challenges include land acquisition, utility shifting, statutory clearances and local stakeholder concerns; material or
skilled labour delays can cascade into timelines and working capital.
Key Projects
• Tungabhadra Dam project: tapping water from the dam, treating it and distributing it to villages in the Koppal area through
pipelines and overhead/underground storage tanks.
• KC Valley project (Bengaluru, BWSSB): secondary treated water is carried through a ~70 km pipeline to the water-scarce Kolar
region, filling ~400 lakes; the water table has improved considerably to ~100-150 ft below ground, supporting irrigation and
agriculture.
• Villages in Kolar have been adopted as model villages by the Finance Minister, and the company is in discussions with central
government teams to replicate similar projects in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.
Order Book & Revenue Visibility
• The order book stands at over INR 8.5 bn as of June-end, balanced across short, medium and long-term projects, providing
visibility for the next 2-3 years.
• The order book excludes the recently won ~INR 3.5 bn order; detailing of its margin profile is in progress as it was bid about a
year ago, but management aims to keep margins within the 25-30% planned range.
• JJM accounts for ~INR 2.8 bn and AMRUT ~INR 1.5 bn, together ~50% of the order book and of revenue.

Dev Accelerator Ltd
Business
• Dev Accelerator (DevX) is a flexible office space operator, founded in September 2017 in Ahmedabad, with operations starting
in 2018. It listed on NSE about a year ago.
• Its focus is managed office space: build-to-suit offices for enterprise clients taking 150-500 seats (~8,000-20,000 sq ft) on long

terms. Management says this fully hedges its lease liability risk.

Guidance

years.

June 2027 and roughly double flex MRR to ~INR 280-290 mn.

broadly flat because the capex is already funded.
• The blended borrowing cost is expected to fall from ~13.1% to single digits by March 2028.
• The portfolio will be kept at ~60% Tier 2 and ~40% Tier 1.
Pipeline and Funding
• Upcoming centres: Bangalore (~0.1 mn sq ft), going live in December 2026-January 2027; Pune (~0.2 mn sq ft), with possession

• Revenue-to-rent targets are at least 2.35x in Tier 2 cities (INR 50 rent earning ~INR 110-125) and 2.1-2.25x in Tier 1.

as it brings new members. Vacated grade A space is typically re-let within 60-90 days.

Diffusion Engineers Ltd
Outlook: Diffusion Engineers is poised for sustained growth with management guiding 20-25% revenue growth for FY27, building
on a five-year track record of approximately 21% CAGR, with the heavy engineering expansion from 9,000 to 18,000 tonnes
targeting INR 8 bn in revenue by FY30. The revenue mix is expected to shift over three years toward wear parts and heavy
engineering reaching around 75% of the business, while consumables moderate to 15-20%, reflecting the industry's structural
move toward ready-to-fit solutions and complete equipment supply. EBITDA margins should remain stable with potential for 100-
200 bps expansion as machining and heat treatment capabilities deepen. The company remains debt-free with no long-term
borrowings envisaged, and demand tailwinds across cement, steel, power and a revitalised mining sector support confidence that
the current capacity expansion will be absorbed faster than initially anticipated, despite near-term volatility from freight logistics
and steel prices.
Business Overview and Product Portfolio
Diffusion Engineers operates across four product baskets: specialty welding consumables for wear protection, flux-cored wires for
automation-friendly hard-facing, wear plates and wear parts, and heavy engineering equipment. The company also provides
epoxy-based coatings for heat-sensitive applications, welding and cutting equipment as a complementary offering, and
automation solutions including special purpose machines for cladding. The heavy engineering segment represents forward
integration, manufacturing complete equipment for cement, steel, power, mining and railways, alongside reconditioning services
and turnkey kiln solutions. The unifying philosophy across all verticals is extending equipment lifetime for customers rather than
merely supplying products.
Capacity Expansion and Growth Outlook
The company is undertaking a significant capex programme that doubles its gross block, with Unit 4 being the primary expansion
site for heavy engineering equipment spanning approximately 30 acres with 32,000 sq m of manufacturing area. The heavy
engineering capacity is being expanded from 9,000 to 18,000 tonnes, targeting a revenue potential of INR 8 bn within two to three
years, with FY30 as a reasonable estimate for full ramp-up. Management guides 20-25% revenue growth for FY27, maintaining the
five-year track record of approximately 21% CAGR, while cautioning that 30-35% growth would be a stretch due to project-based
revenue recognition upon complete delivery rather than stage-wise billing. The order book stands at approximately INR 2.9 bn as
of June, broadly unchanged, with Q3 and Q1 being seasonally subdued while Q2 and Q4 perform better.
Margins and Profitability
Gross margins are highest in consumables at 35-45%, followed by wear parts and engineering at 45-50%, and industrial services at
similar levels though contributing only 10% of revenue. Consumables command premium margins because customers typically
buy on performance outcomes rather than specified compositions, with the company recommending the right product and taking
responsibility for equipment life extension. Management expects EBITDA margins to remain stable or slightly improve, with
potential for 100-200 bps expansion over time as the company adds sophisticated machining and heat treatment capabilities. The
company is debt-free with no long-term debt and does not foresee borrowing in the near future, relying only on working capital
facilities.
Segment Mix and Strategic Direction
The current revenue mix is approximately 30% consumables, 30% wear plates and wear parts, 30% heavy engineering, and 10%
industrial services. Over the next three years, the combined wear parts and heavy engineering share is expected to rise to around
75%, with consumables declining to roughly 15-20% and industrial services remaining at around 10% even as absolute revenue
grows. This shift reflects the industry's move away from buying consumables and hiring specialist vendors toward purchasing
ready-to-fit solutions with clear accountability. The addressable market expands significantly when supplying complete wear parts
rather than just welding wire, as illustrated by the steel industry's requirement for thousands of rollers that can be supplied as
complete assemblies with bearing housings.
Competitive Positioning and Market Share
In specialty consumables for maintenance and repair, Diffusion holds approximately 20-25% market share, competing with Ador,
Fontech, ESAB and Wear Resist. In wear plates and wear parts, the company similarly holds 20-25% share against ESAB and Wear
Resist. In heavy engineering, the market is vast and the company's share is below 1%, competing with ISGEC and AIEA along with
smaller unorganized players. The company deliberately avoids commodity consumables and focuses on specialty solutions where
it can differentiate through quality, delivery and application expertise rather than competing solely on price.
Raw Material Sensitivity and Export Environment
Steel price volatility has been elevated since COVID and the Russia-Ukraine war, though recent ranges are within plus or minus
20%. Short-duration contracts use fixed pricing while longer contracts include price correction clauses. Management estimates
that even significant steel price movements would impact revenue by less than 5%, and the historical 21% CAGR is not attributable
to steel price inflation. Export logistics costs have increased due to geopolitical tensions, causing some customer delays in pickup,
but management views this as temporary with business eventually normalising.

Other Income and Depreciation
Other income includes mutual fund investments and interest from fixed deposits of unutilised IPO proceeds, which will decline as

Key Demand Drivers
The mining sector has transformed from being nearly dormant four to five years ago to a major demand driver following the entry
of private contractors who prioritise high-performance, longer-lasting products over the cheapest alternatives. Cement plant sizes
have doubled from an average of 5,000 tonnes per day to 10,000-12,000 tonnes per day, making production losses significantly
more expensive and driving demand for higher-performance wear protection. The use of alternative fuels and waste-derived fuels
has increased wear and tear, necessitating continuous R&D for new alloy development. Management believes the current capex
cycle is justified by sustainable demand visibility rather than a temporary spike, and the expanded heavy engineering workshop is
expected to reach 80-85% utilisation faster than originally anticipated.

segment, building customised automated test equipment (ATE), RF simulators, checkout and deployable systems that integrate
proprietary software with commercial off-the-shelf hardware. The company listed on the SME platform in January 2026 and the IPO
proceeds are being deployed in Project Udaan, a 65,000 sq ft integrated TMS, EMS and ESS facility at TGIC Hardware Park,
Hyderabad, targeted to commence operations around December 2027. Revenue, EBITDA and PAT have grown at a CAGR of 14.93%,
~40% and 62.51% respectively, as the business mix shifted from low-margin prototype orders to higher-margin production orders.
Management has guided for 25-30% revenue growth and 40-45% EBITDA and PAT growth in FY27, backed by ~65% of opportunities
coming on a nomination basis. The latest published order book stood at INR 310 mn as on 30 May 2026. The company has also
incubated a subsidiary, Avedya Systems, for RF subsystems. The key factors to monitor are Project Udaan execution, conversion of
the tender pipeline, entry of private players into missile production, ramp-up of Avedya and new products, and receivables/working
capital management.
Business Model & Positioning
• A Hyderabad-based defence and aerospace company with ~18 years of operating history, specialising in TMS systems used to
evaluate the onboard electronic systems of guided weapons.
• The company builds customised testing and simulation systems by integrating proprietary software with commercial off-the-
shelf (COTS) hardware, categorised into automated test equipment, RF simulator systems, checkout systems and deployable
systems.
• In-house capabilities span data acquisition, computing, FPGA, RF sensors and software development, catering to radar, missile,
avionics, naval, electronic warfare (EW), communication and field testing applications.
• The company sells systems (not services) to design and production agencies; the customer base has largely been PSUs and
DRDO (e.g., BEL, BDL, HAL).
• Digilogic addresses the import-substitution gap where customers faced long procurement cycles, lack of local support and
imported systems not fully meeting requirements, and supports customers across the full life cycle after deployment.
Industry Tailwinds & Growth Strategy
• Key tailwinds include Atmanirbhar Bharat, indigenisation of obsolete testers, the defence export push, growth in the space
sector, the electronics manufacturing push and increasing private sector participation in defence programmes.
• The company plans deeper penetration in radars, missiles, EW, naval and communication, and expansion into aerospace and
space (avionics, aircraft, satellites and launch vehicles).
• New areas identified for investment include electronic manufacturing services (EMS), environmental stress screening (ESS),
electro-optic systems, single board computers (SBCs) and high-resolution gimbals.
• Development of SBCs, gimbals and indigenous harness testers is underway, with launch planned once customer validation is
completed.
• The company is collaborating with foreign companies for international expansion, targeting exports of test systems, engineering
solutions and locally built products.
Project Udaan – Integrated TMS, EMS & ESS Facility
• Funded through the IPO proceeds raised in January 2026, the facility is located at TGIC Hardware Park (provided by the
Government of Telangana), Hyderabad, spread across 65,000 sq ft, with commencement of activities targeted around December
2027.
• Construction status: footing excavation, footings and plinth beams have been completed and column construction is currently in
progress.
• Layout: the ground floor will house the ESS facility, the first floor the EMS production area along with system integration and
test & evaluation, and the second floor engineering, operations and management workspaces.

• The EMS facility will cover PCB design, PCB manufacturing, schematic capabilities, component assembly, testing and support,

• The team has been formed and R&D activities have been initiated, with systems expected to be ready in the next couple of

Business Economics – Prototype vs Production
• Prototype orders take ~12 months and carry thin margins as specifications keep evolving during development (management
indicated up to ~30% additional specifications by delivery).
• Production orders take 6-8 months as specifications are frozen; margins are higher due to software reusability (porting existing
software rather than redeveloping) and better negotiating power with hardware OEMs on larger volumes. This explains PAT
growing much faster than revenue.
• Once shortlisted in DCPP production programmes, testers are qualified by government agencies, so they must be procured from
Digilogic irrespective of who executes the production (BDL, HAL or private players such as Adani or Tata), making the TMS
opportunity scale with missile volumes.
• Competition exists mainly at the prototype stage; the company's proprietary technologies often become part of the government
specifications.
• Entry barriers for newcomers include MSQAA/CEMILAC certification, documentation expertise and software development
capability.
Order Book & Pipeline
• The latest published order book stood at INR 310 mn as on 30 May 2026; management did not provide an updated figure.
• On the tender pipeline (~INR 1.5 bn referred to by a participant), management did not commit to timelines as tenders can take
anywhere from 3 months to 1-2 years to close.
• Around 65% of opportunities are on a nomination basis (repeat production orders on proven systems), while ~35% are open
competitive tenders.
• Execution typically takes 4-6 months after receipt of the PO; billing is H2-weighted, with a major portion of invoicing in
February-March.
Financial Performance & Guidance
• Revenue has grown at a CAGR of 14.93%, EBITDA at ~40% and PAT at 62.51%, as per the company presentation.
• FY27 guidance: 25-30% revenue growth and 40-45% growth in EBITDA and PAT.
• Management declined to give FY28-FY30 guidance but expects the TMS business to sustain 25-30% growth; any contribution
from Project Udaan would be incremental.
Working Capital & Funding
• The company uses bank cash credit (CC) limits for project funding in addition to administrative needs.

Divine Power Energy Ltd
Divine Power Energy is a winding wire manufacturer (copper and aluminium, bare and insulated conductors) serving the
transformer, railway, automobile and inverter industries, and is now entering continuously transposed conductors (CTC), a higher-
value, next-generation product, through a technical collaboration with a Chinese company that is the world's third-largest CTC
manufacturer. FY26 revenue stood at ~INR 6.26 bn, with Q4FY26 alone contributing ~INR 3.46 bn, a rise management attributed to
higher metal prices rather than seasonality (H1/H2 run-rates are otherwise broadly similar, with H2 typically modestly stronger).
The company operates two complementary facilities: Divine's Sahibabad (Ghaziabad) plant, focused on recycled copper and
primary aluminium, and the Vimlesh Industries plant in Sonipat (acquired in 2025), which uses primary raw materials and serves
large OEMs such as Schneider, Panasonic and Hitachi. CTC production, being set up at the Vimlesh facility with two initial lines
(further expansion planned), is targeted to commence by December 2026, subject to execution timelines. A separate group entity,
Viraj Upkram (set up with newer machinery when initial Vimlesh acquisition talks stalled), is being merged into the group, with
completion expected next financial year; management expects revenue to more than double from the FY26 base by FY28, aided
significantly by the CTC ramp-up. The key factors to monitor are CTC commissioning and customer qualification (given long
warranty requirements), completion of the Viraj Upkram merger, export scale-up from a negligible base, and EBITDA margin trends
as the CTC/value-added mix increases.
Business Model & Positioning
• Divine Power Energy was founded in 2001 as PDRV Enterprises Private Limited, renamed ahead of its public listing, and has
historically manufactured winding wires for the transformer industry, alongside magnetic wire and solar-segment customers.
• The company acquired Vimlesh Industries (now a wholly-owned subsidiary) in 2025, which management said has driven a
multi-fold increase in growth for both entities since the change in management.
• The business spans transformers, railways, automobiles and inverters, giving it a diversified end-market base that reduces
dependence on any single industry's demand cycle.
• The company also has a pan-India customer base across North and South India, providing a geographic demand hedge
alongside its industry diversification.
Product Portfolio
• Products span bare conductors (uninsulated copper/aluminium round wires and flat strips) and insulated conductors across a
range of insulation classes: paper (lowest temperature class, used in lower-end distribution transformers), fibreglass (used in
dry-type transformers and lifting magnets), enamel, and Kapton/Nomex/mica (highest temperature class, up to ~240°C, used in
traction and railway loco transformers).
• The company differentiates itself by focusing on flat wires/strips rather than round wires, a segment it says is harder to execute
consistently and where it has invested in online, AI-assisted defect detection technology imported from China.
• Divine also manufactures specialised inverter-grade aluminium foil using conform casting technology (up to 33 mm wide and
0.6 mm thick, developed in-house beyond standard conform limits), supplying customers such as Luminous and other large
inverter manufacturers.
• By value, copper contributes the larger share of revenue given its higher per-unit value, while tonnage volumes between
copper and aluminium are roughly comparable (~60:40 split).
• Within copper, bare conductors contribute ~18% and insulated conductors ~82% of the segment; within aluminium, the split is
~26% bare and ~74% insulated (aluminium foil is classified as bare).
CTC – New Growth Vertical
• Continuously transposed conductors (CTC) are viewed as the next generation of winding wire, splitting a single large conductor
into individually insulated strips to increase surface area and improve weight-to-current-carrying-capacity efficiency for power
and high-rated transformers.
• The company has a technical collaboration with a Chinese company that is the world's third-largest CTC manufacturer, which
will handhold the company through plant set-up and production quality; some machines have already been received from
China, with others in transit.
• Two CTC lines are currently being set up (at the Vimlesh Sonipat facility, given its larger area and existing OEM customer base),
with production targeted to commence by December 2026, subject to execution; three further machines are planned beyond
this initial phase.
• Target customers are power transformer manufacturers; CTC carries long warranty requirements (20-25 years), creating a high
entry barrier, and the company already supplies the complementary normal conductor to many of these customers, giving it, in
management's view, a natural inside track to capture the CTC portion of the same transformer's winding wire requirement.
• Management sees strong export demand for CTC as well, citing European and Middle Eastern buyers already importing CTC
products from India.
Manufacturing Facilities
• Divine's own plant is located in Sahibabad, Ghaziabad (UP), and focuses on recycled copper, with aluminium sourced as primary
material at both locations.

Dodla Dairy Ltd
Margins and Guidance
• Q1 and Q2 margins are under pressure. Procurement prices rose in Q2 instead of the usual seasonal dip, and sales-price
increases lagged. EBITDA margin has slipped to ~7-8% from a 9%+ aspiration.
• Current gross margin is ~22-23%. Reaching ~9% EBITDA needs ~26-27% gross margin, which management expects in Q3 and
Q4 through price corrections made in the last two months. Management expects Q3 and Q4 to be better than Q1 and Q2.
• Revenue growth guidance is 18-20%, with current growth of 15-16%. Management says earlier guidance is intact, but gave no
bottom-line guidance.
Pricing and Procurement
• The procurement price was ~INR 41 per litre in July and is now ~INR 42.
• In Karnataka, sales prices were raised on 10 September and again on 28 September, by about INR 4 per litre in total. The
procurement price will rise by INR 2 from 1 October. Q1 hikes were ~2% and ~2.5%.
• Karnataka Milk Federation is raising sales prices by INR 4-5. Tamil Nadu co-ops cannot procure enough milk and are delaying
farmer payments by 2-3 months, so Dodla's volumes held despite a wider price gap (earlier INR 6-8 above co-ops).
• Management does not expect procurement prices to go higher. Milk supply is adequate and supply is slightly improving,
though the El Niño impact is seen mainly in July-August.
• Cattle feed prices have been raised twice and farmers are getting remunerative prices. Global skim milk powder prices are up,
but India has no shortage and the North India flush is expected after Diwali.
Costs
• Packaging costs are up 30-40% but are only ~3-3.5% of costs. Transport costs are being optimised, and the combined impact is
under 1%. Some is already passed on.
• Management also cited the West Asia war and the new labour code (higher manpower cost) as one-off pressures this year.
Maharashtra Expansion
• Capex is INR 2.8 bn plus ~INR 400 mn for chilling centres (50 planned, 25 by December, 23-24 already running). The plant is on
track.
• Liquid milk and curd (B2C) start in March 2027. The powder plant will start later, around May-June with the flush or possibly in
September-December.
• FY28 revenue target is INR 5-6 bn, with an exit run rate of ~INR 8 bn. The company already procures ~300,000 litres a day there
and needs 200,000-300,000 more.
• Sales will be in the periphery near Telangana and North Karnataka, not Mumbai and Pune. Management called it incremental
revenue.
• The FDA crackdown on adulteration brings no substantial benefit, since Dodla's model is direct from farmers.
Value-Added Products (VAP)
• VAP is ~30-32% of sales, with a plan to add 1-1.5 points a year.
• Dodla is a late entrant in paneer and is catching up. Paneer grew 60-70% last year, and high-protein paneer is planned.
• Paneer capacity across Dodla and HR Foods is ~17-18 tonnes, against sales of ~6.5-7 tonnes.
• Dodla is the single brand used across products in South India and by HR Foods (a different brand is used in Africa). The
company is pursuing modern trade and e-commerce.
Subsidiaries
• Osam: The business has been fixed through SAP implementation and procurement, plant, quality and SOP corrections, while
route optimisation is still in progress. EBITDA margin is below 5% and may stay slightly below 5% this year, with above 5%
expected next year.
• Africa (Uganda): The business did very well in Q1, slowed in July-August due to a milk shortage, and picked up in September.
Margins are expected at 10-12%.
Cash and Capex
• Planned uses: ~INR 2 bn for Maharashtra (after loan drawdown), ~INR 1 bn for Uganda, INR 100-200 mn for Osam, INR 500-600
mn for backend infrastructure, and ~INR 600 mn of regular capex.
• The rest is for acquisitions (brownfield or greenfield) once projects stabilise, with the dividend policy unchanged. Inventory
build for B2B is also planned after the Maharashtra plant starts.
Inventory
• Bulk fat and powder inventory was built earlier for B2B consistency and has since normalised. Management said it made no
write-offs, only net-realisable-value adjustments.
• Surplus fat will come mainly from the new powder plant.
Competition
• Management says it competes with Heritage, Parag and others in every state, and that nothing is new. It cites a stronger
procurement network.

Dollar Industries Ltd
Business
• Dollar is an innerwear and hosiery maker founded in 1972, with a ~15% domestic market share. The segment mix is ~40% mid-
market and ~40% economy, with women's, thermals and premium making up the rest.
• Brands are Dollar Man, Woman, Junior, Protect, Thermal, Big Boss and Missy, with Force NXT in premium. Force NXT has
grown 20-25% a year and earns 15-20% EBITDA margin.
• A super-premium JV sells ~95% through quick commerce. It grew ~30% last year and targets 20-30% this year.
• Revenue is ~INR 20 bn, with a target of ~INR 30 bn in 3-4 years.
Guidance
• FY27 revenue growth is guided at 12-13%, comprising ~8-9% volume and 4-5% value growth. EBITDA margin is guided at 11.5-
12.5%.
• Management raised prices by ~4-5% in Q1 (May-June) to offset cotton costs. Demand is good this quarter, with thermals
targeted to grow 20-25%.
• Management sees 14-15% EBITDA margins as sustainable for the segment over time, with an 11-12% revenue CAGR to 2030.
• Priorities for the next 2-3 years: reducing working capital days from 164 (March 2026) to 125-130, becoming debt-free, raising
the share of high-margin products from 27% to 35%, and increasing active retailers from ~150,000 to 250,000-275,000.
Restructuring
• Nine group companies, including the one holding the Dollar brand, are being merged into the listed entity, which management
says is a first in hosiery. It is priced at the lowest of the valuations (KPMG and a merchant banker), based on book value.
• This removes ~99% of related-party transactions (the landlord companies were leasing offices and factories) and saves INR 50-
70 mn of rent a year. Completion is targeted by March 2027.

Distribution (Project Lakshya)
• Project Lakshya started in 2019-20, and Phase 1 is complete. Phase 2 activates dormant retailers, with Vector Consulting
advising.
• Management targets >60% of enrolled retailers being active, out of a universe of ~1 mn. It claims retailers benefit directly,
which reduces distributor undercutting.
• Gains were cited in Rajasthan (from #2/#3 to #1) and Haryana.
• About 80,000 retailers are enrolled and 900 large-format stores are served.
Competition
• Peers include Lux and Rupa in the mid-segment, along with a premium player.
• One peer's family settlement could split it into three companies. Management expects aggressive discounting to ease in 2-3
quarters, and says it protected margin during this phase.
Raw Material and Manufacturing

weaker monsoon.
• Backward integration is ~20-25% for yarn, saving INR 5-10 a kg and giving ~7-8% better margin than buying. Cutting is 100% in-

• Four plants: West Bengal (~45% of manufacturing), Tirupur (knitting and bleaching, ~50% of revenue), Delhi and Ludhiana

Channels and Exports

• Exports are ~4-5% of revenue (~INR 750 mn), 90% under the Dollar brand and 10% white label. Orders are coming from the

Other
• GST on innerwear is 5% and no change is expected.
• The new West Bengal government is seen as positive, with subsidy restoration and a textile policy draft expected around 15

D.P. Abhushan Ltd
Business
D.P. Abhushan is a jewellery retailer founded in 1940 in Ratlam and now run by the fourth generation. Its brand pillars are trust,
transparency and quality.
It expanded beyond Ratlam to Indore (2010, after a successful exhibition), Udaipur (2012) and Bhopal (2015). It listed on the SME
platform in 2017, moved to the NSE main board in 2020 and listed on BSE in 2024, and opened 3 stores during COVID.
There were 12 stores as of March 2026, and a 13th opened at Dahod on 24 September 2026 as a strategic entry into Gujarat. The
split is seven in Madhya Pradesh, five in Rajasthan and one in Gujarat. All stores are company-owned (COCO).
Small-to-medium stores are 3,000-5,000 sq ft (average 3,200-3,500), and anchor stores are 8,000-10,000 sq ft (Indore and Ratlam,
~9,500 sq ft each). Management says peers' stores are typically 1,500-3,000 sq ft.
Gold is ~90-92% of sales, of which ~75% is 22K. Studded jewellery is ~5-6%, and silver and gift articles make up the rest. By
occasion, bridal is ~58-60%, festive and gifting ~20%, and daily wear the rest.
The company focuses on Tier 2 and 3 cities, where buyers come with intent to purchase. Conversion is above 80-82% and inventory
turns are ~4.7-5x.
Four Kataria siblings run the business: Santosh (MD and Chairperson), Anil (Whole-time Director), Vikas and Sanjay. Promoters hold
~75%, split equally between two families.
Guidance
The vision is 51 stores and ~INR 150 bn of revenue by 2030, opening 6-8 stores a year. Expansion is planned in Gujarat,
Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra (Vidarbha), with locations already identified.
Blended gross margin is guided at ~7-8% of sales, opex at ~3.5-3.75% and finance cost at ~0.40-0.50%. Management gave a
conservative margin target of ~3.75-4.5% over 5 years.
Diamond share of sales is targeted to rise ~2.5x from ~5% in 2 years, with gold's share gradually falling to ~85-88%.
Priorities for the next 2-3 years: raising hedged inventory from ~12-15% today to more than 50% by March 2027 and 80-90% by
March 2028; increasing the store count to ~28-30 by 2028, after which internal accruals and scheme inflows should fund growth;
and testing the FOCO pilot before scaling.
Store Economics (COCO)
Small-format stores need ~INR 25-30 mn of capex and ~35-50 kg of inventory (~INR 400-500 mn). Anchor stores need ~INR 70-75
mn of capex and ~80-90 kg of inventory (~INR 800-1,000 mn). Inventory runs at ~1.25-1.5x during the season.
Management targets capex payback within 6-9 months of opening. Inventory turns are expected at ~3-3.5x by year 3 and ~4.5-5x at
maturity by year 5.
Franchise (FOCO)
The first franchise pilot is in Jabalpur, launching in October. About 6-8 of the 51 stores planned by 2030 could be FOCO, depending
on how the pilot performs.
Franchisees are only financial partners who are not already in the jewellery business. They fund capex and working capital, while
the company controls design, hiring, operations, marketing and pricing. Pricing and store ambience will be the same as in COCO
stores.
Management said franchising works best where the brand is already known, which is why it is starting in Madhya Pradesh and
building brand awareness before franchising in new regions.
Fundraise
A preferential warrant issue of ~INR 2-2.5 bn is planned. The proceeds will be used only for inventory for new stores, not for debt
repayment.
Sourcing and Operations
There is no in-house manufacturing. About 30-35% of jewellery is sourced through job work and the rest bought outright from
vendors including Sky Gold and Shanti Gold. Diamonds come from DTC sightholders, and some vendors manufacture exclusively
for the company.
The company makes no direct imports and has no forex exposure. It buys concessional UAE CEPA gold under the tariff rate quota
(TRQ) when available, using it for job work as the rules require.
An automated real-time replenishment system first checks other stores and buffer stock, then raises purchase orders with vendors.
Jewellery arrives almost every second day.
Design is done in-house and co-developed with vendors. Frequent design rotation means repeat visitors see new stock within 90-
180 days.

Products and Schemes
Amora, launched two years ago, targets 15-35-year-olds with lightweight, studded daily and office wear. The company is also
selling lightweight and electroforming products and testing 18K and 14K jewellery.
With high gold prices, buyers now shop to a budget rather than a weight. A necklace that used to be bought by grams is now
bought within a ~INR 1.5-2.0 mn budget.
Diamond jewellery earns ~25-30% gross margin, with lower margins on solitaires. Silver sales exceed 10 tonnes a year, also at
higher margins than gold. Polki is also part of the range.
The Swarn Plus scheme, launched in April, sets aside gold each month against the customer's instalment. This removes price risk
for the customer, includes a making-charge waiver at maturity, and gives the company a natural hedge. A gold harvest scheme also
runs alongside it.
Brand awareness is built through events and collections such as Mewar and Polki exhibitions.
Hedging
Until January 2026, the company relied on like-for-like (kg-for-kg) replenishment. It has since set up a hedging desk using three
tools in order of priority: Swarn Plus scheme metal, gold metal loans (GML) with a 180-day window, and MCX futures. The mix
depends on season and spot versus international prices.
About 12-15% of stock is hedged today, with the targets given above.
Industry
The unorganised share of the market has fallen from more than 80% 4-5 years ago to ~40-50%, and management expects it to
reach ~20-30% in 3-4 years as UPI and digital payments grow.
Management says off-book and cash activity is driven by import duty plus 3% GST. It still sees structural formalisation, with card
MDR costs negligible.
Gold is increasingly treated as an investment through jewellery, schemes, digital gold and ETFs, and management sees current
price levels as the new normal.

DU Digital Global Ltd
Outlook: DU Digital is shifting from a pure embassy front-office services provider into a four-engine platform spanning visa
processing, AI-led verification through DU Verify, overseas manpower supply through Global Access, and open-ended visa
issuance through DU Visas. Near-term growth hinges on conversion of a large tender pipeline worth INR 1 bn to INR 5 bn per
contract across Netherlands, Greece, Japan, Australia, KSA, UAE and Singapore, while the recently operational Kuwait contract and
the ramp-up of the manpower vertical give visible revenue through H2. The Saudi contract re-tender and a conditional fundraise
remain the key swing factors to track.
Business Model and Verticals
• The visa front-office business remains the bread and butter, handling administrative and verification work for embassies, and
is the base on which the other three verticals were built.
• DU Verify is the proprietary tool that combines a financial score from bank statements, a travel score from passport and visa
history, and a background score from court, Interpol and ID checks into a single green, orange or red decision aid, with the
embassy or ministry keeping the final call. It currently runs all of Georgia's electronic visa processing and was piloted for South
Korea.
• Global Access and DU Visas are the open-ended, non-contract businesses. Global Access supplies verified temporary workers
from India and neighbouring countries to Europe and the Middle East, and is the newest, high-margin, high-revenue vertical.
• DU Visas issues tourist, five-year and golden visas, notably for the UAE, using the company's own quota, with more than 1,200
travel agents connected directly to its portals.
Pipeline and Contracts
• The company is tendering for roughly ten contracts, with RFPs for Australia, KSA, UAE and Singapore expected in H2.
• Contract values range from INR 1 bn to INR 5 bn, with Australia alone estimated at around INR 5 bn over three years.
• Typical contract tenure is three to five years, and the setup lead time is 1.5-3 months.
Kuwait Contract
• Operations began on 22 July after a competitor's court challenge was resolved with MEA support, and have run smoothly for
about two months.
• Monthly top line is tracking around INR 25 mn against an expected INR 30 mn, with the shortfall attributed to August school
holidays, a slow September restart and the regional war.
• The company expects it to normalise to the INR 30 mn run-rate over the year, with exact margins to be shared in the October
results.
Cost Structure and Margins
• The largest one-time cost is centre setup, covering fit-out, biometric machines, computers and printers, after which running
costs are dominated by manpower at ~50%, followed by rent, utilities and courier costs.
• Staff are largely local Indians in Kuwait trained on the company's systems.
• The company guided to EBITDA margins in the 20% to 30% range across the business.
Revenue Breakup for FY26
• Visa business: ~INR 145 mn.
• Korea and Thailand contracts (started last year): ~INR 45 mn.
• DU Verify (Georgia and Korea missions): ~INR 95 mn.
• Immigration, residency and Global Access: ~INR 260 mn.
Manpower Ramp
• The company sent close to 1,000 workers abroad last year and is targeting 3,000 to 4,000 this year, adding Russia, Japan and
Germany as new geographies.
• Each placement runs on a three- to six-month cycle from job order to visa, so fulfilment and revenue are weighted to H2.
• Alongside the existing B2B network of 300 to 400 labour agents, the company is building a B2C channel through Meta and
LinkedIn sourcing at around USD 100 per candidate for onboarding and checks, with the aim of reducing B2B dependence over
time.
Fundraise and SEBI Matter
• The planned fundraise was deferred because the Saudi Arabia contract, on which the raise was conditional, went back to re-
tender, with bidding expected to reopen at the end of October.
• On the January SEBI order, the company clarified it was never contacted and has no link to the individuals involved. A group of
25 to 26 traders made about INR 9.6 mn on DU among other stocks and were fined roughly INR 19 mn, having traded and
exited the stock back in 2022.

Dynamic Cables Ltd
Dynamic Cables reported a price-led Q1FY27 with soft volumes, consistent with its price-volume seesaw; Q2 growth is also expected
to be largely price-led YoY. The order book stood at INR 8 bn at end-Q1 (1.78x revenue), with 80-90% of orders carrying price
variation clauses. The new plant (~INR 400-450 mn gross block; revenue potential of INR 2.8-3 bn at 6.7x asset turnover) is in
advanced commissioning and expected to start around October-November, with meaningful revenue contribution in Q4FY27.
Supplies to the US have started after product approvals, but Middle East exports are lost in H1 at least due to the war. Management
reiterated its 8-11% margin corridor (80-10-10 structure) and an 18-20% long-term growth trajectory. Key monitorables are on-time
commissioning of the new plant, US order build-up against Middle East losses, and any volume recovery as commodity prices
evolve.
Revenue Dynamics: Price, Volume & Order Book
Q1 growth was price-led YoY as prices were higher than the same quarter last year, while volume growth stayed low. Q2FY27
growth is also expected to be largely price-led YoY.
Price-volume seesaw: value/price growth always comes with low volume growth and vice versa, as customers have a value budget
and defer projects when prices rise.
80-90% of orders carry a price variation (PV) clause, so billing prices follow an escalation formula at the time of supply rather than
company-initiated hikes.
High commodity prices have compressed the order cycle; most orders are now executed within ~6 months.
The order book stood at INR 8 bn at the end of Q1FY27 (1.78x revenue, a typical historical level) and is expected to increase over the
next couple of quarters with the new plant.
New Plant & Capacity Expansion
The new facility is in an advanced stage of commissioning; commencement is expected in October (after the Shradh period, around
Navaratri, close to Diwali/Dussehra).
Revenue contribution in FY27 is expected largely from part of Q3 and full Q4, with meaningful contribution in Q4.
Investment of ~INR 400-450 mn (gross block) and asset turnover of 6.7x give an expected yearly revenue potential of INR 2.8-3 bn.
Order booking for the new facility has not yet begun.
Export Strategy & Geopolitics
Exports were 8-9% of revenue in FY26 and are expected to be slightly higher in FY27; the long-term vision is to take export
contribution from 10% to 20%.
The company has obtained approvals and started supplying cables to the US market this year.
Middle East exports are lost in H1 at least because of the war, pulling down overall export numbers.
Management said it is very early to comment on US margins, citing returning instability, higher sea fares and the longer shipping
distance from India vs other global suppliers.
Export margins are 10-11%, in line with domestic margins. The path to exports is harder than domestic given tariffs, sea fares,
geopolitics and currency.
The low-value regular conductor business is being exited or descaled given its lower margin profile vs value-added cables.
Product Development: Data Centres, HTLS & HVDC
The company is developing power cables for data centres (not communication or fibre cables): 70-80% of the manufacturing
process is the same, 20-30% needs tweaking, and additional machinery will be added in existing plants. No precise timeline; type
testing and approvals are in progress.
HTLS conductors are on hold: commercial production is possible via the TS Conductor tie-up, but the company is not participating
because small utility orders include erection and commissioning, which it does not want to take up.
HVDC cables: The company is working with customers on development.
There is no intention to enter EHV or optical fibre cables for now.
Margins & Competitive Positioning
Management maintains its long-standing guidance of an 8-11% EBITDA margin corridor, built on an 80-10-10 structure (80%
material, 10% other opex, 10% EBITDA), considered fair for a B2B business.

Electrosteel Castings Ltd
Electrosteel Castings, incorporated in 1955, is a pioneer in ductile iron (DI) pipes with ~0.9 MTPA of largely backward-integrated
capacity (~20-22% of the ~4 MTPA industry) across West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh, and exports ~25% of revenue to 130+
countries. The industry has been operating at 50-60% utilisation as central Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) disbursements stalled,
compressing EBITDA margin to ~9% in Q1FY27. Management believes the bad phase is over: JJM 2.0 has an enhanced outlay of INR
8.7 trn (extended to December 2028), and of the INR 670 bn FY27 central budget, ~INR 100 bn has been released with ~INR 100 bn
per month expected in October-December. September saw strong order bookings, the order book has risen to 5-6 months, and
management expects double-digit EBITDA margin in Q3FY27, further improvement in Q4 and a return to ~14% in FY28. Capital
allocation has been permanently shifted away from DI pipe expansion (Odisha greenfield in abeyance) towards valves and industrial
paints, each targeting ~INR 10 bn revenue by 2030, as part of an INR 100 bn revenue vision for FY30. The key factors to monitor are
JJM fund flows, capacity utilisation, coking coal prices, channel inventory, diversification ramp-up and debt reduction.
Business Overview
• Incorporated in 1955, the company is a pioneer in DI pipes, having started with a small capacity in 1994 (~60,000 t) and scaled to
~900,000 tpa of DI pipe capacity that is almost backward integrated.
• Manufacturing plants are located in West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh.
• Exports contribute ~25% of revenue, with presence in 130+ countries supported by wholly owned subsidiaries in Europe, the UK,
the US, the Middle East and Singapore.
• DI pipes are the core product; the company also sells DI fittings (value-added, used in water transportation) and surplus pig iron,
coke, sponge iron and power.
Jal Jeevan Mission & Demand Outlook
• JJM 2.0 is an extension of JJM 1.0, with the outlay enhanced from ~INR 3.6-3.7 trn to INR 8.7 trn and the period extended to
December 2028; the central share of the enhancement is ~INR 1.5 trn.
• The central government has budgeted INR 670 bn for FY27, of which ~INR 100 bn has been released so far; management expects
~INR 100 bn to be released in each of October, November and December, taking cumulative releases to ~INR 400 bn by end-Q3,
along with corresponding state releases.
• Funds released so far have largely been used to clear existing liabilities rather than generate new demand; states have also
allocated funds in anticipation of central releases.
• About 2.5 MT of DI pipes are yet to be supplied under ongoing JJM projects, mainly in Rajasthan, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh;
the bulk of JJM 2.0 demand is expected from Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
• Beyond JJM (till FY29), demand is expected from AMRUT, irrigation and river-linking projects; DI pipe orders from river linking
are expected from Q4FY27/Q1FY28, as large-diameter MS transmission mains are taken up first.
• West Bengal: There has been no material development yet following the change of government, but the state has committed to
a big tender and expects its first central disbursement of the year in October after Durga Puja.
• Uttar Pradesh is seeing strong demand as unexecuted water supply projects are being fast-tracked ahead of state elections next
financial year.
Order Book & Execution
• The company did good order booking in September from EPC contractors, mostly under JJM and partly AMRUT, for supplies to
Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh, to be executed from Q3FY27 onwards.
• The order book has risen to ~5-6 months (versus ~3-4 months earlier) and is gradually increasing.
• New orders are at reasonable margins, factoring in present costs and likely cost increases.

• The company has no material direct JJM receivables, as supplies are made to EPC contractors on secured payment terms.
Industry Dynamics

Margins & Raw Material Costs
• Margin decline over the years was attributed to the demand-supply mismatch, as JJM-led supply additions met a sudden drop in

Diversification & Capital Allocation

• No further expansion in pipes, including other pipe types; the Odisha greenfield DI pipe project is in abeyance, and management
described the capex reallocation as more or less permanent.
Exports & Trade Measures
• Exports are steady at ~25%, with no notable upward or downward trend; the wide geographic presence allows diversion
between markets, so the Gulf situation has not materially impacted export volumes.
• Saudi Arabia (KSA) anti-dumping duty: the company attracts the lowest duty of 17% versus over 30% for other Indian players; it
has filed a first appeal, with an order expected in ~2 months.
• Exports to Saudi Arabia are ~10,000-12,000 tpa (~2% of turnover), so the impact is limited; the company continues to export
there and is diverting volumes to other markets.
Balance Sheet & Other Updates

be used to reduce working capital debt.
• Coal block compensation: the company has received ~INR 1 bn so far and expects to recover its full investment, though timing is
uncertain due to litigation.
• Promoters increased their stake by ~4% in the March quarter and by a further ~4% recently.

Margins

International Expansion

target, particularly given the relatively meaningful position the company already has in its domestic market.
Manufacturing & Production
• The company has increased its in-house production capabilities, which management believes has helped improve production
efficiency and reduce the manufacturing cycle.
• Production cycle time has reduced from around 4 months previously to approximately 2-3 months, following the
establishment of in-house capacity and improvements in planning, tools and operational processes.
• The shorter production cycle has helped the company bring down inventory, providing an operational benefit beyond
manufacturing efficiency through lower working-capital requirements.
Working Capital & Cash Flow
• Working capital had remained elevated over the previous 2-3 years, with increasing inventory absorbing a meaningful portion
of EBITDA and consequently limiting EBITDA-to-operating-cash-flow conversion.
• The company reported an improvement in cash flow in the previous year following the reduction in inventory, with
management attributing the improvement partly to faster production cycles and better working-capital management.
• Management expects cash-flow conversion to improve further as the company continues to focus on working-capital turnover
and remains more cautious about incremental working-capital investment.
Product Mix & Applications
• The growth and profitability characteristics of forming machines depend significantly on the end application, rather than being
structurally determined by the forming-machine category itself.
• The company is experimenting with new applications to expand its addressable market, which could provide an additional
growth avenue beyond the existing product and customer base.
• The discussion highlighted the difference between forming and cutting machines, with cutting-machine players currently
demonstrating higher growth and margins, although management indicated that application-specific economics need to be
considered before drawing broader conclusions.

Diversified Engineering Platform
Fastwell Engineering, which commenced manufacturing in 2016, operates across forging and pipe fittings with end-markets spanning
railways, defence, oil & gas, chemicals, fertilisers, pharmaceuticals, dairy and infrastructure. The company supplies directly to
government entities including HAL, ISRO, BHEL, BEL, Mazagaon Dock and Goa Shipyard, while also servicing projects through turnkey
contractors. FY24 revenue stood at ~INR 650 mn with EBITDA margins of 12-13% and PAT of >INR 50 mn.
Railway Division – Key Growth Engine
Fastwell entered the railway segment in March 2024 through its Boisar, Tarapur facility. The division manufactures both exterior
components, including body shells, side walls, roofs and end walls, and interior products such as FRP side walls, ceilings, windows, seats
and berths. Initial orders of INR 250-300 mn have been secured from MCF, RCF and ICF, with management targeting INR 400-500 mn of
railway bookings by December.
RDSO Approval to Enable Scale-Up
The current period is being treated as a pilot phase, with the company working towards entering the RDSO-approved vendor ecosystem.
Management expects this transition to materially increase order opportunities, targeting railway revenue of ~INR 2 bn in FY27 and INR
2.5-3 bn in FY28. The opportunity is supported by India's increasing coach production, including Vande Bharat, Amrit Bharat and AC
MEMUs.
Expanding Railway Product Basket
Beyond conventional coach interiors and exteriors, Fastwell is developing electrical wiper assemblies for locomotives as a replacement
for legacy pneumatic systems. The company is also working with Jindal Fiber and Bajaj Carpets to develop lightweight, fire-resistant
alternatives to PU foam, potentially expanding its addressable railway component portfolio.
Strong Railway Industry Tailwinds
Indian Railways is targeting a significant increase in annual coach production, from ~10,000 to ~16,000 coaches. Additional opportunities
include modular European-standard toilets, priced at ~INR 1.2-1.3 mn per unit, and refurbishment of ~17,000 locomotives. Fastwell is
targeting these opportunities through products such as modular toilets, waterless urinals and FRP driver desks.
Gujarat Aluminium Forging Project
The company is developing a new aluminium forging facility at Umargam, Gujarat, with a total project cost of ~INR 370 mn, comprising
INR 50 mn land, INR 30 mn construction, INR 180 mn machinery and INR 120 mn working capital. The facility will have 12,000 MT annual
capacity and manufacture components ranging from 50 grams to 60 kg. The project is targeting Korean GIS equipment manufacturer
Hyosung, which currently imports a significant proportion of its aluminium forgings from China.
Attractive Project Economics
Management expects the Gujarat plant to generate INR 2 bn revenue at 50% utilisation in Year 1 and potentially reach ~INR 5 bn at full
capacity. EBITDA margins are guided at 18% in Year 1, 22-23% in Year 2 and up to 30% at 90% utilisation. The project also qualifies for
Gujarat government incentives, including interest subsidy and SGST reimbursement, subject to applicable conditions.
Existing Forging Business Provides Base
The existing forging business has installed monthly capacity of 500 MT, currently operating at 250 MT. Full utilisation of the existing
facility can support revenue of INR 1.5 bn. Oil & Gas contributes 30-40% of revenue, while Marine and Defence account for ~20%; exports
contributed 5% in the previous year. New customer additions already contribute 40% of current revenue, supporting customer
diversification.
Revenue & Earnings Guidance
Management expects the existing business to scale to ~INR 0.9-1 bn in FY25 and ~INR 1.2 bn subsequently. Including the railway
opportunity, management is targeting overall revenue of ~INR 2.5-3 bn with absolute EBITDA/PAT of ~INR 150-200 mn in the indicated
growth period. Railway scale-up and the Gujarat forging facility are expected to be the key contributors to the next phase of growth.
Working Capital & Funding
Railway receivables are largely released against R-notes after supply, with ~5% backed by bank guarantees, while PSU customers
generally operate on 45-90 day terms. The working capital cycle stands at ~90-100 days. The company has an INR 150 mn cash-credit
facility, of which INR 110-120 mn is currently utilised, at an average borrowing cost of ~10-11%. Management is also evaluating a private
funding round around December-February.
Key Growth Drivers
The key growth levers are the transition to the RDSO vendor ecosystem, increasing railway coach production, expansion of the railway
product portfolio, ramp-up of the Umargam aluminium forging plant and higher utilisation of existing forging capacity. The combination
of railway, defence, oil & gas and export opportunities provides scope for greater end-market diversification.
Key Monitorables
Key monitorables include RDSO approval and conversion of pilot railway orders into bulk contracts, achievement of the targeted INR 2 bn
railway opportunity in FY27, timely commissioning and customer qualification of the Gujarat facility, utilisation ramp-up and working-
capital requirements. Execution against the company's aggressive revenue and margin guidance will remain critical as multiple expansion
projects scale simultaneously.

Fineotex Chemical Ltd
Outlook: Fineotex Chemical is undergoing a structural transformation from a traditional textile and hygiene chemical producer
into a fully integrated specialty chemical platform operating across four core pillars: Textile Chemicals, Hygiene & FMCG, Oil &
Gas, and Water Treatment. To support long-term revenue diversification, management is shifting its portfolio revenue split from
35% Textile / 65% Oil & Gas & Specialty toward a long-term target of 70% Oil & Gas & Water Treatment and 30% Textile &
Hygiene/FMCG. Sustainable chemistry already represents over 50% of the company's product portfolio.
Oil & Gas Vertical & CCTL Growth Trajectory
Growth in the Oil & Gas division is anchored by Crude Chem Technology (CCTL), operating in the Permian Basin (Texas), where
~65% of US crude production occurs. CCTL is on track to achieve its USD 200 mn revenue target by FY28 backed by strong volume
demand from marquee clients including Baker Hughes, Halliburton, ExxonMobil, and Nalco. Operations are driven by continuous
upstream/midstream production volumes rather than crude price volatility. Operational efficiency and financial discipline have
driven CCTL's EBITDA margins up to 13-15% (from 8-9% at acquisition), with current capacity utilisation at ~65%.
Global Manufacturing Infrastructure & Fungibility
The company operates six manufacturing plants globally: three in India (two in Ambernath and one in Mahape), two in the US
(Midland and Brookshire, Texas) and one in Malaysia, with a total annual capacity of 260,000 tonnes. Manufacturing lines are
100% fungible across product categories (Textile, Hygiene, Water, Oil & Gas). Dedicated reactors run continuously for high-volume
lines, while batch reactors experience minimal downtime (a few hours to 1-2 days) for cleanup, allowing operational utilisation
targets of up to 90%.
Water Treatment & M&A Expansion
Fineotex is aggressively expanding its Water Treatment vertical across specialised subsegments including Data Centres,
Semiconductors, Oil & Gas, Effluent Treatment Plants (ETP), and pure water. Texas serves as a primary hub for data centre water
treatment, complemented by growing demand in India and Saudi Arabia. Management is actively evaluating acquisition targets to
accelerate scale in the water treatment space.
Textile, Hygiene & FMCG Footprint
Fineotex holds a ~15% organised market share in domestic Indian textile chemistry, serving premier clients such as Trident,
Reliance, Donear, Aditya Birla, and Raymond. In the Hygiene division, the company recently onboarded FMCG majors HUL and
P&G, alongside expanding government contracts. On the health product front, its "Aquastrike" product is progressing through
domestic, WHO, and local plant/regulatory approvals for tendering, with concrete updates expected in upcoming quarters.
Financial Performance & Margin Profile
On a consolidated level, international markets account for 77% of revenue and domestic markets 23%. Standalone figures reflect
Plant 1 (Ambernath) alone, as higher-volume 30,000-litre reactors operate under a subsidiary (Plant 2). While Textile and Hygiene
verticals maintain >20% EBITDA margins, overall blended consolidated EBITDA margin guidance is conservatively pegged at 14-
15% to absorb growth investments, client sampling costs, and market share acquisition. The quarterly working capital cycle stays
normalised at 70-80 days.
Balance Sheet, Capital Structure & Governance
Fineotex maintains a pristine, low-leverage balance sheet with minimal debt limited to short-term LCs and working capital.
Fineotex invested USD 14-15 mn in working capital into CCTL, with any future requirement capped at a maximum of USD 4-5 mn
and zero major building capex required to reach the FY28 target. ICRA recently upgraded the company's credit rating to AA-
(Stable). Shareholders have approved a blanket INR 8 bn limit for strategic M&A flexibility, though no active equity fundraise is
currently planned.

Fractal Industries Ltd
Outlook: Management guides for an EBITDA margin of about 20% and a PAT margin of about 15% going forward. ROE has been
temporarily diluted by the IPO capital and is targeted at 15-20% over the long term. Cash flow will be reinvested in inventory and
warehousing until revenue reaches INR 3-4 bn, about 3-4x the current scale.
Financial Performance: Revenue grew from INR 499 mn in FY24 to INR 855 mn in FY25 and INR 898 mn in FY26 (+5.1% YoY). FY26
EBITDA rose 57.3% to INR 175 mn, and EBITDA margin expanded from 8.3% in FY24 to 13.1% in FY25 and 19.5% in FY26, helped by
value engineering and better selling prices. FY26 PAT rose 71.6% to INR 129 mn, with PAT margin up from 4.6% in FY24 to 8.8% in
FY25 and 14.4% in FY26.
Balance Sheet: Net worth increased from INR 82 mn in FY24 to INR 736 mn in FY26. Net debt-to-equity improved from 1.16x to
0.14x, supported by the IPO proceeds and internal accruals. FY26 operating cash flow was INR 41 mn.
Business Model Evolution: The company has moved through three models, each with higher margins than the last:
◦ Outright sale (since 2021): The company supplies e-commerce platforms on a wholesale basis, and the marketplace
owns the inventory.
◦ Pure-play marketplace/licensed brands (since 2024-25): The company runs design, sourcing, production, inventory and
fulfilment end-to-end under licensed marketplace brand names, paying royalties in exchange for higher operating
margins.
◦ D2C own brand: The company recently launched "789", a premium proprietary brand focused on contemporary
apparel and shackets. It is sold through brand-owned sites, social media and major e-commerce platforms.
Manufacturing & Warehousing: The company has 13 manufacturing units with a combined installed capacity of 1.44 mn units a
year, built to US-equivalent quality standards. Seven warehouses run on WMS, which allows orders to ship from the nearest site
and lowers logistics costs.
Closed-Loop Workflow: Operations follow a five-stage cycle: sense (marketplace demand), design (shorter design-to-shelf times),
source and manufacture, store and fulfil, and learn (feeding returns and customer feedback into the next designs).
Returns Management: Return rates across the apparel industry range from 25% to 55%, the high end being fashion items. The
company's return-handling framework limits the net value lost across the return cycle to just 0.5%.
Nested Brands Subsidiary: The company holds 55% of Nested Brands, which handles digital marketing, trading, distribution and
brand promotion across apparel, perfumes and fabrics. The subsidiary is targeting FY27 revenue of INR 100 mn.
Channel Diversification: To reduce customer concentration, the company is onboarding Amazon, Ajio, Nykaa, Flipkart and Tata
CLiQ, and is exploring B2B and B2C exports to the Middle East. It has no immediate plans for physical retail and remains 100%
focused on online channels.
Industry Tailwinds: India's supply chain management market is projected to grow from USD 1,131 mn in 2025 to USD 2,757 mn by
2031, a 16% CAGR. The Indian apparel market is expected to grow from USD 88 bn to USD 117 bn by 2034, a 3.2% CAGR.
Long-Term Potential: The shift from wholesale to licensed brands and its own D2C brand is structurally lifting margins, and a
deleveraged balance sheet supports the next phase of growth. Reaching the INR 3-4 bn revenue goal while holding margins of
about 20% EBITDA and 15% PAT would mean a several-fold increase in earnings.
