Knack Packaging Ltd
Knack Packaging delivered a strong Q1FY27 with revenue of INR 2.62 bn (+41.1% YoY), EBITDA of INR 590 mn (+53% YoY; margin
22.35%, +170 bps) and PAT of INR 305 mn (+47.96% YoY; margin 11.53%). Margin expansion is driven by solar cost savings (~1.15%
contribution from the 11 MW solar farm) and a structural mix shift towards premium pinch-bottom products (21.1% of revenue vs
10% in FY24). Export share is 56.30% across 74 countries, and the new Mexico plant (commercial operations from April 2026) is
running at full capacity on all 5 machines. Installed capacity is set to rise from 45,000 to 70,000 tonnes by October 2027 via a new
owned plant that phases out rented facilities. Management expects ~40% YoY growth to continue in FY27 and Q2 EBITDA margins of
22-23%. Key monitorables are whether ~40% growth holds through the monsoon quarter, margin sustainability, and volume trends
vs gross profit per kg gains.
Revenue Growth & Product Mix
Q1FY27 revenue of INR 2.62 bn grew 41.1% YoY (from INR 1.86 bn), with both domestic and export segments contributing; export
share is 56.30% (up from ~50% in FY24).
Pinch-bottom (a higher-margin premium category) contribution rose from 10% in FY24 to 21.1% of revenue; management says the
mix shift is structural and expects the trajectory to continue.
Knack added 50 new customers in Q1 (an annual run-rate of 100-120); total customers are 2,000+ (1,950 at FY26-end), with
retention of 93.75%. Export countries rose from 71 to 74 (three added in Q1). The top-10 customers contribute ~40-41% of revenue
and the top-15 ~50%; a US customer (Target) is growing very fast under an exclusive contract.
Gross profit per kg improved from INR 85 to INR 100 over recent quarters, attributed to solar cost savings, premium mix shift and
better export realisations.
Volumes: Asked whether volumes are keeping pace with rising gross profit per kg, management did not directly address volume
trends.
Margins & Profitability
Q1FY27 EBITDA grew 53% YoY to INR 590 mn (from INR 386 mn); margin expanded 170 bps to 22.35% (from 20.65%). The 11 MW
solar farm (commissioned in FY25-26) contributed ~1.15% to EBITDA margin directly via electricity cost savings; solar covers 60-70%
of electricity cost (2.1 MW rooftop plus 11 MW farm).
PAT rose 47.96% YoY to INR 305 mn (from INR 206 mn); PAT margin improved to 11.53% from 11.03%. EPS was INR 3.0.
Multi-year build: EBITDA margin 15.38% (FY24), 19.31% (FY25), 20.2% (FY26); PAT margin 6.98%, 9.88%, 10.99% over the same
period.
Raw-material pass-through: 40-50% of raw-material price movement is passed to customers under agreements, with 98-99% pricing
achieved on the production cycle; the company absorbs the balance. Polymers are easily available and no supply issues are
expected.
Capacity Expansion & Mexico
Installed capacity is 45,000 tonnes across one owned and four rented plants; production is targeted at 40,000-42,000 tonnes this
year, up from 36,000 last year.
The company plans to reach 70,000 tonnes by October 2027, with a new owned plant starting production that month; rented
facilities will be phased out during FY28 as the new plant ramps through efficiency milestones of 60%, 70%, 80%, 85% and 90%.
The Mexico facility commenced commercial operations in April 2026, with all five machines commissioned and running at full
capacity, adding a new growth leg alongside the 74-country export footprint.
Balance Sheet & Returns
Debt-to-equity improved to 0.59x from 0.74x; ROE is 37.45% and ROCE 54.73%.
Working capital is held at 86 days, with inventory at 65 days.
Competitive Positioning & Outlook
Management asserts India offers the cheapest pricing globally for textile and specialised packaging, sustaining competitiveness
against Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.
Asked from whom it is gaining share, management did not name competitors or quantify share shifts.
The company runs digital-first, system-driven operations, having invested INR 47.5 mn in systems in 2017 (roughly one year of profit
at the time).

Krishana Phoschem Ltd
Outlook: Krishana Phoschem is focused on expanding domestic fertiliser capacity and reducing import dependence through higher
NPK/DAP capacity, balanced nutrition products and backward integration. The company recently added ~165,000 MT of NPK/DAP
capacity, which management believes can support ~INR 10,000 mn of incremental revenue at optimal utilisation. Management
expects to build on the strong growth trajectory while maintaining high capacity utilisation and leveraging operating efficiencies.
Capacity Expansion & Growth
The company has total fertiliser capacity of ~615,000 MT following the recent expansion. The additional 165,000 MT NPK/DAP
capacity became operational in March 2026 and is expected to support capacity-led revenue growth. Management estimates
potential incremental revenue of ~INR 10,000 mn at optimal utilisation. No major additional capex is planned currently, with focus
remaining on ramping up the expanded capacity.
SSP Business & Raw Material Costs
SSP profitability has been impacted by higher sulphur and sulphuric acid prices. The company has increased SSP MRP from April to
partially offset the cost inflation, while higher government subsidy support is expected to provide further relief. KPL uses
internally produced BRP from low-grade rock phosphate, which provides some cost protection. Management currently expects
SSP EBITDA of ~INR 1,500-1,700 per tonne, subject to the upcoming NBS/subsidy announcement and market conditions.
Backward Integration
KPL has integrated capabilities across BRP, phosphoric acid and sulphuric acid. Internal BRP production currently meets ~20% of
requirements, with the balance sourced through imports. Phosphoric acid capacity is broadly matched to NPK production
requirements. Captive sulphuric acid capacity can meet >75% of requirements at full utilisation; however, current utilisation is
intentionally lower as sulphuric acid from external suppliers such as Birla Copper and Hindustan Zinc is currently available at a
lower cost.
Green Ammonia
The company has secured 70,000 MTPA of green ammonia for 10 years, with supply expected to commence from 1 April 2029,
implying a financial impact from FY30. The long-term fixed-price arrangement is expected to provide greater ammonia supply
security and reduce exposure to volatility in imported grey ammonia prices. Management also expects the government
compensation mechanism to maintain price parity in case grey ammonia prices fall below the contracted green ammonia price.
Import Substitution & Industry Opportunity
Management sees significant opportunity from India's dependence on imported complex fertilisers, with import substitution and
balanced nutrition remaining key structural growth drivers. KPL aims to increase domestic availability of NPK/DAP and other
nutrient products while utilising its existing manufacturing capacity. Even at 100% utilisation, the company's NPK production of
~415,000 MT remains small relative to India's overall fertiliser consumption, providing headroom for future growth.
Distribution & Market Expansion
KPL has a broad distribution network spanning ~11-12 states, with 2,500-3,000+ wholesalers and 30,000-40,000+ retailers.
Management does not currently see a need for aggressive geographic expansion as existing capacity can be absorbed within the
current markets. Once the recently expanded capacity is fully utilised, the company may explore new geographies, products and
value-added opportunities.
Financial Performance & Working Capital
The company has delivered strong growth, with revenue CAGR of ~66% over the last five years and EBITDA margins generally
sustained at ~13-14%. Fertiliser remains a working-capital-intensive business, with management indicating that ~45% of sales
turnover is tied up in current assets. Working capital is largely funded through bank facilities, while limited incremental capex is
expected to support cash generation going forward.
Capex & Capital Allocation
Management clarified that current-year incremental capex is expected to be ≤INR 600 mn, materially lower than the INR 6,000 mn
figure referred to during the Q&A. With the major NPK/DAP expansion already completed, the company intends to focus on
utilising existing capacity and deploying internal accruals toward value-added products, adjacent opportunities and future
expansion.
Taxation
The company has transitioned from the earlier MAT regime to the revised corporate tax regime, resulting in reassessment of
deferred tax assets and liabilities. Management indicated that the corporate tax rate going forward is expected to be ~25%,
subject to any future changes in tax regulations.

Kwick Forensic Solutions Ltd
Outlook: Kwick Forensic Solutions is an end-to-end forensic solutions provider catering primarily to government and law-
enforcement agencies. The company operates across five verticals: forensic science & physical evidence, cyber & digital forensics,
DNA forensics, mobile forensic vehicles and services. With >200 products/solutions, >130 customers and a debt-free balance
sheet, the company is positioned to benefit from increasing government spending and regulatory focus on forensic investigation.
Management targets 30-35% revenue growth going forward.
Business Model & Customer Base
~95% of customers are government entities, including police departments, FSLs, fingerprint bureaus and crime investigation
agencies. Business is predominantly tender-driven through GeM, state e-procurement portals and direct government tenders. The
company provides products ranging from crime-scene kits and forensic equipment to cyber/digital extraction tools, DNA
equipment and mobile forensic laboratories.
Market Opportunity & Regulatory Tailwinds
The company estimates the current annual tender opportunity for its product categories at ~INR 5 bn. The government has
allocated ~INR 300 bn under various schemes for forensic-related infrastructure over the next five years. Mandatory forensic
investigation for offences carrying punishment of >7 years, along with BNS, BNSS and BSA, is expected to support demand for
scientific evidence, digital evidence and chain-of-custody solutions.
Mobile Forensic Vehicles
Mobile forensic vehicles are a key growth driver, with the company converting vehicles into mini forensic laboratories equipped
for crime-scene investigation and evidence collection. Over 1,000 vehicles are targeted across states, of which ~450 have already
been supplied, ~300 of them by the company in some form. The segment contributed ~10% of FY26 revenue and is expected to
reach ~25% of revenue over the current and next financial year.
DNA & Digital Forensics
DNA forensics is a rapidly growing segment, supported by increasing requirements for DNA profiling and evidence preservation.
Cyber & Digital Forensics focuses on extraction, preservation and analysis of data from mobile phones, laptops, hard disks and
other digital devices. Both segments are expected to benefit from the increasing adoption of forensic and digital evidence.
eForensic Suite & Make-in-India
The Android-based eForensic Suite is in the final stages of development, with POCs underway, and is designed to digitally record
evidence collection, analysis and chain of custody. The company has also converted several previously imported products into

Financial Performance

from INR 20 mn to INR 135 mn. EBITDA margin has improved to ~18%. Operating cash flow turned positive at INR 76 mn in FY26
from negative INR 26 mn in FY24, supported by improved receivable collections.
Growth Guidance & Order Flow

operating leverage. The company has seen increasing order sizes, including individual orders of ~INR 110 mn and ~INR 50 mn in
FY26. Management expects further opportunities from larger government projects but does not currently disclose its order book.
Export Opportunity
The company is evaluating African markets for its Make-in-India products, with a market survey planned in October 2026 and local
tie-ups already initiated. Management does not expect material export revenue in FY27 but expects potential contribution from
FY28.
Working Capital & Balance Sheet
The business is working-capital intensive due to H2/Q4-heavy government procurement and execution of larger orders. Current

proceeds supporting working capital requirements and execution of larger orders.
Growth Drivers

Outlook: Founded in 2013, with production commencing in 2015, Lead Reclaim and Rubber Products (LRRPL) has set a revenue
target of INR 1.8 bn by FY29, driven by completed and ongoing capex.
• Management envisions expanding beyond tyre recycling over the next five years to establish a broader circular recycling
group, exploring potential ventures in solar panel and metal recycling.
• LRRPL maintains strong commercial relationships, evidenced by a 99% customer retention rate since inception and direct
vendor supply to major tyre OEMs such as TVS, JK Tyre and CEAT.
• The company's primary business model centres on collecting end-of-life scrap tyres and converting them into reclaimed
rubber, crumb rubber powder, and by-product steel wires.
• Reclaim rubber provides a major economic advantage for tyre and rubber product manufacturers, as virgin rubber prices
hover around INR 200 per kg while reclaim rubber costs ~INR 55-60 per kg.
• Accounting for rubber content technicalities, reclaim rubber delivers over 50% cost savings for buyers and lowers electricity
consumption during rubber compounding.
• Additional revenues are generated by extracting and directly selling steel scrap and bead wires.
• LRRPL has shifted away from merchant third-party exporters toward direct vendor registration with international
manufacturers, increasing direct exports to 20% of revenue.
• LRRPL has grown its core reclaim rubber capacity from 250 MT per month in 2015 to 1,150 MT per month, currently operating
at 60-65% utilisation with a two-month backlog of pending orders.
• The company is actively expanding its manufacturing footprint by adding 950 MT per month of new crumb rubber capacity to
its existing 960 MT per month facility by October.
• Construction is also complete for a 900 MT per month EPDM profile recycling plant using automated Chinese machinery that
will go active by October.
• Furthermore, LRRPL is developing a 60 MT per day tyre input pyrolysis project expected to be operational by September 2025,
producing roughly 750 MT per month of tyre pyrolysis oil and 700 MT per month of recovered carbon black.
• Once fully scaled, revenue is projected to be split evenly with 50% coming from reclaim rubber and 50% from pyrolysis oil.
• To optimise operating margins, LRRPL is addressing electricity expenses, its largest single cost driver, by installing a 1.2 MW
captive solar power plant, which is projected to cut power costs by at least 60%.
• Profitability is further enhanced by securing government licences from MoEF and DGFT to import restricted scrap tyres, which
yield higher gross margins than domestic scrap; management intends to increase its imported raw material share from 30% to
50%.
• The working capital cycle involves payment terms of 15-20 days for domestic raw material sourcing and 45 days for imports,
with customer receivables averaging 45 days under letter of credit or document against payment terms.
• On the regulatory side, LRRPL benefits from Extended Producer Responsibility rules, earning 1.3 EPR credit units with a base
value of INR 2.52 per unit for every kilogram of reclaim rubber sold, while expecting reclaim rubber blend ratios in tyre
manufacturing to increase from 2-7% to 20% over the next two to three years.

Business Model & Positioning
• The company is a leading CNC machine and special purpose machine (SPM) manufacturer based in Hyderabad, with operations
since 1985. It was founded by Mr Lokeshwar Rao, a technocrat and the current Managing Director; the third generation of
promoters (qualified engineers) has now joined the business.
• The business operates across three verticals: machine tools (CNC and SPMs), auto components (where three hot forging lines
are being commissioned for backward integration) and defence (small arms).
• The company has 5,000+ customers across seven countries and has delivered 9,000+ machines in India to date.
• Installed capacity stands at ~1,500 CNC machines per year and 15,000-18,000 small arms per year, both of which are scalable.
Management indicated that existing capacities can support combined revenue of INR 5 bn+.
FY26 Performance & Sanctions Update
• FY26 was described as a year of the "3 Rs": resilience under constraint, rebuilding the operating base and readiness for
reopening.

• Despite this, the CNC division grew ~29%, costs were reduced by more than 10%, EBITDA margin improved to ~18% from ~12.5%
in preceding years, and PAT improved significantly.
• The sanctions were lifted on 30 June 2026 with support from the Ministry of External Affairs; the company was among the first
Indian entities to be delisted. Overseas supply chains have been restored and exports are expected to resume, albeit from a low

• The company has put in place MNC-style compliance policies (with Indian and US legal advisors) to screen prospective
customers and suppliers for sanctions exposure. Management noted that defence and dual-use technology exports will continue

Order Book & Execution

Business and Q1FY27 Performance
LT Foods is a 70+ year-old basmati and specialty rice company. Revenue CAGR is ~17% and PAT CAGR ~18% over the last 5 years.
Q1 revenue grew 26%, gross profit ~19% and EBITDA ~20%. EBITDA margin was ~11.2%.
Basmati and specialty rice is ~84% of business. Organic and food ingredients are ~12%. Ready-to-heat (RTH) and ready-to-cook
(RTC) are a small but growing segment.
Own brands (Daawat and Royal) are 85%+ of business. Royal was acquired in 2007 at ~USD 35 mn and is now ~USD 600 mn.
Geography: US 48%, India 30%, Europe and UK ~12%, Middle East and RoW ~9%.
Gross margin was flat YoY despite higher realisations. Management attributes this to the lower-GP jasmine rice business, which is
consolidated from June 2025 (it was earlier a JV). Excluding that, GP margin improved.
Guidance and Targets
Growth guidance is 11-12% (7-8% volume plus 4-5% value).
EBITDA margin is targeted at ~14% from ~12%, and ROCE at ~23% from ~20%.
The 15% EBITDA aspiration is a 4-5 year target. Near-term margin stays around 11%, with improvement over 2-3 years as loss-
making segments break even.
Excluding the investment-phase segments, basmati and specialty already earns 14%+ EBITDA.
Management says the combined basket of organic, RTH/RTC, UK and Europe can reach 13.5-14% EBITDA.
Segment-Wise Margin Roadmap
UK and Europe: These are in the investment phase. The UK is expected to lose ~USD 2-2.5 mn at EBITDA this year and Europe ~USD
2 mn, with losses continuing through the year.
Organic: It was loss-making last quarter after the restructuring into a CPG model. Year-end EBITDA margin is expected at ~8% and
~10% the year after.
RTH/RTC: revenue is ~INR 2 bn with an investment loss of ~INR 200 mn. Breakeven is expected in about two years at double the
sales, then INR 6-7 bn of revenue in 4-5 years at a ~10% EBITDA margin.
RTH/RTC is ~1.5-2% of the portfolio today, targeted at 4-5% in 4-5 years.
India Demand
India value grew 23% and volume 12.5% in Q1.
Basmati is only ~5% of India's rice consumption, and ~70% of it is still sold loose. The shift to branded products and higher price
points is driving growth.
E-commerce and quick commerce are ~17-18% of India business (6-7% 3-4 years ago). Margins are within 1-2% of general trade.
There are no D2C plans.
India launches include Daawat biryani kits, Thai curry kits and Kapaar rice. In the US, the focus is RTH (rice with lentil, chana or
ghee).
US and Tariffs
The 50% US tariff ran until about February this year and is now 10%.
LT's US import share rose to ~70% during the 50% tariff period because its US base let it keep importing, while peers could not.
Part of the tariff refund was received in Q1, but it is not recognised in P&L. A portion may have to be passed back to customers, so
the accounting treatment is pending.
Middle East
The Middle East is ~5-6% of revenue. Freight is up as much as 10x in some lanes, and transit times are up 30-90 days.
Management could not pass on the higher cost and margin took a slight hit. Working capital also rose.
Exposure is limited, so management says the impact is smaller than for peers.
Raw Material and Inventory
Last year's crop prices rose 20-25% on supply constraints. New-crop paddy is also currently 20-25% higher YoY.
Acreage is up 2-3% and basmati areas are well irrigated, so management expects prices to be broadly stable with 5-6% inflation. It
considers it too early to call, since the crop runs until December.
Inventory is kept at a minimum of 7-8 months. In June it was ~160,000 tonnes of paddy and ~346,000 tonnes of rice (versus
~316,000 tonnes last year).
Permanent cost changes are passed on to consumers, but temporary swings are absorbed through the P&L. No inventory gains are
booked, and inventory is valued at the lower of cost or market.
Long-term pricing is modelled at 4-6% inflation.
Capex
FY27 capex is INR 5+ bn, including doubling US RTH capacity (~USD 15-16 mn), US land and own warehouses (~USD 18-20 mn), an
organic greenfield plant in India (~INR 1.3 bn) and basmati capacity expansion (~INR 600 mn).
Normal capex from FY28 is ~INR 1.7-1.8 bn a year. That is INR 1.8-2 bn for ~10% volume growth, implying ~4.5-5x asset turn.
Paddy-to-rice capacity is ~88-90% utilised, and 8-10% capacity is being added this year.
The return hurdle is ROCE of 20%+, which US investments may not meet.

• NPK selling price increased from around INR 26,000 per tonne to INR 41,000 per tonne from April.
• Current MRP of INR 41,000 per tonne is supported by around INR 20,000 per tonne of government subsidy, taking the total
nutrient value to around INR 61,000 per tonne.
• Management indicated that pricing is adjusted based on input costs, subsidy levels and the required EBITDA level.
Capacity Utilisation Expected to Improve
• Existing facilities achieved around 100% utilisation last year.
• Utilisation has been lower in the current year due to ammonia availability and other temporary constraints.
• Management expects overall utilisation to reach around 90% by the end of FY27.
• For the Dhule plant, management expects initial utilisation of around 40-50%, rising to around 80% in the following year and
potentially above 100% thereafter.
Backward Integration to Support Margins
• The company is strongly backward integrated across key raw materials, including phosphoric acid and sulphuric acid.
• The phosphoric acid plant is expected to meet the company's requirement even at full capacity utilisation.
• Sulphuric acid requirements will be partly sourced externally, including through an agreement with Birla Copper.
• Rock phosphate remains fully dependent on imports from Jordan and Egypt, while ammonia will be sourced through a mix of
domestic and imported supplies.
Raw Material Prices Remain a Key Margin Variable
• Ammonia prices have declined from ~INR 100,000 per tonne to below INR 70,000 per tonne.
• Sulphur prices have not declined materially, creating pressure on input costs.
• Management expects potential government support/subsidy adjustments to offset the impact of higher raw-material costs.
• Management also expects higher nutrient-based subsidy to offset the impact of higher-cost inventory.
Working Capital and Liquidity Are in Place
• Management indicated that the fertiliser industry typically requires working capital equivalent to around 45% of turnover.
• For the FY27 estimated turnover, the company has sanctioned working-capital limits of around INR 12.25 bn.
• The company has also received more than INR 3 bn through preferential allotment, providing additional liquidity for working
capital and capex requirements.
Product Mix to Remain Focused on EBITDA
• NPK 20:20:0:13 has historically been an important product for the company.
• Management stated that product mix can change depending on raw-material availability and EBITDA margins.
• The company shifted toward variants requiring less ammonia during periods of limited ammonia availability and is now
focusing on products based on EBITDA contribution.

Manaksia Coated Metals & Industries Ltd
Manaksia Coated Metals & Industries manufactures value-added coated steel products (Aluzinc coated steel and pre-painted steel
coils) at its port-based facility in Kutch, Gujarat, located ~40-60 km from Mundra and Kandla ports. Under Phase 1, the galvanising
line was upgraded to Aluzinc and expanded from 132,000 MTPA to 180,000 MTPA in January 2026, while the new colour coating line
(raising pre-painted capacity from 86,000 MTPA to 236,000 MTPA) and a 7 MW captive solar plant (savings of ~INR 70 mn per
annum) are set to commission next month. Phase 2 involves INR 3.5 bn of capex for a 360,000 MTPA cold rolling complex (INR 2 bn)
and a second 180,000 MTPA Aluzinc line (INR 1.5 bn), to be completed in FY28, with full capacity available by FY29. Management
targets 3x volumes (over 300,000 MT) and over 3x revenue by FY29 versus FY26 levels of ~100,400 MT and INR 9 bn, with EBITDA
growing by more than 3x. EBITDA per tonne doubled from INR 5,000 to INR 10,000 in Q1FY27, while exports rose to ~68-70% of
revenue and the order book stands at over INR 4.2 bn. The key factors to monitor are commissioning and ramp-up of the new
colour coating line, Phase 2 execution and funding, the export-domestic mix, sustainability of EBITDA/tonne and working capital
reduction from backward integration.
Business Model & Positioning
• The company has a legacy of over 30 years in manufacturing and is primarily engaged in value-added coated steel products,
supplied pan-India and to export markets.
• Value chain: The company buys cold-rolled (CR) steel and coats it with an aluminium-zinc alloy to produce Aluzinc coated steel,
which is either sold as is or further value-added by painting into pre-painted Aluzinc coated steel.
• Aluzinc coated steel offers ~3x the corrosion resistance of galvanised steel and commands a premium in the market.
• The company focuses on extreme customisation (thicknesses, widths, coatings and performance guarantees), with USPs of small
MOQs, just-in-time delivery and specialised requirements that large primary steel producers focused on volumes cannot offer.
• ~90% of sales are direct to OEMs (B2B), across pharma clean rooms, HVAC, refrigeration, metal wall and ceiling, drywall
partitions, bus bodies and insulated sandwich panels, rather than the trade segment.
• The port-based location enables efficient logistics, raw material imports, exports and coastal shipping to southern states such as
Kerala and Tamil Nadu at costs potentially lower than mills in Maharashtra.
• Distribution footprint includes a service centre in Hyderabad, stockyards in Jammu, Cochin, Bhopal and Guwahati, and
branch/marketing offices across India, supported by an experienced team with 20-30 years in the steel industry.
Phase 1 Expansion: Capacity & Technology Upgrade
• Metal Coating: In January 2026 (FY26), the galvanising line was upgraded from 132,000 MTPA to 180,000 MTPA along with a
technology conversion from regular galvanising to Aluzinc coating.
• Pre-Painted Steel: Capacity of 86,000 MTPA is running at very high utilisation; the new colour coating line will raise capacity 2.7x
to 236,000 MTPA and is set to commission next month (management declined to comment on its current status, as it is price-
sensitive information).
• The new colour coating line will enable specialised finishes such as SMP, SDP and PVDF, demanded by European customers and
Indian OEMs requiring 20-30 year warranties, as well as three-colour printed and hot lamination products, which only 1-2 lines
in India currently produce.
• Captive Solar: A 7 MW plant, targeted to commission next month along with the colour coating line, will convert over 55% of
plant energy requirements to renewable energy and generate power cost savings of ~INR 70 mn per annum from day one.
• All Phase 1 projects have been funded and are nearing completion.
Phase 2 Expansion: Backward Integration

• Total Phase 2 capex is INR 3.5 bn, to be funded through a balanced mix of equity, internal accruals and debt.
• Cold rolling complex: 360,000 MTPA capacity at an estimated capex of INR 2 bn, comprising a slitter, pickling line, acid
regeneration plant, rewinding line and cold rolling mill; described as the most critical capex for the company.
• Second Aluzinc Line: Capex of INR 1.5 bn, doubling metal coating capacity from 180,000 MTPA to 360,000 MTPA to match the
cold rolling capacity and support the expanded colour coating line in-house.
• The new Aluzinc line is being designed with an option for zinc-magnesium (ZAM) coating, which offers ~2x the corrosion
resistance of Aluzinc and is increasingly used in the solar/photovoltaic industry; this is still work in progress.
• The shift from CR steel (a customised product) to hot-rolled (HR) coil (a commoditised product) cuts lead times from 45-60 days
(domestic) and 90+ days (imports) for CR to ~2 weeks (domestic) and 30-45 days (imports) for HR, drastically reducing raw
material inventory.
• Raw material SKUs are expected to fall from over 1,000 to only 4-5 HR SKUs, with all thicknesses and widths produced in-house.
• The conversion cost currently paid to suppliers is INR 4,500-5,000 per tonne, versus an estimated INR 3,000-3,500 per tonne in-
house, adding ~INR 1,500-2,000 per tonne to EBITDA.
• Backward integration is expected to shrink working capital and inventory ageing; Phase 2 projects are targeted for completion in
FY28, with full capacities available by FY29.
Volume, Revenue & Margin Outlook
• FY26 production and sales stood at ~100,400 MT with revenue of ~INR 9 bn; historical volume CAGR has been over 12%.
• FY29 target: over 300,000 MT of sales (3x FY26), revenue of over 3x FY26 and EBITDA growth of far more than 3x.
• The share of pre-painted steel in the mix has increased consistently from 2023 to 2026 despite rising volumes.
• Blended EBITDA/tonne has increased from INR 5,000 to INR 10,000 in Q1FY27; management believes this is sustainable and sees
potential for a further 10-15% uplift from better utilisation, niche OEM/export products and solar power savings.
• EBITDA margins have moved from mid-single digits to early double digits over the last 4-5 years; management believes ~13%
EBITDA margin is not far-fetched with a focus on niche, value-added products.
• Ramp-Up: The new colour coating line is expected to take ~1 quarter to stabilise, with no material change to the earlier
indication of 50-55% utilisation by FY27 exit; the Aluzinc line is at 70-75% utilisation, targeting 80-85% in the coming quarter.
Export vs Domestic Mix & Demand
• Export share has grown from 21% to over 68% in FY26 and is currently at a ~70% revenue run-rate; a participant noted ~87% of
the current order book is exports.
• With capacity increasing ~3x over the next 12-18 months, the mix is expected to become more balanced at ~55-60% exports.
• Export EBITDA has been higher at ~INR 11,000-11,500 per tonne, versus ~INR 8,000-8,500 per tonne in the domestic market,
though this is dynamic and depends on demand-supply.
• The export focus so far was driven by capacity constraints (demand has been ~2x capacity); management believes domestic
OEM and niche customers can deliver similar margins.
• The India-EU FTA is expected to be favourable, providing tariff-free access and larger quota allocation for Indian value-added
steel.
• Domestic demand drivers include urbanisation, infrastructure (airports, metros, bullet trains, railway overhaul), FMCG growth
and rising consumption of appliances, cars and consumer durables, with steel consumption growing in double digits.
• India's addressable market for Aluzinc and pre-painted steel is ~4 mn tonnes, growing at 11-12% per annum, excluding export
opportunities.
Balance Sheet & Funding
• The company is A-rated by credit agencies and has reduced net debt, keeping leverage and borrowing costs in control.
• The order book stands at over INR 4.2 bn across domestic and export customers and is growing, supporting utilisation of new
capacities.
• Interest cost appears high relative to gross debt (~INR 1.5 bn debt vs ~INR 300 mn annual interest, as highlighted by a
participant) due to non-fund-based limits (letters of credit) used for domestic and imported raw material procurement.
• Management clarified that the company is a standalone entity with its own shareholding and management, unrelated to any
other company with similar expansion plans.

Business Profile & Earnings Mix
• Master Trust has a diversified business model spanning retail broking, proprietary trading, NBFC and PMS, with a client base of
~400,000 and ~30,000-35,000 monthly active clients.
• Proprietary trading and broking are the key earnings drivers, historically contributing ~40% and ~60% of PBT, respectively, with
the former cushioning volatility in broking revenues.

Broking Business & Regulatory Impact
• Master Trust has ~0.25% market share in cash equities and ~1.5% in equity derivatives, with brokerage revenue split across
derivatives (50%), cash equities (40%) and commodities (10%).

MTF & Funding

Technology-Led Growth

Mutual Fund Business Deferred

Store Expansion
Store count increased to 98 from 80 stores at the time of IPO listing in April 2026; management targets 150 stores by FY27-end.

Expansion outside Gujarat is planned only after reaching INR 6,000-7,000 mn revenue within Gujarat.
COCO Economics
COCO stores are company-operated and require approximately INR 20-25 mn capex depending on store size.
A mature COCO store can generate ~INR 20-25 mn of monthly revenue, with a 6-7% operating margin and ~5% net profit margin.
COCO currently contributes ~60% of revenue, while FOFO contributes ~40%; management intends to increase the COCO mix given

FOFO Model
Under FOFO, franchisees operate the stores while Mehul Telecom supplies inventory against a deposit and earns around 2-3%
revenue-linked margin/royalty.
Franchisees are incentivised through higher margins of around 8-10%, alongside quicker access to inventory and sales support.
Inventory is recorded in the company's books but is largely backed by franchisee deposits, limiting the company's working-capital
requirement.
Growth Outlook

purchases from brands enable better procurement economics.
This business contributes around 25-30% of revenue and carries relatively healthier margins than standard branded-phone sales.
Strong social-media reach of 1.1 mn followers is used to drive customer footfall and monetise such inventory.
Working Capital
Management indicated that FOFO expansion requires limited incremental working capital as inventory is supplied against
franchisee deposits.
For COCO stores, inventory requirement is the key working-capital component; the company typically receives 8-10 days of
supplier credit.
Management expects to remain largely debt-free, with no major working-capital funding requirement up to the targeted Gujarat
revenue scale.
Geographic Strategy
Gujarat remains the immediate growth market, with management estimating the state's mobile/accessories market at around INR
20,000 mn.
The company currently generates ~INR 250-300 mn of monthly revenue from Gujarat and intends to scale significantly before
pursuing a pan-India expansion.
Recent COCO additions include two stores in Ahmedabad, with further expansion planned across Gujarat.

Business Model

focus area.
Obsolescence Management
• Five semiconductor products have been submitted and are under evaluation, with supplies of three parts already made.
• The business has generated ~INR 100 mn so far, with further inquiries and a likely order position in about four tenders. Each

their own customers, with a signed agreement imminent.

not a JV. The first chip is still about 2-2.5 months away, after which the first delivery will serve as a showcase case study.

• The company has continuous DPSU orders across LCA, radar identification systems, thermal imaging cameras and seeker

Working Capital and Margins
• Trade receivables of INR 370 mn against customer advances of INR 250 mn give unusually low net receivables for a defence
business, helped by advances from a major customer, Apollo Micro Systems.
• The company is confident of holding margins despite steel and freight inflation, since products are customised rather than
high-volume standard parts, and the global memory shortage has limited impact given small order quantities.
• Order execution typically runs 120-180 days, with import-led component lead times of 25-50 weeks making the business
working-capital-intensive, in line with the industry.
• Guidance & View: The company maintained full-year revenue guidance of ~INR 2 bn, with H1 at ~INR 1 bn, build-to-spec
revenue of INR 200-250 mn in FY27, and EBITDA margins of 27-35% for build-to-spec versus 16-18% for build-to-print. The

MMP Industries Ltd
MMP Industries has built a diversified aluminium portfolio across aluminium powders, electrical conductors/cables and
aluminium foil, with the group increasingly focused on higher-growth electrical applications. The company generated revenue of
~INR 8.5 bn in the previous year, including ~INR 4.5 bn from the core powder business, which management expects to grow at a
minimum of 8% annually, with margins of ~11-12%. Management's medium-term growth strategy is increasingly dependent on
newer electrical businesses rather than the mature powder and foil segments.
Electrical Segment to Become the Key Growth Engine
• The company is expanding aggressively across the electrical value chain through LT cables, aluminium wire rod, conductors
and composite silicon insulators. MMP Cables has established 18,000 TPA wire-rod capacity, with the majority expected to be
consumed internally, while LT cable capacity is being expanded from the existing 100 TPA to 600 TPA, including a new 500 TPA
facility expected to commence production in H2FY27. LT cable revenue is expected at around INR 150-180 mn in the current
year, with management indicating potential to reach approximately INR 500 mn next year.
New Businesses Provide Significant Medium-Term Revenue Upside
• MMP Electricals is developing composite silicon insulators, with product approvals and customer audits at an advanced stage.
The company is also evaluating further downstream opportunities such as aluminium forging, although these remain at an
early stage. Management indicated that the major growth over the next three years is expected from insulators, cables, wire
rod and conductors, while the mature foil business is already operating at relatively high utilisation and is unlikely to be the
primary growth driver.
Capacity Utilisation Provides Operating Leverage
• Current utilisation remains relatively high in the established businesses, with the powder division at ~80-85% and foil at ~75%,
while the conductor division is operating at around 45-50% utilisation, leaving room for volume growth without proportionate
near-term capacity additions. The powder business is also shifting towards AAC powder, which management identified as the
fastest-growing and more margin-accretive part of the portfolio, supported by rising exports and a record export order book
across multiple geographies.
Integrated Manufacturing & Downstream Expansion to Improve Economics
• The company is increasing vertical integration by manufacturing aluminium wire rod internally for its conductor business,
while the larger LT cable capacity is being developed under MMP Cables. The use of recycled aluminium is expected to be
particularly relevant for wire rod, unlike powder applications where purity requirements favour primary aluminium. With
electrical demand supported by renewable energy, EVs and broader infrastructure spending, management expects the newer
businesses to materially increase the contribution of higher-value products and drive the group's medium-term revenue
expansion.

Outlook: The company is focused on scaling its AI-native, outcome-led advertising platform across India, emerging markets and
developed markets. Management expects growth to be driven by organic expansion, increasing cross-sell across its full-funnel
platform, premiumisation into CTV/streaming/Apple/digital OOH, AI-native product development and selective M&A. The
company is targeting a 30% growth framework with ~20% EBITDA margins, while international expansion and proprietary
technology remain key strategic priorities.
AI-Native Ad-Tech Platform
• Mobavenue positions itself as an AI-native advertising and consumer growth platform, helping brands identify the right
customers, reach them and drive measurable business outcomes.
• The platform is built around three pillars: Intelligence, Intent and Impact, with a focus on outcomes rather than impressions
or clicks.
• The company was established in 2017 and listed on the BSE in 2025; it currently serves 155 brands across 12 countries with
200+ employees.
• Its seven proprietary platforms collectively reach 2.6 bn devices and process ~1.3 bn consumer signals per day.
• The company raised ~INR 500 mn in February 2026 to fund global expansion, technology investments and potential inorganic
opportunities.
Large Open Digital Opportunity
• Mobavenue targets the fragmented digital advertising ecosystem outside major walled gardens such as Meta and Google.
• The company aims to unify apps, websites, gaming, CTV/OTT, OEMs and digital OOH through a single AI-driven platform.
• Management highlighted India's digital advertising market at ~INR 1,370 bn, with digital advertising growing at ~19% CAGR.
• The platform seeks to address fragmentation, limited transparency, inefficient targeting and inventory bias in the open
digital ecosystem.
Full-Funnel A3 Framework
• Mobavenue's platform covers the complete customer journey across Awareness, Acquisition and Activation.
• Awareness: PRIZMX and DiscoverX target audiences across CTV, mobile, OTT, websites and digital billboards.
• Acquisition: SearchX, PiX, OrbitX and AmplifyX focus on customer acquisition across search, social, mobile and partner-led
channels.
• Activation: ResearchX and PiX support remarketing, retargeting and retention.
• Management sees significant cross-sell and upsell potential by expanding existing clients across the three stages.
Outcome-Based Business Model
• Mobavenue follows an "Outcomes as a Service" model, where clients pay based on predefined and verified outcomes such
as installs, registrations, leads, add-to-cart and purchases.
• The company does not charge traditional software licence fees; technology is embedded within the outcome-based pricing
model.
• 97% of revenue comes from the outcome-led model, while 73.9% of FY26 revenue was generated from direct clients.
• Management believes the model provides alignment between customer spending and measurable business outcomes.
Proprietary Neural Engine
• The platform handles around 40-50 bn ad opportunities per day and processes ~1.3 bn signals per day globally.
• Response time is stated at <15 milliseconds, with models and data retrained hourly using ~50 TB of data.
• The Neural Engine combines neural networks, statistical models and machine learning to identify consumer behaviour,
intent and appropriate advertising opportunities.
• AI-led workflows have reduced campaign launch time to <5 minutes, according to management.
• Technology is fully proprietary and built internally without third-party white-label solutions.
Asset-Light Technology Model
• Mobavenue does not own media inventory or provide minimum guarantees to media owners.
• Inventory is purchased in real time based on expected outcomes, making the model asset-light and inventory agnostic.
• Management highlighted that the platform prioritises expected customer outcomes rather than specific media inventory.
• The company is also developing AI-native workflows and agentic AI across its modular platform.
Strong Growth in Q1FY27
• Q1FY27 outcome volumes increased 57.3% YoY to 14.16 Mn, while revenue per outcome increased 11% YoY to INR 49.94.
• Outcome-based revenue increased 74.6% YoY to INR 707 Mn, driven by both higher volumes and revenue per outcome.
• FY26 revenue stood at INR 2,185 Mn, EBITDA at INR 454 Mn and PAT at INR 293 Mn.
• FY26 EBITDA margin stood at 20.8%, while PAT margin was 13.4%.
• Q1FY27 revenue increased 56.9% YoY to INR 728 Mn, EBITDA grew 77% YoY to INR 154 Mn, and PAT increased 95% YoY to
INR 117 Mn.
• EBITDA margin expanded to 21.2%, while PAT margin reached 16.1%, indicating operating leverage.
• International markets contributed 20.7% of Q1FY27 revenue, across 12 countries.

Moneyboxx Finance Ltd
Moneyboxx is pivoting from a single-product MSME lender to a multi-engine platform with four distinct verticals: secured MSME
(LAP), livestock/dairy finance, rooftop solar and digital lending. The past 18 months were difficult, with AUM stagnation, stress
driven by MFI guardrails and a large ARC clean-up of the legacy unsecured book. However, the company has used this period to
fundamentally reshape its underwriting standards, build partnership-led origination channels (Akshayakalpa, Loom Solar and
Bachatt) and secure FLDG/guarantee-backed structures. AUM stands at ~INR 8.3 bn, with 69% secured by mortgage, and GNPA has
dropped to 0.73% following the ARC transaction. The next few quarters will be about proving that the new engines can deliver
disbursement and AUM growth.
Business Model: Four Growth Engines
• Secured MSME (LAP): The core engine, with ticket sizes of INR 0.8-3 mn (average INR 0.75 mn), a 7-8 year tenor and 22-23%
yield. It is a branch-led model, with opex expected at ~8% at scale once AUM doubles from here.
• Livestock/Dairy Finance: INR 16 bn has been disbursed cumulatively. Under a new partnership with Akshayakalpa (India's first
certified organic dairy, ~INR 10 bn revenue, backed by BII and Rabo Foundation), Akshayakalpa provides leads and transfers
funds for collection, backed by FLDG, with zero sales cost and near-zero collection cost. The average ticket is INR 0.25 mn, with a
~28-month tenor and yield of 26-27% (internal) / 22-23% (partner).
• Rooftop Solar: A partnership with Loom Solar (~INR 10 bn company) is disbursing ~INR 50 mn per month with no sales team,
backed by a 10% second-loss guarantee from Shell Foundation; an MOU has also been signed with SIDBI for lending. The
average ticket is INR 0.45 mn, with a 4-year tenor, yield of 23%+ and opex of 2-3%. The book has reached INR 100 mn of AUM,
and an INR 1 bn term sheet has been received. The segment helps offset weak Q1 seasonality.
• Digital Lending: A partnership with Bachatt (the country's largest small-savings platform, backed by Accel, Info Edge and
Lightspeed, with 2.5 mn customers) started in September 2026. The average ticket is INR 50,000, with a 3-12 month tenor and
yield of >36% net of credit cost, backed by 5% FLDG.
AUM & Asset Quality
• AUM is ~INR 8.3 bn, down from the peak due to the ARC transaction and a deliberate stop on unsecured re-lending. 69% of the
portfolio is secured by mortgage and 5% by FLDG.
• ARC Transaction: INR 1+ bn of legacy stressed assets (secured and unsecured) were sold at a ~50% take rate. Recovery efforts
have been aggressive, with 1,600 warrants issued in under three months and 8,000 Section 138 cases filed between October and
March.
• GNPA improved from 3.59% (March 2026) to 0.73% (June 2026), largely driven by the ARC sale. Underwriting standards for the
new book have been significantly tightened: a 650+ CIBIL score cut-off, no new-to-credit or low-score borrowers, and no secured
loans below INR 0.5 mn. Collateralised houses are worth INR 1.5-2+ mn.
• FY26 credit cost was 3.32%, against a medium-term target of <2%; FY27 is realistically expected at 2-3% as some legacy pain
lingers.
Disbursement & Partnership Ramp-Up
• Partnership-led disbursements are targeted at INR 400 mn per month through the four partnership channels alone, entering
Q3FY27.
• Loom Solar disbursements have already reached ~INR 200 mn in total. The Akshayakalpa and Bachatt partnerships started in
September 2026, with encouraging early traction.
• Additional EPC partners are being onboarded for solar (currently 90:10 Loom Solar versus others) to diversify.
Liquidity & Capital
• Liquidity remains strong, and CRAR is adequate. The company recently raised funds through an NCD issue, and further
fundraising is planned.
• The company has raised funds continuously over seven years and expects no challenges on the capital front.
Guidance
• No specific revenue/AUM guidance was given. The company expects disbursements to pick up very significantly in the coming
months, driven by the four partnership engines.
• Credit cost is targeted at <2% over the medium term (FY27 could be 2-3%), and no further major ARC-type pain is expected.

M-Safe Equipments Ltd
Outlook: M-Safe Equipments is pursuing an integrated manufacturing, sales and rental model for aluminium and steel scaffolding,

fragmented scaffolding industry and entering the aluminium formwork segment. It has reiterated revenue growth guidance of 50-

additions.
Business Model & Rental
The company manufactures, sells and rents aluminium and steel scaffolding, with rental contributing ~46% of total revenue and
sales contributing a similar proportion. Aluminium scaffolding generates a rental yield of ~60-66% with an economic life of 5-6
years, while steel scaffolding generates ~32-38% yield with a 15-20 year economic life. Rental and sales are expected to remain
broadly at a 50:50 mix. Around 95-98% of products are standardised, allowing redeployment across projects.
Capacity Expansion
Aluminium scaffolding and ladder capacity is being expanded from 1.5 mn kg to 2.5 mn kg, with the new facility expected to be
ready by May 2027. Steel scaffolding capacity has increased from 3 mn kg at the time of IPO to 6.285 mn kg and is planned to
reach 9 mn kg. The company believes the planned capacity provides sufficient room for growth over the next 2-3 years.
Aluminium Formwork
The company is entering the aluminium formwork segment, with production expected to commence in October 2026. The initial
facility has a capacity of ~500 tonnes per month, while substantially higher capacity is planned at the upcoming owned facility. The
company intends to introduce a rental model in a segment that is currently predominantly sale-based. Customer overlap with the
existing scaffolding business is expected to support cross-selling, although revenue contribution in FY27 is likely to remain limited
due to a 4-6 month order execution cycle.
Revenue Mix & Growth
FY26 revenue stood at ~INR 1,040 mn, including ~INR 800 mn from aluminium scaffolding and ~INR 140 mn from steel scaffolding.
For FY27, the company expects aluminium scaffolding revenue to reach ~INR 1,100 mn and steel scaffolding revenue to increase
to ~INR 400 mn, while formwork contribution is expected to remain small initially. The company has historically delivered ~51%
revenue CAGR since inception and reiterated 50-70% revenue growth guidance.
Market Share & Competitive Positioning

Margins & Operating Leverage
The company indicated current PAT margins of ~23%, while steel scaffolding carries a lower margin of ~5% and aluminium

Capex & Debt
The company expects to incur additional debt during the current year as IPO proceeds are insufficient to fully fund land and
machinery requirements. Continuous investment in scaffolding inventory is also required to support growth, with the company

expected to be funded primarily through debt in the near term.
Growth Drivers
Growth is expected to be driven by market-share gains in aluminium scaffolding, rapid scaling of steel scaffolding, entry into
aluminium formwork, expansion of the warehouse network and increasing penetration among multi-location contractors. Rising
infrastructure activity across data centres, semiconductor plants, airports, bullet train stations and other construction projects
provides additional demand opportunities.

My Mudra Fincorp Ltd
Overview: My Mudra is positioning itself as a capital-light, phygital corporate DSA platform, with the strategy centred on
expanding its distribution network, increasing in-house sourcing and diversifying into adjacent financial products. Management
remains focused on building a broader customer ecosystem and increasing revenue per customer, while continuing to operate
without taking direct lending/credit risk.
Branch expansion remains a key growth lever: The company is adding branches across Tier-2/3 and emerging markets, where
rentals and employee costs are relatively lower. Management believes this can gradually improve branch-level profitability.
Franchise network continues to scale: New franchisees are being added regularly, with a focus on experienced ex-bankers and
financial professionals. The company intends to train and nurture these partners to build a wider distribution ecosystem.
Greater focus on owned distribution: Management is working towards increasing the proportion of in-house branches, employees
and call centres, which should provide better control over customer acquisition and economics.
Reducing sub-DSA dependence: Historically, a large portion of commissions was shared with sub-DSAs. The longer-term objective
is to internalise more sourcing, potentially improving the economics of the business.
Gold loans are a near-term addition: Management is preparing to launch gold loan distribution, with an ambition to leverage its
existing network and eventually build a pan-India presence.
Mutual funds as a recurring product: The company sees mutual fund distribution as an important long-term, recurring revenue
opportunity, initially targeting its existing customer base and subsequently new customers.
Cross-selling is becoming more important: Management highlighted the ability to offer credit cards, insurance and other products
to the same customer, increasing the revenue generated per relationship rather than relying only on new customer acquisition.
MSME finance is a strategic opportunity: The partnership with UGRO Financial for solar/green MSME financing is being used as an
entry point into the broader MSME segment. Management intends to expand gradually into other sectors rather than pursuing
aggressive diversification.
Focus on underserved markets: Management sees considerable opportunity outside major metros, where credit awareness and
formal financial penetration remain relatively low. The company believes its physical presence can help bridge this gap.
Phygital model remains central: While technology is important for efficiency and customer reach, management does not see a
purely digital model as sufficient. It believes physical distribution combined with technology will be the more effective model for
Bharat.
No direct credit risk: My Mudra continues to operate as an intermediary between customers and lenders. Banks/NBFCs take the
lending and default risk, allowing My Mudra to remain relatively asset-light.
Strong lender ecosystem: The company works with a broad base of banks and NBFCs, allowing it to match customers with
different lenders/products depending on their requirements and credit profile.
Approval rates vary by geography: Management noted that approval rates are better in more financially aware/tech-savvy
markets, while emerging markets face challenges around credit awareness and understanding of CIBIL/credit behaviour.
Long-term industry opportunity remains favourable: Management is structurally bullish on India's credit penetration, supported
by urbanisation, entrepreneurship, housing demand, rising financialisation and increasing use of formal credit.
Overall takeaway: The key theme is "build the distribution first, then monetise the customer through multiple products."
Branch/franchise expansion, higher in-house sourcing and cross-selling could be the main drivers of the company's next phase of
growth.

Outlook: Nanta is targeting ≥30% FY27 revenue growth, with robotics & AI expected to grow ~50% and drive a favourable revenue

automation.
Large-scale deployments are still developing in India, while international customers are adopting robotics at a faster pace.
Cleaning robots currently see the strongest traction, particularly across manufacturing, pharma, airports and hospitality.
Hospitality and warehousing are emerging as key growth verticals, with defence also expected to become meaningful over the
medium term.
POC Conversion Remains Strong
The company conducts paid POCs, which helps filter customers with genuine implementation intent.
Management indicated an ~85% POC-to-order conversion rate.
Three Indian customers have already moved into large-scale implementation.
More than 15 customers have completed POCs and deployed initial robots, and are currently evaluating feasibility and ROI.
Management expects potential conversion from these customers into larger orders by end-FY27 or early FY28.
Domestic Manufacturing Roadmap
Nanta currently relies on external manufacturers, with key robot components such as batteries, chips, actuators and motors

Elderly Care Still Early in India
Elderly-care robotics is more commercially developed in overseas markets, while adoption in India remains at an early stage due
to the relatively higher cost of robots versus human caregivers.
Potential applications include companionship, surveillance, security and routine assistance for elderly individuals.
Management sees future potential through home healthcare providers integrating robotics with human-led services.
International markets, including the US and Dubai, are already seeing more tangible elderly-care opportunities.
Order Book and Execution
The order book stood at ~INR 450 mn as of March, with around INR 300-350 mn of orders already publicly disclosed, largely
related to robotics and AI.

Differentiation through Integration
Nanta's proposition is not limited to supplying robots; its key capability lies in robot design, software/AI integration and customer-

Neetu Yoshi Ltd
The company is targeting revenue of INR 2 bn in FY27 and INR 3.5 bn in FY28, driven by the ramp-up of its newly commissioned
facility, higher utilisation of existing capacities and an expanding railway product portfolio. The company's focus on larger
components and complete assemblies, supported by 20-25 products under approval, provides scope for improved scale and
product diversification. PAT margins are targeted at around 25%, with a debt-free balance sheet and internal accruals expected to
support future expansion. Key monitorables include execution of the revenue guidance, timely product approvals and maintaining
quality and working capital discipline during the scale-up.
Revenue Growth & Management Guidance
• The company is targeting revenue of INR 2 bn in FY27, supported by the ramp-up of its new manufacturing facility and higher
production at existing facilities.
• Revenue is expected to increase to INR 3.5 bn in FY28, driven by capacity utilisation, new product approvals and an expanding
portfolio of railway components.
• Revenue contribution from the new facility is expected to commence meaningfully in H2FY27, alongside a gradual increase in
production at the existing facilities. The second half is expected to witness a sharper growth trajectory than H1.
• No material seasonality: Business performance is largely expected to follow a gradual growth trajectory, with April typically
witnessing relatively lower activity. H1FY27 has been better than the corresponding period in the previous year.
Capacity Expansion & New Facility
• The recently commissioned facility enables manufacturing of larger components weighing up to 1,000 kg, compared with the
earlier facility's capability of handling components weighing up to 100 kg.
• The new facility is expected to generate revenue of around INR 600 mn in the remaining part of FY27, with its full-year revenue
potential estimated at approximately INR 2 bn.
• The facility has commenced production and secured sufficient orders to support the targeted ramp-up. Revenue contribution
in H2FY27 is expected to reflect approximately 50% utilisation of the facility's capacity.
• The original facility, with revenue capacity of approximately INR 1 bn, is operating at 90-95% efficiency. The additional capacity
created through the previous expansion, estimated at INR 500-600 mn, is also being progressively utilised.
• With capacity and orders in place, the key operational priority is to ramp up production while maintaining product quality and
delivery schedules.
Margins & Cost Competitiveness
• The company is targeting PAT margins of approximately 25% over the next 2-3 years, supported by cost efficiencies, product
mix and a debt-free balance sheet.
• The company expects margins to remain broadly similar as new products are introduced, while indicating a potential margin
range of 31-33% for its evolving product portfolio. The timing and product-level applicability of this target were not specified.
• Lower power costs in Uttarakhand, proximity to sand suppliers and access to railway scrap provide cost advantages. The
company also benefits from tax incentives available under Section 115BAB.
• Railway tenders include a price variation clause (PVC), allowing changes in prevailing metal prices to be factored into billing.
Scrap prices typically fluctuate by INR 3-4 per unit, according to the prevailing market scenario.
Product Approvals & Portfolio Expansion
• The company currently supplies over 70 product lines to the railway sector, including components for wagons, coaches and
tracks. Product-specific RDSO, company or grade approvals determine the eligibility to supply.
• Applications have been submitted for approximately 20-25 additional products, primarily larger components that can support
the transition from individual components to complete assemblies.
• The company expects to receive approximately 1-3 product approvals every month, supporting progressive portfolio
expansion.
• The company is moving beyond smaller components towards manufacturing complete assemblies, including couplers and
bogies. Existing capabilities across machining, fabrication and larger-component manufacturing provide the foundation for this
transition.
• The pipeline includes locomotive components, track products such as switches and crossings, and new-generation wagon
components. Product development is being prioritised based on infrastructure compatibility and commercial potential.
Bogie Manufacturing & Integrated Solutions
• The new facility supports the manufacture of larger components and the assembly of complete bogies, marking an expansion
beyond the company's traditional component-focused business.
• The facility could manufacture approximately 500 bogies per week, with an indicative realisation of INR 0.2-0.3 mn per bogie.
However, the facility is not exclusively dedicated to bogies and can manufacture multiple products within its capabilities.
• Most metal components are expected to be manufactured in-house, while spring and rubber components will be procured
externally. The stated procurement cost for these components is approximately INR 35,000-40,000 per bogie.
• The strategic objective is to combine smaller components, larger fabricated parts and assembly capabilities to supply complete
railway systems rather than individual components.

Nelcast Ltd
Business
• Nelcast is a ferrous foundry making grey and ductile iron castings for CVs, tractors, off-highway, PVs and railways. Castings typically
weigh 70-200 kg for both domestic and export markets, with select parts up to 500 kg.
• Management says it has the only moulding line in India for 500 kg castings. Customers include Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors, and
some of those castings may end up in defence vehicles, but there is no direct aerospace or defence supply.
• Capacity is ~160,000 TPA, with a practical peak of ~135,000 tonnes at 85% utilisation. Company-level utilisation is ~55%, and the
Pedapariya plant is at ~25%.
• Exports were ~30% of Q1 revenue. They go ~85% to the US and ~15% to Europe, and ~70% of US exports are for CVs, with the rest for
pickups and SUVs.
• Last year's export slowdown came from North American weakness and tariffs, not loss of customers or share. Management sees
global OEMs diversifying sourcing to India.
Guidance
• FY27 volume is expected to exceed 100,000 tonnes (Q1: ~22,500 tonnes), with ~15% volume growth in FY28.
• FY27 EBITDA is guided at ~INR 15 per kg (Q1 was below INR 10 per kg). Management targets ~INR 18 per kg in 3 years once volume
reaches ~135,000 tonnes and exports exceed 50% of revenue.
• Peak volume of 135,000 tonnes would mean revenue of ~INR 19,000 mn, targeted within 3 years.
• Export share is expected to rise from ~30% in Q1 to ~35% by FY27-end and above 50% in 3 years, depending on how fast domestic
grows.
• Pedapariya utilisation is expected to reach ~40% by Q4FY27. Management says plant profitability becomes very good once utilisation
crosses ~35%.
• Management sees good export demand, with no macro headwinds and Q2 tracking to plan.
Margins and EBITDA per Kg
• Current EBITDA is ~INR 10 per kg for domestic and ~INR 20 per kg for exports. The move from INR 15 to INR 18 per kg will come from
product mix, better realisations and operating leverage at higher volume.
• Raw material pass-through has a one-quarter lag in both directions. In Q1, raw material costs rose more than INR 5 per kg (the
Middle East war was cited), and this was recovered from customers in Q2, so management expects Q2 margins to be good.
• Q2 raw material costs rose only ~INR 1-2 per kg, to be recovered in Q3. The exact price increase varies by customer.
• Forex gains in other income are included in EBITDA per kg because management treats them as operational (timing between invoice
and realisation). Management says it can reach INR 18 per kg even if the rupee stays stable, with volume as the key driver.
• Management did not give a fixed vs variable cost split and tracks performance by EBITDA per kg.
New Products
• The large-casting new products have completed sampling and customer approvals. Ramp-up is underway, with bulk production by
Q4FY27.
• New products should add ~250-300 tonnes a month at peak, and management expects the peak schedule to be sustained.
• The RFQ process began ~15 months ago and development ~1 year ago. Management says there was no unusual delay, since typical
approval cycles are 6 months to 1.5 years depending on complexity.
• When asked about the INR 2,000-2,500 mn of new business, management only reiterated the ~300 tonnes a month addition.
• No capacity capex is needed for the new products because capacity is already available.
Capex and Balance Sheet
• Maintenance capex is ~INR 300-350 mn a year, ranging from ~INR 250 mn to ~INR 400 mn depending on balancing equipment,
furnaces or automation. Last year was lower because little balancing equipment was added.
• Debottlenecking Pedapariya from ~160,000 to ~200,000 TPA would need ~INR 600 mn on top of maintenance capex. The maximum
on existing lines is ~210,000 TPA, and a new moulding line would bring a step-up beyond that.
• Further capex will be decided once volume crosses ~120,000 tonnes.
• The term loan should be repaid this year, leaving only short-term borrowings. These will rise with turnover (an extra ~INR 1,000 mn
was indicated), but management expects them to stay similar as a percentage of revenue despite the longer export cycle.
Competition and Processes
• Management sees limited competition in large and complex castings. Craftsman Automation is mainly in machining and is not a direct
competitor.
• Green sand uses sand, water and additives without chemicals and allows faster, higher-volume production. No-bake uses resin
binders and suits castings from 300 kg to 3 tonnes, but only ~6-7 castings can be made per cycle.
• Management is not targeting new niche segments.
Other
• US exports fall under Section 232 at a 25% tariff, and management expects no change.
• Only ~5-10% of export receivables are hedged, as the company currently benefits from dollar strength. Hedging is decided based on
currency moves.
• Labour shortages in April-May came from election-related migration across the country and are seasonal, lasting 1-2 months a year.
• Management did not give a scrap vs pig iron ratio because it depends on grade and product mix. Scrap cost pressure is industry-wide.
• Management sees no material customer concentration risk after diversifying across products and customers.

NeoChem Bio Solutions Ltd
Outlook: NeoChem Bio Solutions is executing a long-term strategic transformation, moving from a local partnership model and
white-label manufacturing to a proprietary, high-margin branded business. With a 48-year heritage, the company is expanding
beyond its core textile chemicals into non-textile segments, including home care, personal care, paints and coatings. Management
aims to achieve a 5x revenue expansion over five years (~35% CAGR), driven by higher capacity utilisation, deeper export market
penetration and an increasing revenue contribution from higher-margin silicone and bio-based ester products.
Corporate History & Business Model Shift
Founded in 1978 in Ahmedabad as a local business, the company scaled from ~INR 3.2 mn of revenue in 2006 to ~INR 130 mn by
2013 under Managing Director Mr Swapnil Lalitbhai Makati. Historically reliant on white-label manufacturing for multinational
corporations, NeoChem pivoted in 2021 towards developing its own branded portfolio. As a result, the revenue mix has shifted
from 75% white label before 2021 to 75% branded currently, while the non-textile portfolio is 100% branded.
Product Segments & Diversification
The company operates across four core product segments with an aggregate manufacturing capacity of 22,000 MTPA. Silicones and
bio-based esters carry higher margin profiles, with bio-based esters utilising plant derivatives like soy and palm sourced
competitively from Southeast Asia as base materials for fabric softeners and conditioners. Conversely, polymers and surfactants
serve as volume-based, standard-margin products used in textile processing as well as personal care and home care applications.
Currently, company revenues are split ~75% in textiles and ~25% in non-textiles, though management targets a balanced ~50:50
revenue split across both verticals within the next 3-4 years.
Financial Performance & Margin Expansion
EBITDA margins expanded to 18-20% in FY26, from historical levels of 7-15% between FY22 and FY25, primarily driven by the
structural shift towards branded products and specialty categories. Gross margins across the product blend average ~35-40%,
supporting PAT margins of 10-12%. Branding and marketing spend is budgeted at ~3-4% of revenue. On pricing, NeoChem has
demonstrated its ability to pass through costs, successfully passing on ~10-12% raw material price increases.
Capacity Utilisation & Debottlenecking Capex
The manufacturing facility operates 11 interchangeable reactors, with current capacity utilisation of ~53%. Historical growth (~35%
CAGR) is expected to continue until utilisation reaches its operational ceiling of ~85-87% by FY28-FY29. Incremental
debottlenecking involves replacing existing units with larger reactors at a modest cost of ~INR 2.5-3 mn per reactor over 3-4
months. For long-term expansion, NeoChem holds a land parcel 10x larger than its current footprint, where a greenfield expansion
estimated at ~INR 300-400 mn will be initiated once current capacities reach peak utilisation.
5x Growth Strategy & Target Revenue Mix
Management expects its multi-year ~5x revenue expansion strategy to be anchored by deliberate segment, product and customer
realignments. The segment goal targets a ~50% textile and ~50% non-textile split, while the product mix is projected to shift
toward ~50% silicones and bio-based esters alongside ~50% polymers and surfactants. Customer contribution to this incremental
revenue expansion is anticipated to come ~60% from new client acquisitions and ~40% from organic volume growth with existing
accounts.
Global Operations & Geographic Expansion
Exports currently account for ~5% of sales across 12 international markets, including Australia, Indonesia, Thailand, Canada,
Singapore, Vietnam, Egypt, Ukraine and Turkey. The company plans to increase the export contribution to 10% by the end of FY26
and eventually to 15-20% over the long term. Export margins are in line with domestic margins due to competitive dynamics across
Southeast Asia.
Working Capital Dynamics
Working capital days temporarily expanded to ~160 days, with receivables reaching ~INR 1,610 mn, driven by strategic raw
material buffer stocking using IPO proceeds to mitigate global supply volatility, alongside adherence to MSME payment
compliance rules. Management has initiated operational normalisations to optimise cash flows, targeting a reduction in working
capital days to 120 days by March 2026 (end of FY26).
Key Growth Drivers & Risks
Primary growth drivers include scaling plant capacity utilisation toward 85%+, expanding non-textile branded penetration,
increasing export market wallet share, low-cost reactor debottlenecking, and the eventual development of the 10x land parcel. Key
monitorables include the execution pace of reducing working capital days to 120 days, execution timelines and funding structure
for the planned ~INR 300-400 mn greenfield capex, input price volatility in bio-based raw materials like palm and soy derivatives,
and maintaining margin discipline while expanding into competitive non-textile markets.

Neogen Chemicals Ltd
Neogen Chemicals, a bromine and lithium chemistry specialist (bromine since the 1970s and lithium since 1985), is transitioning into
a battery materials player through its subsidiary Neogen Ionics. The base business is at a ~INR 10 bn revenue run-rate across
bromine derivatives, advanced intermediates and contract manufacturing, organolithium and inorganic lithium, with FY27 revenue
guidance of INR 10.5 bn versus INR 8.5 bn in FY26. Battery capex of ~INR 18 bn is nearing completion and is due to be completed by
the end of this year, comprising the Pakhajan greenfield site (30,000 t electrolyte using Mitsubishi technology and 3,000 t
electrolyte salt via the 80:20 Neogen Morita JV) and the Dahej site (2,000 t electrolyte, with salt and additive capacity being raised
to 2,500 t). Battery revenue is targeted to scale from ~INR 0.35 bn in FY26 to ~INR 3 bn in FY27, over INR 10 bn in FY28 and INR 25-
30 bn in FY29, taking consolidated revenue to INR 35-40 bn by FY29. The model is electrolyte for India and electrolyte salts and
additives for the world, with Dahej approved by 4 of 5 US electrolyte makers. The key factors to monitor are commissioning of ~60
GWh of Indian cell capacity, offtake from global salt customers, PLI support, debt repayment from QIP proceeds and working capital
normalisation.
Business Overview & History
• The company was founded by the MD's father, one of the first in India to make bromine from seawater in the 1970s; the plant
near Morbi was destroyed in the Morbi dam failure in the late 1970s, after which he restarted in 1985 with bromine derivatives,
the first being lithium bromide, which began the company's lithium journey.
• Growth journey: revenue of ~INR 10 mn by FY91, ~INR 1 bn by 2016, followed by a plant acquisition in Vadodara that took
revenue to ~INR 3 bn in 3 years, a greenfield plant at Dahej and an organolithium acquisition in Hyderabad 3 years ago.
• The parent company makes bromine derivatives, specialty bromine derivatives, inorganic (non-battery) lithium compounds,
advanced intermediates and contract manufacturing products for pharma, agrochemicals, semiconductors, flavours &
fragrances and engineering sectors; Neogen Ionics caters to battery customers in India and internationally.
Base Business
• The base business is expected to cross ~INR 10 bn of revenue this year: bromine derivatives INR 3-4 bn, advanced intermediates
and contract manufacturing INR 3-4 bn, organolithium INR 1-1.5 bn and inorganic lithium ~INR 1.5 bn.
• FY27 revenue guidance stands at INR 10.5 bn versus INR 8.5 bn in FY26.
• The earlier capex was premised on agrochemicals, which slowed down; the company pivoted to flavours & fragrances and
semiconductors to fill volumes, before a fire at one of its pharma manufacturing blocks at Dahej disrupted operations.
• Post-fire, the plant is expected to restart very soon; the company aims for near-full utilisation this year and full utilisation next
year, with a focus on stabilising the business by FY28.
Battery Materials: Capacity & Technology
• R&D on lithium-ion battery materials began in 2017 (focusing on electrolyte); all electrolyte components were made in the lab
by 2021, and gigascale electrolyte production started in 2024.
• Dahej (existing): 2,000 t electrolyte capacity, already supplying one of India's gigafactories, plus two smaller units; electrolyte
salt capacity of ~200 t until last year is being increased to 2,500 t of salt and additives.
• Pakhajan (greenfield, 65 acres): starting capacity of 30,000 t electrolyte using Mitsubishi technology and 3,000 t electrolyte salt
via Neogen Morita New Materials Ltd (NML), a step-down subsidiary and 80:20 JV with Japan's Morita.
• Total capex of ~INR 18 bn for 30,000 t electrolyte and 5,500 t salt (equivalent to ~45 GWh) is to be completed by the end of this
year, with full utilisation targeted within the next 2 years.
• Business model: electrolyte, which has a short shelf life, will be sold in India, while electrolyte salt, lithium additives and purified
solvents will be sold to international markets.
• The Mitsubishi agreement is non-exclusive, though Neogen is the preferred choice; the Morita JV is the main (exclusive) vehicle
for Morita's lithium salt sales.
Battery Revenue Guidance & Unit Economics
• Battery revenue: ~INR 0.35 bn in FY26, targeted at ~INR 3 bn in FY27, over INR 10 bn in FY28 and INR 25-30 bn in FY29;
consolidated revenue is targeted at INR 35-40 bn by FY29.
• Realisation assumptions at stable lithium prices: electrolyte at ~USD 8 per kg initially (up to 30,000 t) and USD 6-7 per kg
thereafter; salt and additives at USD 20-22 per kg with lithium carbonate at ~USD 20 per kg. If most salt is consumed internally,
~1,000 t would be sold internationally.
