• Incremental capex is estimated at ~60-70% of the base investment (~INR 10-11 bn for the next integrated phase), with
brownfield expansion possible at the existing site up to ~100 KT.
• If fully utilised by FY29, a brownfield expansion from 30 KT to 60 KT would be required; salt capacity may need to be added as
early as next financial year, especially if the battery material PLI comes in.
• Downside scenario: even with zero electrolyte sales in India, selling salt and solvents (the second-highest value component)
would take the business to breakeven or better next year and ~INR 13-14 bn or more of revenue by FY29.
Demand Outlook: India & Global
• Six Indian gigafactories are under construction, adding ~60 GWh of cell capacity: Ola has commissioned, Exide has
commercialised, Amara Raja has set up its own plant, while Waaree, Reliance and Tata are at advanced installation stages
targeting completion before March. Management expects most of the 60 GWh to be installed by March-June 2027.
• Plants typically take 1-2 years to reach full utilisation; at full output, the 60 GWh would need over 60,000 t of electrolyte, so
even ~50% utilisation by FY29 would be enough to fully utilise Neogen's 30,000 t plant. Total targeted capacity of these players
is ~250-260 GWh, with scale-up expected from FY30.
• India imported ~30 GWh of cells last year, and the Ministry of Heavy Industries expects this to rise to 90 GWh next year; Indian
demand is expected to exceed 100 GWh by FY29.
• Indian cell demand is estimated at 600-700 GWh over 10 years, plus 20-25% exports, taking it to ~900 GWh by 2036-37 (China's
current level) and implying ~900 KTA of electrolyte demand; a 30-50% share would mean ~270-450 KTA for Neogen.
• Global battery demand of 1,500+ GWh (China 70-80%) is expected to reach 6,000-7,000 GWh in 10 years, with energy storage
(ESS) emerging as a key growth driver.
• Neogen has electrolyte recipes for 5 of the 6 gigafactories and will demonstrate them during trial production with Mitsubishi;
tech-partner mandates are being addressed through validation clauses in agreements and electrolyte designs that outperform
imports.
Global Opportunity: US & Non-China Supply
• The Dahej site has been approved by 4 of the 5 US electrolyte makers, and the fifth is expected to approve once the new
packaging facility is online next year, giving access to the entire US market.
• US 45X tax credits require battery makers to source China-free materials; there are only 3-4 non-China electrolyte salt suppliers
(Neogen-Morita being one) and only 2 non-China electrolyte additive producers.
• Contracts in place already exceed capacity, and the company expects to keep investing in the battery business over the next 7-8
years.
Policy Support & Competition
• The INR 181 bn ACC PLI is for cell manufacturers; Neogen is an indirect beneficiary as cell makers must meet localisation
requirements. Reliance and Ola have qualified, and the government is re-auctioning 10 GWh with a cap of 3-4 GWh per player,
so most of the six players should get some benefit.
• A battery material PLI is under consideration, under which Neogen could be a direct beneficiary; the government is considering
this instead of customs duty to avoid raising costs for cell makers.
• Electrolyte is difficult to import, with a shelf life of 1-3 months on paper but a practical desired shelf life of only ~14 days; it is
also typically a customised recipe for each cell maker.
• Chinese electrolyte prices can be 50-60% of Neogen's at times, sometimes only 10-15% lower and sometimes higher; importing
all raw materials and blending locally brings costs close to China, while full localisation implies a ~30-40% delta.
• Leading Chinese electrolyte makers operate at 300-350 KT, so scaling to 50-100 KT will narrow the scale gap.
• One other Indian company has announced plans for cathode, anode, additives, electrolyte and electrolyte salts.
Contracts, Debt & Working Capital
• There are no take-or-pay contracts; electrolyte volumes rely on the need for local supply, while international salt customers
have committed to buy at least 40% of volumes directly or indirectly, implying 70-80% salt utilisation and INR 7-8 bn of revenue,
which underpins confidence in over INR 10 bn of battery revenue next year.
• Bonds and Vivriti debt were raised during the major capex and after the Dahej fire (with insurance proceeds coming in slowly);
most long-term debt is expected to be repaid from the recent QIP proceeds, leaving only working capital debt.
• The battery business is expected to run a ~90-day working capital cycle given only 2-3 products, while the base business is
expected to return to ~120-140 days over the next 1-2 years, significantly improving cash flows.

Northern Arc Capital Ltd
Northern Arc is a diversified lender spanning credit solutions (B2B lending to NBFCs), funds, debt syndication and a fast-growing
direct-to-customer book across consumer, MSME and microfinance, with total AUM of ~INR 170 bn. The company holds its FY27
guidance of 22-23% growth, an ROA approaching 3% and credit cost of 2.6-2.8%, with interest rate sensitivity largely neutral given a
matched asset-liability structure. Direct-to-customer is now ~65% of the book and heading to 70%, built on a capital-efficient fintech
partnership model.
Franchise and Scale
Northern Arc was founded after the 2007-08 MFI crisis to help microfinance institutions raise funds, and later expanded into MSME,
consumer, affordable housing and vehicle finance. It has worked with 350+ NBFCs and built its own direct-to-customer franchise
from 2017. The business comprises credit solutions (B2B, AUM ~INR 65 bn), funds (AUM ~INR 30 bn) and debt syndication (INR 120-
130 bn of annual volume at a ~25 bps placement fee).
Direct-to-customer AUM is ~INR 96 bn, and total AUM ~INR 170 bn. The company has been profitable every year, through COVID,
the IL&FS crisis and the over-leveraging cycle; its 15-year AUM CAGR is ~29% and PAT CAGR ~24%.
The fintech digital lending book is ~INR 55 bn, with 35+ live partners. Rural finance (from the slump sale of 150 Smile Microfinance
branches with INR 2.5 bn of AUM) now has 430+ branches and INR 12 bn of AUM. The MSME book is ~INR 36 bn (LAP INR 17 bn,
merchant loans INR 10 bn, and mid-market and supply chain INR 10 bn).
Interest Rate Positioning and Guidance
Banks have quietly raised MCLR by ~15 bps over six months without an RBI move, and market benchmarks (G-Secs, T-bills) are up
30-35 bps, so the trajectory is upward; a 50 bps repo increase is expected across October and December, adding 15-20 bps to the
cost of funds over six months.
Liabilities are ~40% fixed and 60% floating, of which ~30% is T-bill and repo-linked (immediate reset) and 30% MCLR-linked (mostly
resetting in March). On the asset side, B2B credit solutions are floating via an in-house FPLR benchmark reset monthly, while direct-
to-customer loans are largely fixed but short-tenor (12-15 months), so they reprice on fresh lending. Net interest margin is largely
protected, as lending rates move with the cost of funds.
The company holds FY27 growth guidance of 22-23%, with ROA moving from 2.6-2.7% towards 3% by year-end and credit cost of
2.6-2.8%, even as the direct-to-customer share rises from 50-55% last year to 65% now, against a 70% target. The CFO is already
pushing business teams to raise lending rates ahead of the hikes.
Risk Management and Portfolio
The risk framework has evolved from wholesale FI lending to a product-specific and enterprise-level approach, with separate
policies for MFI and MSME LAP, internal scorecards, annual RBI inspection inputs and internal audit review. GNPA and NNPA are
among the lowest in 15 years.
Over the last two months, there has been no deterioration across consumer, MSME or microfinance. MFI disbursements have
recovered from a low of INR 300 mn per month to INR 1,100-1,150 mn, aided by CGFMU cover and MFIN over-leveraging
compliance; MSME has held up despite war-related apprehensions, and consumer (largely urban) continues to outperform.
Capex is light and mainly on technology (LOS, LMS, bonds, funds and co-lending platforms, amortised over five years); the lending
business invests capital in growing the book rather than in fixed assets. Existing products offer enough headroom for 3-5 years, with
inorganic opportunities evaluated continuously.
Fintech Partnership Economics and Capital
Partners such as MobiKwik, Kissht (OnEMI) and MoneyView source loans and act as agent and FLDG provider (5% under RBI norms),
while Northern Arc owns the customer, underwrites, disburses, collects and signs the agreement. On an illustrative 15% risk-
adjusted yield with a 25% customer IRR, ~10% passes to the partner as a servicer fee; MobiKwik yields can reach 32-33%, partners
earn a 6-7% net fee for the 5% FLDG, and the business has delivered 4%+ ROA and a 30%+ CAGR.
Pricing is risk-based: if partner losses run at 7% against a 5% FLDG, pricing is lifted (for example, to 17%) to preserve the target 15%
net yield. Customers are largely urban and bureau-gated, distinct from rural MFI borrowers; ~95% of the consumer book is partner-
sourced. Partners have a vintage of 5+ years, and Northern Arc has in-house collection infrastructure and has taken over portfolios
from underperforming partners.
Guidance
The company held FY27 guidance of 22-23% growth, ROA approaching 3% from 2.6-2.7%, credit cost of 2.6-2.8% and a rise in direct-
to-customer to 70% of the book, with ROE improving from 11% to ~13% this year and 15% next year, and no capital need for 7-8
quarters.

Business Model & Positioning

Subsidiaries & Operations

Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Ltd
Outlook: Nuvoco Vistas is on a growth trajectory to reach 35 MTPA of capacity by FY28. Despite significant inflationary pressure
from rising fuel costs (petcoke and coal), the company remains optimistic about medium-to-long-term demand driven by
government capex and housing spend.
Capacity Expansion & Timeline
• Current Status: Operating at 27 MTPA.
• FY28 Target: 35 MTPA.
• Recent Milestones: 2 MT grinding capacity at Surat was operationalised in July 2026, ahead of the Q3FY27 schedule.
• Upcoming Projects:
◦ Wadraj (Kutch): 3.5 MT clinker capacity by end of Q3FY27; 2.5 MT grinding capacity by April 2027.
◦ Sachana (Gujarat): 1.5 MT bulk terminal for cement handling by Q2FY28 to serve the Ahmedabad market.
◦ East Region: Adding 4 MT capacity by FY28.
• Future Growth: Potential expansion to 44-45 MTPA by FY29/30 through greenfield projects in Gulbarga (5-5.5 MT grinding) or
Western UP/MP (3.5 MT grinding).
Operational Metrics & Strategy
• Market Mix: ~74-75% of volume is sold in the trade segment.
• Premiumisation: Premium category cement sales increased from 34% to 43% over five years.
• Utilisation: Currently hovering around 81%, which is higher than several industry peers.
• Resource Security: Limestone reserves are sufficient for the next 40 years.
Cost & Pricing Dynamics
• Inflationary Pressures: Petcoke prices have risen to USD 175-180 per tonne, and domestic coal prices have increased due to
diversion to the power sector.
• Pricing Action: The industry saw price hikes in March and April 2026, followed by stability through July and a brief moderation
in August. A new hike was initiated around 15 September.
• Margin Protection: Management suggests a net price hike of ~INR 15-20 per bag is necessary to offset current input cost
increases.
• Trade vs. Non-Trade: The price gap between trade and non-trade segments is currently ~INR 40-50 per bag.
Sustainability & Efficiency
• Renewable Energy: Currently meeting ~20% of power requirements via WHRS and solar.
• New Initiative: Partnership with CleanMax to add 46 MW of hybrid renewable power in Rajasthan, expected to be operational
in 15 months.
• Cost Saving Target: Internal target to achieve savings of INR 110-120 per tonne over the next 2-2.5 years through efficiency
and renewables.
Risks & Market Challenges
• Logistics: Railway rake shortages in Q1FY27 led to a loss of 200,000 tonnes in sales volume.
• Regional Demand: Heavy rainfall in Chhattisgarh and West Bengal has negatively impacted demand in the East, while North
and West regions have shown better growth.
• Geopolitical Risk: Middle East conflicts continue to drive volatility in fuel and freight costs.

Oriental Rail Infrastructure Ltd
Oriental Rail Infrastructure is transitioning from a wagon and railway component manufacturer into an integrated, technology-
driven rail freight solutions platform. FY26 and Q1FY27 were about execution and efficiency, with margins rebuilt through
backward integration and in-house component manufacturing. A consolidated order book of ~INR 16.92 bn gives 18-22 months of
revenue visibility, while four new initiatives (smart wagons, high-axle-load wagons, leasing and refurbishment) frame the next
phase of growth, albeit at a nascent stage.
Business and Capacity
• The company operates across rolling stock interiors for passenger coaches (around 30% share in the organised seat and berth
segment) and freight wagons and components through subsidiary Oriental Foundry, with backward integration into artificial
leather, PU foam, silicone foam and engineered boards.
• Freight wagon capacity is around 2,400 wagons per annum at roughly 50% utilisation in FY26, leaving headroom to scale; four
facilities span around 100 acres.
Financials
• FY26 consolidated revenue was INR 5,733 mn, with EBITDA up 21.8% to INR 854 mn (margin of 14.9%, from 11.6% in FY25),
PAT up 44.6% to INR 422 mn (7.4% margin) and diluted EPS of INR 6.37.
• Q1FY27 revenue was ~INR 1,376 mn, up 16.7% YoY; EBITDA rose 43.7% to INR 209 mn, with margin up 286 bps to 15.2%, and
PAT rose 83% to INR 107 mn, with margin up 283 bps to 7.8%; diluted EPS was INR 1.60.
• Profitability improvement was driven by better execution, product mix, operating leverage and cost absorption, with smaller
components such as springs and couplers now made in-house.
Order Book
• The consolidated order book as of 11 August 2026 was ~INR 16,920 mn, of which ~INR 15,260 mn sits with Oriental Foundry for
freight wagons and ~INR 1,660 mn with Oriental Rail for seat, berth and allied products, executable over 18-22 months.
• Most of the order book is from Indian Railways; private player orders for wagon manufacturing are not yet significant, and bulk
Railways tendering has been limited since 2022.
Four Growth Initiatives
• Smart Wagons: Via an exclusive JV with HUM Industrial Technology (USA), moving monitoring onboard for real-time
diagnostics; an RDSO bid for 300-400 smart wagons is out, with an estimated market of ~INR 100 bn, and a dedicated New
Delhi testing facility is expected by the end of FY28.
• High-Axle-Load Wagons: A collaboration with Russia's United Wagon Company (design arm VNICT) to develop next-generation
25-tonne high-axle-load wagons for Indian conditions, with design and prototype submissions in process at RDSO and clarity
expected by February or March next year.
• Wagon Leasing: A leasing platform with regulatory approvals in hand, aligned to the Railways' privatisation push, to be scaled
step by step given its capex-heavy nature, as wagons sit on the balance sheet.
• Refurbishment: Refurbishment and turnkey projects through the ABUR Projects LLP JV with AB Composites, diversifying
revenue using existing interior capabilities; the JV has already participated in 4-5 tenders.
Cash Flow and Production Ramp
• Weak cash generation historically stemmed from sub-optimal capacity utilisation and working capital tied up amid steel price,
gas and wheelset supply disruptions; the plan is to lift utilisation to 60-65% and then 75-80% to turn operating cash flow
positive.
• Wheelset supply from Indian Railways has largely normalised; the Q2 target of 500 wagons (from 300 in Q1) may slip by a
quarter or two, with Q4 at ~560-570 rather than the earlier 600.
Guidance & View
The company guided to stable to improving margins around current levels; freight wagon utilisation rising to 60-65% and then 75-
80% to turn operating cash flow positive; production ramping towards 500 wagons a quarter, with Q4 at ~560-570; and capex for
new initiatives funded largely from internal accruals. Revenue guidance for the new verticals was withheld until a few orders are
executed.
The core order book provides solid near-term visibility and the margin recovery is real, but the growth optionality in smart
wagons, high-axle-load wagons and leasing is early and dependent on RDSO approvals and the pace of railway privatisation. Capex
discipline and the normalisation of wheelset supply are the swing factors for the cash flow turnaround.

Orient Bell Ltd
Outlook: Management guides double-digit volume and revenue growth for the current fiscal year. It expects a favourable demand
environment for the next two years, as real estate projects launched in 2023-24 reach completion. Margin expansion is supported
by narrowing pricing gaps with unorganised Morbi producers, a richer product mix and rising utilisation.
Record Q1 Performance: Q1 revenue grew 43% YoY to above INR 2,000 mn. This is the first time Q1 has crossed the historical
baseline of INR 1,500-1,600 mn. EBITDA margin expanded to 8.7%, up from 5-6% in Q1 last year and 6.4% for the full prior year.
Gross margin stayed strong at 38-39%, compared with 36-38% earlier.
Capacity Utilisation: Utilisation across the three manufacturing locations rose to 70-75% from about 60% a year ago, giving
operating leverage.
Working Capital Discipline: Working capital days fell to 18 from 25-26 in earlier periods, a sign of strict cash discipline.
Product Innovation: New products launched over the past 7-8 quarters contribute 28-30% of revenue, up from 26%. Key
innovation categories include Sinker, Super Gloss and specialised GVT surfaces. Vitrified tiles now make up more than 60% of the
mix, up from 40% five years ago.
Distribution Reach: The network has more than 2,000 distributor touchpoints nationwide. Tier-3 and smaller cities contribute 61%
of revenue, up from 58-59%. North and East account for about 70% of sales and South and West about 30%; the company is
targeting growth in South and West, supported by the Dora GVT capacity.
Digital & Sell-Out Push: Call centres and AI-based visualisation tools help dealers drive secondary sales. Company-driven sell-out
initiatives now account for about 40% of total sales, up from 26% last year.
Morbi Dynamics: High gas and propane prices have shut down non-viable unorganised plants in Morbi. Morbi 2x4 tile prices have
risen from INR 20 per sq ft to INR 27-28 per sq ft. Orient Bell sells at INR 32-33 per sq ft, plus INR 5 per sq ft freight from
Sikandrabad. The price gap has therefore narrowed from INR 10 per sq ft to INR 5 per sq ft, and dealers have shifted 10-15% of
their sourcing to organised players.
Energy Cost Advantage: Orient Bell's natural gas cost was INR 60 per unit in Q1 and is projected at INR 61-62 per unit in Q2.
Morbi's equivalent propane cost is INR 80 per unit. Kilns run only on natural gas, while spray dryers use biofuels that cost less than
half as much as natural gas.
Tile Adhesives (MasterBond): The adhesives business generated INR 24 mn in Q1 from pilot operations in North India. The
company plans to extend distribution across North and East India, opening an adjacent growth category.
Export Headwinds: Industry-wide ceramic tile exports fell from INR 200 bn to INR 180 bn, hit by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and
disruption to Red Sea and Suez Canal shipping. This has redirected supply into the domestic market.
Long-Term Potential: Market share gains from Morbi's cost disadvantage, a higher share of vitrified and new products, and
expansion into South and West India support sustained growth. Rising utilisation, an energy cost advantage and a working capital
cycle of 18 days point to continued margin and return improvement.

• BFSI and mid-market contracts generally do not require bank guarantees, whereas government/PSU contracts may involve
such requirements.
• Orient maintains regular engagement with OEMs through programmes and quarterly meetings to access market opportunities
and larger deals.
• OEMs provide the products, while Orient handles installation, AMC and maintenance/service requirements, particularly for
larger contracts.
Installation vs Services Revenue
• Product/installation revenue is generally recognised when the product is installed/sold.
• AMC/service revenue is recognised over the service period, typically one year.
• The product-to-service split varies by contract, with examples ranging from 60:40 to 80:20 and 90:10.
• Management is actively increasing the contribution of ARR/managed services, given the recurring nature of these revenues.
• Orient operates both NOC and SOC centres at Turbhe.
AI-Led Services
• AI-led revenue models have been initiated through OHMS 2.0, with Orient also becoming an Anthropic partner.
• AI revenue contribution remains insignificant currently, but the company intends to scale data and AI-led businesses during
FY27 and beyond.
• The near-term focus is on building the underlying infrastructure and service capabilities required for enterprise AI adoption.
IPO Funds Utilisation
• Approximately INR 350 mn of IPO proceeds remained unutilised.
• Management expects the balance amount to be fully utilised by 31 December 2026.
• The funds are earmarked primarily toward the DaaS contract/order requirements.
International Expansion
• While Orient has entities/offices in the UAE and Singapore, international expansion is not a major focus currently.
• The Singapore entity is primarily used for USD billing where customers require it.
• Management intends to first scale the India service opportunity before increasing its focus on the Middle East and Singapore
markets.
Gross Margin & Profitability
• Q1FY27 gross margin was in the 15-16% range, while EBITDA margin stood at 7.28%.
• Management indicated that contracts are being executed above the minimum gross-margin threshold required for viability.
• The focus remains on improving the overall margin profile through higher-margin services, ARR-led revenues and operating
synergies.

Paisalo Digital Ltd
Paisalo is a three-decade-old, collection-first NBFC lending to micro enterprises and the MSME-SME segment. It is now on a three-
year plan to double AUM, revenue and PAT (within a six-year cycle) before returning to a five-year cadence, targeting AUM of INR
115-120 bn. The strategy pairs an AI-led lending franchise with new products and geographies, while maintaining pristine asset
quality with credit cost below 2%. The company targets a 25-30% CAGR, FY30 ROE of 20% and ROA of 4-4.5%, with ROE guidance of
13-14% for the current year.
Capital Structure and Performance
Paisalo raised INR 1.84 bn of fresh equity via a foreign issuance; promoters added 5% a year from 2022 to Q1FY25, raising their stake
to 46.71% undiluted in Q1FY27 (42.88% fully diluted). The first FCCB of USD 50 mn was completed three quarters ago, followed by a
debut ECB of USD 15 mn last quarter, and SEBI has approved INR 9 bn of public debt (the first INR 3 bn has been raised).
From 1992 to 2016, the company doubled AUM every 10 years, and from 2017 to 2026 every five years; it is now on a three-year
doubling cycle for six years. The highest-ever credit cost was 3.8% during COVID, cut to under 2% within eight quarters; current
credit cost is 0.9%, GNPA 0.70% and NNPA 0.49%.
AUM stands at INR 67.07 bn, up 28% YoY. Q1 disbursements rose 128% to a record INR 17.3 bn, total income rose 20% to INR 2.6 bn,
and PAT grew 30% to INR 610 mn on net interest income up 16% to INR 1.44 bn. Headcount fell 2% to 3,018 despite the growth,
showing early operating leverage. The company added 696 touchpoints to reach 5,995 across 23 states (424 branches, 3,997
distribution points and 1,574 BC points) and has served 18 mn customers.
AI Transition and Products
The company is shifting from a high-tech, high-touch model to an AI-led franchise across sourcing, underwriting, servicing and
collections. It processes ~180,000 applications per quarter via AI onboarding (up from 160,000), along with 175,000 servicing and
225,000 debt management cases through AI. Monthly AI activity includes 20 campaigns, 25 videos, 0.2 mn outbound calls, 60,000
facial matches and 0.3 mn OCR scans. 80% of new code is tested by AI, and all legacy system maintenance and test case generation
is AI-driven.
Opex is expected to be higher in the near term as distribution and AI investments run ahead of benefits; six new products launched
last quarter are expected to deliver by year-end. Micro enterprise is ~30% of AUM and MSME-SME ~70% (split 30-30, with a 10%
treasury reserve), with themed sub-products in vehicle, equipment and micro-LAP financing across OEM tie-ups, including Hero,
Bajaj, Escorts, Mahindra, Adani and Philips.
93% of the portfolio is secured by movable or immovable collateral; the balance 7% carries a deed of hypothecation over current
assets. No single sector exceeds 25% of AUM: food and hospitality ~23%, agriculture ~15%, street vendors ~15%, industries ~11%,
health and education 6-7%, and vehicles ~4%.
Market Sizing and Collection Discipline
The market is framed from a population of 1.4 bn, with a credit history base of 150 mn and a PAN base of 420 mn; the differential of
informal MSMEs across retail, SME and MSME at a weighted ticket of INR 0.5-0.6 mn implies a market of INR 9,600 bn, validated
against the INR 800-900 bn annual priority sector lending shortfall parked with NABARD. At INR 115-120 bn, Paisalo would hold just
above 1% of this market.
Paisalo positions itself as a collection-first, not disbursement-first, NBFC; it has delivered a 20-22% CAGR over 30 years because it
treats lending as a collection business. Discipline rests on low LTVs, good FOIR and a strong on-ground team, plus in-house
geospatial PIN code mapping across ~19,383 postal codes, updated fortnightly to tighten triggers, pause onboarding or adjust credit
parameters by default band.
Lending is based on income assessment rather than consumption, with no personal or consumption loans at scale. A cooling-off
period applies between two Paisalo loans, and separate categorised loan accounts are required rather than new accounts to service
existing ones, protecting against capital loss; strong debt management recovers within three to four quarters after any weak
collection cycle.
Geographic Exposure and Provisioning
Maharashtra is ~19% of the portfolio, with no single activity above 20% of that; on an INR 60 bn book, this implies exposure of ~INR
2.4 bn to any single activity, where a 2% default would be ~INR 48 mn, already covered given a liquidity coverage ratio of 600%
against the RBI minimum of 85%. Provisioning is maintained at 2% against actual credit cost of 0.9%, held conservatively since
provisions can be rolled back but not forward and are not tax-deductible.
Guidance
The company guided to doubling AUM, revenue and PAT over three years (AUM of INR 115-120 bn), a 25-30% CAGR, credit cost
below 2%, FY27 ROE of 13-14% and cost of funds of 10.5%, with FY30 ROE of 20% and ROA of 4-4.5%.

Pajson Agro India Ltd
Business and Financials
• Pajson Agro is an integrated cashew processor covering global raw cashew nut (RCN) sourcing, processing, and B2B and B2C
distribution. Its consumer brand is Royal Maya.
• Processing volume rose from ~7,000 MT in FY24 to ~16,000 MT in FY26. Existing capacity is 18,000 MT.
• FY26 total income was INR 2,569.2 mn (+37% YoY), EBITDA grew ~25% and PAT ~21%. EBITDA margin was ~14%.
• Q1FY27 revenue was ~INR 680 mn versus INR 450 mn in Q1FY26 (+51% YoY).
• It sells in 19 states, and ~80% of revenue comes from repeat customers.
Capacity and Expansion
• Current plant utilisation is ~93-94%.
• The new Vizianagaram plant adds 35,000 MT, roughly tripling capacity. Trial production is expected in December 2026/January
2027, with only a few weeks of delay from the cyclone.
• Utilisation is guided at 60-70% in FY28 and 85-90% in FY29.
• Management guides ~20% revenue growth in FY27 from the existing plant, plus incremental volume from the new plant. It
then expects 40-45% YoY growth for the next 2-3 years, which it called modest.
• Management agreed with an analyst view that FY28 volumes could effectively double.
• Customers for the new capacity are not yet contracted, since India does not do long-term contracts. Management says current
and new customers are excited about the capacity.
• No fundraise is planned and the company says it is well funded. Capex was not disclosed.
Sourcing
• ~90% of RCN is imported (West Africa: Ivory Coast, Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau) and ~10% is local.
• Sourcing is direct from farmers, cooperatives and local agents, bypassing intermediaries. Management calls this its main moat
and sees no sourcing risk in doubling volumes.
• Kernel outturn is typically 24-25% of RCN.
• Freight adds only ~0.5% to total cost. Management sees no need for long-term shipping contracts.
Margins and Currency
• INR depreciation is pressuring margins. The rupee moved from ~83-84 to ~87-89+ against the dollar.
• Mitigation is partial hedging and paying suppliers in advance, which acts as a natural hedge.
• FY27 EBITDA margin is guided down a few bps from FY26's ~14%. Operating leverage from the new plant should improve
margins excluding currency. Even with currency pressure, margins should stay in the historical range.
• PAT margin is expected to stay in line.
• ASP should improve, though it depends on the market. Management cited W320 realisation of ~INR 820 per kg.
Working Capital and Cash Flow
• FY26 cash flow was negative because large supplier advances were paid in February-March ahead of expected INR weakness.
• It expects to turn cash flow positive this year or next.
• Working capital and finance cost will rise somewhat with the revenue jump.
Products and Brand
• Byproduct processing (e.g., oil) will be added in space earmarked at the existing plant after Q4FY27. It is expected to be ~10%
of revenue at a couple of points higher margin, though this is early-stage.
• Phase 3 is cashew milk and paste. Whether to make them in-house or outsource will depend on demand.
• B2C expansion is selective, focused on profitability rather than chasing revenue. H1FY27 B2C sales already exceeded all of
FY26. B2C is targeted at ~15% of revenue in 2-3 years.
Labour and Automation
• The current plant has ~470 workers, ~90% of them women. About 300 do manual peeling on a piece-rate basis, as in Vietnam.
• Core workforce is ~170, down from ~350 at half the capacity. Labour per kg is expected to fall further at the new plant.
• Monthly wages in India and Vietnam are similar, so cost per kg is comparable to Vietnam on the strength of automation.
Global and Industry
• Africa-based processing is taking share from Vietnam, not from India.
• The company plans to set up processing in Ivory Coast to serve the US and Europe. Management expects some international
footprint by FY28.
• There are no central government benefits, but the state offers subsidies for setting up new plants.
• Seasonality: there is no fixed H1/H2 pattern. It depends on festival and wedding timing.

Revenue Model and DLM-CLM Mix

in FY26. Operating EBITDA grew ~109.5% in FY26, and PAT grew ~441%. Net debt-to-equity declined to ~0.21x from ~0.98x, while
ROCE stood at ~25.6% and ROE at ~18.9%. For Q1FY27, revenue was ~INR 508.4 mn, operating EBITDA ~INR 52.1 mn and PAT ~INR
38.1 mn, a PAT margin of ~7.4%.
Company Scale and Capabilities
Panache has over 25 years of experience, more than 150 customers across over 15 countries, and an operating facility of over
50,000 sq ft. The company describes 360-degree ODM capabilities covering ideation, industrial design, prototyping, production,
quality checks, packaging, logistics, and after-sales support including end-of-life support.
Capacity and Order Book
There is no rated capacity, since lines are interoperable across products, and capacity utilisation cannot be measured precisely,
though the current facility will suffice for ~1-2 years of growth. The company does not maintain an order book, given short cycles,
imported components and dollar pricing, and converts designs into POs on a monthly to quarterly basis.
Capex and Subsidiary Strategy
Technofire Digital's ~INR 1 bn capex is intended for contract manufacturing, with the entity being spun off as a subsidiary to house

Capital Allocation and Margins
R&D expenditure runs at ~1-2% of revenue and is not capitalised, with potential increases depending on product mix. Capital
allocation prioritises working capital and utilising spare capacities of ecosystem partners, with capex focused on protecting design
IP in manufacturing. DLM EBITDA margins are indicated at ~12-15%, with CLM lower and blended rates reflecting the mix.

Parag Milk Foods Ltd
Business and Financials
• Parag Milk Foods is a dairy company, listed since 2016, with four in-house brands: Gowardhan (cow ghee, ~22% share of
branded cow ghee at a premium price), Go (cheese), Pride of Cows (farm-to-home milk) and Avvatar (sports nutrition).
• The company says it is India's largest whey protein producer. Whey was historically a cheese by-product, and now
management treats it as a strategic product in its own right.
• FY26 turnover was ~INR 38 bn, with gross block of ~INR 9+ bn.
• EBITDA margin is ~8-8.5%. Management expects double digits in the medium term and the early teens at INR 100 bn revenue.
It declined to give a segment-wise EBITDA split.
• The distribution network has 29 depots, 4,500+ distributors and 460,000 outlets pan-India, with 300+ bulk milk coolers (BMCs).
New-Age Business (Avvatar)
• New-age is ~13% of Q1FY27 turnover. It grew 90% last year and 59% in Q1.
• Avvatar volume growth is ~84-85%, so it is not driven by pricing alone. Whey isolate prices have risen from ~INR 3,000-3,500
per kg to INR 7,000+ per kg.
• Gross margin for new-age is roughly double the company average.
• Bars are ~8% of Avvatar revenue. Newer formats are protein wafers, ready-to-drink coffee, a 26 g protein RTD coming soon,
and protein pop chips launched about 10 days ago. Chips and bars are subcontracted.
• Newer formats are expected to reach ~40-45% of Avvatar in 2-3 years. No chip revenue target was given.
• About two-thirds of Avvatar sales come from its own website and marketplaces, with the website and quick commerce
growing fastest. General trade is being added for the newer formats.
• Marketing is ~INR 1.4 bn a year, mostly performance marketing, plus KBC (5 years) and India's Got Latent. Avvatar searches
rose ~250%, and 550% on episode days.
Paneer and Cheese Expansion
• Paneer: Capacity will rise 4x from 20 to 80 MT a day for ~INR 1 bn, with commissioning by June 2027 (a conservative estimate).
Paneer has grown ~28% YoY for two years.
• Management cites the regulatory crackdown on analog paneer as a tailwind. It says India consumes ~4 mn kg a day, of which
~70% is analog. Parag expects strong HoReCa demand and 60-70% utilisation on commissioning.
• Cheese: Capacity will double from 60 to 120 MT for ~INR 1.05 bn as a brownfield project. Guidance is for completion by March
2028, but the project has been fast-tracked.
• Industry growth rates are ~12% for paneer, 25-35% for cheese and ~20% for dahi. India's per capita cheese consumption is ~0.5
kg versus 17 kg in the US.
• Ice cream is under consideration, but only with unique positioning.
Milk Procurement and Pricing
• Farmer prices rose after the summer shortage. Parag passed on the cost with calibrated price hikes across flagship products
and schemes, and held blended gross margins.
• Festive demand may keep pressure on until Diwali, with stabilisation expected after.
• Procurement is ~2 mn litres a day against 3.5 mn litres of capacity. About one-third comes via own BMCs, with similar landed
cost from aggregators.
• Management says it needs ~4 mn litres a day at INR 100 bn of revenue. It collects only 11-12% of the milk available in its areas,
so supply is not seen as a bottleneck.
Margin Levers
• A mix shift towards new-age and premium products (Greek yogurt and lactose-free milk).
• Better by-product realisation, such as edible-grade lactose with pharma-grade lactose next.
• Cost optimisation projects with consultants, and fixed-cost leverage from scale.
Capex and Balance Sheet
• Capex is INR 2.05 bn for the two expansions plus INR 800-900 mn a year of routine capex (including cow sheds), or ~INR 5 bn
over three years. No asset-turn target was given, and management says capex is not a constraint to the INR 100 bn aspiration.
• Net debt fell to INR 4.85 bn at 31 March. Debt-to-EBITDA improved from 3.2x to 1.6x, and debt-to-equity is ~0.4x.
• Another ~INR 1.2 bn of preferential warrant money is expected around November 2026 (INR 400 mn received in May 2025).
Management may raise debt toward ~2x EBITDA for the expansions.
Industry and Competition
• The dairy industry is ~INR 10,000 bn, of which 41% (~INR 4,000 bn) is organised. About 35-40% of milk is retained by farmers,
and loose milk and paneer dominate the unorganised part.
• Management does not see a new listed dairy entrant as a threat, since the competition is organised versus unorganised, not
brand versus brand.

Paramount Communications Ltd
Outlook: Paramount Communications is targeting revenue of ~INR 50 bn by FY31, implying a CAGR of under 25%, with ~INR 25 bn
each from the new Narmadapuram plant and existing facilities. The ~INR 3 bn Phase 1 greenfield capex, focused on EHV cables up
to 132 kV and HTLS conductors, is expected to contribute ~INR 12 bn by FY29 at 75% utilisation, with Phase 2 adding 220 kV and
400 kV capabilities. FY27 top-line growth is guided at ~15% with sequential margin improvement to exit near FY25 levels. The
company plans to maintain debt-to-equity below 0.3, having already raised ~INR 1.22 bn in equity, and expects volumes to double
to ~55,000-60,000 tonnes at peak. Key risks are US tariff volatility (though contracts are now structured to shield margins) and
execution of the greenfield expansion.
Company Background and Legacy
Paramount Communications, established in 1955 by S.S. Agrawal as a micro-scale housewire maker, evolved into a leading Indian
wire and cable player across telecom, railways, and power segments. It developed axle counter cables for Indian Railways,
indigenised EPABX exchange cables for Alcatel exchanges, pioneered aerial bunched cables for discoms, and was among the first
Indian firms to set up optical fibre cable and jelly-filled copper cable units. It acquired UK-based AEI Cables in 2007, the world's
oldest cable company, as a gateway to global markets.
Financial Restructuring and Turnaround
The 2008 Lehman crisis and commodity crash pushed the highly leveraged company into CDR by 2010, forcing an exit from new
Indian plants and the UK subsidiary by 2014. It became NPA in 2015, debt was sold to ARC in 2016, and promoters infused ~INR
1.25 bn between 2016 and 2023. The company returned to profit in 2019 but faced a working capital ceiling of ~INR 6 bn until
2022. Promoters liquidated personal assets to keep the company afloat, demonstrating strong commitment.
US Market Entry and Export Trajectory
Leveraging the China-plus-one opportunity, Paramount entered the US supply chain when no Indian company was exporting
cables there. US sales grew from ~USD 1 mn each in 2020 and 2021 to ~INR 1.2 bn in FY22, ~INR 4 bn in FY23, and ~45% of Q1FY26
sales. The company operates on a DDP basis, bearing tariff risk, and faced a sharp setback when the US imposed 25% reciprocal
plus 25% Russian oil tariff (effective ~54%) on India in August 2025.
Tariff Impact and Mitigation
The FY26 US tariff shock turned exports EBITDA-negative for the year, but a strong domestic pivot helped deliver ~3.5% operating
margin. Customers shared tariff burdens in varying ratios, and refunds following the US Supreme Court's cancellation of reciprocal
tariffs began only in Q2FY27. The company has since renegotiated contracts so that tariff changes during shipment are borne by
customers, and some customers shifted from DDP to FOB. It has adopted a wait-and-watch approach for October tariff decisions,
with production for US orders paused.
Domestic Pivot and Growth Resilience
In FY26, H1 sales were ~INR 8.5 bn, with 43% from the US; H2 sales were ~INR 11 bn, with only 15% from the US, demonstrating
sales channel fungibility. Domestic sales grew from ~INR 4 bn to ~INR 8 bn year-on-year. Revenue grew from ~INR 5.9 bn in FY22
to ~INR 8 bn in FY23, ~INR 10.7 bn in FY24, ~INR 15.5 bn in FY25, and ~INR 19.5 bn in FY26, a three-year CAGR of ~34-35%.
Margin Recovery and Guidance
Q4FY26 operating margin was ~5% and Q1FY27 ~6.5%, with sequential improvement guided each quarter. The company expects
to exit FY27 with margins similar to FY25. FY27 top-line growth guidance is ~15%.
Greenfield Expansion at Narmadapuram
The company is investing ~INR 3 bn in Phase 1 capex for a greenfield plant near Bhopal for specialised cables and transmission
conductors, including EHV cables up to 132 kV and HTLS conductors. Phase 1 is expected to complete in two years and generate
~INR 12 bn revenue by FY29 at 75% utilisation (~INR 15 bn potential). Phase 2 will expand into 220 kV and 400 kV cables with an
additional ~INR 2-3 bn capex, targeting an asset turn of ~6x.
Long-Term Vision and Capital Structure
The company targets sales of ~INR 50 bn by FY31, implying a CAGR of under 25%, with ~INR 25 bn from Narmadapuram and ~INR
25 bn from existing plants. Current plants are capped at ~INR 22 bn revenue potential. Volume is expected to double to ~55,000-
60,000 tonnes at peak. The company raised ~INR 1.22 bn in equity (INR 900 mn from investors, INR 300 mn from warrants), with
INR 650 mn earmarked for capex and the rest for working capital. It plans to keep debt-to-equity below 0.3, with total debt at ~INR
1.2 bn against net worth of ~INR 9 bn.
Capacity and Utilisation
Current metal consumption is ~29,600 tonnes (up ~12% YoY), with FY27 volume growth guided at ~5-7%. Utilisation is practically
100%, with every new machine immediately deployed. The company prefers throughput in tonnes over kilometres as a capacity
measure due to its wide product range from 1 sq mm to 1,000 sq mm cables.

Competitive Landscape and US Market Nuances
Competition in the US comes more from Vietnam and South Korea than Indian peers, with Chinese companies setting up

Growth Guidance Remains Strong

expected at 26-27% and PAT margin at 16-17% over the coming years.

Patel Chemical Specialities Ltd
Outlook: Patel Chemical Specialities is an Ahmedabad-based manufacturer of pharmaceutical excipients, with a product portfolio
spanning microcrystalline cellulose (MCC), croscarmellose sodium (CCS), sodium starch glycolate (SSG), calcium CMC and other
cellulose-based excipients. The company operates plants at Vatva and Talod, with a new 6,000 TPA Indrad facility under
development. It is targeting ~20% revenue growth in the current year and aims to reach INR 5,000 mn revenue by 2030.
Manufacturing & Capacity Expansion
Vatva has 3,250 TPA mixed-product capacity and is operating at ~95-98% utilisation. The Talod facility has 4,500 TPA MCC capacity
and is ready for commercial production, with utilisation targeted at ~30-40% initially and >90% next year. The upcoming Indrad
plant will have 6,000 TPA capacity, comprising ~3,000 TPA CCS, ~2,500 TPA SSG and ~700 TPA calcium CMC. Trial runs are targeted
for July-August 2027, followed by commercial ramp-up.
Product & Margin Profile
MCC margins are currently lower as the company entered the segment in 2022 and is still building scale. Sodium CMC margins are
also relatively lower due to competition from Chinese suppliers, while CCS, SSG and calcium CMC offer better margins. The Indrad
plant, with its higher-margin product mix, is expected to support margin improvement.
MCC Opportunity & Competitive Position
MCC is used across pharmaceuticals, nutraceuticals and food applications, with demand expanding into newer food and
nutraceutical applications. Management believes its 4,500 TPA MCC capacity remains small relative to the overall market and does
not currently see significant oversupply or pricing pressure. The company also indicated that established players face supply
constraints, supporting opportunities for additional capacity.
Customer Base & Capacity Utilisation
Around 60% of Talod's targeted utilisation is expected to come from existing customers and customers currently under discussion,
while another ~30-35% is expected from new customers. Vatva's high utilisation currently limits the company's ability to cater to
incremental demand from existing customers, which the new Indrad capacity is expected to address.
Export Expansion
The company exports to 20+ countries, including the US, Russia, Egypt, Europe, Korea, Japan, Malaysia and Thailand. It has signed
an exclusive marketing agreement for MCC in Italy, an exclusive distributorship agreement for calcium CMC in Japan and a non-
exclusive marketing agreement for MCC in Egypt. The company is also expanding its distributor network and participating in
international exhibitions.
Certifications & Manufacturing
Vatva has GMP certification and has been inspected by the US FDA. The company exports to the US through Patel Chem North
America. Certifications for the Talod plant are currently under process. The Indrad facility is planned to use an ethanol-based
manufacturing process, with the required licensing process underway.
Financial & Margin Outlook
Operating margin declined from ~15% in FY25 to ~12% in FY26, primarily due to expansion-related raw-material procurement and
higher operating costs. Management expects margins to remain around previous levels but did not provide a firm EBITDA margin
target due to volatility in fuel and raw-material prices. MCC prices have increased by ~10%, supported by higher fuel and raw-
material costs.
Working Capital & Funding
Current working-capital requirement stands at ~INR 220 mn, with an additional ~INR 35 mn enhancement already applied for with
banks. Further funding may be required for the Indrad project if there is a shortfall. Management also indicated that the business
will require higher working capital as the expanded capacities ramp up.
Growth Guidance
Management targets ~20% revenue growth in the current year, with growth initially driven by the Talod MCC facility and
subsequently by the Indrad plant. For the long-term INR 5,000 mn revenue target, management indicated a conservative ~10% net
profit margin assumption. The company expects export expansion, higher utilisation and the shift towards higher-margin products
to support growth.

Patel Engineering Ltd
Outlook: Patel Engineering is poised for steady growth over the next 3-5 years, driven by a strong hydropower and pumped
storage pipeline worth INR 8,000-10,000 bn, of which it will selectively bid for INR 2,000-3,000 bn. With an order book of ~INR 140
bn, annual order inflow guidance of INR 80-100 bn, and a conversion ratio of 15-20%, revenue is expected to grow at 13-15% CAGR
while maintaining EBITDA margins of 13-14%. Debt is targeted to remain below INR 15 bn, supported by INR 1.5-2 bn annual non-
core asset monetisation, including land parcels and arbitration claims. The company's seven-decade expertise in hydro, tunnelling
and irrigation, strong PSU relationships, and emerging opportunities in desalination and STP plants position it well to capitalise on
India's infrastructure push and deliver consistent, margin-accretive growth.
Business Profile and Order Book
Patel Engineering is a seven-decade-old infrastructure company focused on hydropower, irrigation and tunnelling projects, with
central PSUs such as NHPC, NTPC, SJVN and NEEPCO as primary clients. The order book stands at ~INR 140 bn, with ~65% from
central PSUs and 30-35% from state governments and civic bodies. Hydro, tunnelling and irrigation together account for ~90% of
the order book, with the balance 10% from urban infrastructure and roads.
Growth Guidance and Order Inflow
Revenue has grown at a CAGR of over 15% in the last five years, with profits growing similarly. The company targets INR 80-100 bn
of new orders this year and expects this run-rate to continue for the next four to five years, driven by the hydropower and
pumped storage push. Revenue is guided to grow at a CAGR of over 10-12%, with margins maintained at 13-14%. For the next five
years, management sees at least 13-15% CAGR.
Hydro and Pumped Storage Opportunity
The government has a strong pipeline of hydropower projects, with ~30 GW expected in the next couple of years, translating to
~INR 1,500 bn of opportunity. Pumped storage adds another ~INR 2,000 bn opportunity with 40-50 GW expected. The company
has already bid for over INR 200 bn of work in recent months, with another INR 300-400 bn in the pipeline to be bid by the end of
this year. The overall opportunity is seen at INR 8,000-10,000 bn, of which INR 2,000-3,000 bn will be selectively targeted. The
conversion ratio is expected at 15-20%.
Segment Margins and Retention
Hydro projects carry margins of ~15%, irrigation and tunnelling ~12-13%, and other segments ~8-10%. Blended margins are
maintained at 13-14% due to hydro's dominant share. Retention money is generally 5% of project value, with some projects
allowing retention to be drawn against bank guarantees. Mobilisation advance is typically 5% against bank guarantees, plus
equipment advances of 5-10% of project value.
Bank Guarantees and Surety Bonds
Bank guarantee limits stand at ~INR 40 bn, with ~INR 30 bn utilised. BG costs are ~1-1.5% per annum. Surety bonds from insurers
like New India Assurance, ICICI Lombard and Bajaj Allianz are increasingly being used for bid bonds and performance guarantees,
backed by international reinsurers. Costs are currently similar at ~1%, but may decline as more insurers enter. Contingent
liabilities of ~INR 30 bn are largely performance and retention bank guarantees.
Debt and Finance Cost
Consolidated debt rose to ~INR 12.93 bn, including working capital of ~INR 9.69 bn and term debt of ~INR 3.44 bn. Borrowing costs
have reduced from 11-11.5% to 10.5-11% following credit rating improvement. The company targets keeping overall debt below
INR 15 bn even as new projects require additional working capital. There are ~14-15 banking relationships, and pledge has been
reduced to ~66% across the lender pool.
Non-Core Asset Monetisation
The company plans to generate INR 1.5-2 bn annually from non-core assets over the next 4-5 years, using proceeds for debt
repayment. This year, ~INR 700-800 mn has already been realised from one land sale and sale of equity in a road project. Land
bank is ~INR 8-9 bn, with Nagapattinam land at ~INR 3 bn not being actively pursued. Arbitration claims and awards total ~INR 30
bn, with INR 7 bn awarded and ~INR 23 bn under arbitration. Arbitration timelines are ~5 years, with dedicated teams for
arbitration, legal recovery and real estate monetisation.
Land Monetisation
A 27-acre land parcel near Hyderabad was sold at ~INR 10 mn per acre, and discussions are ongoing for the balance ~400 acres in
the same region. Bangalore land monetisation is targeted for closure this financial year. The 1,500 acres in Tamil Nadu are being
explored for joint development rather than outright sale due to low immediate value.

PNGS Gargi Fashion Jewellery Ltd
Business and Financials
• The company was carved out in November 2021 from the P N Gadgil & Sons group (190+ year legacy, plain gold jewellery
topline of ~INR 50 bn). It is not directly promoted by the group, and it listed on the NSE SME platform through a ~INR 720 mn

• Revenue grew from ~INR 150 mn at carve-out to ~INR 1.45 bn in FY26. FY25 was ~INR 1.25 bn, which included a one-time ~INR
250 mn inventory sale to the parent's shop-in-shop (SIS) stores.
• That sale converted the SIS stores from FOCO to FOFO, because the GST service-tax portion under FOCO piles up and cannot
be claimed as a cash refund.
• Products are 925 silver fashion jewellery and gifting, 14K natural diamond (launched November 2024) and 9K gold (launched
last festive season).
• 14K natural diamond is ~INR 470-500 mn of revenue and 9K gold ~INR 30-35 mn. Silver is the balance.
• Target customers are millennials, Gen Z and working women under ~40. The average ticket size is ~INR 3,500-7,500. Silver
ranges from INR 500-600 to INR 15,000, diamond from INR 8,000-10,000 to INR 35,000, and 9K gold averages INR 10,000-
30,000.
• Customers typically visit 3-4 times a year.
Q1FY27 Performance
• Revenue grew only ~10% YoY, which management called disappointing.
• The cause was the parent changing to just-in-time inventory transfer (about 7 days ahead) instead of push sales. Consumer-
level sales at the 34 SIS stores rose from ~INR 160 mn to ~INR 270 mn.
• Management also cited weak April-May demand (West Asia conflict, inflation, job uncertainty), with recovery in June during
the monsoon sale.
• Management says the company's own inventory procurement is unaffected and that the policy change has no profit impact.
Network and Expansion
• The network is now 100+ outlets. It started with 34 SIS stores at the parent's showrooms and has added third-party SIS
(Shoppers Stop) and EBOs in malls and on high streets.
• There are four models: company-owned COCO, FOCO with the parent, parent SIS on FOFO, and Shoppers Stop SIS on FOFO.
• Management guides 20-25 new locations this year, with 12 done and 3 more due within 1-2 weeks.
• Same-store growth is expected at 25-30% for new stores and no lower than ~15% at maturity. The oldest parent store is ~20
years old.
• Management expects 20-25% YoY growth, barring extreme conditions.
• Seasonality: Q3 and Q4 are the strongest (Dussehra, Diwali, Christmas, Valentine's Day), Q1 is a little better and Q2 is the
weakest.
Unit Economics and Margins
• SIS stores under the parent operate on a fixed-margin arrangement, with the company selling to the parent at a 37.5%
discount to the retail price.
• Company-run EBOs keep the full retail margin but bear rent, power, hospitality and staff costs. They break even in 15-18
months, and sales are ~2-2.5x inventory.
• EBO costs will drag EBITDA and PAT margins by ~200-300 bps over the next 2-3 years. Management expects margins to recover
to earlier levels once EBOs mature and fewer new ones are added.
• The stated priority is profitable growth, not cash burn.
Strategy and Positioning
• The focus is silver, 14K natural diamond and 9K gold, positioned as a lifestyle brand backed by the Gadgil legacy.
• Management has no celebrity or heavy brand-marketing plans.
• There are no plans for lab-grown diamond. Natural diamond in 14K gold keeps buyback value.
• Management said BlueStone is a higher-end player (INR 40,000-75,000 AOV) and the company's diamond AOV is ~INR 30,000.

Polite Powertech Ltd
Outlook: Polite Powertech is positioned for strong growth over the next few years, underpinned by an order book of INR 11.3 bn, a
dominant underground cabling opportunity across Gujarat and other states, and a government push toward underground cabling
and GIS substations through 2032. The recent acquisition of a cable manufacturing unit enables backward integration, captive
consumption and margin protection, while the emerging operation and maintenance division and GIS substation vertical add
higher-margin, recurring revenue streams. With FY25 revenue of INR 3.41 bn and PAT of INR 130 mn, and a stated target of INR 6.5
bn topline for the current year, the company expects to sustain over 100% growth while maintaining PAT margins of around 11%.
Key monitorables include the timing of the IPO, conversion of L1 orders into LOAs, working capital discipline as operating cash
flow turns positive, and execution ramp-up in the newly acquired cable business.
Company Overview and Positioning
Polite Powertech Ltd is a Gujarat-focused EPC player incorporated in March 2023, with operations concentrated in underground
cabling and GIS substations. The company has an order book of INR 7.3 bn in hand plus INR 4 bn where it is L1 with LOA pending,
taking total visibility to INR 11.3 bn. Of this, roughly 85% is underground cabling work involving ST, NLT and LT cables. The
company recently acquired a house wire and flexible cable manufacturing company, handed over in the last week, marking
backward integration into cable manufacturing.
Backward and Forward Integration Strategy
The acquired cable manufacturing unit is located in Baroda near other cable companies such as Ahrar Cable, GAC, Diamond Power
and Waltemp. Existing house wire and flexible cable capacity can generate approximately INR 1.5 bn revenue at full utilisation. A
new expansion of INR 300 mn is underway for a 630 sq mm single core LT cable plant, targeting total revenue capacity of INR 3 bn.
Further expansion of INR 500 mn is planned for FY27-FY28, including elastomeric cable manufacturing, which could take total
capacity to INR 8-9 bn revenue. The strategic rationale is captive consumption of cables for EPC projects, which currently account
for 2-3.5% of purchase cost, helping maintain PAT margins of around 11% in a competitive environment.
Order Book and Execution
The current order book of INR 11.3 bn carries an average PAT margin of approximately 11%. Execution timelines vary by order,
broadly divided into 12-month, 15-month and 18-month categories. The company qualifies for single orders up to INR 1.5 bn
directly, and participates through JVs where it does not independently qualify. The major customer base includes Gujarat state
PSUs such as BGVCL, UGVCL, DGVCL, GETCO and MGVCL, along with private clients including Siemens, Suzlon and Polykem India
Ltd. Competitors include Rajesh Power, Park Electrical, Viviana Powertech and Edwin Energy. The company holds GETCO A-Class
approved contractor status and participates in GIS substation tenders up to INR 2 bn.
GIS Substation Opportunity
Management highlighted GIS substations as a major forward integration focus, replacing ageing AIS substations across metro and
mega cities. GIS offers 70-80% land savings, a 40-year lifespan versus 25 years for AIS, lower annual maintenance shutdown
requirements, higher reliability and better safety. The company has already won a GIS substation project and is bidding for
another tender in Daman involving build-install-maintain over 35 years with 100% subsidy and a distribution licence requirement.
The GIS vertical is cited as the highest-margin vertical, with a 30% gross margin.
Operation and Maintenance Division
A new recurring revenue division is being built around operation and maintenance of RMUs and HT connections. Gujarat currently
has approximately 20,000 RMUs, of which 5,000 are in the DGVCL area of South Gujarat. The current INR 11 bn order book
includes 2,000 RMU installations, with maintenance targeted at INR 80,000-90,000 per RMU per year, implying roughly INR 170-
180 mn annually. Additionally, around 4,000 private HT customers in South Gujarat are targeted for annual maintenance contracts
of approximately INR 0.1 mn each. This division carries 45% gross margin and provides recurring revenue visibility.
Financial Performance and Cash Flow
FY25 revenue stood at INR 3.41 bn with PAT of INR 130 mn, while H1FY26 revenue was INR 970 mn with PAT of INR 107 mn. The
company reported over 100% revenue CAGR over the past two years. Operating cash flow has remained negative at INR 4.646 mn
and INR 81.6 mn respectively, which the CFO attributed to the inherent working capital intensity of EPC businesses, including
retention money and tender-related margins. Management expects the operating cycle to trend toward zero and turn positive
over time as the business matures. Inventory days are around 6-7 days. Current fund-based limits are INR 200 mn and non-fund-
based limits are INR 800 mn, totalling INR 1 bn. The company has not availed mobilisation advances despite eligibility, preferring
to use internal accruals and working capital. Payment cycles from Gujarat government PSUs are 45-60 days, and management
noted no historical payment delays from these profitable PSUs.
Risk Mitigation
The company avoids overhead transmission line work, which constitutes less than 1% of the order book, because of right-of-way
and private property objections that cause project delays. Underground cabling is laid along highways, municipal roads and
panchayat roads, making approvals easier. Price escalation clauses are built into most government tenders and are typically
closed, insulating margins from metal price fluctuations. Insurance covers theft, third-party damage and force majeure for large
orders.

Prime Cable Industries Ltd
Outlook: Prime Cable Industries is positioned for strong growth, guided by 40-50% near-term revenue growth and a minimum 40%
CAGR through FY29-FY30, supported by a projected 5x expansion of the Indian cable market by 2030 and a persistent five-year
supply deficit across LV, MV and HV segments. The company is expanding its MV presence from 7 to 21 states, commercialising a
new INR 1.5 bn MV facility with peak potential of INR 2.5 bn by March 2027, and targeting 85% utilisation across three plants by
FY28. With a balanced 50:50 LV-MV revenue mix by FY28, a growing EPC-driven order book, 80% of orders protected by price
variation clauses, zero bad debts and a conservative funding policy based on internal cash generation, Prime Cable appears well-
placed to capture India's underground cabling, solar and grid modernisation demand while sustaining blended EBITDA margins of
12-12.5%.
Revenue and Guidance
• Prime Cable Industries targets 40-50% near-term revenue growth and a minimum 40% CAGR through FY29 and FY30. The
company quadrupled manufacturing capacity by 2020 and has broadened approvals across 20+ state transmission and
distribution boards, all Navratna companies, and every operating oil refinery in India for LV cables.
Market Size and Demand
• The 2024 Indian cable market was valued at ~INR 1,000 bn, with MV cables representing 30% or roughly INR 300 bn. The total
market is projected to expand 5x by 2030. A structural demand-supply gap exists across LV, MV and HV segments, expected to
persist for five years. Key demand drivers include the government's shift from overhead to underground cabling for disaster
resilience, exemplified by the Robust Gujarat project requiring approximately INR 220 bn in MV cables, alongside sustainable
energy, grid modernisation, and nationwide electrification.
Revenue Mix and Customer Channels
• By FY28, the target mix is 50% LV cables (solar, conductors, power, control, instrumentation) and 50% MV cables (3.3 kV to 33
kV). EPC contractors now generate over 50% of revenue, up from 30% two years ago. The strategy involves supplying state
power boards and Navratna companies first to build track records, then unlocking higher-volume EPC orders on superior
payment terms. MV utility presence expanded from 1 to 7 states, with plans to enter 14 more over two years.
Product Portfolio and Certifications
• The company manufactures LV and MV cables from 3.3 kV to 33 kV across 600+ SKUs, with third-party quality verification for
nearly all MV SKUs. It secured in-house NABL certification for its MV testing laboratory, enabling testing of sensitive cables for
state utilities and Navratna enterprises. In solar cables, against an INR 50-60 bn domestic market, Prime Cable obtained a BIS
licence after a 365-day accelerated UV ageing test, generating initial orders of INR 70-80 mn. BIS certifications were expanded
across aluminium conductor standards IS 398 (Parts 2, 4, 6), with AL59 conductors developed, STLS conductors under research,
and covered conductors added.
Margins and Cost Savings
• LV cables yield 9-12% EBITDA margins; MV cables yield 14-15%. At peak utilisation across all three plants by FY28, blended
EBITDA margin is projected at 12-12.5%. Continuous process optimisation, material polymer experiments, and R&D design
efforts aim to minimise production costs and maintain price competitiveness.
Order Book and Breakup
• Prime Cable holds MV orders from four major Navratna companies. In LV, it serves 600+ EPC contractors, maintains approvals
in 20+ state transmission and distribution boards, and is approved with every operating oil refinery in India. Initial order sizes
in new institutional segments are capped until a proven utility supply track record is built. PQRs, type testing, third-party lab
validations, and BIS licences are prerequisites.
Capacity, Utilisation, and Expansion
• LV capacity was quadrupled by 2020 and reached over 350 units by 2024, with MV entry in 2025. The Ghiloth campus in
Rajasthan is at 80% utilisation. Management targets 85% peak utilisation across all three plants by end-FY28. A new MV
expansion goes live next month, adding INR 1.5 bn initial revenue capacity, with peak potential of INR 2.5 bn by March 2027.

• The MV manufacturing cycle is 40-45 days, plus 40-60 day client payment terms, creating an 80-100 day baseline working

Business model: Priority Jewels is a pure-play B2B, design-led diamond-studded jewellery manufacturer with end-to-end
capabilities from design to manufacturing, serving 200+ customers across India, the Middle East, Europe and the US.
Affordable jewellery focus: The company is focused on lightweight, affordable and everyday-wear diamond jewellery, using
design and technology to offer larger-looking products at lower price points.
Strong design engine: The company develops 8,000+ new designs annually, supported by customer sell-through data, market
research and trend analysis, which remains a key competitive differentiator.
India-led business: India contributes ~50% of revenue, with the balance coming from the Middle East, US and Europe. Q1FY27

Studded jewellery dominates: Studded jewellery contributed ~80-85% of Q1FY27 revenue, while the company also has a growing

Customer diversification: The top five customers contributed ~33% of overall revenue, while the contribution of the largest

Affordable category growth: Everyday affordable jewellery is growing at ~14% CAGR, with rings and earrings being the fastest-
moving categories. Management expects continued opportunity from Gen Z and working-women segments.

because the mix shifted sharply from 18-carat to 14-carat and 9-carat jewellery as gold prices increased.

CAGR during FY24-26 and PAT at a 57.1% CAGR.
Improving returns and leverage: ROE improved to 18% and ROCE to 27.7% in Q1FY27, while the debt-equity ratio declined
materially from 1.32x to 0.76x.
Gold price risk largely hedged: Gold is procured through Gold Metal Loans from banks, with ~118 days available to complete the

Exports offer runway: The company has customers across the US, Middle East and Europe, including both Indian-origin retailers

Prostarm Info Systems Ltd

BESS, competing largely with global MNCs (Schneider, Vertiv, Eaton, Hitachi) rather than local players in its critical/customised UPS

segment growth for FY27, EBITDA margins of 13-14%, and per-vertical UPS revenue potential of INR 1-1.5 bn over the next 1-2 years.
Operating cash flow was negative INR 480 mn at March-end, improving to negative INR 150 mn in June. Key monitorables are
lithium pricing and China supply-chain developments, execution of the Bihar and Karnataka BESS projects, data centre/export order
conversion, and margin trajectory.
Business Model & Positioning
• Prostarm has operated since 2008, initially focused on IT and BFSI (banks, ATMs), before broadening into UPS, inverters, hybrid
solar inverters, lithium batteries and, more recently, energy storage systems.
• A 2020 acquisition of a Pune-based UPS technology company enabled entry into metro, airport, railway, healthcare, toll and
defence applications, with installations at Patna metro, Bengaluru and Nagpur airports, and UPS/storage supply to Northern and
Western Railways.
• The company also supplies customised UPS for continuous-process machinery (laser cutting, laser welding) and complex oil &
gas applications requiring transformers, servo stabilisers and control panels; few Indian players compete in this segment.
• Management's stated strategy is to compete mainly against global MNCs (Schneider, Vertiv, Eaton, Hitachi, Fuji) in these
critical/customised verticals rather than local players, which it sees as an easier position once initial qualification barriers are

Business Profile and Main Board Migration

Raama Finance Ltd
Outlook: The company is positioned to benefit from the growing demand for short-tenure digital personal loans, supported by a
large underserved customer base, increasing digital penetration, repeat borrowers and expansion across Tier-1/2/3 cities. The sharp
Q1FY27 improvement demonstrates the scalability of the model; however, sustainability of growth remains unproven as
management has not provided forward guidance. Asset quality, NPAs, funding costs and collection efficiency will remain key
monitorables, particularly given the unsecured portfolio and high customer APRs.
Business Model
• The company focuses on short-term, unsecured personal loans under the "Fast Salary" brand, with ticket sizes of INR 5,000-
120,000 and average ticket size of ~INR 45,000.
• Loan tenure is 30-60 days, with a fully digital journey enabling disbursal within 45-60 minutes.
• Target customers are salaried individuals aged 25-45 years, earning INR 25,000-100,000 per month, primarily in Tier-1/2/3 cities.
• It uses AI, APIs, KYC automation and rule-based underwriting to assess customers and process loans digitally.
Q1FY27 Performance
• The company disbursed INR 440 mn to 10,373 customers in Q1FY27, with loans processed of INR 485.2 mn.
• Revenue stood at INR 213.1 mn, including INR 174.3 mn of interest income; PBT was INR 65.9 mn.
• Business was supported by renewed focus on the segment and greater use of digital customer-acquisition tools.
Collection Efficiency
• Around 40-45% of customers pre-close their loans before the due date, while ~50% repay on the due date.
• Overall, ~90% of scheduled collections are received by/on the due date, with the remaining ~10% requiring additional collection
efforts.
• Loans are entirely unsecured, with no collateral/security taken.
Customer Proposition
• The competitive advantage lies primarily in speed, convenience and digital execution, rather than lower interest rates.
• The company targets customers underserved by banks who require quick, short-tenure credit for needs such as medical
emergencies, weddings, home renovation and other exigencies.
• Repeat customers account for ~70% of the customer base, supporting lower acquisition friction and repeat business.
Growth Opportunity
• Raama Finance is currently focused on the short-term personal-loan segment, with no immediate diversification indicated.
• Its presence has expanded to 500 cities and 6,700+ PIN codes, with 1,200+ employers integrated into the platform.
• Management highlighted a large underserved market, with digital lending expected to expand significantly and NBFC
participation gaining share from banks.
Growth Outlook
• Management indicated that the business should improve but did not provide forward-looking guidance on quarterly
performance, loan-book growth or customer additions.
• The strong Q1 performance was attributed to renewed business focus and better utilisation of available digital tools.
• Management's current priority remains scaling the existing business rather than entering new lending segments.
Interest Economics
• Customer APR currently ranges from 470% to 500%, varying based on credit history and prior relationship with the company.
• Management could not provide the current cost of borrowing, stating that the data would be shared subsequently.
• High customer APR reflects the short-tenure, unsecured nature of the product and the risk profile of the target segment.
Asset Quality
• Management did not disclose the current NPA level or expected impairment cost during the call and committed to revert with
the numbers.
• Given the unsecured nature of the portfolio, asset quality and collection performance remain key monitorables.
Digital Platform
• Loan disbursement currently happens through the company's website, rather than a mobile application.
• A dedicated app is under development and is expected to be introduced subsequently. The digital journey covers application,
KYC, documentation, e-signing, e-mandate, approval, disbursement and repayment.
Competition
• Management believes the addressable market remains sufficiently large, with a significant portion of customers still
underserved. Rather than competing aggressively for an existing customer pool, the company is focused on penetrating the
untapped Tier-1, Tier-2 and Tier-3 customer base.
• Management did not comment specifically on competitors such as Apollo Finvest.

Raj Rayon Industries Ltd
Raj Rayon Industries is a polyester filament yarn turnaround story, taken over by the SVG group about three years ago, with
integrated value addition from polymer to chips, chips to POY and POY to DTY. The company added ~50 TPD of capacity during a
brief shutdown in April 2026 and is now running at ~400 TPD, with all capacity sold out. An expansion to ~700 TPD over the next two
years has been announced, with a capex of ~INR 6.5 bn funded through ~INR 3.5 bn of primary equity (also bringing promoter
holding down to 75%), INR 1.5-2.0 bn of debt and internal accruals. EBITDA margin has improved from ~1% to ~6% over three years
and is targeted to rise to 10-12% as value-added products scale up. Management targets revenue of ~INR 30 bn within 2-3 years (at
earlier, pre-hike prices). Raw material price increases have been fully passed on so far, and Q2FY27 is expected to be better than Q1
on both volume and realisation. The key factors to monitor are the equity raise and its timing, capex execution, crude/PTA price
volatility and spreads, value-added product mix, export ramp-up and related-party dependence on SVG.
Business Model & Positioning
• Raj Rayon is a turnaround story, taken over by the SVG group about three years ago; since then, production, topline and bottom
line have increased significantly.
• The company is integrated across multiple value-addition stages (polymer to chips, chips to POY and POY to DTY), with further
downstream processing done by SVG, which provides insulation in sales and pricing.
• SVG is a market leader in polyester athleisure and athletic wear, known for customised textile solutions for high value-added
clients; Raj Rayon aims to follow the same culture and lead in value-added products rather than volume.
• Raj Rayon's product is well established and sought after in the market, with a value-added and customised product basket
comparable to top industry players; all capacity is currently sold out.
Capacity & Expansion Plan
• ~50 TPD of capacity was added during a brief shutdown in April 2026; the company is now running at ~400 TPD, with the added
capacity reflecting in Q2FY27 along with value addition.
• An expansion plan has been announced to increase capacity to ~700 TPD over the next two years, effectively doubling capacity,
with value addition increasing alongside.
• New machinery being added is for value-added products, vertical integration and value addition at each stage.
• Growth over the past three years has come from a mix of volume increase, value addition and product mix, and this trend is
expected to continue over the next two to three years.
Funding & Shareholding
• Total capex is ~INR 6.5 bn, of which ~INR 3.5 bn will be raised as primary capital, with the balance through debt of ~INR 1.5-2.0
bn and internal accruals.
• Promoter holding is high and must be reduced to 75%; the primary capital raise will help achieve this.
• The dilution is planned over the next ~6 months; the route (QIP, rights issue or similar) is being finalised with merchant bankers,
with the aim of bringing growth capital into the company.
Related Party Transactions
• SVG produces ~40 TPD, of which ~25-30 TPD is bought from Raj Rayon at arm's length, which is very small relative to Raj Rayon's
~400 TPD production.
• Going forward, not more than ~15% of Raj Rayon's production is expected to go to SVG.
• Raj Rayon and SVG do not compete with each other; competition from SVG's followers is seen as normal and not a concern for
marketing.
Raw Material, Spreads & Demand
• Crude-led raw material price increases have so far been fully passed on to customers; if prices keep rising, demand could
plateau and pressure margins. New upstream paraxylene capacity in China could narrow supplier spreads and ease raw material
prices.

• Spreads compressed in April-May 2026 as players booked inventory gains and sold cheaply, expecting the price rise to be

Japan, many of which SVG itself imports today.
Industry Outlook
• India imports ~2.4 mn tonnes of PTA; MEG is not structurally short. GAIL and IOC Paradip PTA capacities (expected in ~6 months)
should make India self-sufficient in 2027, and Reliance's ~3.2 mn tonne Dahej plant (end-2027 or early 2028) would create a
surplus.
• With self-sufficiency, domestic PTA pricing is expected to move from import parity to below import parity, which could widen
spreads for Raj Rayon by ~1-2%, along with a possible price war and consolidation favouring newer, efficient plants.
• No significant polyester capacity is expected in the next 1-2 years after Sanatan; IOC's announced ~1,000 TPD Odisha plant and
Reliance's plans are unlikely within 2-3 years. India could be ~2,000 TPD short, similar to current import volumes, so oversupply
risk is low.
• Polyester demand grew 7-8% last year (versus 5-6% historically), and polyester is the only fibre that can meet incremental global
demand. India is expected to expand capacity as the main alternative to China.
Exports & Sustainability
• Export enquiries are increasing; India currently faces a ~2-4% price disadvantage versus China, and domestic realisations are
better, so the company prefers the domestic market for now.
• As domestic raw material surplus emerges, exports are expected to rise sharply, with value-added and customised products
exported first; management expects significant exports to start by end-2027. Newer plants such as Raj Rayon are expected to
gain the lion's share.
• FTAs (UK, EU) will benefit fabric exporters and indirectly lift yarn demand as customers export more, rather than impacting Raj
Rayon's yarn sales directly.
• SVG has recycled 300 mn+ bottles through a certified, traceable process over two decades; Raj Rayon is planning recycled and
responsible manufacturing, targeting a net-zero waste and emissions plant, and will meet SVG's recycled yarn demand along
with broader brand demand.
