Distribution & Retail Expansion
The company has 60+ super stockists, 600+ distributors and 40,000+ retail outlets across 15+ states, with Gujarat contributing ~50-
60% of revenue versus ~80% five years ago. Freezer deployment remains a key growth driver, with ~8,000 freezers deployed
annually over the last five years. The company plans to increase this to ~12,000-15,000 in the current year and further scale
deployment from the following year. Each freezer generates ~INR 0.2 mn of annual revenue on average.
Quick Commerce & Channel Expansion
Quick commerce is currently at an early stage, with products recently listed across 300+ Blinkit stores. The company is in
discussions with Zepto and Swiggy Instamart and plans to expand aggressively across platforms. Domestic sales remain largely
driven by general trade, contributing >98% of domestic revenue, while quick commerce is expected to support broader brand
availability over time.
Manufacturing & Capacity Utilisation
The company operates two manufacturing units, with the main Amreli facility having ~200,000 litres per day of milk processing
capacity, alongside capacities of ~1.7 mn candies, 1.1+ mn ice cream cups and ~700,000 cones per day. Overall capacity utilisation
is ~75% annually and reaches ~100% during summer. A small expansion is underway, while a new plant may be considered as
demand increases.
Product Portfolio & Innovation
Ice cream remains the core and highest-margin business, with 200+ SKUs across cups, cones, candies, novelties and take-home
packs. The company is expanding premium products such as 3D-shaped and fruit-shaped ice creams and is developing high-
protein and low/no-sugar variants. High-protein flavoured milk and lassi products are also being introduced, while fruit juices are
currently not under consideration.
Exports & Ready-to-Eat Products
Exports contribute ~7-8% of revenue and have grown consistently since entry post-COVID, with Japan, the Middle East and the US
among key markets. Growth is primarily driven by ready-to-eat/ready-to-cook and frozen products. A dedicated facility has
recently been commissioned for this segment after the existing plant reached peak capacity.
Cost Efficiency & Integration
The company has undertaken backward integration across corrugated boxes, packaging sleeves, biscuit cones and chocolate
syrup/toppings, while directly procuring milk from farmers and bulk unions. It operates 70+ refrigerated vehicles, helping manage
distribution costs, with freight expenses targeted at ~5-8% of revenue. More than 75% of electricity requirements are met through
captive renewable assets, supporting cost efficiency.
Margins & Milk Procurement
Ice cream remains the company's highest-margin business, while the company continues to focus on dairy as its core segment.
Recent milk price increases were attributed to higher demand for regular paneer following restrictions on analogue paneer in
Gujarat and Maharashtra. The company has been able to pass on higher milk costs through price increases and pack-size
adjustments, while paying farmers/bulk unions within 3-4 days to secure cash discounts.
Growth Strategy
Revenue has remained broadly flat at ~INR 3,400-3,500 mn over the last five years, impacted by slower general trade expansion,
higher freezer deployment costs and the time required to establish new markets. Going forward, growth is expected to be driven
by aggressive freezer deployment, expansion across core and newer markets, quick-commerce penetration, premiumisation,
exports and scaling of ready-to-eat/ready-to-cook products. Recently raised funds are being deployed towards freezer expansion,
advertising and branding.

Shera Energy is a Jaipur-based non-ferrous metals company and one of India's largest winding wire producers, manufacturing PICC,
enamelled and superfine enamelled wires, bunched conductors and busbars, with the group spanning copper, aluminium and brass
across recycling (Rajputana Industries), processing and finished products, and exports to 15+ countries. Consolidated revenue grew

MTPA capacity. Q1FY27 was the highest-ever quarter, with revenue of INR 4,877.7 mn (+26% YoY), EBITDA of INR 309.1 mn (+57%)
and PAT of INR 126.4 mn (+79%), and H1FY27 revenue has crossed INR 10 bn. Management's FY30 vision is 25-30% annual revenue
growth, aided by new value-added products (CTC, bunched PICC, PV ribbon) and the Zambian copper cathode project, where trial
production yielded 8.6 MT of 99.99% pure cathode, with revenue of ~INR 0.9-1.0 bn expected in the first year and INR 3-4 bn in the

(ore sourcing, sulphide recovery and capacity expansion), PGCIL approval for CTC, resumption of Hitachi Energy supplies, the
Rajputana amalgamation, main board migration, PAT margin expansion and operating cash flow.
Business Model & Positioning
• Established in Jaipur in 2003 by the CMD, who had worked with transformers, the company began by making winding wires for
the electrical industry and is today a Jaipur-based non-ferrous metals company exporting to more than 15 countries.
• Product range includes paper insulated copper and aluminium conductors (PICC), enamelled winding wires, superfine enamelled
wires, bunched conductors and busbars; the group also produces rods, tubes and sections of copper and brass.
• Group structure: Shera Energy holds 85.55% in Shera Metal Pvt Ltd (forward integration), 51.01% in listed Rajputana Industries
Ltd (recycling and upstream) and 99.5% in Shera Zambia Ltd (copper cathode).
• Rajputana recycles non-ferrous scrap into usable metals, wires and rods, helping the group recover value and control part of its
supply chain; India's developing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework for non-ferrous metals offers a further
opportunity for qualified recyclers.
• End markets include power transformers, T&D equipment, motors, appliances, industrial machinery, automobiles and solar
modules; ~80-85% of revenue comes from transformer manufacturers (mainly low and medium voltage) and ~15-20% from
other applications.
• Winding wires contribute ~80% of revenue; the closest listed peers are Precision Wires, RR Wires and Vidya Wires, though the
company also does aluminium, in-house recycling and brass, which limits like-for-like comparison.
• Copper price risk is hedged through a hedging desk that books all daily sales back-to-back with suppliers on LME basis, with no
open positions, so profitability is not affected by copper price movements.
Financial Performance
• FY23-FY26: consolidated revenue grew from INR 6.96 bn to INR 16.4 bn (~33% CAGR), EBITDA from INR 400 mn to INR 940 mn
(~33% CAGR) and PAT from INR 90 mn to INR 370 mn (~60% CAGR).
• Production rose from ~21,300 MT to ~36,500 MT (~20% CAGR); management attributed the ~33% revenue CAGR to ~20%
volume growth and ~13% value upgradation.
• Capacity utilisation reached 78% in FY26 versus 74% in FY25, on a total capacity of ~46,000+ MTPA, which includes the recycling
and forward integration businesses.
• Q1FY27 consolidated revenue stood at INR 4,877.7 mn (+26% YoY, highest-ever quarter), EBITDA at INR 309.1 mn (+57%) and
PAT at INR 126.4 mn (+79%), entirely from existing operations, as new value-added lines and Zambia are not yet in commercial
production.
• PAT margin improved from ~2.25% in FY26 to over 2.5% in Q1FY27; management expects further improvement from operating
leverage and value-added products but did not quantify a target.

Shri Kanha Stainless Ltd
Business
Shri Kanha makes stainless steel coils, sheets and circles at Ringas, ~55 km from Jaipur. The promoter family has 35+ years in steel,
the company was incorporated in 2015, and it listed in December 2025 at an IPO price of INR 90.
Capacity is ~14,000 tonnes a year, with utilisation of ~60-70%. Coils are ~90-95% of sales.
It rolls from 0.08 mm to 2 mm thick. Management says only 1-2 Indian makers go as thin as 0.08 mm, against ~0.15-0.2 mm for
most, which earns a price premium. Material of 0.08-0.2 mm is ~25-30% of sales.
Customers span textiles, automotive, electronics, utensils, sinks and elevators. About 90% of sales go through distributors, many
with 10+ year relationships, and the top 10 make ~70% of repeat orders.
FY26 revenue was ~INR 2,050-2,100 mn (+41%) and PAT ~INR 90-110 mn (+51%). EBITDA margin is ~9-10%, up from ~3-3.5% before
the IPO after the move into thinner gauges. The promoter family holds ~68-69%.
Guidance and Capex
A 1,250 mm 4-high AGC rolling mill is being installed for ~INR 120 mn, with the machine advance already paid and no further
fundraise needed. Management says it will be the third such mill in India.
It is expected to be operational by ~September 2027.
Management agreed that revenue could reach ~INR 3,000-3,600 mn after the expansion, without providing formal guidance.
Utilisation of ~80-85% is targeted by end-FY29.
PAT margin is expected at ~5-7%, and the capex payback at ~4-5 years.
Future plans include a solar mounting structures plant, a return to exports (Europe and Latin America, paused because of taxes) and
backward integration into melting scrap at ~40,000 tonnes of demand.
Working Capital and Balance Sheet
The order book is ~INR 120-130 mn and executes in 4-5 weeks. Orders are not taken beyond ~2 months, and prices are locked at the
time of order.
Pass-through of steel price changes is achieved by repricing new orders. Management uses stock levels as its only hedge.
Debtors are ~INR 890 mn, of which ~INR 240 mn is older than 6 months, with credit periods of 15 days to 4 months. Management
says all of it is recoverable.
Debt is ~INR 530 mn at ~8-9% interest.
Raw material comes from Jindal Stainless and importers. BIS quality control orders on stainless steel imports support domestic
demand.
Listed peers cited include Hisar Metal.

Simplex Castings Ltd
Simplex Castings is a heavy engineering castings and fabrication company (founded in 1970) with two units in Chhattisgarh (a
foundry at Bhilai and a fabrication/equipment-building unit at Tedesara, Rajnandgaon district), capable of single-piece castings up to
65 tonnes and fabricated pieces up to 80 tonnes. The company reported revenue of INR 2+ bn in FY26 and is targeting INR 3+ bn in
FY27 and INR 5+ bn in FY28, driven by thermal power, steel and railways. The order book stood at ~INR 1.5 bn at the end of Q1FY27,
deliberately maintained at this level to avoid liquidated damages (LD) risk. Railway bogie orders (targeted at INR 500 mn for FY27)
have been delayed, but management has made the Bhilai unit fungible with BHEL-approved fabrication capacity and maintains FY27
guidance of INR 3 bn with ~19% EBITDA margin, with or without railways. Management is targeting ~40% growth through FY31,
supported by completed capex, an INR 470 mn preferential issue and a recently announced ~INR 1 bn fundraise. The key factors to
monitor are railway order inflows, thermal order execution, commodity price pass-through, inventory levels, captive solar
implementation and margin sustainability.
Business Model & Positioning
• The company was founded in 1970 as a partnership firm and converted into a private limited company in 1980. It operates a
dedicated foundry with machine, fabrication and CNC shops at Bhilai, and a fabrication/equipment-building unit at Tedesara
(Rajnandgaon district) making large equipment such as torpedo ladle cars and sucker rod pumps.
• Simplex is known for heavy castings, ranging from a few kilos to 65 tonnes in a single piece, and fabricated pieces up to 80
tonnes; it is recognised for import substitution products.
• It is the only company apart from L&T making torpedo ladle cars, and is the market leader in zero-leakage coke oven doors
supplied to steel plants in India and abroad.
• The company has supplied 12,000+ bogies running on Indian Railways, has exported to GE and Electro-Motive Diesel (USA), is a
star export house and has been part of the bogie design standards committee.
Revenue Guidance & Segment Mix
• Revenue was INR 2+ bn in FY26; the company targets INR 3+ bn in FY27 and INR 5+ bn in FY28 with the addition of thermal
power projects.
• Management is targeting a similar ~40% growth rate till FY31, while acknowledging it as a challenge.
• Targeted segment mix: ~40% steel, ~40% thermal (till 2032) and ~20% shipbuilding, defence, machine tools and others. Railways
are expected to scale up to ~40% to replace thermal after 2032.
• The strategic aim is to have ~40-50% repetitive railway items in both units (cast and fabricated) for shorter working capital cycles
and fixed-line utilisation, with the balance capacity used for higher-margin niche products.
Thermal Power & Steel
• Thermal power is seeing a strong upcycle with projects awarded to BHEL and L&T; tendering is via GeM, with 9,000-10,000
tonnes of orders released every month. Around 48 power plants are to be established by 2032.
• Both units are approved for thermal orders for four years; the company has previously won BHEL's best supplier award. The
Bhilai fabrication division is approved by BHEL, with Adani and L&T approvals in the pipeline.
• Demand exceeds industry capacity, with the industry approaching the PMO for imports from China, which was declined. Only
four to five players operate in heavy technological structures (e.g., Simplex Engineering among others), while other companies
are also expanding.
• In steel, Simplex has won the door bodies in all four recent coke oven work orders released in India (a virtual monopoly in zero-
leakage doors); one order has gone to ThyssenKrupp, and management is confident of winning that as well.
• Nuclear is a future opportunity, where the company has supplied certain materials.

SIS Ltd
SIS is a diversified business services company spanning security, facility management (FM) and cash logistics in India, along with a
large international (Australia-led) security business. FY26 marked a return of growth momentum along with the AP Securitas
acquisition, consolidated in H2FY26. Q1FY27 grew ~20% YoY and management expects ~18-20% growth for FY27, with PAT expected
to rise 18-20% to ~INR 4.35-4.40 bn. India security is growing ~15%, FM ~11-12% (with EBITDA growth of over 15%) and
international over 20% on currency tailwinds and large domestic wins in Australia. Management sees stable margins of ~5.5% in
India security (from 5.1%), ~4.4% in international (from ~4%) and ~6% in FM. FCF of ~INR 4.5 bn is expected in FY27, with at least 30-
33% to be returned to shareholders and the balance largely for debt reduction. The new labour codes are expected to accelerate
formalisation and market share gains for organised players. The key factors to monitor are AP Securitas margin integration, gratuity
recovery from clients, state-level labour code implementation, working capital, capital allocation between buybacks and debt
reduction, and the UDS stake.
Business Overview & FY27 Outlook
• FY26 was a strong year with business growth momentum returning and the AP Securitas acquisition consolidated in H2FY26; its
full effect is visible in Q1 and Q2 of FY27, after which the base resets from Q3.
• Q1FY27 was ~20% higher YoY, and Q2 is expected to show similar growth. Management expects ~18-20% growth for FY27, which
it considers "in the bank".
• India security is growing ~15%; FM growth is picking up at 11-12% with EBITDA growth of over 15%; international is expected to
grow over 20%, aided by currency tailwinds and large wins in the domestic Australian market.
• While the company does not give formal guidance, management is confident of 18-20% PAT growth in FY27, implying PAT of
~INR 4.35-4.40 bn as the quarterly run-rate inches up.
• Pricing in the business is stable with no erosion or increase; growth is driven by volumes and new wins.
Segment Margins
• International: margins fell to ~3.5% after client attrition and a management change at a high-margin subsidiary, and recovered
to ~4%. Management models ~4% as stable in the near term, returning to the historical ~4.4-4.5% in about a year.
• FM: margins had dropped to ~4%; after renegotiating or exiting low-margin contracts, FM is now operating at ~6%, which
management considers optimal, with scope to go higher over time.
• India security: historically ~5.5%; currently ~5.1% due to consolidation of the lower-margin AP Securitas (~4%). Management
expects to lift AP Securitas margins by ~100 bps to ~5% over two years, taking India security back to ~5.5%.
AP Securitas Acquisition
• AP Securitas was acquired at ~4% EBITDA margin; it has ~INR 1.2 bn of monthly revenue and has grown at an ~18% CAGR over
the last five years (15%+ YoY currently).
• It is one of the top six to seven security companies in India, with a stable management team and strong BFSI clients (such as
HDFC Bank), filling SIS's gap in BFSI exposure. Management stated it was a value acquisition, not a distressed purchase.
• The current structure is 51:49; SIS is obligated to buy out the remaining 49% by the end of FY28.
• The brand will continue separately, while back-office and HR functions will be integrated over the next two to three years.
Capital Allocation & Cash Flows
• SIS has maintained 70%+ OCF/EBITDA since listing and generates 100%+ of PAT as FCF; FCF of ~INR 4.5 bn is expected in FY27,
with a larger number next year.
• FY27 EBITDA is expected at ~INR 8.5 bn, with 70-75% conversion into OCF.

• At least 30-33% of cash generated is expected to be returned to shareholders through dividends, buybacks or a mix; buybacks

Labour Codes & Gratuity Provision
• Following the labour code notification in November, the company took a conservative upfront gratuity provision in Q3FY26
(initially INR 2.8 bn, revised to INR 2.4 bn), as the definition of basic wage was revised to 50% of total emoluments, creating a
retrospective liability.
• The provision is non-cash and not an immediate liability. The labour codes came into legal effect from 9 May 2026.
• The company is renegotiating ~25,000 contracts in line with the new codes. Recovery is expected from continuing customers
over time, while recovery from discontinued customers is uncertain. High attrition means part of the liability may never
crystallise, and some customers may reimburse on actual payout. The split between continuing and discontinued customers was
not available.
• States have not yet formally enacted the labour code rules (draft model rules are out); management expects notification within
two to three months.
Working Capital
• Overall DSO is ~63-65 days: international ~45 days (automatic payments), India security ~75 days from start of duty (~45 days
post bill submission) and FM ~85-90 days.
• Clients have not yet started paying earlier. To comply with the requirement to pay wages by the 7th of the month, SIS is
proposing to move the wage cut-off to the 20th-25th so that invoices are processed and paid by the 5th-6th; negotiations are
ongoing and adoption will be gradual.
Cash Logistics & Other Businesses
• ATM exposure is only ~15-18% of the cash business; SIS does not own ATMs and has no managed service provider model, acting
as a pure service provider on fixed-price bank contracts.
• The business focuses on bank and retail cash movement, which is growing in line with GDP. MDR implementation from 15
October is expected to bring more cash back into the economy.
• Growth in cash logistics has slowed but not declined. The SIS Prosegur IPO has been deferred given the sharp fall in the market
leader's (CMS) stock.
• Vprotect (electronic security) saw tenders largely stall over the last 1-1.5 years due to the STQC certification requirement for
cameras; the long-term outlook remains positive, as remote surveillance costs ~INR 6,000-7,000 per month versus INR 60,000-
70,000 for two fully compliant guards.
Industry Dynamics & Strategic Stake
• The security market is ~INR 1,000-1,500 bn, of which only ~20% is organised; the top 10-15 players account for INR 200-250 bn,
with SIS at INR 80-90 bn in security.
• Labour code digitisation (single challan, Labour Identification Number, Shram portal visibility for clients) is expected to make
low-margin informal players unviable, shifting business to large organised players.
• Rising minimum wages (e.g., 50%+ increase in Haryana) are positive for SIS, as its management fee is charged as a percentage of
wages.
• SIS's FM business is at ~INR 28 bn, expected to become an ~INR 30 bn pure-play FM business next year. SIS acquired a ~10%
stake in UDS (INR 20+ bn FM plus ~INR 10 bn other services) at an attractive price, seeing long-term consolidation potential;
management clarified there has been no communication with UDS and all options, including exit, remain open.
• AI is not seen as a direct threat; it could indirectly affect demand via slower commercial real estate build-out, but tech-enabled
solutions (cameras, access control, robo dogs, monitoring centres) make services more effective, though ROI does not yet justify
replacing manpower. SIS works with defence establishments in Australia but there is no such opportunity in India.

Growth Outlook and Guidance
• The company expects to deliver 1.5-2x the underlying industry growth on a blended basis, driven by increasing content per
vehicle, premiumisation, cross-selling and new product introductions.
• It remains focused on sustaining high growth while maintaining EBITDA margins above 25%, with FY26 EBITDA margin at

Business Mix and Content per Vehicle

Optical Glass and Display Business

Export Opportunity and Margin Profile

• Export business generates ~4-5 percentage points higher EBITDA margins than domestic business, supported by India's cost
competitiveness in labour-intensive and complex printing products.
• SJS supplies products to more than 22 countries and serves ~170 customer locations globally, with established relationships
across automotive and appliance customers.
• The company is expanding its international reach through customer cross-selling, sales representation in Germany and a
variable-cost agency model, supported by recently added manufacturing capacity.

SKP Bearing Industries Ltd
Revenue Growth & Outlook
• 15% organic growth target: Management expects revenue to grow at ~15% organically, with margins remaining sustainable.
Growth could improve further if external factors turn favourable.
• FY27 revenue trajectory: Despite discontinuing low-margin trading sales that had adversely impacted profitability, management
expects revenue to increase over FY26 levels, with improved margins.
• India revenue potential: At full plant utilisation and the targeted product mix, the Indian business could generate revenue of ~INR
1,500 mn. Management expects a steady increase in utilisation and revenue over the next 2-3 years.
• Export growth ambition: Exports are targeted to increase from ~4% of revenue currently to 10% by FY28, supported by new
global customer relationships and cross-border sourcing opportunities.
India Capacity Expansion & Utilisation
• Roller capacity ramp-up: The expanded roller capacity is operating at ~78% utilisation, with further capacity additions planned
during FY27. Management indicated that the business is already operating at healthy utilisation levels.
• Ball capacity ramp-up: Ball plant utilisation stands at ~17%, but management expects a sharp improvement during FY27. Three
customers are expected to account for ~75% of the newly added capacity.
• OEM approvals driving growth: The company has secured approvals from major OEMs for its ball products, with commercial
volumes expected to ramp up as customers increase production. The timing and pace of volume conversion remain key
monitorables.
• High-return capacity additions: Management highlighted attractive returns on incremental investments, with capacity expansion
being undertaken alongside customer demand visibility. However, the ball division's low current utilisation indicates scope for
operating leverage as volumes scale up.
France Acquisition
• Revenue recovery remains the key priority: The French subsidiary, acquired in 2024, was generating annual revenue of ~EUR 8-
8.5 mn before the acquisition, while incurring losses of ~EUR 2 mn. Management is targeting a recovery towards EUR 16 mn
revenue as quickly as possible.
• Customer re-engagement progressing: Several legacy customers discontinued supplies following the ownership transition.
Management indicated that discussions with these customers have continued, with some customers already returning and
others undergoing supplier evaluation.
• Turnaround largely focused on revenue recovery: Management stated that cost-optimisation initiatives are nearing completion,
with the focus now shifting towards higher volumes, customer reactivation and improved capacity utilisation.
• ~EUR 3 mn cash outflow to date: Cumulative cash outflow from India towards the French entity is approximately EUR 3 mn,
including the operating losses and associated investments over the three-year period. Management stated that the acquisition
itself involved no upfront purchase consideration, with employee liabilities and subsequent operating/upgrade costs constituting
the financial commitment.
• Significant operating leverage potential: The French facility has substantial installed capacity and a large asset base, including
~400 machines/assets. Management is prioritising higher utilisation through customer orders and operational improvements
rather than asset disposal or fresh capacity expansion.
India-France Synergies & Global Customer Strategy
• Dual-continent manufacturing proposition: The India and France facilities provide global customers with manufacturing options
across Asia and Europe, supporting supply-chain diversification and risk mitigation. Management believes this is particularly
relevant for multinational OEMs seeking to reduce dependence on China.
• Technology and cost synergies: The company is integrating manufacturing capabilities across India and France, including sourcing
materials and services from India to optimise costs at the French facility. Certain machines from France have also been
redeployed to India.
• Cross-selling opportunities: SKP intends to leverage its combined product portfolio and geographic footprint to access
multinational customers operating across multiple countries. Management highlighted that global sourcing decisions involve
lengthy qualification and approval processes.
• Legacy customer recovery remains gradual: While customer discussions and evaluations are progressing, the timing of order
conversion remains uncertain, given the stringent requirements of global OEMs and their focus on supplier stability.
Margin Outlook & Product Mix
• Standalone margins expected to remain sustainable: Management indicated that Indian business margins are broadly sustainable
at historical levels, excluding the weaker Q4FY26, which was affected by an unsuccessful product initiative and associated
spillover costs.
• Ball margins structurally lower than rollers: Management highlighted an approximately 30% margin differential between balls
and rollers, with balls being relatively more commoditised. The product mix will therefore be important as ball capacity utilisation
increases.
• Trading sales discontinued: The company has exited certain trading activities that were not economically beneficial and had
adversely affected margins. The resulting improvement in profitability is expected to support margin expansion despite
potentially lower incremental revenue from trading.
• Renewable energy supports profitability: The company's wind and solar assets are fully depreciated and debt-free, according to
management. Captive renewable power provides a cost advantage and contributes positively to profitability.

Business
• SMC has been in broking for 30 years and runs four businesses: broking (full-service SMC Global and discount broker
StocksCart), an NBFC (Moneywise Financial Services), insurance broking (SMC Insurance Brokers) and wealth management and
distribution.
• The group has ~2 mn clients in total. Full-service broking has ~1 mn, StocksCart ~0.4 mn, and other entities the rest. The group
opens ~15,000-20,000 demat accounts a month.
• Broking DP AUA is ~INR 1,650 bn, and the broking margin trading (MTF) book exceeds INR 11,000 mn, separate from the NBFC.
• Clients are ~40% in the North, ~30% East, ~20% West and below 10% South. There are 190+ branches.
• Group net worth is ~INR 12,500 mn: ~INR 5,000 mn in the NBFC, ~INR 7,500 mn in broking and wealth, and ~INR 200-250 mn in
insurance.
• FY26 ROE was 8.2% and ROCE 11.5%.
Guidance
• FY27 revenue is budgeted to grow ~20% YoY (as given in the annual report), and management is confident of meeting it. No
EBITDA margin guidance was given.
• The 5-year target is a ~20% CAGR, led by broking and wealth plus the NBFC once its portfolio rebalancing is complete.
Insurance will contribute, but not as the main driver.
• NBFC AUM is expected to stay flat for about a year during rebalancing, then grow at more than 20% CAGR.
• Wealth AUM of more than INR 60,000 mn is targeted to quadruple in the coming years.
• Capital allocation will stay at ~35-40% for the NBFC and ~60-65% for the other businesses. The NBFC is expected to raise its
own capital in future.
Broking
• Q1 fee and commission income and MTF interest income rose, lifting standalone broking profit.
• StocksCart revenue grew ~250% YoY. It was the fourth-largest broker on the NSE by active clients added in FY26.
• StocksCart is India's first subscription-based discount broker, charging a subscription for unlimited trading instead of a per-
order fee.
• Full-service SMC focuses on research (20+ SEBI-registered analysts), physical presence and doorstep service.
• Full-service broking has a client acquisition cost of ~INR 2,000-3,000 and revenue of ~INR 25,000 per client a year. For
StocksCart, these are ~INR 800-1,000 and ~INR 11,000, respectively.
• SMC has 3-in-1 account tie-ups with six banks, including South Indian Bank and PNB, to build presence in the South. This
channel already adds ~2,000-3,000 accounts a month.
NBFC (Moneywise)
• Moneywise is a middle-layer NBFC with AUM of INR 10,250 mn as of June 2026, down from INR 11,910 mn. It operates in five
states, with ~40 branches and 500+ employees.
• Products are micro-LAP, gold loans, healthcare equipment finance, MSME business loans and onward lending to smaller
NBFCs.
• The AUM decline reflects deliberate rebalancing: unsecured loans are now ~20% of the book (down from ~50% three years
ago), new LAP lending has shifted to small tickets of ~INR 1.5 mn (from ~INR 20 mn earlier), and yields on new LAP loans are
~18% (versus ~30% earlier).
• On the new secured retail book (micro-LAP and gold loans), yield is above 18% and incremental cost of funds ~10.1%. That
gives an unlevered spread of ~8%, a levered NIM of ~12% and opex of ~6%. Blended yield should rise ~1-1.5% as the book
shifts.
• Gross NPA is 2.99% and net NPA 1.9% (June 2026), similar to a year ago. Most NPAs are backed by collateral, so management
expects good recoveries. Unsecured loans are written off at 180+ days past due, and provisioning follows Ind AS ECL.
• Management said it has no plans to sell or partner the NBFC, as monthly secured disbursements are rising.
Insurance Broking
• The business places ~INR 30,000 mn of premium a year. Motor insurance is ~90% of volume, and the mix is ~90% general and
~10% life.
• Most general insurance comes from motor insurance service provider (MISP) tie-ups with Honda and Kia. Cross-sell overlap
with broking clients is below 1%, so it runs as an independent channel.
• Q1FY27 revenue was INR 1,670 mn, up from INR 1,150 mn (+~45% YoY), but PBT was only ~INR 21.7 mn. Management said Q1

• The company is hiring to scale the business.

Solarium Green Energy Ltd
Solarium Green is positioned for continued growth through a combination of large-scale EPC execution, residential rooftop expansion
and the ramp-up of its 1.2 GW module manufacturing facility. Captive module consumption should improve supply and price control,
while the all-in-one solar kit provides an additional scalable channel in the highly fragmented residential market. The deliberate shift
towards private-sector EPC customers and larger projects could support execution quality, although margins may remain below the
historical residential-led levels. Key monitorables remain module utilisation, conversion of the EPC order pipeline, residential kit ramp-up
and working-capital discipline.
Strong Growth Trajectory
• FY26 revenue stood at INR 3.68 bn, with 3-year revenue CAGR of 55%; EBITDA was INR 350 mn, with 3-year CAGR of 83%.
• Management remains confident of sustaining a strong growth trajectory but is refraining from providing formal FY27/FY28 revenue
guidance given the company's relatively young operating history.
Module Manufacturing Ramp-up
• The 1.2 GW fully automated module facility was commissioned in March 2026 and received ALMM certification in July 2026; the
company is focused on 725 Wp+ G12 TOPCon modules and is applying for 745 Wp certification.
• Around 50-60% of module output is targeted for captive consumption, primarily supporting the EPC business, while the balance can
be sold to external customers/export-oriented players.
EPC Scale-up
• The company is moving towards larger 50-100 MW ground-mounted projects, with two 65 MW projects currently in the
pipeline/execution.
• Execution of ~250 MW of orders by FY26-end is expected to strengthen technical and financial eligibility for larger government
tenders; margins remain lower than residential projects but are considered sustainable.
Shift towards Private Sector
• Government project contribution has been deliberately moderated after FY26, with greater focus on private developers and agencies
with stronger cash positions to reduce payment-cycle risks.
• This shift should improve working-capital quality, although the larger-ticket ground-mounted business carries structurally lower
margins than residential rooftop projects.
Residential Rooftop & Solar Kits
• Solarium remains the second-largest vendor under PM Surya Ghar, with >450 Sarthi partners across 25 cities and ~250-270 partners
generating orders each month.
• The all-in-one solar kit addresses the fragmented residential market by bundling ~25-30 SKUs under one brand, along with warranty,
insurance and remote-monitoring support.
Kit Distribution Opportunity
• Residential EPC plus kit distribution is expected to reach INR 150-160 mn of monthly revenue over the next 3-4 months, although
standalone residential EPC has faced execution-related constraints.
• The kit model provides an opportunity to scale through city-level distributors without extending credit, as customer payments are
collected directly by Solarium.
Module Cost & Margin Outlook
• Aluminium is the most relevant commodity exposure, with frames accounting for ~10-15% of module cost; the company does not
expect direct commodity-price movements to materially determine margins.
• Captive module production should provide better price and supply control, although the overall margin benefit may be moderated by
the increasing contribution from large ground-mounted EPC projects.
Backward Integration
• There are currently no near-term plans to backward integrate into solar cell manufacturing, with management expecting domestic
cell capacity to increase sufficiently over the next 6-12 months.
• The company intends to first stabilise its module facility and assess market conditions before considering further integration or
related capex.
Energy Storage
• The company has executed a small 2 MW energy-storage project and is monitoring the BESS opportunity, but is currently cautious on
bidding for larger storage tenders.
• Sharp increases in lithium battery prices and uncertainty around project economics are key reasons for waiting until the market
stabilises.
Balance Sheet & Working Capital
• No major equity fundraise or large capex is currently envisaged over the next 12-18 months, with growth expected to be supported
through internal accruals and bank financing.
• Elevated receivable and inventory days are partly due to the shift towards C&I/government projects and year-end revenue
concentration.

Solex Energy Ltd
Solex Energy, an early renewable energy player (since 1995), has transformed into a solar PV module manufacturer after a change in
control in 2019, building towards ~4 GW of module capacity, including a fully automated 2.2 GW line (one module every 14
seconds) set up with LONGi's support. Around 70-80% of manufacturing is for IPPs such as KPI Energy, Sprng Energy and Zelestra,
and the company has done OEM manufacturing for Jinko Solar and LONGi. The order book stands at ~INR 33-34 bn, of which ~INR
12-13 bn is backed by POs and advances. Management targets FY27 revenue of INR 22-24 bn, heavily H2-weighted, after Q1 was
impacted by uncertainty around ALMM List-II for cells. Non-DCR G12R module prices have softened to INR 12.5-13 per Wp, while
DCR modules sell at ~INR 22 per Wp. Backward integration includes a 2.2 GW cell line (~INR 10.5 bn) targeted by December 2027
and a further 3 GW by 2030, with a long-term vision of 10 GW cells, 2 GW ingot/wafer and 10 GW BESS involving ~INR 40 bn of
capex over FY27-FY30 at 70:30 debt-equity. The key factors to monitor are ALMM-II timelines, module pricing, cell import and
freight costs, conversion of stage 2/3 orders, cell line execution and the BESS foray.
Business Overview & Journey
• Started in 1995 by Mr Kalpesh Patel, the company was initially engaged in solar thermal equipment and EPC projects
(streetlights, ground-mounted and rooftop), including several government projects.
• Listed on the NSE SME platform in 2018; in October 2019, current CMD Dr Chetan Shah, Mr Vipul Shah and other investors
acquired a majority stake.
• The company launched a 4 GW module giga-facility, with the first 700 MW mono PERC line commencing manufacturing in
October 2022.
• Solex did OEM manufacturing for Indian module makers and for Jinko Solar (100+ GW capacity in China); after ALMM, it
manufactured for LONGi, whose team inspected and approved the factory, with material procured from LONGi on LC and
supplied to LONGi's customers such as Welspun and Zelestra. Management stated it is the only company globally to
manufacture for both Jinko and LONGi.
• The company benchmarks itself on quality, cell breakage and compliance parameters against large global Tier-1 manufacturers
rather than domestic peers.
Manufacturing & Technology Edge
• Solex was the first to implement a manufacturing execution system (MES) in its facility, integrated with machinery and providing
end-to-end traceability (raw material source, breakage, efficiency), enabling customers to carry out inline inspection remotely.
• G12R modules (620+ Wp) were launched in October 2024, a year ahead of larger peers with 10+ GW capacity (October 2025),
with megawatt-scale production since September 2025.
• An expansion was announced in March 2025 (800 MW followed by ~2.5 GW of TOPCon module capacity); the latest 2.2 GW line,
with equipment procured with LONGi's support, is AI-enabled, fully automated (zero-touch) and produces one module every 14
seconds.
• An in-house lab performs testing similar to UL India (without the NABL tag yet), with NABL accreditation expected by next year-
end; this allows full-scale ramp-up without waiting on independent lab results for first lots.
• The company holds certifications for the US (top performer in Kiwa PVEL testing) and European markets; US exports are
currently not possible due to US policy, while a dedicated resource has been appointed for Europe, and small export quantities
have been executed on 100% advance.
Customers & Order Book
• Since last year, 70-80% of revenue/manufacturing has been for IPPs, and Solex is among the top 5 vendors for IPPs when
allocating orders.
• Key customers include KPI Energy (350 MW order in February 2025 when the company's capacity was only 700 MW), Sprng
Energy (a Shell subsidiary, now acquired by the Aditya Birla Group) and Zelestra (a Spanish group operating in 12 countries).

ALMM Policy Update
• ALMM-I was introduced in 2019 and implemented in 2022 after four extensions, when module capacity reached ~40 GW against

• ALMM-II was not extended when it became effective on 1 June; after ~45 days it was extended to December (announced on 15

• Initial cell plan of 5 GW in two phases: Phase 1 of 2.2 GW with DCCO targeted by December 2027, and a further 3 GW by 2030
after Phase 1 ramp-up.

the CCD term sheet received and sanction expected shortly; the balance ~INR 7 bn through term loans, for which banks have
been approached.
• Technology tie-ups with a Tier-1 Chinese cell manufacturer (involved from design, vendor negotiation and plant operation, on a

• The cell line was delayed due to land acquisition challenges in Gujarat (land, water and power), which are now cleared;

BESS Foray & Long-Term Vision

followed by BESS within about a month.
• Initially, BESS will be OEM-based with parts manufactured by the partner and assembly in India; the first 6 months will focus on
market building and the next 6 months on installation and operations.
• Long-term vision: ~4 GW of modules (with additions as required), 10 GW of cells, 2 GW of ingot and wafer and 10 GW of BESS,
involving ~INR 40 bn of investment over FY27-FY30, funded at a 70:30 debt-to-equity ratio.

Somany Ceramics Ltd
Outlook: Management targets an FY27 EBITDA margin of 11.3%, about 200 bps higher than last year. Volume growth is guided at
5-6% (mid-single digits) for FY27. A new South India greenfield plant will add 9 mn+ sq m of 100% GVT capacity, commissioning by
the end of FY28 and contributing revenue from FY29. Over the long term, management aims to raise GVT's share of revenue to 70-
75%.
Q1 Margins & Pricing: Q1 EBITDA margin was 11.6%, helped by restricted outsourced supply from Morbi. It is expected to
normalise over Q2-Q4 to the full-year target of 11.3%. The company has held on to the 17-18% price hike it took in Q1, passing 95-
96% of gas cost inflation through to consumers. It also plans to increase advertising and promotion (A&P) spending to win share
from unorganised players as the price gap narrows.
JV Turnaround: The joint ventures lost about INR 110 mn in each of Q1 and Q2 last year (INR 110-120 mn in Q2) and INR 50 mn in
Q3. They turned profitable in Q4 and delivered a net profit of INR 30 mn in Q1FY27, even though Q1 is usually the weakest quarter
because of plant shutdowns. The recovery came from a better product mix at the Max plant, following investments made in Q4,
and from plant and equipment upgrades that come into commercial use in Q3 and Q4.
Volume & Demand Trends: Q1 volume grew about 3% (2.5-2.7%), and Q2 growth is expected to roughly double to 5-6%. Domestic
demand is stable to decent. Receivables continue to improve without the company offering extra credit terms. Private
institutional projects make up 10-12% of the business, and management is deliberately limiting further growth in this segment to
an additional 3-4% to protect the balance sheet from longer working capital cycles.
Capacity Base: Total capacity is 56-57 mn sq m across four hubs: Haryana/Kassar (about 25 mn sq m), Kadi in Gujarat (11-12 mn sq
m), the Morbi JVs and outsourcing (about 12 mn sq m), and the South cluster at Chittoor.
Capacity Expansion: Balancing equipment at existing plants will add 4-5 mn sq m, coming into commercial use in mid-Q3 and Q4.
In addition, the greenfield South plant will add 9 mn+ sq m of GVT capacity, placing the company closer to key demand markets.
GVT Mix Shift: GVT makes up about 60% of capacity. Including double charge, the share is about 65%, and adding
Duragres/Durastone takes it to about 70%. By the end of FY27, 2.5 mn sq m of wall ceramic capacity will be converted to flexible
GVT capacity.
Fuel Flexibility: The plants can run on LPG, propane or natural gas. The Haryana plant has pooled natural gas supply agreements
with GAIL and can switch 20-25% of its fuel to LPG. Propane is currently INR 11-12 per SCM cheaper than natural gas, a cost
advantage of about 15%, and 80-85% of Morbi production has switched to propane. Management expects gas prices to remain
high and volatile for the next 6-8 months, driven by winter demand in the West, replenishment of global reserves and geopolitical
conflicts.
Morbi Cluster Stress: Exports, which used to be 35% of Morbi's output, have collapsed, causing severe inventory and working
capital stress. About 15-20% of Morbi capacity has shut down long-term, and another 25-30% of units will close for a month from
mid-October to reduce inventory and force a price increase. That takes total Morbi capacity offline to about 50%. An industry-wide
price hike is expected in November, after Diwali.
Organised Share Gains: As the historical price gap between unorganised Morbi suppliers and national brands narrows, organised
players are winning market share.
Competitive Landscape: Management dismissed "lab-grown marble" tiles as a marketing gimmick for standard tiles. It noted that
the effect needs standard machinery costing INR 200 mn, slows plant speeds and gives poorer aesthetics than natural marble at
INR 400-600 per sq ft. The anti-dumping duty on Chinese tiles comes up for a sunset review in February 2027. Indian production is
currently more cost-competitive than Chinese production because of China's energy costs and global freight economics.
Long-Term Potential: Morbi capacity going offline, a narrowing price gap and higher A&P spending support organised share gains.
The JV turnaround, a richer GVT mix and 13-14 mn sq m of new capacity point to margin expansion and growth through FY29.

Spandana Sphoorty Financial Ltd
Outlook: The company is focused on rebuilding its loan book through customer acquisition while maintaining stringent
underwriting standards, with FY27-end portfolio guidance of ~INR 65 bn and an FY28 target of INR 90 bn. Improving collection
efficiency, lower borrowing costs and branch rationalisation should support gradual margin expansion and operating leverage.
Management is targeting a 2% ROA over FY28-FY29, driven by yields of around 25% and operating costs declining towards 7.5% of
assets. Key monitorables include the sustainability of asset-quality improvement, execution of growth targets amid elevated
rejection rates, normalisation of credit costs and the pace of individual lending expansion.
Asset Quality & Collections
• Sustained improvement in asset quality: X-bucket collection efficiency of over 95% over the past 18 months, with Q1FY27
collection trends improving further in Q2FY27.
• Q2FY27 collections remain stable: Collection efficiency in July and August was broadly in line with Q1FY27, while the last two
months showed an improvement over June levels.
• Low reported delinquencies: Loans overdue by more than 90 days accounted for approximately 0.4% of the balance sheet,
with the company highlighting strong repayment behaviour across the current portfolio.
• State-level trends remain stable: Collection efficiency across the top five states, which contribute 60-65% of business, was
broadly stable or better in Q2FY27 compared with Q1FY27.
• Weather-related disruptions remain localised: Heavy rainfall may temporarily disrupt collections in certain pockets, but
management expects repayments to normalise within one to one-and-a-half months as conditions improve.
• Recoveries from written-off loans remain steady: Recoveries are currently ~INR 150 mn per month, below management's
initial expectations, with an ambition to increase this to INR 170-180 mn per month.
Growth & Disbursement Strategy
• Disbursement momentum remains intact: The company has been disbursing ~INR 5 bn per month, in line with its H1FY27
plans, despite elevated rejection rates of ~70-75%.
• Customer acquisition remains a key growth driver: New borrower additions increased from 60,000 in Q3FY26 to 113,000 in
Q4FY26 and 140,000 in Q1FY27, with management targeting over 150,000 additions in Q2FY27.
• New customers account for a rising share of disbursements: ~60% of Q1FY27 disbursements were directed towards newly
acquired borrowers, reflecting the company's focus on expanding its borrower base.
• FY27 growth guidance remains intact: Management expects the portfolio to reach approximately INR 65 bn by FY27-end,
followed by a target of ~INR 90 bn in FY28.
• High rejection rates reflect tighter underwriting: Rejections remain elevated due to stricter KYC checks, borrower indebtedness
and delinquency screening, with management prioritising credit quality over volume-led growth.
• Competitive intensity remains manageable for Spandana: Management believes its relatively smaller portfolio and presence
across ~1,300 branches should support the achievement of near-term growth targets, although sustaining similar growth
beyond FY28 may become more challenging.
Operating Efficiency & Cost Rationalisation
• Branch rationalisation supports operating leverage: The company closed or merged 357 branches during FY26, reducing
operating expenses from ~INR 2 bn to INR 1.55-1.6 bn.
• Operating cost reduction remains a key earnings lever: Management expects operating expenses to decline from ~10% of
assets currently to 7.5% in FY28, supported by improved productivity and a leaner branch network.
• Growth will require limited incremental costs: Higher disbursements may entail some additional operating expenditure in
H2FY27, but management does not expect a corresponding increase in branch count or headcount.
• Balance-sheet optimisation is improving profitability: Lower excess cash balances have reduced negative carry and supported
the overall cost structure, while maintaining adequate liquidity.
Margins, Cost of Borrowings & Profitability
• Portfolio yields stood at ~24.6% in Q1FY27, with management targeting ~25% by FY28, supported by normalisation of legacy
portfolio-related pressures.
• Marginal borrowing costs have reduced by ~170-180 bps from the Q3FY26 peak of ~13.2%, with further improvement
expected in Q2FY27.
• NIMs currently stand at ~13-13.5%, with management expecting a gradual improvement through H2FY27 as funding costs
decline.
• Management is targeting a 2% ROA over the medium term, supported by higher yields, lower funding costs, operating
leverage and normalisation of credit costs.
• Credit costs could remain marginal this year, although they may increase in FY28 as recoveries from older delinquent and
written-off portfolios moderate.

October.
• Weather Disruptions: July volumes saw a 12% decline due to flooding in Assam, though recovery was noted in August and
September.
Financial Strategy
• Funding: Rajasthan expansion will be funded through internal accruals and debt.
• Debt Target: Aiming to keep net debt-to-EBITDA at 1.5-1.7x.
• Peak Debt: Peak debt is expected not to exceed INR 15 bn.

Steelcast Ltd
Steelcast's board has approved an 8,500-tonne capacity addition (~30% above the 29,000-tonne base) to be commissioned by

FY29, implying a ~24% three-year volume CAGR from the FY26 base, with new capacity expected to generate ~INR 3 bn of sales over

Capacity Expansion & Utilisation Roadmap
The board has approved 8,500 tonnes of additional capacity (~30% above the current 29,000-tonne installed base) on 100,000 sq m
of land (INR 186 mn, from the Gujarat government) 12 km from the present facility; commissioning is targeted by March 2028,
compressed from a normal two-year timeline.
Total capex is ~INR 2.25 bn through FY29 (INR 1.2 bn for the new facility plus ~INR 1 bn for the existing facility), fully covered by cash
accruals over FY27-FY29, with reserves of INR 1.22 bn maintained at current levels. The company has been debt-free since FY23.
Utilisation of the existing facility is guided at 60% in FY27, ~76-79% in FY28 and 90% in FY29, beyond which bottlenecks make going
higher imprudent.
New capacity is expected to generate sales of ~INR 3 bn over ~3 years from commissioning; it will serve the same nine end-user
industries, with no segment considered high or low margin.
The ramp-up is underwritten by new parts developed over the last two years entering serial supply, rupee depreciation, China-plus-
one share gains with existing customers, and three-year procurement horizons shared by customers.
Visibility gap: Firm orders cover only four months; the 12-month forward view is refreshed monthly from customer indications, not
a contracted backlog. Management acknowledged that customer projections have often diverged from actual procurement over the
last decade, but argued that on a 3-5 year lens, "by and large, whatever the customer says does happen".
Growth Trajectory
The plan implies a ~24% volume CAGR over three years from the FY26 base (FY28 volume growth ~32%, FY29 ~15%), a sharp
acceleration from the ~7% PAT CAGR over FY23-FY26 (PAT of INR 700 mn in FY23 to INR 880 mn in FY26).
Management attributes the muted last two years to the industrial cycle and new parts not yet in serial supply; it did not directly
reconcile the gap between past and projected growth.
End-user industries are expected to grow 5-6% YoY for the next 2-3 years, supported by Indian infrastructure spending and high
commodity prices. Exports are expected to stay at 50-55% of sales through FY29.
Management urged a 3-5 year lens rather than the immediate two years.
Margin Structure & Sustainability
EBITDA margins are running at 28-29%, lifted by rupee depreciation and a few other benefits that may not persist; the long-term
sustainable band is 25-26% and the current year is expected to be similar to last year.
Higher utilisation could push margins above 25-26%, but management did not commit to it. The 9.5 MW captive power project
(commissioned 23 March) provides a continuous cost benefit.
Margin strength is attributed to material procurement efficiencies, productivity, quality assurance and world-class facilities, not
niche positioning. The company tracks only percentage margins (not EBITDA per tonne); peer margins are unknown as most
competitors are closely held.
Raw material costs were flat QoQ. The company does not hedge forex or raw materials; raw material inventory is 40-45 days and
pass-through is reviewed quarterly. All sales are ex-works, so freight increases pass to customers.

Steel Exchange India Ltd
Outlook: Management guides blended EBITDA of INR 10,000 per tonne, up from its earlier guidance of INR 7,000 per tonne. It
expects EBITDA margins to expand by 200-500 bps as higher volumes absorb fixed costs. Revenue is expected to rise from the

Capacity Expansion: The company runs a 0.50 mn tonne steel plant. The newly commissioned reheating furnace has effectively
doubled output. A three-phase expansion with capex of more than INR 50,000 mn will raise capacity to 1.50 mn tonnes. The
company has signed an MoU with the Government of Andhra Pradesh for industrial incentives.
Expansion Timeline: The three phases are:
◦ Phase 1: Capacity rises to 1.0 mn tonnes through a new rolling mill, targeted for late 2027 or March 2028.
◦ Phase 2: Adds round bars, wire rods and an electric arc furnace (EAF) by March 2029.
◦ Phase 3: Targeted for completion by late 2030.
Volume Ramp-Up: Output was about 0.18 mn tonnes in FY25/FY26. August-September production reached 50,000 tonnes after
the reheating furnace was commissioned, an annualised run-rate of 0.30 mn tonnes. Daily output is currently 800 tonnes and
should rise to 1,200-1,300 tonnes after the festive season, or about 40,000 tonnes a month. The FY27/FY28 volume target is 0.36
mn tonnes, about 70% utilisation.
Steel Pricing: Finished steel prices rose 20-25% in Q2 to above INR 70,000 per tonne, compared with the usual range of INR
50,000-55,000 per tonne, driven by regional power and coal shortages.
Premium Products: The company has been re-approved for five years to supply CRS/HSCRM defence-grade steel across coastal
India, at a realisation premium of INR 3,000 per tonne. Its move into special green steel alloys adds a further margin premium of
about 2% over standard products.
Demand Catalysts: The company is empanelled with Adani for the flagship Google data centre project in Visakhapatnam. It also
supplies hotel projects in Visakhapatnam, where 10-15 new hotels have signed up. It is positioned to benefit from steel demand in
the INR 1,000 bn Amaravati capital region build-out.
IMR Partnership: The company has partnered with IMR Resources, a global commodities major. IMR's owner, who runs a USD 3.5
bn enterprise across 20 countries, has joined the company's board. IMR provides letter-of-credit support for working capital,
global sourcing of coking coal and raw materials, billet trade access, export network integration and support for low-cost debt
refinancing.
Balance Sheet & Funding: About INR 2,000 mn of balance warrant money is expected within 3-6 months. The operating cycle has
shortened from 161 days toward 120 days, with a target of 60-90 days within two years. A credit rating upgrade to BBB+ has
opened talks with banks on single-digit interest rates for borrowings and working capital facilities.
Logistics Park & Land Bank: The company owns a 500-acre land bank with a three-lane railway siding connected to
Visakhapatnam Port. Under an initial MoU with the AP government, it is setting aside 100-150 acres for a logistics industrial park
and goods shed terminal. This will run as a wholly owned logistics and trading subsidiary with estimated revenue potential of INR
10,000 mn.
Sales Mix & Geographic Expansion: About 90% of revenue currently comes from Andhra Pradesh. Of total revenue, 70% is B2C
through the Simhadri TMT brand and 30% is B2B. In the short term, the company aims to raise sales outside AP to 20-30%, and
within two years to reach a 50:50 split between AP and other regions plus exports.
Long-Term Potential: The expansion to 1.5 mn tonnes, higher EBITDA per tonne, the IMR partnership and infrastructure-led
demand in Andhra Pradesh support a path to more than INR 50,000 mn of turnover. The logistics park and an improving balance
sheet add further levers for value creation.

Sunlite Recycling Industries Ltd
Business
Sunlite was set up in 2012 in Kheda, Gujarat, to make copper products from recycled scrap. Its products are copper rods (FRHC and
OFC), wires, strips, ATC wire for solar and busbars for transformers and switchgear.
In 2026, it acquired Sunlite Aluminium (aluminium rods) as a wholly owned subsidiary.
Copper capacity is ~30,260 tonnes a year and aluminium ~12,000 tonnes. About 85% of rod output is sold as rod, and ~15% is
processed further into higher-value products.
FY26 revenue grew ~98% on ~50% volume growth, and Q1FY27 revenue grew ~75% on ~15% volume growth, mostly from higher
copper prices. Aluminium revenue was ~INR 1,550 mn in FY26.
ROE is ~36% and ROCE ~34%. Working capital is ~10 days, with inventory turning ~42 times a year.
Guidance and Capex
A busbar expansion adds ~1,000 tonnes a year for ~INR 130 mn, against current value-added capacity of ~2,500 tonnes.
A ~20,000-tonne copper plant will be built in the aluminium subsidiary for ~INR 240 mn, to use its income tax, capital and interest
subsidies.
Machinery is ordered, with commissioning targeted for February-March 2027 and first-year utilisation of ~30-40%. Management
expects a significant ramp-up from FY28.
The earlier copper cathode plant plan was dropped, because many large cathode plants are coming up and margins may not justify
the capex.
Revenue and volume should both grow in Q2. Management would not give H1 margins ahead of results.
Margins and Hedging
EBITDA is ~INR 25-30 per kg. Rod EBITDA margin is ~2.1-2.2%, and ATC wire gross margin is ~4.5-5% (~3.5-4% at low utilisation).
Utilisation is ~90% for rods, ~60-65% for ATC wire (which management says is close to full practical capacity) and ~40-45% for
busbars.
Margin percentage falls when copper prices rise even though absolute profit grows.
The company is fully hedged: every purchase is matched by a sale, and import prices are fixed against sales close to when the
container arrives. Aluminium is priced off the M6 benchmark.
Procurement
About 40% of scrap is imported and ~60% domestic, but the mix shifts with relative prices and imports can reach 70-80%. Copper
scrap carries no import duty, and shipping cost is passed on.
Supplier contracts run 15-25 days, and management sees no shortage of scrap so far. Sharp price spikes cause only 1-2 days of
disruption.
The company runs on green energy with no oil-fired furnaces, and its scrap yard is in Nadiad. A GST provisional attachment on the
Kheda factory was removed about a year ago.
Any benefit from the April 2026 EPR rules awaits government guidelines.

Suryoday Small Finance Bank Ltd
Outlook: The bank is tracking in line with plan across its three pillars of microbanking, retail assets and digital, and reiterated
guidance of roughly doubling FY27 profit on a growing paying book and improving credit quality, aided by CGFMU claims.
Microfinance is ~50% of the book in the near term and will be gradually pared down while remaining a key revenue engine.
Collections are better than in the prior quarter, with isolated stress in drought-affected Maharashtra, and the bank retains an exit
ROA target of ~1.5-1.6% with credit cost of 1-1.2%.
Performance and Pillars
The bank has received ~INR 8 bn of CGFMU claims over the last two years, pertaining to the last three base years, with all
anticipated levers playing out. The three pillars of microbanking, retail assets (CV and mortgage) and digital are all delivering; micro
mortgage saw a small slippage that is now under control, while CV is seeing good growth.
Digital is showing strong traction, with 30-40% of incremental deposits raised through digital channels and customer acquisition
through partner tie-ups (including a BC and CLOU model) growing 20-30% per month. Headcount was barely added in Q1; growth
will come from productivity and existing customers.
The bank is running at an annualised partner customer acquisition rate of 2.7+ mn, plus 0.5 mn through internal channels, and is
targeting 3+ mn additions for the year. Branch expansion is deliberately limited, with the focus on leveraging existing branches.
Profit Trajectory and Margins
Q1 PSLC gains, while one-off within the year, recur every year; the doubling of profit versus last year rests on paying book growth
and credit cost improvement expanding operating income, with the same trend expected in Q2.
Deposit rates remain elevated for small finance banks, so funding uses a mix of retail deposits (85%+ of the total), refinancing and
revived IBPC transactions over the next three quarters. A 25 bps rate hike is seen as possible by December.
LAP is fully floating; the fixed-rate book sits in MFI, where pricing will be reviewed and repriced if a hike materialises. Yield on the
loan book fell ~110 bps QoQ to ~16% and NIM fell ~70 bps, largely due to impairment; in Q2, the impaired book should be written
off (helped by trust guarantee claims) and a rising paying book should lift yields.
Insurance, Asset Quality and Digital Economics
Insurance is not material: total insurance income in the P&L is INR 200-300 mn, of which the IRDAI impact is ~INR 100-150 mn at the
PBT level. Credit-attached products account for a little over half of insurance income, largely MFI credit life; the bank would rather
forgo commission and charge a slightly higher fee, with leeway on the asset-attachment side.
Collections are better than in the prior quarter; drought pockets in Maharashtra show a ~50 bps impact on collection efficiency (35-
40% of AUM is in Maharashtra), but April and May were decent and no deterioration is seen. The post-November 2024 book, built
on propensity and scorecard-based lending, is intact, and exposure to the northern floods is limited.
The bank positions itself more as an individual lender than a group lender, with JLG under 25% of microbanking; customers are new-
to-loan and new-to-bank, with standing instructions in place, and three-fourths pay on time through savings accounts, effectively
the top end of the microbanking segment.
Digital partner economics are ROA-accretive, above the bank's average ROA; one partner's live retail asset base is ~INR 11 bn.
Conversions on early assisted journeys are in single digits and are expected to reach double digits. UPI MDR is a double-edged
sword: it is accretive on network volumes, but FDs booked digitally through UPI are not yet exempt from MDR, making it broadly a
zero-sum game.
Capital, Mix and Outlook
The board approved a Tier 2 raise of INR 2 bn at a coupon of a little over 10%, as flagged on the Q1 call; more may be discussed on
the Q2 call. There are no plans for a universal banking licence in the near or medium term, although an AD Category I licence may
be added later.
The AUM mix of inclusive finance to retail assets is to stay at ~50:50 in the near term, with microfinance pared down over time but
still a leading revenue engine. On MFI industry asset quality, ~75-80% of customers pay regardless of the cycle; current strength
reflects tighter selection amid limited capital, with the industry customer base down by ~20 mn and borrowers migrating to gold
loans and other products.
Guidance
The bank reiterated guidance to roughly double FY27 profit on paying book growth and credit cost improvement, with an exit ROA
of ~1.5-1.6%, credit cost of 1-1.2% and a near-term 50:50 mix of inclusive finance to retail assets; Q2 is expected to be in line with
the FY27 trajectory.

Susan India Electronics Ltd
Outlook: For FY27, management plans to shift the mix sharply toward HT cables and MVCC, targeting 30-35% of revenue from
about 5% today, as these carry the highest margins. Installed capacity supports annual revenue of INR 6,000-7,000 mn, more than
2x the FY25 base. Commissioning the CCV line will unlock qualification for large state tenders, and revenue from UP alone is
expected to double.
Q1FY27 Performance: Revenue grew about 3.8x YoY (+278%) to INR 950 mn from INR 250 mn. PAT was INR 60 mn, a turnaround
from a loss in Q1FY26. FY25 turnover was INR 2,700 mn, with a historical PAT margin of about 6.5%.
Order Visibility: As of 30 June, the unexecuted order book was INR 1,420 mn. Active tenders are expected to bring further wins of
about INR 1,500 mn, taking total order visibility to INR 2,920 mn.
Segment Margins & Mix: EBITDA margins are 9-10% for LT cables and conductors, 10-11% for winding wires and strips, and 12-
13% for HT cables and MVCC. The FY27 target mix is 30-35% HT cables and MVCC, about 35% winding wires and strips, and 25-30%
LT cables and conductors.
Raw Material Protection: Contracts use variable, pass-through pricing for copper, aluminium, XLPE and PVC. This shields
operating margins from commodity price swings.
Capacity Expansion: Capacity has been raised from 7,500 km per annum to 12,000 km per annum through additional Sioplas lines,
ahead of the timelines given in the RHP. The target is 13,000-14,000 km per annum by December. The plant runs 24/7 on double
shifts at 70-80% utilisation.
CCV Line: The company built its continuous curing vessel (CCV) line in-house for INR 70 mn, compared with about INR 140 mn at
market prices. It has a 100-metre nitrogen dry-curing tube that needs 120 metres of floor space, and commissioning is expected
within 1-1.5 months.
CCV-Linked Tender Access: A CCV line is a mandatory supply qualification in major states, including UP, Rajasthan, Karnataka,
Uttarakhand, Gujarat and Haryana. The company previously missed an INR 10,000 mn tender in UP because its CCV line was not
yet commissioned.
Customer Mix: Revenue is split evenly between state discoms and private EPC contractors such as Raja Electricals, Roy
Construction, Parth Electricals and Offshore Ltd. Vendor registrations are in the final stages with NTPC, BHEL, IOCL and Power Grid,
in addition to the existing registration with Indian Railways.
Geographic Footprint: The company supplies in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Bihar, Andhra
Pradesh and Telangana. Vendor registration in Maharashtra is under way.
HTLS Conductors: High-tension low-sag (HTLS) conductors, a high-margin product, are under active R&D. The company imports
core materials, which avoids INR 200-250 mn of capex on in-house core manufacturing. Samples enter type testing within 10-15
days, and the company targets trial orders of INR 20-50 mn this fiscal year.
Entry Barriers: Pre-qualification requirements demand 2-3 years of proven supply history covering 20-40% of a tender's volume.
The company holds 10 BIS licences and type-test certifications from CPRI, ERDA and NTH.
Long-Term Potential: Capacity that supports more than 2x current revenue, access to state tenders through the CCV line and a mix
shift toward higher-margin HT cables and MVCC together point to strong revenue growth and margin improvement. PSU
onboarding and HTLS conductors add further growth options.

Symphony Ltd
Outlook: Symphony enters FY27 with its core India air cooler business on a clean slate after full trade inventory normalisation,
though the September and December quarters will be cautiously managed amid elevated raw material costs and a ~12% price
hike, with consumer demand confined to March-July. The BISP portfolio, already roughly one-fourth of standalone revenue and
~48-49% of consolidated revenue, is the key growth and de-risking engine, with calibrated entry into RAC, BLDC fans and air
purifiers from the December quarter under an asset-light outsourcing model targeting reasonable ROIC rather than price-led scale.
The ~INR 50 bn air cooler market, with ~19% penetration, is expected to double in 5-7 years at ~8-10% CAGR, aided by a shift from
unorganised to organised players and BIS and energy-rating regulatory tailwinds where Symphony is already largely compliant.
Overseas, Mexico and Australia are diversified and on cleaner footing, while China has turned around and repaid its intercompany
loan. Overall, Symphony is positioning for steadier, less weather-dependent growth with both ISP and BISP engines firing, though
near-term margins may stay mixed as new categories scale.
India Summer Portfolio Normalisation and Demand Outlook
Symphony's core domestic household air cooler business enters FY27 from a clean slate, with trade inventory fully normalised
across channel and company after a strong summer in 2026. The company took a price hike of up to ~12% across models in the
core category post-July to offset raw material inflation, with plastics being the key input linked to crude and forex movements.
Management is cautious on the September and December quarters, balancing advance collection from dealers against billing at
elevated input costs, to avoid creating high-priced inventory if commodity prices normalise later. Consumer sales for air coolers
remain confined to March-July, so Q2 and Q3 revenue depends on advance orders and billing against them for the next summer
season.
BISP Portfolio as a De-Risking and Growth Engine
The beyond-Indian-summer-products portfolio, comprising large venting cooling, water heaters, tower fans and kitchen cooling
fans, contributes roughly one-fourth of standalone revenue with positive EBITDA. Symphony has announced entry into three new
India categories from the December quarter: residential air conditioners, BLDC fans and air purifiers. All three will follow an
outsourcing, asset-light model with no in-house manufacturing capex, and entry will be highly calibrated by SKU, geography and
channel, scaling only if predefined operational and commercial parameters are met. Management expects the product mix to tilt
toward BISP over the medium to long term given the far larger addressable market of INR 500+ bn versus ~INR 50 bn for air
coolers. On a consolidated basis, BISP already stands at ~48-49% of revenue on a TTM basis.
Residential Air Conditioner Entry and Competitive Positioning
Management clarified that RAC is classified under BISP and not ISP because ~62% of RAC sales occur in summer while ~38%
happen off-season, unlike air coolers where nearly 100% of consumer sales are summer-linked. The RAC market is mature and
crowded with 80+ brands, but Symphony argues the manufacturing and sourcing ecosystem, distribution overlap with ~1,000+
distributors and 90%+ alternate channel partners, and its authorised service provider network covering 95%+ PIN codes provide
leverage. The stated intent is not to buy scale through a price war but to offer superior price-value, especially on after-sales
service, and to earn a reasonable ROIC on incremental working capital only, with initial category-level losses being negligible in
absolute terms.
Air Purifier and BLDC Fan Opportunity
The air purifier market is currently small at ~INR 5-6 bn but is seen as having exponential runway across household, commercial
and industrial use, with no clear domestic leader and a less crowded competitive field, giving Symphony a potential shot at
leadership over the medium to long term. Margins in these new categories will initially be below the air cooler business, but
management sees scope to leverage brand, sourcing and distribution relationships, and to capture operating leverage at the
EBITDA level over time as fixed costs remain largely fixed under the outsourced model. BLDC fans are noted as a fast-growing
category with a large runway and year-round sales, further reducing weather dependence.
Overseas Business Diversification and Balance Sheet Reset
In Mexico, a weak summer has been offset by a diversified portfolio now including stand fans, room heaters, washing machines
and RAC alongside room coolers. In Australia, legacy issues and the balance sheet reset were addressed in the March quarter,
leaving the business on a cleaner slate with a diversified mix including room heaters and RAC, with RAC already contributing
roughly one-fifth of revenue. In China, the business has turned around and repaid its intercompany loan to the parent, making
capital efficiency comparable to Symphony India.
Air Cooler Industry Structure and Regulatory Tailwinds
The household air cooler market is ~INR 50 bn with penetration of only ~19%, and management expects it to double over the next
5-7 years, implying a CAGR of ~8-10%. The unorganised segment still commands ~65% of the market, mostly metal cooler
fabricators, but a consumer shift from metal to plastic coolers is underway on aesthetics and performance. BIS certification
became mandatory from 1 November 2025, and energy rating standards become mandatory from 1 July 2027; Symphony already
has ~75-80% of its portfolio at 5-star rating, giving it a compliance advantage over both branded peers and unorganised players.

was provided for the new RAC, BLDC fan and air purifier categories, though management confirmed a concrete internal business
plan exists for sourcing, distribution and medium-to-long-term scale.

Product Portfolio & Diversification

Growth & Financial Targets

Long-Term Potential: The bank combines a 105-year record of uninterrupted profits and 104 years of dividend payouts with
ample capital headroom, best-in-class asset quality and an expanding distribution and MSME franchise. This positions it to sustain
above-industry growth with ROA of 2%+, while CASA recovery and the resolution of legal cases are further triggers.
