Tarachand Infra Logistics Solutions Ltd
Outlook: The company is targeting 20-25% revenue growth in FY27, led by equipment rentals and specialised services, supported
by an executable order book of INR 2,048 mn and continued deployment in renewable energy and power. While Q1FY27
profitability was affected by project-related losses, subdued steel logistics activity and prior-period charges, management expects
margins to recover in H2FY27 towards its 37-38% medium-term band. The expected settlement of the disputed project, improving
fleet utilisation and the contribution from recent capex are key earnings drivers. Moderating capex, improving receivable days and
disciplined leverage management remain important to sustaining growth and cash-flow generation.
Revenue Growth & Guidance
• Management has guided for 20-25% YoY revenue growth in FY27, driven primarily by equipment rentals and specialised
services, supported by recent capex and a healthy executable order book.
• Executable order book stood at INR 2,048 mn as of July 2026, of which 74% was contributed by equipment rentals and
specialised services, providing revenue visibility for FY27.
• Growth is expected to be driven by both market expansion and market-share gains, with renewable energy and power
emerging as key end-market opportunities.
Equipment Rentals: Utilisation & Margins
• Equipment rental utilisation stood at 79% in Q1FY27, while standalone rental EBITDA margin declined to 54% from the usual
58-62% range, primarily due to project-related demobilisation costs.
• Specialised services margins declined to 10% from 18% following a unilateral scope reduction by a client after machinery
mobilisation, resulting in revenue and profitability losses.
• Management expects the affected project to be settled by Q3FY27, with the machinery already redeployed to another project;
the settlement proceeds are expected to provide a potential earnings benefit.
• Renewable energy and power contributed 31% and 26%, respectively, of rental revenue in Q1FY27, taking their combined
share to 57% versus 24% in FY26, reflecting the company's increasing exposure to these sectors.
Warehousing & Transportation: Recovery Outlook
• Segment revenue declined to INR 187 mn in Q1FY27 from INR 295 mn in Q1FY26, while EBITDA margin contracted to 1% from
16%, reflecting subdued steel movement, the absence of an earlier RINL contract and the ramp-up of the new SAIL Dhankuni
contract.
• Higher fuel costs, which could not be passed through under existing contracts, further affected transportation activity and
profitability; management indicated that revised contractual provisions would address such cost escalations going forward.
• The segment is expected to recover in H2FY27, with Q3 and Q4 traditionally representing stronger quarters for steel handling
and transportation volumes.
Capex, Fleet Expansion & Asset Productivity
• The company incurred INR 428 mn of capex in Q1FY27, taking the gross block to INR 6,010 mn, with FY27 capex targeted at
~INR 800-1,000 mn.
• Management expects annual capex to moderate to INR 600-700 mn from FY28 onwards, including replacement of older
equipment, subject to business opportunities and deployment visibility.
• Equipment rental yields currently range between 2.8% and 3.0% of the deployed fleet's gross block, with utilisation generally
ranging from 79% to 85%.
• The fleet has an average age of approximately five years, with equipment typically replaced after 8-10 years and a targeted
resale value of 50-60% of the original purchase cost.
Profitability & Earnings Trajectory
• Q1FY27 revenue grew 11% YoY to INR 676 mn, while EBITDA stood at INR 210 mn, translating into a margin of 30.7%; PAT was
INR 17 mn and cash profit was INR 176 mn.
• Management expects H1FY27 EBITDA margins to remain below its earlier 37-38% medium-term band, with recovery
anticipated in H2FY27 as specialised services stabilise, equipment deployment improves and the disputed project is settled.
• The company also recognised ~INR 22 mn of prior-period charges, including a revenue write-off of INR 18.6 mn and an
exceptional charge of INR 3 mn relating to an old earnest money deposit.
Balance Sheet & Working Capital
• Net debt-to-equity stood at 0.87x at Q1FY27, compared with 0.90x in the previous year, despite continued fleet expansion.
• Management is targeting a reduction in receivable days from ~97 days to 80 days, which should support operating cash flow
and reduce working-capital intensity.
• Equipment purchases are partly funded through interest-free supplier credit, typically involving 20-25% upfront payment and
the balance payable after 1-2.5 years; the outstanding amount subsequently converts into bank debt, with loan tenures of 4-5
years.

Tars Aerospace
Outlook: Tars Aerospace is developing a modular missile system designed to provide a long-range, low-cost alternative to existing
Indian systems such as Pinaka. The company is pre-revenue, operating at TRL 3 and moving towards TRL 4. It is seeking a seed
round of INR 100 mn as part of a larger funding requirement of ~USD 3 mn to reach its third year of development.
Product Suite & Technology
• Modular Design: A single design platform that can be configured into three variants: unguided rockets (200 km range), guided
precision missiles (160 km range) and ground-launched glide vehicles (250 km range).
• Technical Approach: Focuses on surface-to-surface strikes using INS/GPS guidance for stationary targets, with future plans for
seeker-based capability against moving targets.
• Development Status: Has completed the configuration phase and is moving into the detailed design phase.
• IP Strategy: Aims to secure ~30 IPs across various subsystems.
Business Model & Market Strategy
• Revenue Streams:
◦ B2G (Primary): Direct sales and upgrades for the Indian Armed Forces.
◦ B2B (Secondary): Sale of subsystems, such as solid rocket propulsion for assisted launches, to drone companies.
• Market Positioning: Aims to bridge the gap between current systems (120 km range) and future DRDO requirements (200+ km
range) through a Make-II (suo motu) proposal to ensure IP retention and assured procurement.
• Competitive Edge: Focuses on faster R&D iterations and shorter development times than traditional players, and avoids the
high-risk, high-cost market for aircraft-integrated glide bombs.
Financial Projections
• Revenue Targets: Initially projected cumulative revenue of USD 2 bn over nine years, although analysts flagged this as
potentially unrealistic compared with established firms such as BDL.
• Margins: Expects ~50% margins per unit, with higher margins anticipated on international exports.
• Production Plan: Intends to use existing vendors initially to minimise capex, with a long-term goal of in-house production of
50-100 missiles per month.
Risks
• Regulatory: Requires various licences (including from DPIIT) within the next 1.5-2 years.
• Supply Chain: Explosives will be outsourced to established partners in Hyderabad due to high compliance and safety risks.

The company is positioned to benefit from its leadership in domestic plastic labware, rising import substitution and a capacity

margins lower due to the trading subsidiary.
Q1FY27 Performance
• Revenue grew ~20% YoY at both standalone and consolidated levels, with growth seen across domestic and export markets;
FY26 standalone revenue stood at ~INR 3.3 bn and consolidated revenue at ~INR 4.5 bn.
Raw Material & Pricing
• Polymer prices rose 40-60% from end-FY26; the company absorbed costs in FY26 and took partial price hikes in the domestic
market from FY27, leading to a 2-3% dip in gross margin, while export prices were kept unchanged due to competitive

~15%, diagnostics 10-12%, academia ~10% and hospitals and IVF 5-10%.

products; the US contributes 40-45% of export revenue, followed by Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia; enquiries that
were paused due to US tariffs have revived, with some converting into large orders.
US Tariff Risk
• The company did not lose any customers when US tariffs rose to 50%, though it offered discounts, and tariffs were
subsequently reduced to 25%; US revenue is ~INR 300-400 mn (~10% of consolidated revenue), and management indicated
that a 100% tariff would effectively halt India-US trade.
Capacity Expansion

Capex & Utilisation

be operational by year-end, and future capex limited to INR 200-300 mn per year.
Return Ratios
• Industry asset turnover is ~0.6-0.7x, and management expects ROCE and ROE to improve meaningfully once the new capacity
reaches full utilisation in 3-4 years; fixed employee costs for the new plants are already in the P&L, with variable wages to rise
only alongside revenue.

Outlook: TIPCO Engineering is poised for a transformative scaling phase, targeting 30-40% annual standalone revenue growth,

tangible assets and a clear competitive edge over European imports on lead times and pricing, TIPCO is well-positioned to sustain
momentum, although macroeconomic slowdowns, export trade halts and reduced customer R&D capex remain key risks to

Revenue and Growth Guidance
• TIPCO Engineering targets standalone revenue growth of at least 30-40% a year, with the current base marking the start of a
broader scaling phase. Peak revenue capacity across the Sonipat plant and the upcoming Pune facility is projected to exceed
INR 5-6 bn. The company has grown from a base turnover of INR 5 mn under Chairman and Managing Director Ritesh Sharma.
Revenue Mix and Margins
• Operating leverage has played out in recent quarters, and management expects margin expansion as higher-margin
specialised products scale up and production volumes increase. Initial gross margins for specialised products will remain stable
or slightly higher, while regular batch production in Pune will enhance overall profitability. Standard catalogue models account
for ~70% of orders and customised machinery for 30%.
Capex and Capacity Expansion
• TIPCO is developing a world-class 5-10 acre facility in Pune using funds raised from its recent IPO and preferential issue. The
Pune facility will expand overall production capacity 3-4x over current levels once fully operational. The Experience Centre and
assembly unit were expected to be functional in Q4FY26, with major factory operations commencing in Q1FY27-Q2FY27 and
full operational scale by Q2FY27-Q3FY27.
Order Book and Dynamics
• Orders under INR 5 mn take ~1 month to finalise, standard machinery orders of ~INR 10 mn require 2-3 months for client
decision-making, and large turnkey projects exceeding INR 200 mn involve a six-month cycle of evaluation, RFQ, technical
comparison and trial runs. Standard catalogue models can be produced in 1-2 months, while customised machinery requires
additional design and delivery time. TIPCO is receiving active order enquiries from major corporate brands but is currently
constrained by production capacity at its Sonipat plant.
Core Processes and Technical Capabilities
• TIPCO specialises in basic engineering design and manufacturing across four core process verticals: mixing, milling,
homogenising and chemical reactions. Its machinery handles a wide spectrum of processes, spanning low to high viscosity and
low to high temperature requirements. The company has evolved from a simple equipment supplier into an end-to-end
turnkey solution provider, now executing single turnkey projects worth up to INR 800 mn out of client equipment capex
budgets of INR 2 bn.
Fabrication and Manufacturing
• TIPCO keeps 90% of its fabrication and machining in-house, ensuring strict quality control and precision engineering. The
existing Sonipat facility operates on a half-acre footprint with a monthly capacity of 50-60 machines; it is running at close to
100% utilisation with a full order book, handling general mixing machinery and standard projects, primarily serving North
India.
Pune Plant and Specialised Focus
• The Pune facility will feature a dedicated Experience Centre allowing clients to conduct R&D, product trials and slurry test runs
before placing orders. The site will focus on specialised, high-margin machinery such as planetary mixers, pharmaceutical
equipment, cosmetic machinery and EV battery slurry systems.

Trishakti Industries Ltd

• Trishakti Industries has undergone a significant transformation into a focused infrastructure equipment rental platform, with

Aggressive Capex Backed by Strong Demand & High Utilisation
• The company is pursuing a cumulative INR 4,000 mn capex programme, of which ~INR 2,700 mn had been deployed by

UGRO Capital Ltd
Emerging Market Lab (Secured Micro SME)
• The business has 318 branches across 13 states (none in Eastern India; Tamil Nadu is the largest, with 56 branches), of which
~200 were added in the last two years.
• It targets micro SMEs with turnover below INR 30 mn, offering secured-only loans of INR 0.75-5 mn at an 18-18.5% yield with a
~10-year tenure. AUM is ~INR 40 bn, with GNPA of 2.1%.
• Each branch has 5-6 sales staff, one credit officer, one operations officer, one branch manager and one collections officer. Direct
sourcing in Tier 3-5 towns keeps pre-closure and foreclosure rates low.
• Productivity is ~INR 8 mn per branch per month (industry benchmark: INR 7-8 mn), against a target of INR 10 mn. Many
branches opened last year are yet to complete 12 months, a key productivity milestone.
• Monthly disbursals are stabilising at INR 2.4-2.5 bn, with an exit run-rate target of INR 2.8-3 bn per month.
• No further branch additions are planned for the next two years; the focus is entirely on productivity improvement and AUM
monetisation.
Embedded Merchant Finance (GrowX Technologies)
• This 100% subsidiary was acquired ~2 years ago. Its technology platform is embedded in PhonePe, Paytm and BharatPe, and
now in e-commerce platforms such as Meesho.
• The product is QR code-based lending to small retailers, with a ticket size of ~INR 0.1 mn, a one-year tenure and daily
repayment.
• AUM is ~INR 30 bn. The business crossed 400,000 customers in September (up from 350,000+ in June) and is adding 60,000-
70,000 customers a month. About 50% of PhonePe disbursals go through UGRO.
• It disburses INR 7-8 bn a month, but INR 5-6 bn comes back as daily repayments, so the business generates high income but is
not a major AUM builder. The AUM target is INR 45 bn.
• GNPA is 2.1% and is expected to stabilise at ~2.5%. Unit economics comprise a 30-36% customer yield, a 10% payout to the
originator and a 5-6% credit cost reserve, leaving a clean ROA of ~4%.
Strategic Realignment & Financials
• UGRO discontinued its DSA-led prime business (customers with turnover of INR 30-150 mn) due to high pre-closure rates, as
customers were being refinanced at 9.5% after one year versus UGRO's 13.5%.
• UGRO tactically acquired Profectus Capital (one-fourth of UGRO's size, in a similar segment). It cut ~INR 1.2 bn of opex at
Profectus and INR 800 mn by winding down the prime vertical, for total opex savings of ~INR 2 bn.
• Q1FY27: Total AUM of INR 150 bn, gross disbursements of INR 25 bn, PBT of INR 610 mn, GNPA of 2.6% and ROA of 2.6%. The
cost of borrowing is declining but needs to fall faster.
• The focus portfolio is 46% of the total book (up from 32%), with a target of 85% by FY29. A yield improvement of 100-120 bps is
expected as the mix shifts.
• Co-lending income was 24% of total income last year, with a target of below 5% by FY29. This will make earnings more annuity-
and cash-based and reduce volatility.
Liability & Ratings
• Borrowings come from 65+ active lenders: 45% from bank loans, with a large DFI/FI and capital market component. By
instrument, 50% is term loans and the rest ECBs and NCDs.
• UGRO is rated A+ with a positive outlook and expects an upgrade next year, which would reduce its cost of borrowing. The ECB
mix is increasing (five-year tenure versus three years for domestic borrowing) to improve ALM, and ECBs are 100% hedged.
• No equity raise is needed for 2-3 years, as profit accretion is sufficient for expansion plans.
Shareholder & Other Updates
• The largest shareholder is IFU (Danish government, 15.5%). The original PE backers are Samena Capital (~12%), ADV Partners
(~12%) and TPG NewQuest (~9%). The TPG fund has reached the end of its life and is selling, while ADV has taken an extension.
• There is no impact from the RBI's proposed revolving credit rules, as UGRO offers only term loans, and minimal impact from the
IRDAI commission cap regulation, as insurance is an attached product with a low share of income.
• Branch breakeven requires AUM of INR 50 mn, with opex of ~INR 0.4 mn per month; ~50% of branches are already profitable,
and the rest are expected to break even this year.
Guidance
• The ROA target is 3-3.5% (from 2-2.5% currently). The focus portfolio is expected to reach 85% of AUM by FY29, with a 25-30%
CAGR, and GNPA is expected at ~3% in steady state.
• AUM may be broadly flat this year as the low-yield book runs down, but the focus verticals will grow materially. No equity raise
is planned for 2-3 years.

Ujjivan Small Finance Bank Ltd
Ujjivan SFB has entered FY27 on a strong footing, with record PPOP, normalised asset quality across microbanking and its newer
secured verticals, and margins sustained at 8.5% over the last two quarters. The bank reiterated FY27 guidance of ~25% growth, a
56% secured mix by year-end and ROA of 1.8-1.9%, while flagging the IRDAI insurance distribution draft as the principal overhang,
which it is working to mitigate, assuming an implementation date of 1 April 2027.
Growth and Book Mix
• Growth is coming from all segments, secured and unsecured; microbanking has shown good trends for four quarters, and the
secured verticals built over the last 3-4 years are performing without capacity constraints.
• Q1 showed 29% YoY growth, helped by a low microbanking base; H1 benefits from the base effect before growth settles
towards 25%, with possible upside of a couple of percentage points if conditions hold.
• The secured mix is guided to reach 56% by the end of FY27 and is on track, given the sequential product growth seen in Q1.
Margins, Rates and Funding
• NIM was sustained at 8.5% across the FY26 exit quarter and Q1FY27; the floating book is ~18% of assets, with the housing
product fixed for the first 39 months. The treasury expects a 25 bps rate action on 8 October.
• Q1 looks like the trough in cost of funds; some favourable repricing was captured in Q2, and the June rate hikes have flowed
through without meaningful impact. Cost of funds in H2 is expected to be within 5-10 bps of Q1.
• In the prior hiking cycle, NIM moved from 8.8% (FY22) to 9.8% (FY23), then 9.1% (FY24) and 8.8% (FY25), with the sharpest
compression of ~70 bps in FY24, partly reflecting the diversification journey.
Affordable Housing
• The bank is comfortable holding yields in the near term despite larger banks entering, growing the book at the bank's trend
level of 25-26% while other secured products grow faster.
• Around 16-20% of customers are balance-transferred in; dedicated retention teams keep balance transfers out below the
industry level. The product runs through 560-580 branches, with the top 10 cities accounting for under 25-30% of
disbursements, and roughly one-third is sourced internally, with low DSA dependence.
Asset Quality and Newer Verticals
• There has been no change in high-frequency metrics between Q1 and Q2; Q1 credit cost was at the lower end of the guided
range and looks set to hold. Collection efficiency held through April-June, with only localised rainfall pockets.
• Newer secured products (gold, agri, vehicle and micro mortgage) are tracking within priced static pool curves but have not yet
broken even at the bottom line; most higher-yielding products are self-sourced for quality control, with contribution expected
once each product reaches AUM of INR 15-25 bn.
• The new MSME book carries a credit cost of 0.6%; affordable housing and micro mortgages are already profitable at the
operating level and, in a small way, at the bottom line.
Insurance Overhang and Management
• Credit life was ~55% of FY26 insurance income; FY26 insurance income was ~INR 1.75 bn, out of roughly INR 11 bn of other
income (~15%). The bank plans to reduce this dependence and will use pricing, processing fees and product redesign to
mitigate the impact, working with insurers and collectively approaching IRDAI.
• The only recent top management change is the early exit of the MD and CEO on health grounds; no other senior exits have
been reported to the exchanges. A capital raise is planned for H2FY27, with CRAR at 20.4% as of Q1.
Guidance & View
The bank reaffirmed FY27 guidance of ~25% growth, a 56% secured mix at year-end and ROA of 1.8-1.9%, with a base case that the
IRDAI insurance draft is implemented from 1 April 2027 and so does not dent the current year; a January implementation would
be the bear case. The capital raise is slated for H2FY27.
Execution risk looks contained given normalised microbanking, record PPOP and industry-leading asset quality, but insurance
distribution economics remain the key uncertainty into FY28, and the quantum of mitigation is not yet knowable. The spread
across geographies and the self-sourced, higher-yield mix lend durability to the ROA band.

UniHealth Hospitals Ltd
Outlook: UniHealth Hospitals is pursuing a dual-market healthcare strategy across India and East Africa, with hospitals and medical
centres as the core growth engine, supported by healthcare consultancy, pharmaceutical and medical consumable exports and
distribution, and Medical Value Travel (MVT). The company currently has 400 commissioned beds across India and Uganda and is
targeting 1,000 commissioned beds by CY28. Management expects growth to be driven by occupancy ramp-up at Navi Mumbai
and Nashik, the planned Pune expansion, further East Africa expansion and potential hospital O&M and acquisition opportunities.
Current Bed Capacity & Occupancy
The company has 400 commissioned beds, comprising 150 beds in Uganda, 50 beds in Navi Mumbai and 200 beds in Nashik.
Uganda is the mature market with occupancy of 68-72%. Navi Mumbai, which had a soft launch in October 2025 and full services
from February 2026, has ramped occupancy from 15-16% initially to 35-40% currently. Management expects Navi Mumbai to cross
50% occupancy over the next couple of months as insurance empanelments are completed. Nashik commenced operations on 1
September 2026, initially with OPD and diagnostics, followed by in-patient services, with meaningful occupancy ramp-up expected
from November 2026.
India Expansion
The company is building a healthcare network across Maharashtra, with Mumbai/Navi Mumbai, Nashik and Pune forming its
strategic "Golden Triangle". Pune is the next planned addition, with 125 beds expected to be added, taking commissioned capacity
beyond 500 beds. The company is also evaluating an operational or management takeover or collaboration with an existing Pune
hospital, which could potentially accelerate revenue contribution. Following Pune, the company plans to expand further in
Mumbai.
East Africa Expansion
East Africa remains an important high-margin market, with management targeting an increase in capacity from the current 150
beds to 450 beds. Expansion is planned across Tanzania and potentially Kenya by CY28. The company had earlier targeted a 100-
bed hospital acquisition in Tanzania; however, the transaction has been deferred pending statutory, taxation and bureaucratic
approvals, as the target hospital is operated under a trust. Commercial terms have reportedly been agreed, with revenue
contribution now expected to shift to the next financial year.
FY26 Guidance & Revenue Outlook
Management is targeting INR 2,000 mn of consolidated revenue for FY26, based on conservative assumptions of 40-45%
consolidated occupancy across the 400 commissioned beds and ARPOB of INR 30,000-32,000 per occupied bed per day. Earlier
revenue expectations were around INR 2,500 mn, with the revision primarily reflecting the deferment of the Tanzania hospital
acquisition. Navi Mumbai is expected to contribute more significantly from Q4FY26 as occupancy crosses 50%, while Nashik is
expected to start contributing meaningfully from Q4FY26 and Q1FY27.
FY27-FY28 Growth Targets
By FY27, management expects commissioned capacity to exceed 500 beds, including the planned 125-bed Pune addition. Average
occupancy is targeted in the mid-50% range, implying 275 occupied beds, while ARPOB is expected to increase toward INR 35,000
per day. Management expects a substantial increase in revenue as Navi Mumbai and Nashik mature and new capacity is
commissioned. During FY27-FY28, another 250-350 beds are expected to be added, with the overall target of reaching 1,000
commissioned beds by CY28.
FY28 Financial Outlook
Management targets a conservative consolidated revenue of INR 3,400-3,500 mn by FY28 based on 500+ mature beds, 55-62%
occupancy and ARPOB of INR 34,000-35,000 per day. This translates to 325 occupied beds at the targeted occupancy levels. Any
accelerated O&M hospital takeovers or acquisitions, including the Tanzania opportunity, could provide additional revenue above
this base case. Consolidated EBITDA margins are expected to remain at 30%+.
Margins & India-East Africa Mix
East Africa currently generates EBITDA margins in the early-40% range, supported by mature operations and attractive market
economics. New Indian facilities are expected to initially incur setup-related operating losses before stabilising at early-to-mid 30%
EBITDA margins. Management expects some moderation in consolidated percentage margins as the India business scales, but
believes absolute EBITDA will increase significantly with higher capacity and occupancy.

Victoria Hospital: Share Swap
UniHealth completed a no-cash share swap to increase its ownership in Victoria Hospital Limited, which owns the real estate and
150-bed flagship hospital in Uganda. UniHealth previously held 50%, with the balance held by local partners. Effective 2
September 2026, UniHealth acquired an additional 49.81% equity by issuing fresh UniHealth shares, taking its stake to 99.81%.
Victoria Hospital became debt-free in September 2025 and benefits from a corporate tax holiday until 30 June 2034. The
transaction is expected to substantially reduce minority-interest deductions from PAT and allow UniHealth to capture a greater
share of Uganda's profits and cash flows for further expansion.
Working Capital & Receivables
The company has been addressing elevated trade receivables, including the previously highlighted INR 1,200 mn debtor balance.
Significant payments have been received from its largest debtor, the Uganda People's Defence Forces. Further quarterly payments
are expected, while Uganda's Ministry of Defence is working toward reducing debtor days to 180 days. Management expects the
consolidated receivables profile to improve materially as Navi Mumbai and Nashik scale up. Separately, long-outstanding
receivables of INR 60 mn reported in the FY26 annual report relate primarily to consultancy and export and distribution activities
rather than Uganda government receivables. Management expects a majority of these amounts to be recovered within 2-6 weeks.
Medical Value Travel (MVT)
UniHealth has established interlinked patient referral teams between Uganda and India. More than 15 international patients were
treated through the MVT channel during the last 4-5 months. Management expects MVT to become a more meaningful
contributor to the Indian hospital business from FY27 onwards, leveraging the company's established African patient network.
Healthcare Consultancy
The consultancy business is actively negotiating hospital setup and design projects covering 250-350 beds, with agreements
expected to be concluded in Q3. The consultancy vertical operates at EBITDA margins of 55-60%, providing a high-margin,
relatively asset-light revenue stream alongside the hospital business.
Pharmaceutical & Medical Consumables
Pharmaceutical and medical consumable export and distribution remains one of the company's supporting verticals. Some of the
older receivables highlighted in the FY26 annual report originated from this business. The vertical complements the company's
healthcare network in Africa and provides additional exposure to the region beyond hospital operations.
Sub-Specialities: IVF & Ophthalmology
The company launched an IVF centre in Uganda in January 2025, which management described as performing exceptionally well.
IVF is expected to be an anchor sub-specialty incorporated from day one into new tertiary-care facilities planned in Tanzania and
Kenya. In Uganda, the company is also expanding ophthalmology services covering cataract procedures, phacoemulsification and
retinal surgeries, with plans to replicate these capabilities across East Africa.
Doctor Engagement Model
UniHealth follows a mixed doctor engagement model. Full-time doctors provide 24/7 coverage across six core specialties: General
Medicine, General Surgery, Orthopaedics/Spine, Cardiology, Emergency and ICU. Visiting consultants are engaged under revenue-
sharing arrangements, while super-specialists are typically engaged through a minimum-guarantee plus revenue-share threshold
model.
Manpower & Operational Synergies
The India expansion is expected to create a larger pool of trained nursing, technical and administrative personnel. Management
intends to leverage this manpower base for its East African operations, with employees potentially taking 1-3 year assignments in
Africa before returning to Indian facilities within the group. The company's Mumbai roots and established local doctor networks
are also expected to support expansion across Maharashtra.
Capital Structure & Fundraising
The company currently has a single term loan of INR 220 mn, raised in November 2025 for Nashik equipment. Management
remains open to conservative debt for equipment purchases and asset acquisitions. Funding for the planned 600-bed expansion
toward 1,000 beds is expected to come from internal accruals (particularly Uganda cash flows), bank debt and equity dilution.
Management is evaluating a QIP or preferential allotment in Q3 or Q4.
Key Growth Drivers & Risks
Growth is expected to be driven by occupancy ramp-up at Navi Mumbai and Nashik, the 125-bed Pune addition, expansion across
East Africa, higher ARPOB, consolidation of Victoria Hospital's earnings, MVT growth, high-margin consultancy projects and
expansion of IVF and ophthalmology services. Key monitorables include the pace of occupancy ramp-up, insurance
empanelments, execution of the Pune expansion, Tanzania acquisition timelines, receivable collections and debtor days, funding
requirements and equity dilution, margin normalisation as India scales, and the ability to execute the 1,000-bed target by CY28.

Updater Services Ltd
Business
UDS is a ~40-year-old facilities management and business services company founded by Raghunandana Tangirala. Revenue is ~INR
32,000-33,000 mn across two segments.
Integrated Facilities Management (IFM) is about two-thirds of revenue (~INR 22,000-23,000 mn in FY27) and ~55% of EBITDA. It
covers housekeeping, technical and engineering (MEP) services, production support, warehousing and catering. The catering arm,
Fusion, has revenue of ~INR 1,400-1,500 mn with industry-leading margins. Washroom Hygiene Concepts (sanitary waste disposal)
is a small but very high-margin business.
Business Support Services (BSS) is about one-third of revenue (INR 10,000+ mn in FY27) and ~45% of EBITDA. In sales enablement,
Denave sells for global B2B tech clients such as Google, SAP and Lenovo, while Athena runs outbound sales calls for banks and
NBFCs. In assurance, Matrix conducts employee background checks and supply chain audits for FMCG and food companies. Airport
ground handling at 23 airports brings in ~INR 600-700 mn a year.
IFM is strongest in South India and in industrial, warehousing and infrastructure clients. UDS deliberately stays out of residential and
is weak in commercial.
The promoter family owns ~60%. The board has six members, three of them independent, and Group CFO Ram Praveen joined
about three months ago.
Guidance
No formal guidance was given. Q1FY27 PAT was INR 303 mn on revenue of INR 7,640 mn. Management said annualising Q1 gives
PAT of ~INR 1,210 mn against a normalised FY26 base of ~INR 1,040 mn, and it hopes to beat that, without committing.
FY27 revenue growth is expected at ~10-12% in what management calls a stabilisation year, with some acceleration thereafter. Q2
results are due in 2-3 weeks and are tracking well.
EBITDA margins should improve slowly, about 50 bps at a time (for example, from 6% to 6.5% to 7%), driven by scale and a richer
service mix. Double-digit margins are not expected in the near term, and pricing is not a margin lever in this industry.
Management describes UDS as a cash compounder: ~INR 4,000 mn of cash, ~INR 800-900 mn generated a year and zero debt.
Why Growth Slowed
Growth fell from ~18-20% to ~10% because of setbacks in three BSS businesses. Management says all three have now stabilised.
Avon: An incident last year led UDS to shut down the transport brokerage division entirely, so that revenue is gone.
Matrix: The IT hiring freeze hit background verification. Management sees green shoots and is diversifying away from IT clients.
Athena: Four large clients were lost to their own corporate actions rather than service issues, including Citi's sale to Axis, Standard
Chartered's retail exit and ICICI Securities' merger. No further clients have been lost, and new ones are being added.
UDS avoids GCC and commercial work routed through property consultants such as JLL and CBRE, because it would act as a
subcontractor on thin margins and wait 3-5 months for payment. It will try to win GCC clients directly instead.
IFM Operations
About 99.9% of contracts pass through wage increases, including minimum wage and labour code changes, to the client. Where
large hikes cannot be passed on, UDS exits the contract.
The labour codes caused a one-off ~INR 50 mn charge last year for non-billable staff. Management sees the codes reinforcing three
industry tailwinds: formalisation, outsourcing and consolidation.
About 95% of IFM business renews each year. An estimated 60-80% of revenue comes from clients served for more than five years,
and some for decades.
Contracts lost to rivals' unrealistically low bids often come back within a year.
IFM working capital is ~70-72 days.
UDS adds ~100 new clients every half year across its businesses.

Bharat Connect Conference CompendiumPost Conference Note
Business
• Vaibhav Global is an electronic retailer of fashion jewellery and lifestyle products selling through TV and digital channels in the
US, UK and Germany, under brands including Shop LC. It has ~40 years of experience in jewellery manufacturing and sourcing,
and also owns Ideal World and Mindful Souls in the UK.
• FY26 revenue grew ~13%, or more than 10% excluding one-off duty refunds, with better profitability. Management said this
was in line with its guidance.
• Digital is ~46% of revenue and in-house brands ~58%. Lab-grown diamond (LGD) jewellery is more than 13% of revenue, and
lifestyle categories (beauty, apparel and other fashion) ~40%.
• All diamonds sold are certified, which management uses as a selling point to build customer confidence.
• Customer retention was ~38-39% in FY26 and is falling as the digital share rises, because TV customers are more loyal than
digital ones. Retention among customers with 20+ purchases is ~80%.
Guidance
• FY27 revenue growth is guided at 9-11% with EBITDA margin improvement, and management reaffirmed this on the call.
• Digital is expected to exceed 50% of FY27 revenue, and in-house brands to exceed 60%.
• Lifestyle categories are targeted at ~50% of revenue over the medium to long term.
• Management expects ~10% constant-currency growth next year, as digital growth of ~17-19% offsets roughly flat TV sales (~1%
across the US, UK and Germany).
• Germany is growing ~8-10% in local currency and should return to double digits once the benefits of the digital platform
migration come through.
Digital and Technology
• The company moved all six brands from Salesforce Commerce Cloud to Shopify, a platform built for direct-to-consumer brands
with more plug-and-play features. There were a couple of months of teething problems, and digital share has been rising again
since August-September.
• The migration cost less than USD 1 mn for all six brands, against ~USD 2 mn for the US website migration alone in 2022.
Management credits AI-assisted coding for the lower cost and minimal disruption.
• AI is also lifting productivity in campaign optimisation across Meta, email, push notifications, apps and OTT. Technology costs
are falling because most AI tools need only subscriptions.
• Digital sales grew at a ~12% CAGR in local currency over the last 4 years with little paid marketing. Paid spend on Meta and
TikTok is now being stepped up, and management cited pure D2C jewellery retailers in the US growing 30-40% through these
channels.
Platforms and Categories
• TV is slowing because of US cord-cutting and because viewers are moving to livestreams on the company's website and apps.
Web growth is offsetting the TV decline.
• LGD demand remains solid on both TV and Meta. The range is expanding into fast fashion at USD 50-100 price points, from
engagement rings to daily-wear earrings.
• Natural diamonds and some coloured gemstones are slowing, while opal and tanzanite are seeing traction.
• The company is launching supplements this year, including protein products aimed at customers on GLP-1 drugs, alongside
beauty products for its core audience of women.
Geographies
• UK: The UK is profitable on a standalone basis. Margins dipped because the company is paying double leases from March to
December 2026 while consolidating four buildings into one, and management expects profitability to improve after December.
• Germany: A regulatory change cut Vodafone's cable base from 13 mn to 9 mn households, because tenants now need
individual connections, which hurt TV sales last year. Growth has since returned, and Germany has just broken even.
Management noted that an established peer generates ~USD 2 bn of revenue in Germany with a similar audience.
• New markets: No new countries will be added until Germany's past losses are recovered and existing markets are more stable.
Capital Allocation
• Management sees acquisition opportunities in the US but is focusing on organic digital growth first. It said earlier acquisitions
had partly diverted focus from organic growth.
• The company will keep ~USD 50 mn as a cushion against tariff and AI-related uncertainty before considering buybacks or
acquisitions.
• Inventory runs at ~200-220 days, which management says is needed for its channels and production and expects to stay at that
level.

Vibhor Steel Tubes Ltd
Business
• The company started in 2003 in Raigad, Maharashtra, with ERW black and galvanised steel pipes. The first unit had one tube
mill and 1,000 tonnes per month of capacity.
• The MD joined full time around 2006-07 and scaled the business with Jindal Pipe as the anchor partner. Maharashtra pipe sizes
grew from ½"-4" to ½"-8", capacity rose to ~10,000 tonnes per month, and volumes reached 7,000-8,000 tonnes per month
around 2010.
• A second plant in Telangana, of similar capacity, was profitable from day one. Pipe sizes there went from ½"-12" to ½"-14".
Highway crash barriers were added there about 4 years ago, with steady sales since.
• The third plant at Jharsuguda, Odisha, started operations last October. It makes pipes (up to 10"), crash barriers, transmission
line towers (TLT) and octagonal and high-mast poles. The company recently received its first monopole certificate (132 kV,
CPRI).
• A fourth plant is being set up at Hisar, Haryana. It will start with crash barriers and then add other products. Construction
companies are already enquiring.
• Management says the company is now recognised as an infra supplier and contractors have started approaching it.
Jindal Pipe Arrangement
• This is a contract manufacturing arrangement in place since 2003-04. Jindal passes on dealer enquiries, the company bills
Jindal, and Jindal bills its dealers.
• It is the sole supplier to Jindal in Maharashtra, Telangana, and Odisha and the Northeast. Jindal has a similar arrangement with
only one other manufacturer (in Bangalore). In the North, Jindal manufactures itself at Ghaziabad.
• Jindal contributes ~80% of revenue. The arrangement means no distribution or marketing budget, no salesmen and no debtor
chasing.
• Management sees the dependence as mutual. The newer products are small in turnover today but carry better margins.
• The company also has its own distribution in Europe and Australia. Indian enquiries are routed through Jindal, and
management could sell directly if needed.
• If Jindal offtake ever fell, management would fall back on exports, end-user and firefighting-contractor enquiries, or on other
galvanised products (e.g., a 1,000-tonne RSJ order currently deferred). Some export enquiries are being turned down to keep
the regular dealers supplied.
Financials and Margins
• Q1 revenue was INR 2.93 bn versus INR 2.3 bn last year. Management attributes the growth mainly to Jharsuguda and says it
was volume-led, with steel prices having little effect in Q1.
• EBITDA margin has stayed at ~4% for years.
• Management attributes the margin gap to peers to two factors: higher depreciation from Jharsuguda, and peers already
having a richer product mix (hollow sections, crash barrier, TLT).
• The near-term priority is customer acquisition in the Northeast and turnover. Margins on new business are ~3-4% and kept
above zero, with incentives given to win customers.
• Steel prices are on an upward trend, so inventory gains should support margins for the rest of the year. Management calls this
cyclical and does not count on it.
• EBITDA should improve as the newer products contribute, while pipe and crash barrier margins stay constant. Management
expects stability in about 2 years.
• Interest cost has stayed at ~INR 140-160 mn over FY19-FY26. Management says no large term loan was taken for Telangana
and the working-capital cycle has been steady. Interest cost should rise slightly with the new plant's term loan.
• No credit is given on the new products (payment before dispatch), so debtor days are near zero. Working capital could
improve as the mix shifts.
• Inventory is kept at no more than 1.5x sales when the market is strong, and at about 1x when it is weak. Management suggests
tracking turnover, debtor days, inventory days and the working-capital cycle.
Product-Wise Status
• Telangana sells ~6,000-7,000 tonnes (of which 1,000-1,500 tonnes is crash barrier, the rest pipe), stable QoQ.
• Jharsuguda's order book is:
◦ Pipe: ~1,500-2,000 tonnes.
◦ Crash barrier: 1,000-1,200 tonnes.
◦ TLT: a 1,500-tonne order.
◦ Poles: ~300 tonnes, which it cannot yet produce for lack of galvanising capacity.
• Poles have had an order book of 200-300 tonnes for 3 months against ~100 tonnes of capacity. New machines have arrived and
some are being modified. The target is to meet ~300 tonnes within this financial year.
• TLT sales are 150-200 tonnes now, from state electricity orders. Power Grid orders are expected in Q3, or Q4 at the latest, with
a few documents pending that could clear in October-November. This could lift TLT volumes above 1,000 tonnes, about 5x.
• State TLT orders carry lower margins. Management expects Power Grid and large EPC players (Adani, L&T, Bajaj, Tata Projects)
to bring better margins and repeat orders.
• The current order of priority is pipe dealers, then crash barrier, then TLT, then poles. TLT is expected to become the top
priority once Power Grid orders flow.

• Jharsuguda's product mix could move towards ~50% non-pipe, though pipe will likely remain the largest because of the 20-
year pipe franchise.
Capacity and Capex
• Galvanising is the bottleneck, so utilisation is judged on galvanising tanks rather than machines.
• Maharashtra (2 tanks, ~5,000 tonnes per month) and Telangana (2 tanks, ~3,500 tonnes per month, with one for pipe and one
for crash barrier) are at maximum levels.
• Jharsuguda utilisation is ~25-30% (the MD called it "quite low"). A second galvanising tank has been commissioned, with
production started and a revenue impact from October.
• The first target is ~3,000 tonnes per month from the two Jharsuguda tanks within this financial year, hopefully in Q3.
• A third tank is likely next year, after watching how the two perform. Management indicated ~3,500 tonnes per month at the
next milestone and ~5,000 tonnes per month after the third tank.
• Capex is being added cautiously and only when orders are visible.
Growth Outlook
• Each plant has added ~INR 5 bn of turnover historically: INR 5 bn (Maharashtra), INR 10 bn (with Telangana), INR 15 bn (with
Jharsuguda) and ~INR 20 bn (with Hisar). Turnover could exceed INR 20 bn if the new products deliver. Management said this
is a trend rather than guidance.
• Becoming an EPC contractor for TLT and monopoles is a longer-term option and not being pursued now.
Peers
• Management says APL Apollo (hollow sections) is not a like-for-like peer, since Vibhor's presence in hollow sections is almost
zero.
• Closer peers named are Goodluck, Hi-Tech and Rama Pipe.

Vikran Engineering Ltd
Outlook: Vikran Engineering has strong near-term visibility, with an order book of ~INR 65 bn, FY26 standalone revenue guidance
of ~INR 22-25 bn and margins sustained at ~14-17%. The NOPL Solar acquisition is the key value driver, adding 969 MW with ~INR
5.25-5.5 bn of annual revenue at an ~88-90% EBITDA margin and ~INR 1.3-1.4 bn of annual post-tax free cash flow, with most
commissioning expected in FY26 and completion before June 2027. The asset-light, agile model supports diversification into solar,
data centres and battery energy storage, while overseas forays through the UAE target ~15-20% margins. Execution remains
largely on track, with ~90% of land tied up and panel prices secured, although receivables and the pending NTPC land parcel
warrant monitoring. Overall, the outlook is positive, with ~20-25% growth targeted and revenue of INR 30 bn seen as comfortably
achievable by FY28.
Business Profile and Positioning
Vikran Engineering is an asset-light EPC player operating across power transmission and distribution, substations, solar EPC and
development, water infrastructure (including Jal Jeevan Mission, groundwater and surface water extraction, treatment plants,
sewage treatment plants and pipeline laying) and overhead electrification for Indian Railways. The company has executed projects
in tough terrain across Arunachal Pradesh, Kashmir, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Naxal-affected belts of Madhya Pradesh,
Jharkhand and Bihar. It has worked across ~22 states, maintains ~4,000 registered vendors and contractors on SAP, and counts
Power Grid, NTPC and MSEDCL among its key clients.
Financial Guidance and Order Book
FY25 revenue stood at ~INR 12.25-12.5 bn, with an EBITDA margin of ~14%. FY26 guidance is ~INR 22-25 bn on a standalone basis,
nearly a 2x jump, with similar margins. The current order book is ~INR 65 bn, of which roughly one-third is targeted for completion
this year. The company aims to close FY26 with ~INR 55-60 bn of orders, maintaining order book visibility at ~2.5-3x revenue. The
typical project duration is ~2-5 years. The average ticket size is INR 3-5 bn, with a minimum threshold of ~INR 1 bn, although INR
500-600 mn orders are accepted if they are quickly executable or credential-enhancing. The win rate is ~10-20%.
NOPL Solar Acquisition and Developer Economics
The NOPL Solar acquisition adds a 969 MW AC solar development contract in Maharashtra, with total capex of ~INR 42 bn already
tied up with lenders. The central government subsidy is ~INR 10,175 mn. The tariff is INR 3.074 per unit versus prevailing market
rates of ~INR 2.4-2.5. The project allows non-DCR panels, reducing capex by ~INR 10-12 mn per MW, and uses 15 MW modular
blocks at a single location with existing 220 kV and 132 kV evacuation infrastructure. Once commissioned, it is expected to
generate ~INR 5.25-5.5 bn of annual revenue at an ~88-90% EBITDA margin, with average free cash flow of ~INR 1.3-1.4 bn per
year post-tax over 25 years. The improvement in net worth is estimated at ~INR 20 bn. About 60-65 MW is already commissioned,
another ~150 MW is expected within 30-45 days, and full commissioning is targeted before June 2027, with most revenue falling
in FY26 and some spillover into FY27.
Funding and Capital Structure
The company has ~INR 1.8 bn of fund-based limits and ~INR 4.1-4.2 bn of non-fund-based limits, totalling ~INR 5.9 bn of bank
limits with ~70-75% utilisation, plus ~INR 2.5 bn of sanctioned but unutilised non-fund-based limits. For the INR 42 bn NOPL
project, ~INR 30 bn will be debt and ~INR 12 bn equity, of which ~INR 6-7 bn will come from internal accruals and ~INR 1.4-1.5 bn
has already been raised through NCDs and a term loan, with ~INR 3 bn more raisable as needed. The company targets 80:20 or
85:15 debt-to-equity for projects to improve equity IRR, while ensuring cash flows support debt servicing. The minimum equity
IRR threshold is ~15-18%, in addition to attractive EPC margins.
Water Segment and Receivables
The Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) order book is ~INR 6-7 bn across UP, MP and Chhattisgarh. Working capital for JJM has been capped
at ~INR 1.2 bn, with collections reinvested village by village. No additional working capital is needed even if the scheme extends to
FY28, and escalation clauses protect margins. A ~INR 65 mn provision was taken in Q1 primarily on water, with reversal expected
on recovery. The company is confident of recovering government receivables, and payments have improved versus last year, with
completion expected within a year.
Growth Strategy and New Verticals
The company follows a satellite business model, shifting towards government focus areas such as power, water, railways and now
renewables, with future interest in battery energy storage systems and data centres. Its FY30 vision includes growing ~20-25% a
year, comfortably crossing INR 30 bn of revenue by FY28, and exploring long-term private partnerships with large funds to finance
the equity requirements of large projects while Vikran handles execution. In data centres, the initial focus will be on GIS and AIS
substations and connecting data centres to the nearest substation, later graduating to MEP and civil work. In battery energy
storage, engineering and execution capabilities are in place, but the company has avoided aggressive bids and will not commit to
unrealistic pricing that risks bank guarantee encashment.

Overseas and Competitive Positioning
Overseas enquiries total ~INR 15 bn, with a UAE subsidiary planned to target Africa and other international markets, leveraging

Vilas Transcore Ltd
Vilas Transcore is expanding from its core CRGO lamination business into higher-value transformer components, with radiators
and nanocrystalline cores already commercialised and copper conductors being added to the portfolio. The company has
expanded CRGO lamination capacity from 12,000 MTPA to 36,000 MTPA, while Unit 3 houses 240 MTPA of nanocrystalline
capacity and 7,200 MTPA of radiator capacity. Nanocrystalline sales reached ~30,250 kg in H2FY26, generating INR 34.8 mn of
revenue, with management targeting ~15 MT per month utilisation in FY27. The radiator facility has recently commenced
commercial production and management sees strong growth potential as approvals and tenders are completed. In the
management meeting, radiator production was indicated at 50-60 MT per month versus installed capacity of 600 MT per month,
highlighting significant headroom for ramp-up. CRGO production reached 19,856 MT in FY26, and management has guided for 45-
50% CRGO volume growth and 40-50% revenue growth in FY27, with EBITDA and PAT margins expected to be maintained. Copper
conductor Phase I of 1,550-1,800 MTPA is targeted for completion by September 2026, with revenue contribution expected from
H2FY27. The key factors to monitor are the ramp-up of radiator and nanocrystalline capacity, CRGO volume growth, tender and
approval conversion, copper conductor commissioning, product mix and margin sustainability.
Business Model & Positioning
• The company has expanded its portfolio into nanocrystalline cores, radiators and copper conductors, moving towards a
broader transformer value-chain offering.
• The company operates three manufacturing facilities in Vadodara, with Unit 3 housing the newly added product capacities.
• Management is targeting higher wallet share from existing transformer customers through the expanded product portfolio.
CRGO – Core Business & Capacity Expansion
• CRGO lamination capacity has increased from 12,000 MTPA to 36,000 MTPA, following the commissioning of the additional
24,000 MTPA capacity in July 2025.
• FY26 CRGO production stood at 19,856 MT, compared with 12,069 MT in FY25.
• The additional capacity is expected to support the company's targeted volume growth going forward.
Radiator Business
• Radiator capacity stands at 7,200 MTPA, equivalent to around 600 MT per month.
• Current production was indicated at around 50-60 MT per month, implying significant available capacity for ramp-up.
• The radiator facility has recently commenced commercial production and is expected to contribute to revenues in FY27.
• Management expects approvals and tenders to be completed during FY27 and FY28, supporting the growth opportunity in the
radiator business.
• The radiator business is expected to be an important incremental growth driver as utilisation increases.
Nanocrystalline Business
• The company has installed 240 MTPA of nanocrystalline core capacity. Commercial production commenced during FY26.
• The business generated INR 34.8 mn of revenue in H2FY26, with sales volume of ~30,250 kg.
• Management expects utilisation to reach around 15 MT per month or ~180 MTPA in FY27.
• Production was at around 13-14 MT per month, consistent with the company guidance of moving towards 15 MT per month.
Copper Conductors
• The company is entering the copper conductor segment as part of its strategy to expand across the transformer value chain.
• Phase I will include copper PICC, CTC conductors and paper-insulated aluminium conductors. Phase I capacity is planned at
1,550-1,800 MTPA.
• The project has an estimated capex of INR 250-300 mn, funded through term loan and internal accruals.
• Phase I completion is targeted for September 2026, with the latest management commentary indicating revenue contribution
from H2FY27 onwards.
FY27 Growth Guidance
• Management has guided for 45-50% CRGO volume growth in FY27.
• Revenue growth guidance stands at 40-50%, depending on the product mix.
• Management expects EBITDA and PAT margins to be maintained despite the ongoing capacity ramp-up.
• The growth is expected to be supported by higher CRGO utilisation, radiator contribution, nanocrystalline ramp-up and the
eventual addition of copper conductors.

Virtual Galaxy Infotech Ltd
Business
Virtual Galaxy is a Nagpur-based software product company founded in 1997, and all its products are developed in-house.
Products cover core banking (e-Banker) for banking and financial services, e-governance, cybersecurity and healthcare. AI is built
into all of them, and management calls the company "AI-first".
It operates in ~20 Indian states and 4 African countries (Tanzania, Malawi, Botswana, Zimbabwe).
Core banking clients rarely switch, because migration is complex and the system handles regulatory reporting to RBI, NABARD and
other bodies.
Top 10 client concentration fell from 47% to 21%, and management expects ~20-25% as the normal level.
Guidance
FY27 growth is guided at 40%+, to ~INR 2,000 mn of revenue, and management says it is on track. It agreed with a participant that
~INR 5 bn by FY29-FY30 is the target. H1FY26 revenue was ~INR 860 mn, and H2 is always stronger.
Margins are expected to stay at current levels. Management said costs rise in line with clients, so it does not expect operating
leverage.
The order book is ~INR 1,500 mn, up from ~INR 1,100 mn in June. About 40% of revenue is recurring, and ~20% of bids convert.
Contracts run 1-7 years.
Growth Drivers
NBFCs: The RBI is pushing NBFCs onto core banking systems, starting with the largest tier. Management sees an opportunity of
more than USD 1 bn across 10,000+ NBFCs.
Cybersecurity: Revenue has started. Virtual Galaxy owns its SIEM and SOAR security platform, which management compares to IBM
QRadar. It has bid in defence tenders and is ranking first or second. Management sees the Make in India preference as an advantage
over foreign vendors, plus a price edge. Management did not disclose cybersecurity's share of revenue or the order book.
Africa: An ERP order from the Botswana Development Corporation is being implemented, and more are in the pipeline.
AI: Management sees AI as helping, not threatening, its product business.
Other
Fixed assets rose because of data centre investment, product development and IPO proceeds.
Employee cost looks low because part of salaries is booked as R&D. R&D spend will stay at a similar share of revenue.
There are currently no plans to appoint a Big Four auditor, though management will consider it. No acquisitions are under
discussion.
Management did not have figures for capex, R&D share or cybersecurity revenue, and said it will respond through investor
relations.

Viviana Power Tech Ltd

supply versus 60% earlier and debtor days expected to fall below 120. The key factors to monitor are order inflow and bid
conversion, order book execution, receivable-day reduction, transformer ramp-up and margin sustainability.
Business Model & Positioning
• The company is transitioning from a predominantly EPC-led model towards an integrated power infrastructure platform.
• The addition of transformer manufacturing is expected to diversify the revenue mix beyond EPC.
• Management expects manufacturing to contribute more than 30% of revenue over the next 3-5 years.
• The company is expanding beyond Gujarat, with projects across multiple states and participation in international tenders across
four countries.
Order Book & Bid Pipeline

Power T&D Opportunity

Transformer Manufacturing

Growth Guidance

Welspun Corp Ltd
Outlook: Welspun Corp has secured its largest-ever HFIW pipe order worth ~USD 412.5 mn (~INR 40 bn) through its US subsidiary,
Welspun Tubular LLC. The pipes will be manufactured at its newly upgraded HFIW mill in Little Rock, USA, with execution
scheduled across FY28-FY29. With this order, the company's global order book has reached a record USD 4.7 bn (~INR 450 bn). The
order strengthens revenue visibility, supports higher utilisation of its upgraded US manufacturing capabilities and reinforces the
company's position in the global pipe market.
View: We view the order positively, as the sizeable INR 40 bn order provides strong medium-term revenue visibility and further
strengthens the company's already-record order book. The order also validates Welspun Corp's US manufacturing capabilities and
ability to secure large international projects. Execution over FY28-FY29 should support sustained growth and provide better
visibility on future volumes and capacity utilisation. We have a Buy rating on the stock.
Business
Welspun Corp says it is the world's largest welded line pipe maker. Its pipes carry oil, gas and water, and it sells in 50+ countries
from plants in India, the US and Saudi Arabia.
Line pipe capacity is ~1.3 mn tonnes in India and ~0.5 mn tonnes in the US, rising to ~1.0 mn tonnes by end-CY26.
In Saudi Arabia, it holds 22% of East Pipes (~0.5 mn tonnes of spiral pipe). A new wholly owned subsidiary is building LSAW pipe
and ductile iron (DI) pipe plants there.
Other businesses are DI pipes in India (~0.6 mn tonnes), Welspun Specialty Solutions (stainless pipes and bars) and Sintex (water
tanks and plastic pipes, still being built up).
Net cash is above INR 23,000 mn after Q1, working capital is negative and ROCE is ~23%. New projects must clear a ~20% ROCE
hurdle, and net debt-to-EBITDA will stay below 1x.
Guidance
FY27 revenue is guided at ~INR 200 bn (up ~19%) and EBITDA at ~INR 28.5 bn (up ~20%).
EBITDA should grow at a ~20-25% CAGR for the next few years. Management says EBITDA per tonne is the better measure,
because steel prices are passed through and move revenue up or down.
The full benefit of the US and Saudi expansions should show in FY29. The Saudi plants start contributing in FY28.
EBITDA per tonne by region: US line pipe at USD 300+ (up from USD 200-250 earlier), India line pipe at ~USD 125 (range of USD
100-150), Saudi LSAW at USD 250-300, Saudi DI at ~USD 200 and India DI at only INR 5,000-7,000 per tonne, against INR 15,000-
20,000 two to three years ago, hit by Jal Jeevan Mission funding delays and overcapacity. DI is below 10% of FY27 EBITDA
guidance.
Order Book
A record HFIW pipe order of ~INR 40,000 mn was announced on the day of the meeting, the largest for that product in company
history. It is for refined-product lines in the US, with delivery in FY28-FY29.
Last month, the company won ~USD 1.8 bn (~INR 170 bn), which management called the largest pipe order in company and likely
industry history. It is for gas pipelines from the Permian Basin to Gulf Coast LNG terminals.
The consolidated order book is a record ~INR 450 bn (~USD 4.7 bn), ~80% of it in the US. US capacity is booked through FY29. India
orders are smaller and shorter-cycle.
US customers are midstream companies such as Energy Transfer, Kinder Morgan, Venture Global, Enbridge and Enterprise.

Expansion
US: The HFIW line is commissioned and stabilising. The LSAW plant is due by end-CY26.
Saudi Arabia: Welspun has supplied Saudi Aramco for ~20 years, and management says Aramco is pushing for early commissioning.
About 30% of Saudi pipe demand and ~50% of DI demand is still imported; the new DI plant should start replacing these imports
immediately after commissioning. Demand drivers include Aramco's Master Gas Phase 4, talk of a second East-West pipeline after

Operations and Capital Allocation
Steel is bought back-to-back when bidding for line pipe, so customers carry the steel price risk. DI uses iron ore and coking coal, with
its own risk policy.
The US site has 800+ acres and offers paid warehousing of raw material and finished pipe, plus logistics. Inventory is funded by
customer advances, so it carries no balance sheet risk.
Cash will be used only for the core business. Options to return cash, such as buybacks or dividends, will be clarified by the end of

Welspun Enterprises Ltd
Welspun Enterprises is a diversified infrastructure player across roads, water and tunnelling, following an asset-light model of
executing projects ahead of schedule and divesting road BOT/HAM assets after stabilisation at 18%+ equity IRRs. The order book
stands at ~INR 190 bn, with 55% in water, 15% in tunnelling and 30% in roads (largely the INR 73 bn Pune-Shirur BOT project). FY26
revenue was ~INR 36 bn, and management guides 10-15% revenue growth in FY27 (~INR 40 bn), 15-20% revenue CAGR over the
medium term and EBITDA margin of 18%+ (Q1FY27: 22.9%). Order wins of INR 80-100 bn are targeted, largely in H2FY27, taking the
order book to ~INR 250-280 bn by FY27-end, with ~20% order book CAGR. The Anta-Simaria divestment (~INR 10 bn enterprise
value) is expected to be accounted for in Q2FY27, reducing consolidated debt by ~INR 8 bn. The balance sheet remains strong, with
~INR 18 bn of cash, INR 10 bn of warrants and a recently upgraded CRISIL AA/Stable rating. The key factors to monitor are order
inflows, execution of Mumbai water projects, Pune-Shirur financial closure and appointed date, receipt of Anta-Simaria proceeds,
tunnelling scale-up and the oil & gas block development.
Business Model & Positioning
• Welspun Enterprises began its infrastructure journey in 2010 with the acquisition of MSK Projects; after internal restructuring, it
became the Welspun group's dedicated infrastructure company and has remained listed throughout.
• In roads, it won India's first HAM project (Package 1 of the Delhi-Meerut Expressway) in 2016 and completed it 11 months ahead
of schedule. It also acquired stalled BOT/HAM projects from other groups and completed them.
• The asset-light strategy involves completing construction ahead of schedule and divesting BOT/HAM projects once recurring
revenue is established in the first year post-construction, delivering equity IRRs of 18%+. In 2022, six projects were divested to
Actis at an EV of ~INR 90 bn.
• The company entered water in 2020 and tunnelling through the acquisition of Michigan Engineers (now Welspun Michigan
Engineers, 60.01% stake). Management remains selective, bidding only for large projects that support 18%+ construction-phase
margins.
Order Book & Guidance
• The order book stands at ~INR 190 bn: 55% water, 15% tunnelling and 30% roads (largely Pune-Shirur).
• Order wins of INR 80-100 bn are targeted in FY27, largely H2-weighted; the order book is expected at ~INR 250-280 bn by FY27-
end, with an order book CAGR of at least 20%.
• FY26 revenue was ~INR 36 bn; FY27 revenue growth is guided at 10-15% (~INR 40 bn), with revenue and EBITDA growth broadly
in line for the year.
• Medium-term revenue CAGR is expected at 15-20% (high teens), implying close to a doubling in about three years, with EBITDA
margin of 18%+ (Q1FY27 EBITDA margin: 22.9%).
• Execution was impacted in Q1 by supply chain disruptions and Mumbai construction stoppages; Q2 is expected to improve, with
H2 making up for lost ground and guidance maintained.
• Water and tunnelling are expected to remain over 50% of the mix combined, with roads being more selective.
Roads
• The Pune-Shirur BOT project is the largest road project the company has won, with a project cost of ~INR 73 bn (EPC component
of ~INR 54 bn), covering 54 km, including a 35 km elevated highway connecting key industrial areas in Maharashtra. The
appointed date is expected soon, with execution beginning in H2FY27.
• The project will be funded with a debt-to-equity mix of ~70:30 to 80:20; the construction period is ~4 years, though the EPC
contractor has been mandated to complete it in 3 years. The project is expected to follow the divestment model post-
construction with high-teens equity IRRs.
• The Anta-Simaria (Bihar) project is being divested to Alpha Alternatives at an enterprise value of ~INR 10 bn; it will be accounted
for in Q2FY27 (by year-end at the latest), with cash receipt likely in Q3FY27, reducing consolidated debt by ~INR 8 bn.

Welspun Living Ltd
Guidance and Outlook
• Management reaffirmed double-digit revenue growth with low-teens EBITDA margin for the full year. The medium-term
revenue aspiration is INR 150 bn by FY29.
• Q1 revenue growth was ~23%. Q2 should still grow in double digits, but the Vapi plant shutdown from the recent flood will
have a minimal impact, which management says it will mitigate through other plants and outsourcing. It expects to recover
most of it in H2.
• FY27 capex guidance is INR 4-5 bn, and the dividend will be maintained. Management says it will invest more if growth
opportunities arise.
• ROCE was ~12.5% at 30 June, with a medium-term target of 15-18%. Levers are operating leverage, input cost normalisation,
unwinding of tariff sharing, and scale in high-margin pillows, advanced textiles and brands.
Balance Sheet (FY26)
• Net debt was more than halved to ~INR 7.75 bn. Free cash flow was ~INR 9.56 bn and working capital was 82 days.
US and Tariffs
• The US now applies a uniform 10% tariff to India, in line with Pakistan and Bangladesh. China and Vietnam are at 12.5%.
• Last year's 50% tariff was managed with no customer lost, and FY26 EBITDA margin averaged ~10%. Management does not
expect tariffs above 18-20% going forward.
• On FOB business, Welspun pays the tariff, and on non-FOB business, the customer does. Costs are shared with customers case
by case, and some refunds have been received.
• US demand is recovering, and the US share is expected to stay in a similar range.
• About 70% of the core business is replenishment-based, giving 6-9 months of visibility.
UK and EU
• The UK and Europe account for ~18% of the business today. Welspun is the largest Indian supplier there, working with John
Lewis, Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, IKEA, Action and Jysk.
• The UK FTA is in force, and the India-EU agreement is expected around Q1 of next year. Pakistan holds more than 50% of these
markets in Welspun's categories, so share gains will come from displacing it.
• Double-digit growth is already visible. Two customers have placed new programmes that ship from Q4 or Q1 next year.
• UK and EU customers largely differ from US ones, and the ramp is expected to be steady rather than sudden.
Flooring
• The business is now profitable. EBITDA margin is at its highest in over two years, swinging from a loss of ~10% last year to a
profit of ~10%. This adds ~1% to overall margin.
• Revenue will be soft this year, as unprofitable sales were deliberately dropped. Capacity utilisation is only ~40% at the
Hyderabad plant (capex of ~INR 12 bn).
• The focus is soft flooring and area rugs for export (20%+ CAGR potential), commercial and hospitality, and new markets
(Australia, New Zealand, Canada, GCC). India flooring has grown in double digits for four quarters.
• There are no demerger plans. Rug-level revenue and margin are not disclosed, and management disputed a brokerage's ~10%
rug margin figure.
Advanced Textiles
• Margins are healthy: management cited double-digit EBITDA, with a 3-5 year average of ~20% excluding the tariff-hit period.
• It is moving from commodity spunlace to value-added products: printed and dyed cotton, biodegradable, baby and femcare,
healthcare, sustainable diapers, wipes, protective apparel and jacket insulation (needle punch) for a global sports brand.
• No three-year targets were shared.
Pillows and Brands
• Pillows are growing ~100% YoY. US revenue was ~USD 27 mn last year and is set to roughly double this year.
• One plant costs USD 10-12 mn and can generate USD 40-45 mn of peak revenue. With two plants, revenue could reach ~USD
100 mn next year.
• Branded revenue is ~19% of total (domestic ~6%, global ~12%).
Margin and Capacity Levers
• Home textiles capacity is largely utilised, while other categories have headroom. Debottlenecking and automation are being
used to extract more from existing capacity.
• A better product mix could add margin, but management says it depends on market demand.
• Cotton is mostly domestic, and imports are used only for customer specification or cost reasons.
• Management does not see online or quick commerce as a threat, since premium share is offline and it also supplies online
through drop-ship with big-box retailers.
• The vision is to be the world's largest home textile solutions company. The Anjar facility runs on 100% renewable power.

Western Carriers (India) Ltd
Outlook: Management plans to double or triple volumes at the Dewalia terminal over the next 6-8 quarters. FY27 capex is set at
INR 1,000 mn for phased deployment, and debtor days are targeted to fall structurally over the next 2-3 quarters. The business is
supported by large long-term contracts, a dual-coast terminal network and a growing domestic multimodal franchise.
• Q1FY27 Performance: Revenue from operations grew 11.8% YoY to INR 4,650 mn from INR 4,160 mn, the fifth straight quarter
of top-line growth. EBITDA was above INR 190 mn, a margin of 4.1%, reflecting an operational turnaround and sequential
margin recovery. Profit rose about 13-14% QoQ on better asset utilisation and faster turnaround times. For context, FY26
revenue was INR 18,300 mn, up from INR 14,700 mn in FY23.
• Volume Momentum: Total container throughput grew sequentially in Q1FY27 over Q4FY26. This runs against the usual
pattern, since Q4 is normally the peak quarter and Q1 the weakest. Domestic volumes rose about 37% YoY to 23,909 units
from 17,498, supporting the strategic push into domestic multimodal supply chains. EXIM volumes grew 3.2% YoY to 34,352
units despite congestion at JNPT (a 30,000-container backlog) and global shipping disruptions.
• Dewalia Terminal: The 42-acre multimodal terminal in Saurashtra, Gujarat, has been formally flagged off by the Railway
Minister. Propane supply to the Morbi ceramics hub has fully normalised, so volumes have recovered to levels seen before the
Iran conflict.
• Dual-Coast Network: The company recently acquired the Kolkata Port Railway Terminal under Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port
Trust. This links Morbi, a major production hub in the west, directly with Kolkata, a major consumption hub in the east. Pan-
India coverage includes active nodes in Guwahati, Patna, Dadri/Delhi NCR and the Bangalore-Chennai belt.
• Capex & IPO Proceeds: FY26 capex was about INR 700 mn, spent mainly on specialised containers and handling equipment.
More than INR 910 mn of IPO proceeds remains unspent and is held in fixed deposits. Management says deployment is being
staggered deliberately in line with macro conditions, not because of operational delays.
• Receivables & Contracts: Trade receivables rose to INR 6,950 mn in FY26 from INR 3,500 mn in FY23. That takes receivable
days from about 87 to about 139. Two factors drove the increase. New terminals are attracting small and mid-sized non-
corporate clients who take longer to pay. The company has also signed large long-term contracts: Vedanta Group (INR 18+ bn
over four years) and Jindal Stainless (INR 12.5-13 bn). Debtor days started falling in Q1FY27.
• Margin Protection: A Diesel Price Variation Clause (DPVC) covers road transport across all major contracts, passing fuel
volatility through to customers. Rail logistics is protected by a Railway Haulage Clause, so tariff revisions or discounts pass
straight through.
• 4PL Business Model: Management deliberately avoids low-margin commodity road transport and price-war reverse auctions.
Instead, it focuses on customised 4PL and value-added multimodal services, including first-mile and last-mile handling,
modular warehousing, containerisation and just-in-time inventory.
• Client Base: The company has long-standing relationships with blue-chip industrial groups that are expanding capacity,
including JSW Steel, Tata Steel, Hindalco, Vedanta, HUL and GSK.
• Sector Tailwinds: India's GDP is projected to grow 6.5-7.0%. The freight and logistics market is expected to expand from USD
315 bn in 2026 to USD 476 bn by 2031, roughly a 9% CAGR. The 2,800 km Dedicated Freight Corridor network is expected to lift
rail's share of freight from 13-14% to 20-25%+. The Union Budget FY27 allocates INR 142 bn to infrastructure, up 9% from INR
131 bn in FY26.
• Long-Term Potential: The domestic volume surge, the Dewalia ramp-up, dual-coast connectivity and large multi-year contracts
support continued growth. Pass-through clauses and the asset-backed 4PL model protect margins. Reducing receivables and
deploying unspent IPO funds are the key monitorables for cash flow.

Zodiac Energy Ltd
Zodiac is entering its next growth phase with a clear shift toward an integrated energy model, combining solar EPC and IPP with
BESS and transmission infrastructure. Near-term growth should remain anchored by the INR 2.68 bn EPC order book, C&I

FY26 performance: Revenue grew 33.3% YoY to INR 5,435 mn, while EBITDA rose 49% to INR 580 mn, driven by stronger project
execution and operating efficiency.
Integrated energy strategy: Zodiac is transitioning from a pure-play solar EPC company toward an integrated energy platform
spanning solar EPC, solar IPP, BESS and transmission infrastructure.
IPP expansion: Operational IPP capacity stands at ~55 MW, with another 45-50 MW under execution; management targets ~90-

BESS entry: Zodiac has acquired a majority stake in ZenWatt Clean Energy to accelerate its BESS entry and avoid building
capabilities from scratch.
BESS manufacturing: A 2 GWh per annum facility near Ahmedabad is being established for cell-to-pack, pack-to-module and
module-to-BESS integration, targeted for commissioning within 6-12 months.
BESS revenue potential: Management expects ~INR 500 mn of revenue from BESS by March 2028, scaling to ~INR 1.5 bn and INR
3-3.5 bn over the following two years, with EBITDA margins targeted at 14-15%.
Solar EPC order book: The current EPC order book stands at ~INR 2.68 bn, primarily C&I, with an additional bid pipeline of INR 3+
bn and a historical bid-win ratio of 20-25%.
C&I focus: C&I currently contributes ~55% of the portfolio and management expects its share to increase, supported by industrial
solarisation, cost-effective power requirements and ESG and carbon-border considerations.
Residential mix declining: Zodiac is reducing dependence on residential rooftop projects due to lower ticket sizes under PM Surya
Ghar and is shifting toward larger C&I, ground-mounted and developer-led projects.
Exports scaling up: Africa is becoming a key growth market, with projects executed in Zambia and Kenya and further projects
underway; management sees significant opportunity in large-ticket ground-mounted projects.
Working capital discipline: Cash conversion cycle improved from 118 days in FY24 to 94 days in FY26, while debtor days declined
from 106 to 57 days; management expects the cycle to remain around 90-100 days despite larger projects.
Transmission opportunity: Zodiac plans to initially participate in standalone transmission-line projects for state and central
utilities, leveraging its existing experience in transmission work attached to solar EPC projects.
BESS as future EPC component: Management expects solar-plus-storage to become increasingly important as renewable
penetration rises and grid curtailment increases, with BESS potentially becoming an inherent part of future solar projects.
Group captive opportunity: Zodiac is actively pursuing group-captive renewable projects with C&I customers, allowing industrial
users to secure renewable power while reducing certain third-party charges.
IPP economics: The existing 55 MW of operational capacity is under long-term PPAs, while the 45-50 MW pipeline also has PPAs in
place; management does not currently see material tariff pressure on its IPP portfolio.
Funding approach: Near-term BESS and expansion investments are expected to be funded through internal accruals and debt;
management is not currently planning an equity raise, though it may consider one later if required.
Distribution business: Solar panel and inverter distribution remains an important business, offering lower margins but faster cash
conversion, while EPC delivers higher margins but requires greater working capital.
Policy environment: Management sees the renewable EPC market remaining structurally strong; the key near-term change is the
transition toward DCR modules, for which Zodiac says it is prepared.
Curtailment supports storage: Existing IPP assets are facing curtailment, reinforcing management's view that rapid BESS
deployment will be necessary to improve grid integration and utilisation of renewable generation.
